Are you certain your highs and lows are directly related to your cycle?  It's possible that there are at least some contributing factors, even if they are  as a result of hormonal fluctuations.For example, at the start of your period, do you have that "I feel great" feeling, or are you tired and down?  Mid-cycle (assuming your periods are regular), do you find yourself napping or ready to run a race?  Either way, how you feel may be leading you to behaviors that contribute to your changes in energy and optimism. Let's say that the few days before your period, you feel cranky, bloated and want salty food.  Your natural inclination might be to isolate, stay inside and eat chips.  The next day, you feel even more tired, cranky and bloated.  It STARTS with a hormonal symptom, but what you do with that can change how you  end up feeling.  So if you notice feeling cranky, bloated and craving salt, what if you pull up a restorative yoga video online, spend an hour being restful and centered in your body and have a good meal with a healthy balance of fats, proteins and carbs, with fresh veggies and fruits before you turn in early to give your body the rest it is asking for ?  That sets you up to feel MUCH better!And those "on top of the world days" - who doesn't love them??  But even those days, be mindful of how you are treating yourself.  Exercise for sure, but don't do twice the workout you normally would just because you can!  You might feel super energy and skip meals which sets you up for poor sleep and feeling crummy after a day or two.All that aside, if you have a couple rough days before your period, pay attention to what is bugging you.  Christiane Northrup, MD, likens our menstrual cycle to the tide.  When the tide is out (just before your period), you see all the garbage cluttering up your ocean floor, but you don't have the energy to address it, so there it stays, bugging you.  At the height of physical and emotional energy (usually mid-cycle/ovulation), the tide is back in and you don't see all that annoying stuff you saw before.  Since you have good energy at this time, take advantage of it by doing some "clean up" on the things you saw there when you felt crummy.  Maybe it's that conversation you have been putting  off with your partner, or having the long-delayed closet clean out, or searching for a job that feels/pays/fits you better.  Whatever it is, those "PMS blues" may hold important messages for you.If taking good care of yourself, staying tuned in to your needs and keeping an eye on the "tides" don't help, then  see your doctor.  Something else may be going on - our hormones all work together like a symphony - it only takes one to be out of tune to throw the whole thing off!

I have a bad habit of thinking and worrying about what others may think of me. I really want to stop it and enjoy things.

We all experience that to a different level, depending on who you ask.  It's actually born out of a good quality---prosocialness.  When we care what others think of us, we are also attuned to how we are treating them and what's socially right vs wrong.  It definitely does feel like it's more about ourselves, however--meaning it feels like we worry about what others think because we don't want to be socially outcast or rejected.  That's also (again, to a certain level) a healthy quality.  It means you want connection.  Connection is crucial to mental health and, according to some available research, physical health.  No matter how mentally healthy or socially confident you are, if you care about connection, you're going to care about what people think of you to an extent.  So the work here is to figure out what worry is warranted vs what is just causing you suffering.  A good way to tell the difference here is to write it out in list form.  Write out all the socially-anxious thoughts you have and scale them from "needed" or "helpful" to "unnecessary" or "unhelpful".  Some may fall in the gray area here.  For example: if you worry that others think you are inconsiderate, so you often say sorry---weed out what's actually inconsiderate vs what you feel is maybe inconsiderate because you feel like a burden to others.  Getting in someone's personal space would warrant some worry and an apology.  Asking for help when you need it is something you don't have to apologize for.  Something else to consider here is there's probably some underlying shame.  Shame is a cluster of really tough feelings and if it had a voice, it'd say things like, "you're not good enough", "you aren't likeable", "you are annoying and no one wants to be around you", etc.  Those feelings typically create the worry you experience about others.  Shame survives and is strengthened by the attention you give to it.  The more you compete with it, the less powerful it becomes.  Sometimes that comes in the form of noticing the wonderful qualities in yourself.  Sometimes it takes practice putting yourself out there when it's really scary.  No matter what, shame's nemesis is connection---to yourself and to others.  That's how you prove it's wrong.  Try not to take shame at face value!If you are struggling with using these techniques or just don't know if they are right for you, a counselor can help you out and give you a more individualized approach.  Sometimes it's just figuring out that specific formula that works for you that makes all the difference.  And of course, counseling is built on a strong connection.I wish you all the best!

How long can you store cooked food in refrigerators?

A common misconception is the assumption that food "loses nutrients" when it's refrigerated. That is not as true as you think it is. It is always good to ask 2 follow up questions
What nutrients exactly? And by how much?
It turns out that water soluble vitamins are the most unstable and easily lost nutrients, but fun fact: most of the loss happens during cooking, not refrigeration. It is heat that destroys vitamins, not cold. In fact, in an airtight container, most cooked food will last 2-3 days at the minimum and up to a week in many cases. In the freezer, food will last up to 6 months (assuming no power cuts). All biological activity slows down with temperature.

There are a few exceptions - plain cooked/steamed rice can sometimes be infected by a bacteria that doesn't mind low temperatures, so it's best to consume it within 1-2 days.

Bonus point: Indian food, is uniquely fridge friendly because it tends to be spicy, salty and sour - these are three conditions microbes absolutely hate.

Recently, there was a major family conflict that caused tension and arguments between me and my siblings. It felt like everything became emotionally chaotic and unsafe. My role in the family has also changed due to shifting dynamics, which brought up unresolved issues from the past. How can I navigate through these family challenges while preserving my mental well-being?

Navigating through family challenges can be tough, especially when it feels like everything has become emotionally chaotic and unsafe. It's understandable that the recent major family conflict has affected your mental well-being. When faced with such situations, there are a few strategies you can try to help preserve your mental well-being:

1. Communication: Open and honest communication is key in resolving conflicts within families. Consider expressing your thoughts and feelings calmly and assertively to your siblings. Avoid blaming or attacking them, but rather focus on using "I" statements to express how their actions have impacted you.

Identify what is acceptable and unacceptable behavior towards you, and communicate those boundaries clearly to your siblings. It can be incredibly challenging when anxiety starts to dominate your life and affects your ability to make decisions or complete even small tasks. The constant worry and "what if" thoughts can be overwhelming, leaving you feeling trapped in a cycle of fear. 

One suggestion I have is to start by exploring the root causes of your anxiety. Sometimes, understanding why we feel anxious can help us gain some clarity and perspective. It might be helpful to reflect on any past experiences or traumas that could be contributing to your current state. Journaling or talking to someone you trust about your feelings and experiences may also provide insights.

Another strategy that could be beneficial is practicing mindfulness and grounding techniques. These techniques can help bring your attention back to the present moment and reduce the intensity of anxious thoughts. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or engaging in activities that promote relaxation (such as yoga or meditation) can all be effective ways to manage anxiety.

Additionally, it might be helpful to challenge and reframe your anxious thoughts. Often, our worries are based on irrational or exaggerated beliefs. Take some time to examine the evidence for and against your anxious thoughts. Are there alternative explanations or more balanced perspectives? By questioning the validity of your anxious thoughts, you can begin to break free from their grip.

Lastly, seeking support from a mental health professional can be extremely valuable. They can provide guidance tailored specifically to your situation and offer evidence-based strategies to address your anxiety. A therapist can help you explore underlying issues, develop coping mechanisms, and provide ongoing support throughout your journey towards breaking free from this cycle.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and effort, but with patience and perseverance, it is possible to regain control over your life.

Work-related stress has led to a decline in my overall well-being. I find it difficult to relax or enjoy leisure activities because my mind is constantly preoccupied with work responsibilities. I'm hoping to discuss strategies to create boundaries between work and personal life and restore balance.

It can be challenging when work-related stress starts to impact your overall well-being. It's important to prioritize self-care and find ways to create boundaries between work and personal life in order to restore balance. Here are some strategies that may help:

1. Set clear boundaries: Establish specific times for work and non-work activities. This could involve creating a schedule where you allocate dedicated time for work tasks, as well as time for relaxation and leisure activities. Stick to these boundaries as much as possible to avoid letting work spill over into your personal time.

2. Create a designated workspace: Having a separate area at home solely for work can help create a physical boundary between your professional and personal life. When you're in this space, it signals that it's time to focus on work, and when you leave the space, it's time to switch off and engage in other activities.

3. Practice mindfulness and relaxation techniques: Engaging in mindfulness exercises or relaxation techniques can help calm your mind and reduce stress. Consider trying deep breathing exercises, meditation, or yoga to help shift your focus away from work and promote relaxation.

4. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to prioritize activities that bring you joy and relaxation outside of work. Whether it's spending time with loved ones, pursuing hobbies, or engaging in physical exercise, dedicating time to self-care is essential for restoring balance and overall well-being.

5. Disconnect from technology: Constantly being connected to work through emails and notifications can make it difficult to detach mentally. Set aside specific times during the day to check and respond to work-related messages, but try to disconnect from technology outside of those designated times. This will allow you to fully engage in leisure activities without the constant distraction of work responsibilities.

Remember, finding the right balance takes time and experimentation. Be patient with yourself as you explore different strategies and adapt them to fit your needs. If you continue to struggle with work-related stress, it may be helpful to seek support from a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and assistance.

Does counseling really do anything that can help people?

I love this question! Some people shy away from counseling because they think since they already talk about how they feel to their relatives or friends they shouldn't need a counselor. However, if you are having a difficult time, counseling can be beneficial in helping you move forward and get your life back on track. Counseling is not like the kind of talking we do to people we know. For one, your counselor does not have a history with you and has no expectations of how you will act and what you will do. In that way, counselors come to a session without judgement and expectation. This gives you the platform to truly explore your thoughts and feelings. Lately, I've been feeling on edge all the time, even in seemingly safe situations. It's like my body is constantly in fight-or-flight mode with rapid breathing, tense muscles, and a racing heart. This level of constant alertness is exhausting, and I find it difficult to relax or enjoy anything. I'm wondering if there are any specific coping strategies that can help me manage these intense feelings of anxiety and regain a sense of calm.

One way to begin managing these intense feelings of anxiety and regain a sense of calm is through deep breathing exercises. Taking slow, deep breaths can help activate the body's relaxation response and reduce tension. You can try inhaling deeply through your nose for a count of four, holding your breath for a count of four, and exhaling slowly through your mouth for a count of four. Repeat this pattern several times whenever you're feeling overwhelmed.

Another technique to consider is progressive muscle relaxation. This involves tensing and releasing different muscle groups in your body to help promote relaxation. You can start by clenching your fists tightly, then slowly releasing the tension. Move on to other muscle groups such as your shoulders, jaw, and legs, tensing them for a few seconds before letting go. Practicing progressive muscle relaxation regularly can help you become more aware of areas of tension in your body and release that tension when needed.

Engaging in regular physical exercise can also be beneficial for managing anxiety. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters and stress relievers. Find an activity you enjoy, like walking, jogging, dancing, or yoga, and aim to engage in it for at least 30 minutes most days of the week. Not only does exercise have physical benefits, but it can also provide an outlet for pent-up energy and contribute to a greater sense of well-being.

In addition to these techniques, it may be helpful to incorporate mindfulness practices into your daily routine. Mindfulness involves paying attention to the present moment without judgment. You can start by simply taking a few moments each day to focus on your breath and observe any thoughts or sensations that arise without trying to change them. There are also various mindfulness apps available that can guide you through meditation exercises if you prefer more structure.

It might also be worthwhile to examine the sources of stress in your life and explore ways to address them. Consider making a list of any triggers that contribute to your anxiety and strategize ways to minimize or manage them. This could involve setting boundaries, practicing assertiveness skills, delegating tasks, or seeking support from loved ones. Remember that it's okay to ask for help when needed and to prioritize self-care.

Finally, try to be patient with yourself throughout this process. Managing anxiety is a journey, and it takes time to find what techniques work best for you. If symptoms persist or worsen, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide additional guidance tailored to your specific needs.

I have trouble falling asleep because my mind constantly races with worries and what-ifs. It's as if my thoughts are overtaking my ability to relax and rest. This lack of sleep is leaving me exhausted during the day and making it harder to concentrate on tasks. Is there any way I can calm my anxieties before bedtime?

One approach you can try to help calm your anxieties before bedtime is establishing a routine that promotes relaxation and helps shift your focus away from worries. Here are some suggestions:

1. Create a peaceful environment: Make sure your bedroom is comfortable, quiet, and dark. Consider using earplugs or a white noise machine to block out any distracting sounds.

2. Wind down before bed: Engage in calming activities for at least an hour before sleep. This could include reading a book (preferably not something overly stimulating), listening to soothing music, taking a warm bath, or practicing deep breathing exercises.

3. Write down your worries: Before going to bed, spend 10-15 minutes writing down your worries and what-ifs on a piece of paper. This can act as a "brain dump" and help reduce racing thoughts. Once done, set the paper aside and mentally let go of those concerns for the night.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: If you find yourself caught in a cycle of worrying, try to challenge and reframe those negative thoughts. Ask yourself if there is evidence to support your worries or alternative explanations for the things you're concerned about.

5. Practice relaxation techniques: Experiment with different relaxation techniques to see what works best for you. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided imagery exercises can all help induce a state of calmness before sleep.

6. Limit exposure to screens: The blue light emitted by electronic devices can interfere with sleep. Try to avoid using screens like smartphones, laptops, or televisions at least one hour before bedtime.

7. Establish a consistent sleep schedule: Go to bed and wake up at regular times to regulate your body's internal clock. This consistency may help signal to your brain that it's time to wind down and prepare for sleep.

Remember, finding the right strategy may require some trial and error, so be patient with yourself. It might also be helpful to consider speaking with a mental health professional for additional guidance and support tailored specifically to your needs.

Who was Charles Guillaume Loys de Bochat

Charles Guillaume Loys de Bochat (born 11 December 1695 in Lausanne, died 4 April 1754, also in Lausanne) was an 18th-century Swiss jurist and antiquarian (Lausanne at the time was a subject territory controlled by Berne).

He studied theology in Basle, which he interrupted for health reasons, and later changed his subject to law, in which he graduated in 1717. He became professor of law in Lausanne in 1718, but he was granted leave to travel for three years, which he spent in Halle, in Leyden and in France.

From 1721, he taught law at the Lausanne Academy, where he acted as rector from 1727 to 1730. In 1738, he proposed to transform the academy into a full university, without success.

Loys de Bochat is best known for his major work, Mémoires critiques pour servir d'Eclaircissemens sur divers points de l'Histoire ancienne de la Suisse, which appeared in three volumes in 1747-1749. This work is dedicated to examining the early history of Switzerland, especially the Gaulish Helvetii, and their legacy in Swiss toponymy.

That's some tough stuff to be dealing with.  Have you ever tracked those highs and lows?  I often have clients graph out those changes to see what kind of patterns show up.  You obviously are very insightful already and maybe having a visual of what you know can help you prepare for some of those lows.  Another curiosity I have is if you have seen your primary provider about what your body is going through.  It's hard to give individualized recommendations without knowing more about your symptoms, but reaching out to your doctor could be a way to advocate for yourself.  Do you ever feel manic when you have a lot of energy?  How long do the "highs" last?  Do your highs interfere with sleep?  And what impact do your lows have on your functioning?  Sometimes I have clients get checked out by a doctor to rule out physical issues that could be underlying the intensity of their symptoms.  PMS definitely fits in this category, but it's always possible there's some other imbalance (e.g., lack of certain vitamins, thyroid dysfunction, etc.).  Your doctor could even help collaborate with you to find some methods to deal with the depression/PMS.With the research we have on hormones and their impact on the body, it's pretty crystal clear that exercise has a huge benefit across all levels of emotional dysregulation.  It has immediate positive impacts in the brain and body, and keeps the body running efficiently.  Same with sleep--it's one of our most underrated functions.  If you think of it like a house, your foundation represents those basic functions.  If your foundation is shaky, it's going to be tough to support the rest of the house.  Exercise is hard to push through, but it's really just those first 10-15 minutes that feel the worst.  And you don't have to start somewhere super intense--even walking is wonderful for the body.Hope this helps a bit!

It is very difficult to move from being the child to be the care giver as in your situation. Your mother's behavior as you describe it is a part of this disease. As the disease progresses and she is less aware of the present including her surroundings and who she is speaking to. Your response of anger and frustration are understandable. It is also a part of the grief process as you see you mother slipping away mentally. In the moment that you feel the anger step away, take some deep breathes and give yourself time to calm down. Then return to whatever you were doing with her. Caregivers of Alzheimer's patients need a lot of support themselves. There are support groups  as well as respite services available in many areas that will help you understand the process that each of you is going through. You can get more information about Alzheimer's disease and local resources by going to www.alz.org

How does a person start the counseling process?

The easiest way to start the counseling process is to do a little research online. A quick search for the type of counseling you are looking for can be helpful. There are lots of Counselors out there to choose from, so many times you will have to take it a few steps further than that. Check out their website, social media, and any reviews (but remember, people are not always very nice). If you plan on using insurance to pay for at least part of the services, look for one that is in your network. You can find out if someone is in your network by looking for providers on your insurance's website. If your coverage isn't that great and you know you're going to be paying for it all anyway (because you're an all-star and verified your coverage already with the insurance company), then you can really pick any Counselor you want, but working with one that is at least out of network will give you the benefit of having it applied to your deductible. If you have any questions about that process or just want some help in getting your benefits from the insurance company once you've started counseling, Better is a good option. Once you've found a Counselor you think is a good fit for you, normally the best step to take here is to call and schedule your very first appointment. With many Counselors you can now send an email, but a phone call can normally tell you quite a bit about someone and their clinic. Once you're all scheduled, they will either get you to do some paperwork before you come in, or many times they just let you fill it out once you get there. From there, all you have to do is show up!

Hello. It sounds to me like you are carrying an enormous amount of emotional weight, and maybe even an equally enormous amount of guilt and feelings of failure about your marriage. I cannot imagine how challenging this is for you right now. Marriages take lots of work, and often the only examples we tend to have are of those we saw when we were young - good, bad, or indifferent. There are no easy answers to your questions, and I won't presume that my response to you will be the linch-pin that heals all your pain. But I can maybe give some thoughts and reflections. First and foremost, cut yourself some slack. No one is perfect. We fail more often than we succeed, but in the end we learn, and that learning helps us grow. Yes, you're right, the abusive aspects of your marriage are not good, and need to stop. You probably are doing more harm than good in that regard, and this will quickly destroy anything you have in your marriage that is even remotely in your favor. Seeing a therapist for yourself, and then seeing a therapist as a couple is a good approach. You have issues that you need to resolve, that, while they impact your marriage because they are part of the history of your life, they are separate from your marriage in many respects.Joining a marriage support group can also be helpful. You can find these through local counseling resources. Sometimes your local crisis numbers can provide services in your area that can be helpful. If you belong to a religious or spiritual community, then you might see if there is any type of counseling offered for free or at a reduced rate. Sometimes pastoral support is focused on the spiritual side of any issues addressed, so if you feel this is important it might be a viable option for you.Lastly, parents are imperfect. Yep...its true. They had no more of a guaranteed parenting success manual than you do at having chances for a perfect marriage. We limp along and do our best. Having said that, we can still take the best from our past and apply to our future, no matter how small or insignificant it might be for us. The bad stuff serves as lessons of what to avoid, and we are each responsible and accountable for our actions in this life. Both with ourselves, and toward other people. So this becomes a guiding principle in our actions. It may be that you discover that the marriage you are in is not a good fit.  I am sure that remains to be seen, but either way you both must be involved in saving it. If only one of you cares, then 100% of the energy to salvage the marriage rests on the shoulders of one person. That's not fair. So be sure you have a clear understanding from your wife about what she wants, and work to create an amicable solution. All of this said, seek out supportive friends, and actively work to do your part to make the changes you want to see in your life. One way or the other, you will benefit from it.Be well.

How do you increase your output on a Peloton ride?

If you want to increase your output on a Peloton ride there are definitely a few tips and tricks to follow to ensure progress. First off, I would always recommend using the same official Peloton equipment (Peloton Bike or Peloton Bike+) to ensure you are tracking consistent metrics between your rides. I would also recommend doing a Functional Threshold Power Test (FTP Test), to get a baseline of your maximum performance as well as get a power meter for each of your rides. From there, a big amount of increasing your power comes from consistency of both riding frequency as well as consistency in overloading your leg muscles during those durations. Taking Power Zone rides (PZE, PZ, PZMax) or Power Zone programs is a great way to increase your output over time. These rides/programs are tailored to your max level of effort, and as you progress over time, so will your 7 power zone levels. Besides consistently riding and keeping track of your metrics/FTP, there is a quick trick for increasing your output which is not that sustainable. The trick is to ride out of the saddle and crank the resistance all the way up (75+). If you can move your legs at 50+ cadence and over say an 80 resistance, you will be putting up over 300 output. If you can sustain that for a minute at a time and do that 3-5 times during a ride, you will easily increase your total output. Lower cadence is not ideal for increasing your power from a longevity strategy, but is a quick answer for breaking a personal record. Good luck on your future rides, and don't forget to send love with some highfives!

I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it.    How should I deal with this?

Thanks for writing in. Several things come to mind:I don't know how you are communicating, but there is a great deal of difference between communicating through videoconferencing compared to text message when discussing subjects like this. Being able to hear and/or see each other will help you to be able to gauge a lot of the emotions connected to what is going on.Are you in a place where you can ask your girlfriend questions about this crush and actually listen to her answers? If you can listen non-defensively and ask questions about what is actually going on (kind of like an investigative reporter might), you are likely to hear about her experience, thoughts, feelings, etc., so you can actually see what the crush is like for her and how you want to react to that.Then you could see if she is willing to listen to your questions and answer them for you.Another tip: Find out when is a good time to have this conversation. If you are talking to your girlfriend after she just worked a 10 hour shift and she is frustrated about that, it is likely that the emotion will transfer to the conversation that you are having even though it doesn't have anything to do with that.Find a way to keep yourself grounded and centered during the conversation. Notice your feet on the floor or your hips in the chair. Mindfully play with an object or something like a paperclip or a pen. Doing this mindfully (by being aware of your senses) will help you to not feel so overwhelmed during the conversation.After you have more details, communicate about what it is that you want or wish for. It is often easier to hear and discuss as opposed to talking about something that you need.Remember that while anger is a very real emotion, there is always something else under it. Be aware of what else could be there: hurt, disappointment, betrayal, fear, etc.
I have a fear of something and I want to face that fear to overcome it, but I don't know how. What can I do?

Fear is a part of life. In fact, our five main emotions are joy, fear, sadness, shame, and anger. We tend to spend a lot of time and energy running away from or trying to get rid of most of those emotions and the more we do that, the more we set ourselves up for failure and disappointment. As a result of viewing our human emotions as "bad" or "wrong," we often get caught up in a trap of thinking we have to overcome them or get rid of them before we can do what matters to us. In reality, you can do what is important to you while having your fears! My question for you is, what would you do if this fear was completely gone? What behaviors would you have if you were the ideal you? What skills, knowledge, or personal qualities would you develop? What kind of relationships would you have?I imagine your fear has kept you from achieving those goals because your mind tells you you can't do it until the fear is gone. I challenge you to do the following exercise:What is a goal you would like to achieve? Example: I would like to change careersWhat actions are necessary to complete this goal? Example: see a career counselor to determine my ideal career, go back to school/get a certification, network with others in my desired industryWhat thoughts, feelings, or urges might get in my way? Example: thoughts of "What if I fail? I'm not smart enough. I can't do it. I'm too busy to put energy into this." Feelings of fear, shame, excitement. Urges to distract myself through drinking or watch tv instead of taking action.It would be helpful to remind myself that: example: It is natural to have these thoughts, feelings, and urges but I can take action anyway. I deserve to have a fulfilling life.The smallest and easiest step I can take now: example: research career counselors in my area and write down their phone numbersThe time, day and date that I will take that first step, is: example: Tonight at 7pm At least think through these answers but it is most beneficial to write them down. I hope this helps!

It hurt me deeply because I expected their support and understanding. Can you guide me on how to deepen our emotional intimacy and discuss our needs openly?

Building and maintaining emotional connection in an intimate relationship is crucial for its growth and fulfillment. It's understandable that you're feeling disconnected and questioning your partner's level of interest and care. Let's work together to address these concerns and find ways to deepen the emotional intimacy between you and your partner.

1. Create a Safe Space: Start by creating a safe and non-judgmental space where both you and your partner can express yourselves openly. Be mindful of your tone and approach when communicating your feelings, ensuring that it encourages open dialogue rather than defensiveness or blame.

2. Practice Active Listening: Actively listen to each other during conversations without distractions. Put away electronic devices, make eye contact, and show genuine interest in what your partner has to say. This will help foster a sense of being heard and understood.

3. Set Aside Quality Time: Dedicate quality time to do activities together that facilitate emotional connection. Engage in shared hobbies or interests, go on dates, or participate in new experiences that allow for meaningful conversations and bonding opportunities.

4. Express Appreciation and Gratitude: Regularly acknowledge and express gratitude for the positive aspects of your relationship. Show appreciation for gestures, actions, or qualities you admire in your partner. This creates a positive atmosphere and reinforces the emotional connection between you.

5. Foster Emotional Vulnerability: Encourage vulnerability by sharing your own feelings and thoughts with your partner. When both individuals feel safe expressing their vulnerability, it fosters a deeper understanding and strengthens emotional bonds.

6. Explore Each Other's Love Languages: Discover and understand how you and your partner prefer to give and receive love. Take the free online quiz about love languages and discuss the results together. This knowledge helps you meet each other's emotional needs more effectively.

7. Seek Professional Help If Needed: If despite your efforts, you continue experiencing difficulties in deepening emotional intimacy, consider seeking professional assistance from a licensed couples therapist. They can provide personalized guidance and support tailored to your specific situation.

Remember, it takes time, effort, and open communication to rebuild emotional connection in a relationship. By implementing these suggestions and reflecting on each other's needs, you'll lay the foundation for a stronger and more satisfying emotional bond between you and your partner.

Social situations terrify me. Whenever I'm in a group setting, I become extremely self-conscious and anxious. The fear of judgment consumes me, and I start overthinking every word I say or action I take. As a result, I tend to isolate myself to avoid these uncomfortable situations altogether. But deep down, I long for meaningful connections and friendships. How can I overcome this social anxiety and build healthier relationships?

I can understand how social situations can be really overwhelming and anxiety-inducing for you. It's completely normal to feel self-conscious and anxious in group settings, especially when the fear of judgment starts taking over your thoughts. It's great that you recognize the importance of meaningful connections and friendships, as they can bring so much joy and support into our lives.

To overcome social anxiety and build healthier relationships, here are a few suggestions:

1. Start small: Begin by gradually exposing yourself to social situations that make you slightly uncomfortable. You don't have to jump into large gatherings right away. Maybe start with one-on-one interactions or smaller group settings where you feel more at ease.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: When you catch yourself overthinking or worrying about what others might think of you, try to challenge those thoughts. Ask yourself if there is any evidence supporting these fears, and remind yourself that everyone has their own insecurities and worries too.

3. Practice self-compassion: Be kind to yourself during these moments of anxiety. Remember that it's okay to make mistakes or feel nervous. Treat yourself with the same understanding and compassion you would offer to a friend who was going through something similar.

4. Focus on the present moment: Instead of getting caught up in overthinking every word or action, try to shift your focus to the present moment. Engage actively in conversations, listen attentively, and allow yourself to enjoy the company of others without constantly analyzing everything you say or do.

5. Seek common interests: Look for activities or groups centered around your interests. Joining clubs, classes, or online communities focused on hobbies or topics you enjoy can provide an opportunity to connect with like-minded individuals who share similar passions.

6. Take care of yourself: Prioritize self-care and overall well-being. Engaging in regular exercise, practicing relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or meditation, and maintaining a balanced lifestyle can help reduce anxiety and improve your overall confidence.

Remember, building healthier relationships takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself throughout this process, as it's completely normal to face setbacks or feel uncomfortable at times. Celebrate small victories along the way and acknowledge your progress. You deserve meaningful connections and friendships, and I believe in your ability to overcome social anxiety and cultivate those relationships.

Is it normal for people to cry during therapy, or is it just me?

Yes, it is very normal. Some people cry frequently, but not fully. They’re good at crying but never seem to heal from what’s hurting them.Crying is supposed to be good for you. Tears contain toxins, after all. And feel-good chemicals are released in the body whenever we cry tears of sadness.Never judge your feelings while you’re having them; there’s always a reason something’s a big deal to you.Cry for your own pain, not just for others’. Crying in movies and when listening to sad songs is a good way to let off some built-up emotion. But you may not be dealing directly with your own hurts when that happens. Remember it’s okay to cry for yourself. Let yourself cry over spilt milk. You don’t have to wait till somebody dies. You can cry about anything that triggers you, no matter how seemingly trivial.Don’t set a time limit on tears. Your heart will decide when enough is enough. If you connect with the true source of your pain, you’ll find it’s finite. But you don’t get to dictate a time limit for your sorrow. Be patient. Pick up where you left off. If you have to keep a stiff upper lip, perhaps because you’re at work, check in with yourself later and see how you feel. Reflect on the incident in private if you feel it’s unresolved. Don’t stress out if you can’t recapture the pain. Tears are like cats: You can’t lead them on a leash. Speak only kind words to yourself. When you cry, watch for self-critical and invalidating self-talk like this:It’s not that big a dealI’m too sensitiveBig boys/girls don’t cryInstead, say, “I’m sorry” and “I’m with you” and “I love you.” Don’t say these things in order to make yourself stop crying. Say them in order to be compassionate to yourself. Cry in public. If you’ve never cried in public before, you may be surprised to find that many people will be drawn to you. Your tears make you vulnerable, and therefore no threat to others. Kindness is a frequent response to public tears.If you remember just one thing from this post, let it be self-compassion.

It's great that you've reached out for help and are actively seeking ways to combat your depression. It can be incredibly challenging when sadness feels overwhelming, but there are steps you can take to alleviate some of the burden.

One possible treatment option for depression is therapy, specifically cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and behaviors that contribute to depressive symptoms. By working with a therapist, you can examine and challenge any self-blame or feelings of unworthiness that may stem from childhood trauma. This type of therapy can also help you develop healthier coping mechanisms and improve your overall mood.

Another option to consider is medication. Antidepressant medications can be prescribed by a healthcare professional who specializes in mental health. They work to rebalance certain chemicals in the brain that may be contributing to your symptoms. However, it’s important to note that individual responses to medication can vary, so finding the right one might involve some trial and error.

In addition to therapy and medication, lifestyle changes can play a significant role in managing depression. Regular exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms and improve mood, as it releases endorphins that act as natural antidepressants. Engaging in activities you once enjoyed, even if they don't bring immediate joy, could also help counteract the grayness you're experiencing.

Finding a support system can be immensely helpful too. Connecting with others who have experienced similar struggles can provide validation and understanding. Whenever I'm faced with uncertainty or unfamiliar situations, anxiety takes hold of me. Simple tasks like going to the grocery store or attending a social gathering cause excessive worry and panic. I start imagining worst-case scenarios and struggle to control my racing thoughts. This anxiety often leads to avoidance behaviors, limiting my opportunities for growth and connection.

It can be challenging when anxiety takes hold of you in uncertain or unfamiliar situations. The excessive worry and panic that arise when faced with simple tasks like going to the grocery store or attending a social gathering can feel overwhelming. It's understandable that imagining worst-case scenarios and struggling to control racing thoughts adds to your distress. This anxiety has also led to avoidance behaviors, which limit your opportunities for growth and connection.

One suggestion I have is to try practicing relaxation techniques when you start feeling anxious. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation can help calm your mind and body. These techniques can be done anywhere and at any time, providing you with a sense of control over your anxiety.

Another strategy that may be helpful is gradually exposing yourself to the situations that trigger your anxiety. Start by breaking down the task into smaller steps and gradually work your way up to more challenging situations. For example, if going to the grocery store causes anxiety, you could begin by visiting during less crowded times or bringing a friend along for support. Over time, as you become more comfortable, you can increase the difficulty level.

It might also be beneficial to challenge the negative thoughts and worst-case scenarios that come to mind. Ask yourself if there is evidence to support these thoughts or if they are based on assumptions. Try reframing them into more realistic and positive statements. Remember, our thoughts can greatly influence our emotions and behavior, so it's important to address any negative thinking patterns.

Additionally, finding healthy coping mechanisms that work for you can make a significant difference. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and provide a sense of accomplishment can help distract from anxious thoughts. This could include hobbies, exercise, spending time in nature, or connecting with loved ones. Taking care of your physical health through regular sleep, a balanced diet, and avoiding substances like caffeine or alcohol can also contribute to overall well-being.

Remember, everyone's journey with anxiety is unique, and it may take time to find the strategies that work best for you. If these suggestions don't seem to alleviate your symptoms or if they become too overwhelming, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support.

Our relationship ended about 7 years ago, but don't know how to let go. How can I get over that person and move on?

What you're most likely trying to get over is to be attracted to the qualities which you felt attracted to in the person.The problem isn't releasing yourself from the person, per se.   Letting go of a person means separating yourself from the qualities in a partner which you value.Two possibilities exist.Either you continue to feel strongly that the qualities in the past relationship are still meaningful and you'd like to base your next relationship on these qualities.Or, the person had qualities which are no longer relevant or necessary in your life and this is the reason the relationship ended.It is possible that even if you had an adequate exposure to certain qualities in someone that you simply miss the companionship of a relationship.See if you can figure out whether you need the qualities this person gave you or whether you simply like being part of a couple.If you like the particular qualities of your previous parter and these are still relevant to your life, you'll attract a partner who has similar qualities.Basically people attract what they need.The more open you are to attracting what you need in a partner, the more likely your next partner will have these qualities.In this way, you'll get over the particular person and still have the satisfaction to be in a relationship.

I have a fear of something and I want to face that fear to overcome it, but I don't know how. What can I do?

Biologically, fear is designed to protect us from harm. Fear is not always a bad thing, and in fact can be quite healthy and appropriate depending on the situation. A phobia, however, is different. You used the term "fear" rather than "phobia". A phobia is an irrational fear - meaning it is not rational for you to fear that thing. If your situation is a phobia, exposure therapy can help. This consists of gradually exposing yourself a little at a time to the thing you are afraid of. Some people with phobias find that the irrational fear interferes with their life and they do need to overcome it. Someone who is afraid to drive over bridges may go to great lengths to avoid routes that have bridges. People who are afraid of elevators may always use the stairs instead, which may not always be feasible. If overcoming a phobia will improve the quality of your life, then by all means, seek professional help to overcome it.Everyone has fears, or things that make them nervous. Public speaking, asking a person out, fear of failure. Examine what your fear is and try to determine the reason for the fear. When you can get to the root cause of the fear, you can deal with that issue. A lot of times, it is a self-esteem issue. You may be able to peel back the layers of the fear and find out what's causing it and deal with the real issue. Some fears are caused by trauma. Someone with PTSD is going to have an exaggerated fear response and will find themselves being kicked into "fight or flight" mode over things that someone without the trauma experience wouldn't notice or react to. In cases like this, exposure therapy would be the wrong approach and could actually make things worse. If there is a possibility that a past trauma is the cause of your fear, I strongly urge you to seek a therapist - not just any therapist, but one who is trained to work with trauma and abuse victims.

You are describing some of the most common symptoms of depression: low self esteem, difficulty sleeping, changes in appetite, sad mood, feelings of hopeless and feelings of worthlessness. A full assessment/evaluation with a mental health professional is warranted to understand if indeed you meet criteria for a Major Depressive Disorder i.e.., are delressed. One thing I often tell patients is that "Do you think you are depressed?" People often answer yes or no, but many individuals respond with a question: How would I know? To that I often explain that if I stopped watching movies or better, stopped enjoying watching movies that would be a clear indication for me that I am delressed. It would be a sign that I have lost pleasure or interest in the activity that I typically enjoy most . I'll ask you to think of one activity which you really really enjoy.  It could be anything from reading, to being with friends, to skiing to watching tv.  I would like to now ask you if you have stopped enjoying that activity or can't find the motivation to engage in it? This is another symptom of depression: loss in pleasurable activities. The good news is that there are many effective, available treatment if you are indeed in a depression or simply, you want to modify/decrease your depressive symptoms i.e., you want to stop feeling so tired and so worthless. Treatment includes one or more of the following: psychotherapy, medication, exercise. Any one or combination of both of these can help to improve your mood. The even better news is that feeling that you are doing something wrong can diminish with appropriate treatment over time.  I hope you find this information helpful. The most important next step is to get evaluated by a mental health professional typically a psychologist or psychiatrist, and for both you and the professional to better understand your symptoms and your mood in the context of what is going on in your life.

I have been experiencing intense anxiety lately, and it's really affecting my day-to-day life. I constantly worry about everything – from small decisions to big life choices. It feels like my heart races all the time, and sometimes I even have trouble breathing. I'm always on edge and find it difficult to relax or enjoy anything because I'm consumed by these anxious thoughts. Experiencing intense anxiety can be overwhelming and have a significant impact on your day-to-day life. It's difficult when worry consumes your thoughts, making it hard to relax or find enjoyment in things you used to enjoy. Thankfully, there are techniques you can learn to better manage your anxiety and find peace of mind.

One helpful technique is deep breathing exercises. When you feel your heart racing or having trouble breathing, take deep breaths in through your nose, hold for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This can help regulate your breathing and slow down your heart rate.

Another technique you can try is practicing mindfulness. Mindfulness involves focusing your attention on the present moment without judgment. You can start by simply paying attention to your breath, body sensations, or the sounds around you. By redirecting your focus away from anxious thoughts towards the present, you may find some relief.

Creating a daily routine that includes activities you enjoy and self-care can also make a difference. Engaging in hobbies, exercise, spending time with loved ones, or engaging in relaxation techniques such as listening to calming music or taking warm baths can provide a sense of calm and distraction from anxiety.

Additionally, consider challenging your anxious thoughts with rational thinking. Often, our minds tend to blow things out of proportion and catastrophize situations. Take a step back and evaluate the evidence supporting your anxious thoughts. Ask yourself if there are other possible explanations or more balanced perspectives to consider.

It might also be helpful to seek support from trusted friends or family members. Talking about your feelings and concerns with someone who understands and cares about you can offer comfort and perspective.

Remember, managing anxiety takes time and practice. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. If your anxiety continues to significantly impact your day-to-day life, I encourage you to reach out to professionals experienced in mental health who can tailor the necessary therapies and interventions specific to your needs.

Hi Texas, Thanks for your honesty; it helps me know where to go in answering you. What strikes me in your question is that you describe several ways in which your husband is hurtful/abusive/controlling with you, and then you ask "Should we call it quits?". We? I wonder if maybe the first step is for you to start seeing this decision as yours, rather than yours together. The way your husband treats you is not your fault, Texas. Your lies are a natural and normal way of you avoiding situations and encounters that feel unsafe for you. The problem is not your lying. The problem is that you don't feel safe enough to be honest with a person you're supposed to be able to trust.There's an analogy that I sometimes use; I don't know if this is scientifically true or simply a useful story, but it's powerful either way, so I will tell it to you.If you take a frog and drop it into a pot of boiling water, the frog will jump out immediately, knowing instinctively that if it stays in the pot, it will die. If you take a frog, however, and put it in a pot of cold water, and slowly, slowly, heat it to boiling, the frog will boil to death because it will fail to recognise the moment when it no longer has the energy to jump out of the pot; by the time it realises it's dying, it has lost its strength. It's called "learned helplessness". When your power or your voice has been taken away for a long time, you get used to that, and you fail to see the options that are available to you. You have a toddler, and you may be under the impression that staying in the marriage is best for the child. The dynamics within my family have become increasingly difficult, and I'm hoping counseling can assist me in navigating these relationships. My parents often argue and involve me in their conflicts, which has taken a toll on my emotional well-being. I want to find healthier ways to cope with their discord and strengthen our bond as a family.

For instance, just last week, my parents had a heated argument during a family dinner. Their angry voices echoed through the house, causing distress for everyone present. As a result of being caught in the midst of their conflict, I felt overwhelmed and helpless. Witnessing their continuous disagreements makes me question if there's something wrong with me or if it's my fault that they fight so much.

Emotionally, this constant exposure to familial arguments has left me feeling anxious and emotionally drained. I worry about their relationship falling apart and what the consequences might be for me and my younger siblings. It's challenging to focus on other areas of my life when I am constantly preoccupied with their problems.

To give you some context, my parents have always struggled with effective communication. They come from different cultural backgrounds and have difficulty understanding each other's perspectives. This leads to frequent misunderstandings and escalations in their arguments.

In terms of coping mechanisms, I try to distance myself emotionally during their conflicts, but it's becoming harder to maintain healthy boundaries. I recognize that their issues are not mine to solve, yet it's challenging not to get involved when they continually draw me into their disputes.

Could you please provide guidance on how to establish healthier boundaries and navigate the complexities of familial conflicts? How can I offer support to my parents without compromising my own well-being?

Navigating complex family dynamics can be difficult, but it's great that you're seeking guidance on how to establish healthier boundaries and cope with your parents' conflicts. Here are some suggestions to consider:

1. Recognize that you are not responsible for their arguments: It's essential to remind yourself that your parents' conflicts are not your fault. Their disagreements stem from their own issues, and taking the blame will only add unnecessary stress to your life.

2. Set clear emotional boundaries: While it may be challenging, it's important to distance yourself emotionally from their conflicts. Remind yourself that their arguments do not define who you are as a person or reflect on your worth. Practice self-care techniques such as deep breathing exercises or mindfulness to help regulate your emotions during these situations.

3. Communicate your need for space: In a calm and assertive manner, let your parents know that you require space and time away from their arguments. Explain that while you love and care about them, their conflicts are affecting your well-being. This way, they might become more aware of their impact on you.

4. Seek support outside of the family: Building a network of supportive friends, mentors, or even online communities can provide an outlet for you to process your emotions. Talking to someone you trust can help alleviate some of the anxiety and emotional strain caused by your parents' conflicts.

5. Focus on what you can control: It's natural to worry about the potential consequences of your parents' fights, but try to redirect your energy towards things within your control. Concentrate on your personal growth, hobbies, education, or other aspects of your life that bring you joy and fulfillment.

6. Encourage open communication: If and when the opportunity arises, gently encourage your parents to work on their communication skills. Suggesting couple's therapy or providing resources on effective communication strategies could potentially help them navigate their conflicts in a healthier manner.

7. Practice empathy and understanding: While it's crucial to distance yourself emotionally, finding ways to empathize or understand their perspectives can help create a more supportive environment. Remind yourself that they are individuals with their own struggles, and try not to internalize their conflicts as a reflection of your relationship with them or you as a person.

Remember, these suggestions may not resolve all the challenges within your family overnight, but establishing healthier boundaries and focusing on your own well-being is a vital step towards navigating familial conflicts in a more constructive way.

Work-related deadlines and pressures often cause significant stress in my life. I notice a strong sense of irritability during these times, and I tend to snap at colleagues and loved ones over minor issues. It affects my relationships and overall well-being. Through counseling, I aim to develop healthier ways to manage stress and communicate effectively during challenging situations.

Managing work-related stress and finding healthier ways to cope can greatly improve your relationships and overall well-being. Here are some suggestions that may help you in this process:

1. Recognize your triggers: Start by identifying the specific situations or deadlines that tend to cause the most stress for you. This awareness will allow you to anticipate and prepare for these stressful periods.

2. Take breaks and practice self-care: Make sure to prioritize self-care activities during hectic times. Schedule regular breaks to engage in activities that help you relax and recharge, such as taking a walk, listening to music, or practicing deep breathing exercises.

3. Practice effective communication: When feeling irritable or overwhelmed, it's important to communicate assertively and respectfully with colleagues and loved ones. Take a moment to pause and collect your thoughts before responding. Focus on expressing your needs, feelings, and concerns calmly and clearly.

4. Set boundaries: Establish clear boundaries between work and personal life. Avoid bringing work-related stress home by creating dedicated time for relaxation, hobbies, and spending quality time with loved ones.

5. Seek support from trusted individuals: Sometimes just talking through your stress with someone who understands can provide immense relief. Reach out to friends, family members, or supportive colleagues who can listen without judgment and offer perspective or advice when needed.

6. Engage in stress-reducing activities: Find healthy outlets to reduce stress outside of work. Engaging in physical exercise or hobbies you enjoy, like painting, dancing, or reading, can help divert your attention away from work-related pressures and promote a sense of balance in your life.

7. Explore relaxation techniques: Incorporate relaxation techniques into your daily routine to manage stress. These could include guided meditation, progressive muscle relaxation, or yoga. Experiment with different techniques until you find what works best for you.

Remember, managing work-related stress takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself as you develop new coping strategies. If your symptoms persist or worsen, consider seeking professional support from a counselor or therapist who can provide personalized guidance to help you navigate through these challenges.

The recent loss of a loved one has left me feeling lost, lonely, and consumed by sadness. Grief seems to wash over me unexpectedly, making it difficult to focus on daily tasks or engage in social activities. I hope that therapy can provide me with guidance on navigating through the stages of grief and finding healing.

Losing a loved one can be an incredibly difficult and painful experience, and it's completely understandable that you're feeling lost, lonely, and consumed by sadness. Grief is a natural response to loss, and it can often feel overwhelming and unpredictable.

In therapy, there are several strategies and techniques that can help you navigate through the stages of grief and find healing. Firstly, it can be helpful to acknowledge and express your emotions in a way that feels comfortable for you. This might include talking about your loved one, sharing memories, or engaging in activities that honor their memory. It's important to give yourself permission to grieve and not suppress your emotions.

Additionally, self-care is crucial during this time. Taking care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally can support your healing process. This might involve getting enough sleep, maintaining a healthy diet, engaging in regular exercise, and seeking moments of relaxation and rest. Finding outlets for stress relief, such as journaling, listening to music, or participating in creative activities, can also be beneficial.

It may also be helpful to establish a routine and structure in your daily life. Engaging in simple tasks and setting achievable goals can provide a sense of stability and purpose, even when faced with immense grief. However, please remember to be patient with yourself and allow for flexibility, as some days may be harder than others.

Building a strong support system is also essential. Reach out to friends, family members, or support groups who can offer a listening ear and emotional support. Sharing your thoughts and feelings with compassionate individuals who understand and validate your experiences can be incredibly comforting.

Finally, don't underestimate the power of professional therapy. A therapist can guide you through the grieving process, providing coping mechanisms, validating your emotions, and helping you develop resilience. They can also assist in exploring any unresolved issues related to the loss and finding ways to incorporate your loved one's memory into your life moving forward.

Remember, healing from grief takes time and everyone's journey is unique. Be gentle with yourself as you navigate through this difficult period and remember that it is possible to find peace and healing in time.

I believe my anxiety started after a traumatic event in which I was involved in a car accident. Since that incident, I've been struggling with recurring intrusive thoughts and a heightened sense of danger, making daily life incredibly challenging.

One specific trigger for my anxiety is driving. Whenever I get behind the wheel, my palms become sweaty, and my heart races uncontrollably. The fear of losing control or being involved in another accident engulfs me, often leading to avoidance of driving altogether.

My anxiety symptoms are frequent and intense. I experience panic attacks at least once a week, accompanied by physical symptoms like shortness of breath, chest pain, and dizziness. These episodes last for around 20 minutes but leave me emotionally drained for hours afterward.

To cope with my anxiety, I've tried relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation and visualization exercises. While these methods provide temporary relief, they don't seem to alleviate the underlying anxiety on a long-term basis.

What strategies do you use to treat anxiety disorders? Are there any medications that might help reduce the intensity of my panic attacks? I'm open to exploring different approaches to managing my anxiety symptoms.

Managing anxiety can be a complex process, but there are several strategies you can try to help reduce the intensity of your symptoms. It's important to note that everyone is different, so finding what works best for you might involve some trial and error.

One approach to treating anxiety disorders is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). This type of therapy focuses on identifying and challenging negative thoughts and beliefs that contribute to anxiety. By learning to reframe these thoughts and replace them with more positive and realistic ones, you may experience a reduction in anxiety symptoms over time.

Another strategy that could be helpful is exposure therapy. This involves gradually exposing yourself to situations or activities that trigger your anxiety, such as driving. Through repeated exposures, you can learn to tolerate and manage your anxiety more effectively. Start by taking small steps, like sitting in a parked car, and gradually work your way up to short drives around familiar routes. Remember to go at your own pace and be patient with yourself.

In addition to therapy, medication can sometimes be beneficial in reducing the intensity of panic attacks and other anxiety symptoms. While I'm not able to prescribe medications myself, it's worth discussing this option with a healthcare professional who can evaluate your specific situation and provide appropriate recommendations if necessary.

Aside from therapy and medication, self-care practices can also play a role in managing anxiety. Regular exercise, such as walking or yoga, can release endorphins and help decrease overall stress levels. Prioritizing sleep, eating a balanced diet, and practicing relaxation exercises, like deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation, can also contribute to a greater sense of well-being.

Remember, managing anxiety is a journey, and it's important to be patient and kind to yourself along the way. Consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support as you navigate through this process.

Deep breathing can help activate your body's relaxation response and bring a sense of calmness.

Another approach you can explore is mindfulness meditation. Mindfulness involves bringing your attention to the present moment without judgment. Set aside some time each day to sit quietly and pay attention to your thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations. If anxious thoughts arise, acknowledge them without getting caught up in them or trying to push them away. Instead, gently guide your focus back to the present moment. With consistent practice, mindfulness can help you develop a greater awareness of your anxiety triggers and learn to respond to them in more helpful ways.

Engaging in regular physical activity can also be beneficial for managing anxiety. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Whether it's going for a walk, practicing yoga, or participating in any other form of exercise that you enjoy, finding an activity that gets your body moving can potentially reduce anxiety symptoms and increase feelings of well-being.

Additionally, make sure to prioritize self-care in your routine. This can include activities such as getting enough sleep, maintaining a balanced diet, connecting with loved ones, and engaging in hobbies or activities that bring you joy. Taking care of your overall well-being can provide a solid foundation for managing anxiety.

Remember, everyone's journey with anxiety is unique, and it may take time to find the techniques and strategies that work best for you. It can be helpful to reach out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support on your path toward managing anxiety.

There may be several reasons for his actions, some of which may have nothing to do with how he feels for you. Learning about what is going on for him will likely answer your questions and, depending on his response, may cause some relief. When initiating conversations about subjects that are sensitive, there are a few things that you want to remember. Tell him how you are feeling and what you are experiencing, rather than blaming him or telling him what he is doing wrong. Avoid using extreme, black and white language (i.e. always and never). For example, you may say something such as, "I feel confused that we are rarely intimate and I'm wondering if you've also noticed this change" versus "You are never intimate with me anymore." Don't be afraid to ask him questions. You deserve to know what is going on, as his behavior is effecting your well being. I like to ask open-ended questions instead of yes and no questions. It allows for more clarity and deeper explanation. Lastly, ask yourself (and possibly him) what part you play in the recent changes. Does he feel that you've been distant? There are some great thoughts offered by others here. I would just add that typically the most natural response to fearful thoughts is to want to stop, avoid, or get rid of them - which doesn't work if you're really caught up in a cycle of OCD or other form of anxiety. In the long run, the more effective thing to do is the harder and less intuitive option: to have those uncomfortable thoughts on purpose. This may mean writing out in detail what the worst case fear you are thinking of is, and then reading it over and over again until it becomes boring. It may also mean pausing through the course of the day to merely observe all the thoughts going on, and realizing that thoughts are merely thoughts. She hasn’t asked yet, but she has been insinuating that she wants to babysit my child. How do I go about saying no without creating an issue?

Hi Fontana,Thanks for providing all the details needed in order to respond to your question. It seems very clear to me that "no" would be the appropriate response. I like your healthy boundaries, and I'll help you explore possible ways to respond to her. First, she hasn't asked yet, and you don't know that she will. Right now, you can pleasantly ignore her hints. They're not hurting you and if you ignore them, they're more likely to go away. You can address and reduce your own anxiety about the possibility of her asking by reassuring yourself that you have the right as parents to make this decision, and that if she's offended, that doesn't mean that you're being mean; it means that she has unrealistic expectations. So, the first goal is to put it out of your mind as a worry. You might never have to face that moment. But, I understand that you want to be prepared.As her son, perhaps your husband is the best one to answer the question, should it ever come. Is he willing to do this? But if you are comfortable, and if you're the one she asks, you can confidently give her a simple, honest response about why it won't happen. And I would suggest presenting a firmly closed door, rather than saying "but maybe later". No need to apologize or hum and haw..."We love that you want to be around Junior, and we definitely want you in his/her life. (try to leave out the "but" here). "Anxiety has been taking over my life recently. It started with just a few anxious thoughts here and there, but now it's affecting my sleep, appetite, and daily activities. I feel like I need professional help to overcome this anxiety and live a normal life again."

Experiencing anxiety can feel overwhelming, but there are steps you can take to manage and overcome it. Here are some suggestions:

1. Understanding your anxiety: Take some time to reflect on what triggers your anxious thoughts and how they affect your sleep, appetite, and daily activities. This awareness can help you gain a better understanding of the root causes and patterns of your anxiety.

2. Deep breathing exercises: When you notice yourself feeling anxious, try deep breathing exercises. Breathe in slowly through your nose, holding it for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This simple technique can help calm your nervous system and reduce anxiety levels.

3. Grounding techniques: Engage your senses to ground yourself in the present moment. Focus on things around you - the sensation of your feet on the ground, the sound of birds chirping, or the texture of an object in your hand. By redirecting your attention to the present, you can lessen the impact of anxious thoughts.

4. Self-care practices: Prioritize self-care activities that promote relaxation and well-being. Engage in regular exercise, get enough restful sleep, maintain a balanced diet, and practice mindfulness or meditation. These actions can contribute positively to your overall mental health and help alleviate anxiety symptoms.

5. Gradual exposure: If certain situations trigger anxiety, consider gradually exposing yourself to them in manageable increments. Start with small steps and gradually increase exposure to build up your resilience over time. For example, if social settings cause anxiety, attend small gatherings or meet-ups instead of diving into larger events right away.

6. Seek support: Sharing your experience with trusted friends or loved ones can provide understanding and emotional support. Sometimes, just talking about your worries helps relieve anxiety. While they may not be professionals, those closest to you can still be great sources of comfort and encouragement.

7. Relaxation techniques: Explore different relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery, or listening to calming music. Experiment with various methods and find what works best for you to create a sense of calm during anxious moments.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time, patience, and persistence. These suggestions can serve as a starting point on your journey towards managing anxiety in your daily life. If your symptoms persist or worsen, it may be beneficial to consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support.

Hello, and thank you for your question. It certainly sounds like you don't like how things are going. Here are a few thoughts and ideas:1. If you haven't seen a primary care provider in a while, you may want to. There are health conditions that can affect your mood and energy levels, even at your age. It doesn't hurt to get checked out. If they find the cause, they may be able to treat it and improve the symptoms. In addition, most primary care providers are trained to be able to manage medication for patients who have mild, moderate, and sometimes severe depression. So, don't be surprised if your primary care doctor offers to put you on an anti-depressant if they diagnose you with depression. Medication is not the only way to treat depression, but sometimes it is necessary depending on different factors.2. You may want to consider counseling, since it is another effective way to treat depression. A counselor will help you explore the factors that may be leading to depressive symptoms in the first place. This could include thoughts, behaviors, beliefs, life experiences, and other things. 3. Finally, to answer your question about whether these feelings are "normal." These symptoms could be the sign of an underlying general health or mental health condition. It is important to remember that even if these symptoms are "abnormal" it doesn't mean that YOU are. Millions of people struggle with depression. So remember, the symptoms are the problem, not YOU. Hope this helps. Be well.Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

It's important to remember that you're not alone in feeling this way, as many people go through similar experiences. While I cannot diagnose you or replace the expertise of a mental health professional, I can offer some guidance and suggestions based on your concerns.

One possible explanation for why you may be feeling this way is negative self-talk. Our minds have a tendency to focus on the negative aspects of ourselves and our actions, which can lead to feelings of self-criticism and worthlessness. Challenging these negative thoughts can be a helpful first step. Instead of automatically accepting them as true, try questioning the evidence behind these thoughts. Is there any concrete proof that nobody cares about you? Are there past experiences or interactions that support this belief?

Social anxiety is a common mental health condition characterized by fear, discomfort, and avoidance of social situations due to feelings of embarrassment, self-consciousness, and perceived judgment from others. This fear can manifest in various ways, such as difficulty making eye contact, speaking up in groups, or even attending social events.

To help you overcome this challenge, we can explore various therapeutic approaches. One effective method is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on changing negative thought patterns and behaviors. We can work together to identify and challenge the thoughts and beliefs that contribute to your social anxiety, such as the belief that you must always be perfect or that others are judging you. We can also practice various techniques, such as relaxation exercises, role-playing, and exposure therapy, to help you build confidence and improve your social skills.

Another approach that may be helpful is mindfulness-based interventions, which can help you become more aware of your thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations in the present moment. By learning to accept and observe these experiences without judgment, you can reduce the emotional intensity of social situations and improve your ability to connect with others.

Ultimately, the goal of our therapeutic sessions will be to help you develop a deeper understanding of your social anxiety and the ways it manifests in your life. Through a collaborative and compassionate approach, we can work together to identify the root causes of your feelings of isolation and disconnection and develop effective strategies for overcoming them.
