My boyfriend’s sneaky and puts his friends before me. He fights just to leave. One day, he's happy. The next, he's mean and blames me for everything. He can't admit faults. He thinks he's perfect and does no wrong.

Hi, Ontario. I live in the other Ontario; in Canada. I'll try to help you sort this out. You have a long list of complaints about your boyfriend! It sounds like he's maybe a bit immature and moody, and these things affect you, for sure. I get it. It's got me curious, and if I was working with you, I'd want to know a lot more about how long you've been together and what's actually working well between you two. I would also ask a lot of questions about the details of your description. What tells you he's 'sneaky'? Does he lie? How do you know he lies to you? Also, are you wanting to make things better with him, do you just want an ear to vent to, are you looking for validation, or do you hope someone will help you wake up to an unhappy situation?  It helps me if I know what you want.Whenever I meet someone who has a lot of complaints about their partner or boyfriend, I encourage them first to look at the language they're using. Some of your words tell me that you think you know what he's thinking (that he wants to fight so he can leave, that he thinks he's perfect). It's always tricky when we assume what someone's thinking, and in an argument or dialogue, these kinds of statements tend to lead to defensiveness and an escalated argument. I'd encourage you to focus on his actual behaviours and how they affect you, rather than the motives or beliefs you think are behind the behaviours (because you really can't know what he's thinking unless he tells you). As a general rule, the "When you do X, I feel Y" sentence goes far in helping others understand what we feel.So, it's fair to say "when you lie to me, I can't trust you", or "when you end our date early to hang with your friends I feel like I'm not important to you", or "your mood swings are difficult for me", or "I don't seem to get apologies from you". Try to focus on his actual behaviour when you talk to him about this stuff. A relationship counsellor can help you each understand the other better beyond the surface behaviours if you want to improve the relationship.That said, I have to ask...if you haven't been with Mr. Not So Great for very long, is it maybe time to rethink the relationship? Unless there is a balance of really loving and positive behaviours that you're leaving out, you don't seem happy. A good therapist can help you understand why you are stuck in an unhappy relationship, if that is what's happening. There's a lot to sort out here...how to communicate about your needs, how to know when to call it quits if something doesn't feel good... I wish you the best as you continue to examine these questions with assistance from friends or professionals.

I was raped a couple months ago, Since then, along with other unfortunately events that have occurred, I have been having trouble feeling emotions. It's almost as if I'm a sociopath lacking any feeling. What can I do to change this?

Hi!This is a great question!The term you are looking for is alexithymia, the inability to identify and describe emotions in the self. However, just because you are not able to feel or express emotions, does not mean that you do not have emotions.After such a traumatic event that you experienced, your central nervous system goes into defensive mode (dorsal vagal nerves) that protect you from any further harm. What this means is if you were to feel your emotions related to your rape, you would have a sense of being overwhelmed, possibly re-experiencing the traumatic event.Not feeling emotions is your body's way of protecting you from any further trauma. Unfortunately, when the (parasympathetic) dorsal vagal system (shutting down feeling) is activated and suppresses your painful emotions (pain, shame, guilt, sadness, anger), it also shuts down your positive and relational emotions (love, joy, contentment, connectedness, happiness).I am very sorry that you had to go through such a traumatic experience as being raped. No one knows what is going on inside of you as a result. You don't know what is happening to your emotional wellbeing! The best (and at times, difficult and scary) thing is to process your emotions related to your trauma. This processing is done carefully, with a trained counselor, in a place that you feel safe, heard, and not judged. Although the thought of proceedings (addressing) emotions may be anxiety-inducing, it brings on a huge sense of relief and validation.What you are going through is normal, considering what happened to you! I hope you reach out for more help.If you have any questions feel free to contact me, Catherine at clevelandemotionalhealth.com

I get so much anxiety, and I don’t know why. I feel like I can’t do anything by myself because I’m scared of the outcomes.

The are two ways that such anxiety can be dealt with. One is an attempt to replace maladaptive thinking by examining the distorted thinking and resetting the fight-or-flight response with more reasonable, accurate ones. As an example "I'm scared of spiders." But if you change the thinking from being scared to "I'm bigger than the spider," it allows the mind to reach a calmer state of mind. Mindfulness-based therapy can also help  focus on the bodily sensations that arise when you feel anxious. Instead of avoiding or withdrawing from these feelings, remain present and fully experience the symptoms of anxiety. Instead of avoiding distressing thoughts, open up to them in an effort to realize and acknowledge that they are not literally true.Although it may seem counter-intuitive, fully realizing the experience of anxiety enables the release of over identification with negative thoughts. You can practice responding to disruptive thoughts, and letting these thoughts go.By remaining present in the body, you'll learn that the anxiety being experienced is merely a reaction to perceived threats. By positively responding to threatening events instead of being reactive you can overcome an erroneous fight-or-flight response.

How is the white color created?

The color white is created when all colors in the visible spectrum are combined in equal amounts. This can be seen in a prism or a rainbow, where sunlight is separated into its component colors. When all these colors are combined, the result is white light.

In terms of pigments, white can be created by using a substance that reflects all colors and absorbs none. This means that when white light hits the surface of the object, it is reflected back to the viewer as white. Titanium dioxide is a common pigment used in white paint, for example, because it is highly reflective and opaque.

In the digital world, white is often created by using RGB color values of 255, 255, 255, which means that all three primary colors (red, green, and blue) are at their maximum intensity. This creates a pure white color on electronic displays.

How can I know if I'm just being paranoid?

Hi Texas,Oh, that's a powerful idea, isn't it? It burrows into your head. Let's figure this out. First, has your partner given you any concrete reason not to trust them? Have they cheated before? If not, then they deserve the benefit of the doubt until there is evidence. If it's a "yes", then it's natural that these fears would be triggered and you can simply let your partner know what triggers the fear and what you need. "When you refuse to let me see your phone I worry that you're hiding something. I need openness". If they haven't cheated on you in the past, there are three possible scenarios here. I invite you to take a moment and write down what the evidence is that cheating is going on. What is the specific thing that's triggering your fears? When you have your data recorded, read on...The first scenario is that you have been personally hurt in the past by someone else and you've developed fears that you will be hurt again or that you're not enough to keep someone interested (this is just fear...people cheat for their own reasons, not because we're not interesting). This may be true if what you wrote down is "They didn't really do anything wrong...there is no evidence. I'm just scared and suspicious". That's a cue to do some self reflection and calm yourself with thoughts like "nothing has really happened. I can trust."If what you wrote down was vague evidence, like for example your partner has been distant or irritable, or you're having less sex than usual, you can try to approach the situation without making assumptions. Trust your gut, but your gut isn't seeing evidence of cheating...it's evidence of "something". Ask your partner what's up with accusations or assumptions.The third possibility is that there is some clear evidence that they are cheating. Maybe there are texts on a phone, or someone has told you something they saw. I'd say when there is some evidence, it's okay to present this to your partner and ask what's going on. If this happens repeatedly, and your gut is screaming and there are only excuses or explanations that don't make sense, then it's okay to do a bit of "research" and be extra aware of what's going on around you. I hope that helps.

Understanding and accepting your own sexuality can indeed be a challenging and emotional journey, but you have already taken an important step by seeking guidance and support. It's commendable that you are open to gaining clarity about your sexual orientation and developing self-compassion.

Firstly, it's essential to acknowledge the confusion and inner conflict you're experiencing regarding attractions towards people of the same gender. Remember that everyone's journey is unique, and exploring your sexuality takes time. It's important not to rush yourself or put undue pressure on finding all the answers right away.

The feelings of guilt and shame you mention may stem from societal expectations and upbringing that predominantly recognize heterosexuality as valid. These emotions are valid too and indicate the need for self-acceptance and understanding. It might help to remind yourself that there is no right or wrong way to feel or love, and your experiences are authentic and meaningful.

Witnessing your friend coming out can create a sense of reflection within yourself, questioning why it's difficult for you to do the same. Self-reflection is valuable, but comparing your journey to someone else's isn't always productive. Everyone progresses at their own pace and has different circumstances influencing their readiness to embrace their true identity.

It's positive to see that engaging in online communities with similar experiences has been helpful for you. Connecting with others who share similar struggles and stories can provide support and validation, making you feel less alone. In terms of embracing your true identity and finding self-acceptance, here are some suggestions:

1. Self-exploration: Take the time to reflect on your attractions, desires, and fantasies without judgment. Journaling your thoughts and feelings can be a useful tool in this process.

2. Education and information: Educate yourself about human sexuality, including diverse sexual orientations and experiences. Resources such as books, documentaries, podcasts, and reputable websites can provide valuable insights.

4. Supportive communities: Besides online spaces, look for local support groups, LGBTQ+ centers, or organizations in your area that offer safe and supportive environments for individuals questioning their sexual orientation. These communities can provide additional resources, workshops, and opportunities to connect with others facing similar challenges.

It feels like anxiety has permeated every aspect of my life. From work-related pressures to personal relationships, I'm constantly second-guessing myself and anticipating negative outcomes. The persistent feeling of impending doom takes a toll on my mental health, leaving me drained and unable to enjoy the present. I long for techniques that could alleviate this overpowering anxiety and restore a sense of tranquility.

One possible technique that could potentially help alleviate anxiety is mindfulness. Mindfulness involves focusing your attention on the present moment, without judgment or attachment to any particular thoughts or emotions. This practice can help bring a sense of calm and tranquility when you feel overwhelmed by anxiety.

Another helpful technique is deep breathing exercises. When you start feeling anxious, take slow, deep breaths in through your nose, hold it for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This simple but effective method helps activate your body's relaxation response, which counters the physical symptoms of anxiety.

Engaging in regular physical exercise can also be beneficial. Exercise releases endorphins, the brain's natural mood-boosting chemicals, which can help reduce feelings of anxiety and stress. Find an activity you enjoy, whether it's going for a walk, practicing yoga, or dancing, and make it a part of your routine.

Additionally, it may be helpful to challenge negative thoughts and replace them with more positive and realistic ones. When you catch yourself anticipating negative outcomes or second-guessing yourself, try to identify the evidence supporting these thoughts and consider alternative explanations or perspectives.

Journaling can be a useful tool as well. Taking the time to write down your thoughts and feelings can provide clarity and help release pent-up emotions. You can use this as an opportunity to reflect on your fears and anxieties and explore ways to address them more effectively.

Lastly, seeking support from loved ones or joining a support group can offer you a sense of connection and validation. Sharing your experiences with others who may be going through similar struggles can be comforting and help you realize that you're not alone in your journey.

Remember, everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, so it may take some trial and error to find the techniques that work best for you. Don't hesitate to reach out to licensed mental health professionals if you need additional support and guidance on your path towards finding peace and tranquility.
I have a fear of something and I want to face that fear to overcome it, but I don't know how. What can I do?

Fear is a part of life. In fact, our five main emotions are joy, fear, sadness, shame, and anger. We tend to spend a lot of time and energy running away from or trying to get rid of most of those emotions and the more we do that, the more we set ourselves up for failure and disappointment. As a result of viewing our human emotions as "bad" or "wrong," we often get caught up in a trap of thinking we have to overcome them or get rid of them before we can do what matters to us. In reality, you can do what is important to you while having your fears! My question for you is, what would you do if this fear was completely gone? What behaviors would you have if you were the ideal you? What skills, knowledge, or personal qualities would you develop? What kind of relationships would you have?I imagine your fear has kept you from achieving those goals because your mind tells you you can't do it until the fear is gone. I challenge you to do the following exercise:What is a goal you would like to achieve? Example: I would like to change careersWhat actions are necessary to complete this goal? Example: see a career counselor to determine my ideal career, go back to school/get a certification, network with others in my desired industryWhat thoughts, feelings, or urges might get in my way? Example: thoughts of "What if I fail? I'm not smart enough. I can't do it. I'm too busy to put energy into this." Feelings of fear, shame, excitement. Urges to distract myself through drinking or watch tv instead of taking action.It would be helpful to remind myself that: example: It is natural to have these thoughts, feelings, and urges but I can take action anyway. I deserve to have a fulfilling life.The smallest and easiest step I can take now: example: research career counselors in my area and write down their phone numbersThe time, day and date that I will take that first step, is: example: Tonight at 7pm At least think through these answers but it is most beneficial to write them down. I hope this helps!

One technique that you might find helpful is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. By recognizing and reframing these thoughts, you can develop more realistic and positive perspectives, which may help reduce your anxiety symptoms.

Another therapeutic approach that has been found beneficial for managing anxiety is exposure therapy. This involves gradually exposing yourself to situations or triggers that cause anxiety in a controlled environment, allowing you to build up resilience over time. It can be helpful in reducing anxiety related to specific situations such as presentations at work.

Mindfulness practices could also be beneficial for managing your anxiety. Regular practice of mindfulness exercises, such as mindful breathing or body scans, can assist in grounding yourself during moments of anxiety.

In addition to these therapeutic techniques, lifestyle changes can play a crucial role in managing anxiety. Engaging in regular physical exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding excessive caffeine or alcohol consumption can all contribute to overall mental well-being and potentially lessen anxiety symptoms.

Building a support network of friends, family, or even online communities who understand and empathize with your experience can provide valuable emotional support. Sharing your feelings and experiences with others who have similar struggles can help alleviate some of the burdens of anxiety.

Managing stress in the workplace can be challenging, but there are strategies you can try to help restore balance and improve your overall well-being. Here are some suggestions:

1. Prioritize and set realistic goals: Take a step back and evaluate your workload. Identify tasks that are most important and tackle those first. Break big projects into smaller, manageable tasks. Setting achievable goals can make your workload feel less overwhelming.

2. Learn to delegate: If possible, delegate some tasks to others who may be able to assist you. Delegating responsibilities can lighten your workload and free up time for you to focus on important tasks.

3. Practice effective time management: Organize your schedule by blocking out specific times for different activities or tasks. Prioritize important deadlines and allocate sufficient time to complete them. Avoid overcommitting yourself and learn to say 'no' when necessary.

4. Establish healthy boundaries: Draw clear lines between work life and personal life. Set aside time for relaxation, hobbies, and spending quality time with loved ones. Engaging in activities outside of work can help reduce stress and promote a healthier work-life balance.

5. Engage in stress-reducing activities: Find activities that help you relax and unwind from work-related stress. This can include exercise, mindfulness meditation, deep breathing exercises, listening to music, or engaging in creative outlets such as painting or writing.

6. Seek social support: Reach out to friends, family, or colleagues who can provide emotional support. Sometimes talking about your stressors and concerns with someone you trust can help alleviate stress and gain a fresh perspective.

7. Take care of your physical health: Ensure you are getting regular exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, and getting enough sleep. These factors greatly contribute to your overall well-being and can enhance your ability to manage stress effectively.

Remember that everyone's experience is unique, so it may take time to find what works best for you. It can be beneficial to consult with a mental health professional who can offer specialized guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Before I begin counseling, I'd like to know more about the fundamentals of the therapeutic relationship. What should I expect from a mental health professional during our sessions? How can I build trust and establish a strong rapport with my counselor? Are there any boundaries or limitations to the therapeutic relationship that I should be aware of? I want to make sure I have a clear understanding of this important aspect before diving into therapy.

It's great that you're taking the time to understand the fundamentals of the therapeutic relationship before starting counseling. Building trust and establishing a strong rapport with your counselor is crucial for a successful therapy journey. Here are some things you can expect from a mental health professional during your sessions:

1. Active Listening: Your therapist will actively listen to what you have to say, providing a safe space for you to express your thoughts and emotions without judgment.

2. Empathy and Understanding: A mental health professional will strive to understand your experiences and feelings, showing empathy towards your struggles.

3. Confidentiality: Your therapist will prioritize confidentiality, ensuring that what you share in therapy remains private unless there are legal or safety concerns.

4. Collaboration: Therapy is a collaborative process, where you and your counselor work together to set goals, explore challenges, and develop strategies for personal growth.

5. Supportive Environment: Your therapist will create a supportive environment where you feel comfortable sharing your concerns, fears, and aspirations.

To build trust and establish a strong rapport with your counselor, consider these suggestions:

1. Open Communication: Be open and honest about your feelings, thoughts, and expectations. Sharing openly can help your therapist better understand your needs.

2. Clarify Goals: Discuss your therapy goals with your counselor so they can tailor their approach to meet your specific needs.

3. Ask Questions: Don't hesitate to ask questions if something is unclear or if you want more information about the therapeutic process. This can help you gain a clearer understanding and ease any uncertainties.

4. Give Feedback: Provide feedback to your therapist regarding what works well for you and what doesn't. Honest feedback helps them adjust their approach to better support you.

Regarding boundaries and limitations in the therapeutic relationship, it's important to be aware that therapists maintain professional boundaries to ensure ethical practice. These boundaries may include maintaining appropriate physical distance, refraining from dual relationships, and focusing on your well-being rather than personal friendships or connections outside of therapy.

Remember, every therapeutic relationship is unique, and it's essential to find a mental health professional who aligns with your needs and values. I hope this information helps you gain a clearer understanding of the therapeutic relationship and prepares you for a positive counseling experience.

Recently, I've been experiencing intense fear, trembling, and feelings of impending doom. The possible triggers for my anxiety are crowded spaces and driving on highways. It can be challenging to deal with severe anxiety and panic attacks, so I'm glad you reached out for support. The symptoms you described, such as intense fear, trembling, and feelings of impending doom, are common experiences during panic attacks. It's understandable that crowded spaces and driving on highways trigger your anxiety, as these situations can feel overwhelming. 

Firstly, it's important to acknowledge how difficult it must have been for you when you had a panic attack while stuck in traffic on the highway. Racing thoughts, chest tightness, and dizziness are uncomfortable symptoms and can make you feel quite distressed. The fact that these symptoms occur sporadically but tend to be present when encountering triggers is significant and something we can explore further.

Considering your past trauma during childhood, it's possible that it contributes to your current struggles with anxiety. Trauma can have a lasting impact on our mental well-being and may manifest in various ways, including anxiety symptoms. Understanding and exploring this connection in therapy could potentially help improve your overall well-being.

Coping by avoiding crowded spaces and taking alternative routes is a valid short-term strategy to manage your anxiety. However, as you mentioned, it does come with limitations, affecting your mobility and social interactions. Exploring therapeutic options would indeed be beneficial for you.

In counseling, we can work together to develop coping mechanisms specifically tailored to your needs. Therapists often use evidence-based techniques like Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) to address anxiety disorders. CBT aims to identify and challenge unhelpful thought patterns that contribute to anxiety, as well as helping you develop effective strategies to manage panic attacks.

Additionally, relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or progressive muscle relaxation, can be helpful tools to reduce anxiety symptoms in the moment. Learning to recognize early signs of anxiety and practicing these techniques regularly can empower you to better navigate triggering situations.

Furthermore, therapy sessions provide a safe space for you to express your feelings and explore the root causes of your anxiety. By working through these underlying issues, you can gradually build resilience and develop new coping mechanisms.

It's important to remember that everyone's journey is unique, and progress may take time. Patience and self-compassion are key as you embark on this therapeutic process. With consistent effort and support, it's possible to manage and alleviate your anxiety symptoms, allowing you to lead a more fulfilling life with greater freedom and social engagement.

"I've been experiencing significant challenges in my role as a parent and want guidance on how to navigate them better. As a single parent, balancing work and parenting responsibilities often leaves me exhausted and overwhelmed. There are moments when I question if I'm doing enough for my child. For example, recently, my child started having behavioral issues at school, which sparked feelings of guilt and self-doubt. I sincerely need advice on effective parenting strategies to support my child's growth and create a harmonious home environment."

Navigating the challenges of parenthood can be overwhelming, especially as a single parent juggling work and caregiving responsibilities. It's completely normal to feel exhausted and question whether you're doing enough for your child. Let's explore some effective parenting strategies that could support your child's growth and create a harmonious home environment:

1. Communication: Regularly engaging in open and honest communication with your child is key. Create a safe space where they feel comfortable expressing their thoughts and emotions. Active listening and validating their feelings can go a long way.

2. Consistency and Boundaries: Establishing clear expectations and consistent routines can help provide structure and stability for your child. Setting age-appropriate boundaries helps them understand what behaviors are acceptable and creates a sense of security.

3. Positive Reinforcement: Recognize and praise your child's positive behaviors and achievements. Offering specific compliments can boost their self-esteem and motivate them to continue making good choices.

4. Establishing Consequences: It's important to have appropriate consequences for challenging behaviors. Instead of focusing solely on punishment, aim to teach your child about responsibility and accountability. Logical consequences (related to the behavior) can be more effective than punitive ones.

5. Problem-Solving Skills: Encourage your child to develop problem-solving skills by involving them in finding solutions. This empowers them and promotes independent thinking. You can guide them through brainstorming ideas and evaluating potential outcomes.

6. Self-Care: Prioritizing your own well-being is crucial. Remember to take time for self-care activities that recharge and rejuvenate you. When you're in a better mental and emotional state, it positively impacts your ability to navigate challenges and support your child effectively.

7. Seek Support: Consider connecting with other parents who may be experiencing similar challenges. Local parenting groups or online communities can offer valuable insight, empathy, and practical advice. Additionally, trusted friends or family members might be able to provide support.

Remember, every child is unique and what works for one may not work for another. Be patient with yourself and your child as you explore effective strategies together. Embrace the learning journey and celebrate small victories along the way. You are doing an incredible job, even if it may not feel that way sometimes.

"Being a parent has been overwhelming. I constantly doubt myself and feel guilty about the decisions I make. I want to develop effective parenting strategies and gain confidence in raising my child."

Parenting can definitely be overwhelming at times, and it's common to have doubts and feel guilty about decisions you make for your child. It can help to remember that there is no one "perfect" way to parent, and it's normal to make mistakes along the way. Developing effective parenting strategies and gaining confidence can take time and patience, but here are a few suggestions that might assist you:

1. Educate yourself: There are many reputable resources available on effective parenting techniques and strategies. Consider reading books or articles written by experts in child development or attending workshops or classes specifically designed for parents. These resources can provide valuable insights and offer guidance on how to navigate different situations.

2. Seek support from other parents: Connecting with other parents who may be going through similar experiences can be incredibly helpful. Sharing your experiences and learning from others can provide different perspectives and validate your feelings. Look for local parenting groups or online forums where you can engage in conversations with other parents.

3. Establish routines and boundaries: Children often thrive on routine and structure. By establishing consistent daily routines and setting clear expectations and boundaries, you can help provide them with a sense of security and stability. This can also make decision-making easier for you as a parent, as you'll have established guidelines to follow.

4. Practice self-care: Taking care of yourself is crucial in order to be an effective parent. Make sure to set aside some time each day for activities that recharge and rejuvenate you. Whether it's exercising, engaging in hobbies, spending time with friends, or simply taking a few moments to relax, self-care will not only improve your overall well-being but also enhance your ability to handle the challenges of parenting.

5. Show yourself compassion: Remember that being a perfect parent is not realistic, and making mistakes is part of the human experience. Be kind and gentle with yourself when doubts or guilt arise. Remind yourself that you are doing the best you can with the knowledge and resources available to you.

6. Celebrate small victories: Parenting is a journey filled with milestones, big and small. Take time to acknowledge and celebrate your successes, no matter how small they may seem. Recognizing the positive moments can help boost your confidence as a parent and remind you of your abilities.

Remember that effective parenting strategies are not one-size-fits-all, and it's important to find what works best for both you and your child. Don't hesitate to reach out for support when needed, whether it be from friends, family, or professionals who specialize in parenting support.

This has strained my relationships, as my loved ones don't feel comfortable around me anymore. It's important for me to learn healthy ways to express and control my anger so that it doesn't continue to damage my relationships.

Learning to manage anger can be a challenging but worthwhile journey. It's great that you recognize the impact it has on your relationships and want to find healthier ways to express and control your anger. Here are a few suggestions that may help you in this process:

1. Take a step back: When you feel anger building up inside you, try taking a moment to pause before reacting. This can give you some time to reflect on what triggered your anger and respond in a more composed manner.

2. Identify triggers and patterns: Pay attention to situations or specific events that tend to trigger your anger. Understanding your triggers can help you develop strategies to prevent or defuse them. Keep a journal where you note down these incidents and explore any patterns or common themes that emerge.

3. Practice relaxation techniques: Engaging in activities that promote relaxation and stress reduction can help you manage your anger. Deep breathing exercises, meditation, yoga, or even listening to calming music can provide a sense of calmness and help you regain control over your emotions.

4. Communicate assertively: Instead of exploding in rage, practice expressing your feelings and needs assertively. Use "I" statements to effectively communicate how certain situations make you feel without blaming others. Learning effective communication skills will not only help you express yourself better but also improve your relationships.

5. Seek support: Consider reaching out to supportive friends or family members who can listen to you non-judgmentally. Talking about your frustrations with someone you trust can provide a fresh perspective and emotional support during difficult times.

6. Engage in healthy outlets: Find healthy ways to channel and release your anger. Physical activity such as jogging, dancing, or engaging in sports can help dissipate the pent-up energy associated with anger. You could also consider creative outlets like painting, writing, or playing an instrument to express and manage your emotions constructively.

7. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of your overall well-being is crucial. Make sure you are getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and engaging in activities that bring you joy and fulfillment. When we neglect our basic needs, it can contribute to heightened feelings of irritability and anger.

Remember, managing anger takes time, patience, and self-reflection. If you feel overwhelmed or find it difficult to make progress on your own, consider seeking guidance from a mental health professional who can provide tailored strategies and support throughout your journey.

What is the difference between mean, mode, and median?

Mean, mode, and median are different types of averages. The mode is the most commonly occuring element in a sample. The median is the element occuring at the 50th percentile, or halfway through an ordered sample, and is therefore resistant to outliers. Mean is found by summing all of the values in a sample and dividing that total by the count of the items in the sample. Mean is perhaps the most common colloquial meaning of the word "average", but is less resistant to outliers than both mode and median.

What advice might you offer?

With any type of criticism, it is usually best to introduce the topic at a neutral time, ie: when both of you are relaxed, with no current stressors involved, having fun, etc.  Begin with a non-judgmental reflective comment about a recent bothersome event, as if it were just then crossing your mind (therefore not something you've been consumed with ruminating over - eases the impulse for him to dive straight into defense mode).Then share how you felt at the time of the event.  Just say when.... Certainly counselling can help. however, there is a caveat, namely, you will need the right counsellor with the right approach. This leads to two questions: 1) What are the identifiers for the right counsellor, and 2) What is the right approach?1) What are the identifiers for the right counsellor? The right counsellor will almost certainly have a lot of experience. He or she will have done a lot personal work and have an ongoing practice of inner work both on their own and with the support of an experienced therapist. This person will be viewing you as a human being with challenges, not as a diagnostic category. He or she will be willing to work with you over an extended period of time and have experience doing such work. Further they will be well versed in approaches that are responsive to you in the moment and overall. The in-depth work will be collaborativel designed in an ongoing way that is responsive to you, the moment, your overall life experience, and their in-the-moment experience. It goes without saying that you will subjectively evaluate the felt sense of connection with this person and the feeling that they are invested in their work with you, value you as a human being, and value the connection. As well, it is crucial that you feel this connection and that your therapist 'gets you.' 2) What is the right approach?  As Carl Jung stated, "When the doctor sits down with the patient he (or
she) must drop all theories and learn the theory of this person." The approach must include a bond between you and your therapist that is in a continuous process of development, attention to pre-verbal imprinting, development of awareness ability, ongoing development of the ability to attend to and stay with inner experience, development of a process orientation, attention to egoic structures that were seeded from the earliest days in the service of perceptions of threats to needs being met, identification of current egoic states and work with these inner selves and their relationship with each other to facilitate movement from developmental points of arrest, increased ability to access and contain non-ordinary states of consciousness, attending to what is, and working with this in the service of moving towards optimal human development.depression is generally experienced as the system shutting down. anxiety is a signal that something is wrong. anxiety is not the problem. it is a sign that there is a problem. the core of these issues is a lack of inner security that is the outcome of insufficient bonding. the work of psychotherapy is to establish an environment and relationship that will facilitate work with the bonding ruptures and re-initiation of the developmental process that stopped at an early stage.

Managing stress can be challenging, especially when it feels like a constant presence in your life. It's positive that you're seeking assistance and looking for effective techniques to manage your stress. Here are some guidance and suggestions that might help:

1. Begin by identifying your stress triggers: Take some time to reflect on the situations, people, or thoughts that tend to trigger stress for you. Is it work-related tasks, deadlines, conflicts at home, or something else entirely? Understanding what specifically causes your stress can empower you to address it effectively.

2. Prioritize self-care: It's important to make self-care a priority in your daily routine. Consciously allocate time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation such as exercise, reading, spending time with loved ones, or engaging in hobbies. Taking care of yourself physically and emotionally can significantly reduce stress levels.

3. Practice mindfulness or meditation: Mindfulness is about staying present in the moment and being aware of your thoughts and feelings without judgment. Consider incorporating mindfulness exercises into your daily routine, whether through meditation, deep breathing exercises, or simply taking moments throughout the day to observe your surroundings and focus on your senses.

4. Establish healthy boundaries: Setting boundaries is crucial for managing stress. Evaluate if you have clear limits in place both at work and at home. Communicate your needs to others and learn to say no when necessary. Remember, you don't have to take on more responsibilities than you can handle.

One major source of stress for me is my strained relationship with my family. Their constant criticism and lack of support take a toll on my mental health. Today, I'd like to delve into my family dynamics and explore how they contribute to my stress levels.

Navigating strained relationships with family members can indeed be challenging and impact our mental well-being. It's great that you're taking the initiative to delve into your family dynamics and understand how they contribute to your stress levels. Here are some suggestions and guidance to help you navigate this situation:

1. Reflect on your emotions: Take some time to reflect on how your family's criticism and lack of support make you feel. Identifying and acknowledging these emotions can provide valuable insights into the specific areas that need attention.

2. Set boundaries: Establishing clear boundaries is crucial when dealing with strained family relationships. Consider what behaviors or comments are unacceptable to you, and communicate those boundaries assertively but respectfully. This can help create a healthier dynamic and protect your mental well-being.

3. Practice self-care: Engaging in activities that promote self-care is essential for managing stress. Find healthy coping mechanisms that work for you, such as exercise, meditation, journaling, or spending time with supportive friends. Prioritizing self-care will help you build resilience and better handle the challenges within your family dynamics.

4. Seek support outside the family: Sometimes, finding support from individuals outside the family circle can be beneficial. This could include close friends, mentors, or even joining support groups where you can connect with others who have experienced similar situations. Sharing your feelings and experiences with trusted individuals can provide validation and alternative perspectives.

5. Improve communication skills: Enhancing your communication skills can positively influence your interactions with family members. Focus on active listening, expressing yourself clearly and calmly, and practicing empathy. Effective communication can foster understanding and potentially lead to more constructive conversations within your family.

6. Consider professional guidance: If you find it difficult to manage the strain on your own, seeking professional guidance from a therapist or counselor might be helpful. They can provide you with additional tools and strategies tailored to your specific situation, helping you navigate your family dynamics more effectively.

Remember, every family dynamic is unique, and finding the right approach may take time. Be patient with yourself and celebrate small victories along the way. You have the strength to navigate these challenges and prioritize your mental well-being.

Basically, your response is the fight, flight or freeze reaction
which is hard wired into the human nervous system, specifically, the autonomic nervous system (called the autonomic response).  This system
is responsible for regulating the heart, digestion, respiratory rate
as well as other aspects which match the symptoms you describe.  It is largely an unconscious function, but
with training it can be managed such as a public speaking course in which you
prepare and even have some exposure to smaller experiences to help you prepare
and cope for larger presentations.  One of the greatest applications of
addressing this response is the NASA program which exposes the astronauts to situations
they will encounter while in space which will trigger the response so that when
it does happen (not if but when) that they are able to move through the
challenge with success.  You can learn
more about his by going to TED Talks “What I learned about going blind in space” It is
a truly inspiring look at what you are experiencing as well as how to deal with
it.

Lately, the constant demands and responsibilities have been causing intense stress in my life. I feel overwhelmed and it's impacting my ability to relax and enjoy moments with loved ones. Through counseling, I hope to develop healthy coping mechanisms to reduce stress and find a sense of calm amidst chaos.

Finding healthy coping mechanisms to reduce stress and find a sense of calm amidst chaos is definitely something worth pursuing. It's great that you recognize the impact of constant demands and responsibilities on your well-being, as it's important to prioritize self-care in order to maintain a balanced life. Here are some suggestions that may help you develop those coping mechanisms:

1. Identify triggers: Start by pinpointing specific situations or circumstances that tend to cause the most stress for you. By recognizing these triggers, you can better prepare yourself mentally and emotionally for their occurrence.

2. Break tasks into smaller steps: When faced with overwhelming responsibilities, try breaking them down into more manageable tasks. This can make them feel less intimidating and allow you to tackle each step one at a time, rather than feeling overwhelmed by the whole picture.

3. Practice time management: Developing effective time management skills can greatly reduce stress levels. Consider creating daily or weekly schedules to allot specific time slots for work, relaxation, and quality time with loved ones. Prioritizing and organizing your tasks can create a sense of control over your schedule and decrease feelings of being overwhelmed.

4. Incorporate relaxation techniques: Engage in activities that promote relaxation and mindfulness. These could include deep breathing exercises, meditation, yoga, listening to calming music, going for walks in nature, or engaging in hobbies that bring you joy and peace.

5. Reach out for support: Don't hesitate to lean on your loved ones for support during stressful times. Talking to someone you trust about your feelings and concerns can be cathartic and help alleviate stress. Additionally, consider joining support groups or seeking online communities where you can connect with others who may be facing similar challenges.

6. Take care of your physical health: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle can significantly impact your ability to cope with stress. Ensure you're getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and incorporating regular exercise into your routine. Physical wellness goes hand in hand with emotional well-being.

7. Set boundaries: It's crucial to establish boundaries in order to protect your mental and emotional health. Learn to say "no" when you feel overwhelmed or stretched too thin. Remember that it's okay to prioritize your own well-being, even if it means disappointing others occasionally.

Remember, finding healthy coping mechanisms takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself as you explore different strategies and techniques that work best for you. And most importantly, be gentle and kind to yourself throughout this process. You deserve happiness and peace amidst life's demands.

"I'm having difficulties maintaining healthy relationships and it's causing me distress. I often feel misunderstood by my friends and family, and communication breakdowns frequently occur. This leads to arguments and frustrations that strain the connections I have with loved ones. I want to explore why I struggle with trust and open up better lines of communication."

Building and maintaining healthy relationships can be challenging, but it's great that you are actively seeking to improve this aspect of your life. Here are some suggestions to help address the difficulties you mentioned:

1. Self-reflection: Take some time to reflect on your own thoughts, feelings, and behaviors in different relationship scenarios. Consider any patterns or triggers that may contribute to the communication breakdowns. This self-awareness can provide valuable insights into why you struggle with trust and may help you identify areas for personal growth.

2. Communication skills: Improving communication is key to fostering healthier relationships. Practice active listening by giving your full attention to others when they speak, rather than thinking about how to respond. Validate their feelings and perspectives, even if you don't agree. Express yourself clearly and assertively, using "I" statements to communicate your needs and concerns without blaming others.

3. Building trust: Trust takes time to develop, and past experiences can impact our ability to trust others. Start by setting realistic expectations for yourself and others. Be consistent in your words and actions, as consistency builds trust over time. Avoid making assumptions or jumping to conclusions about others' intentions, as these can affect your trust level.

4. Boundaries: Establishing clear boundaries is crucial for healthy relationships. Understand and communicate your own boundaries while also respecting those of others. It is okay to say no or express what makes you uncomfortable. Boundaries can foster open and honest communication while also promoting respect and understanding within relationships.

5. Seek support: Consider reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or mentor who can offer guidance and support during this process. Sometimes an external perspective can help shed light on blind spots or offer new strategies for building healthier relationships. Just remember to choose someone who will be supportive and non-judgmental.

Remember, building healthier relationships takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself and others along the way. Celebrate the progress you make, no matter how small, and be open to learning from both successes and challenges.

Every winter I find myself getting sad because of the weather. How can I fight this?

The winter blues can be really tough to deal with, and are quit common. Because the winter blues can be caused by a variety of things, if you have not been evaluated by your healthcare provider I highly recommend you do so.  Here are some key tips I use to help individuals cope with the winter blues:1) The winter blues can be caused by the seasonal invariable fluctuations in daylight.  Using light box therapy is one way to help.  Light box therapy mimics outdoor light. Researchers believe this type of light causes changes in the brain that lifts your mood and eases other symptoms of the winter blues.  All light boxes are designed to do the same thing, but one may work better for you than another. For some, the use of light box therapy may be more effective when combined with other treatments for the winter blues such as counseling and/or medications for depression. it is always best to talk to your health care provider about choosing and using a light box so the treatment and dosage is right for you.2) Keep a consistent routine that does not vary with seasons, vacation, feeling well or feeling bad. Consistency is key to keep a stable mood.  Keep consistent with sleep and wake times, the times of day you eat, exercise, and socializing with others.  The more consistent you can be the better. Your brain knows what to expect from you and when.3) Exercise!  Exercise is not only great to help you sleep better and shed pounds.  Exercise is also the world's most underused anti-anxiety and ant-depression tool.  When you exercise your brain literally releases its own (endogenous) chemicals to alleviate anxiety and depression such as serotonin (a common substance in anti-depression and anti-anxiety medications).  Exercising every day is giving yourself a dose of your body's anti-anxiety and anti-depression substances, which is amazing.4) Sleep is a huge predictor of mood.  In fact, sleeping longer than 7-9 hours per day is a strong predictor of a depressive episode.  Just as insomnia and depression are intimately related.  Consistently practicing sleep hygiene is key to preventing a mood episode. The more consistent you are the more you will go to sleep and stay asleep during the times you want to.  This includes 1) going to bed at the same time every night; 2) waking up at the same time every morning (even if you slept poorly the night before); 3) avoiding naps, but if you need a nap it is best to do so every day around the same time before 2pm and to not nap for more than 30 minutes; 4) using the bed for sleep and sex only (so, no TV, no computers, no smart phones); and 5) limiting caffeine to no more that 250 mg/per day (two 8 ounce cups).  The phone app Sleepio is a tool that can help you adopt the above steps.  If you are having trouble adopting or maintaining this routine, see your health care provider or counselor for further evaluation and help you get on track.5) Limit alcohol intake and other substances of abuse. Most of which "depress" your nervous system.  When you add a depressant to an already depressed nervous system, even though you may feel temporary relief, you create a ceiling for how much your mood will improve.  For specific guidance on "safe drinking" guidelines see the CDC's Facts About Moderate Drinking at: https://www.cdc.gov/alcohol/fact-sheets/moderate-drinking.htm.6) Keep your social life.  Positive social support is the strongest and most robust tool we have to cope with stress, low moods and adversity in life.  Social support can be a friend you know will pick of the phone when you call.  It does not have to be someone that is nearby.

It's completely understandable that you have been feeling extremely anxious lately, and I can see how it is affecting your daily life. In order to manage your anxiety better, it would be helpful to explore coping mechanisms together. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) could definitely be incorporated into our sessions as it has proven to be effective in managing anxiety. CBT focuses on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns and beliefs, helping you develop healthier ways of thinking.

Outside of therapy sessions, there are several self-help resources and strategies that may benefit you. One common technique is progressive muscle relaxation, where you systematically tense and then release different muscle groups to promote physical relaxation. This can help reduce tension and relieve some of the physical symptoms of anxiety.

Another strategy you can try is journaling. Writing down your thoughts and feelings can provide an outlet for self-expression and help bring clarity to your mind. Additionally, engaging in regular exercise, such as walking or yoga, can also be beneficial for managing anxiety. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters.

When it comes to family dynamics, it seems like your upbringing might play a role in your anxiety. Remember to be patient with yourself as you work towards regaining control over your thoughts and emotions. Consider educating yourself about different aspects of sexuality and exploring resources that promote healthy, consensual relationships. Finding safe and supportive spaces to have open conversations about sexuality can also be tremendously helpful. Look for local organizations or social groups that focus on promoting acceptance and inclusivity. Additionally, consider seeking therapy from a qualified mental health professional specializing in issues related to sexuality and identity. They can offer guidance, support, and practical strategies tailored to your unique situation. Therapy provides a confidential and non-judgmental space where you can explore your feelings, address any underlying shame or guilt, and work through barriers to expressing your needs more comfortably.

Remember, this journey towards embracing your own sexuality takes time and patience. Be kind to yourself throughout the process and celebrate every small step forward. Surround yourself with positive influences, whether it's supportive friends, LGBTQ+ affirming media, or empowering literature. Good for you for recognizing that a change has to be made quickly. Regardless of whether or not your girlfriend leaves your relationship, taking control of your anger needs to happen sooner than later. If left unresolved, it will follow you into any relationship you have. Have you talked to a therapist? I would suggest you take that step first. A therapist will help you explore the source of your anger and teach you new, adaptive ways of dealing with your anger. Until you're able to get some professional help, I would advise that you start recognizing when your emotions are becoming escalated and take a time out before the anger turns into aggression. If you feel yourself becoming heated, excuse yourself from the situation, go to a quiet place or on a walk, and practice some deep breathing. Clear your mind of the problem and focus only on your breathing as you inhale slowly counting to four and exhale slowly counting to six. Don't get discouraged if it doesn't work right away. Deep breathing takes practice! Return to the situation or your girlfriend only once you have calmed down and are confident that you are not going to hurt anyone. You might also want to ask your girlfriend to remind you to take a break when she recognizes that your emotions are escalating. Know that with help and support, especially from a therapist, the issues you have can be resolved and new ways of coping can be learned. Good luck!

How do I decide if I should end my relationship with my boyfriend?

Deciding to end a relationship is a big question that deserves your full care and attention.  One of the first questions you may ask of yourself and consider for your boyfriend is whether you are both willing to work on the relationship.  A relationship, no matter how great or hard, can't work unless both people are invested in working on it.  This means that both people are willing to take responsibility and work on their on stuff when things are hard rather than blaming the other.  If one of you is not willing or able to work at this then the relationship can't really grow or get better.  Perhaps spend some time really asking yourself if you this is the person you want to work on things with.  All relationships are hard and require care and attention and also ask us to really take responsibility for what we contribute.  This should be done in a relationship where you want to do this work for yourself and the other.  Also, if you are fully in and ready to do the work but your partner isn't.  If they say things like "this is just how I am" or "we have problems because of your issues" then you also may want to really slow down and consider if this will be workable.  You and your boyfriend need to be invested and committed to the relationship even when things are hard.

That really sucks to go through.  There are tons of ways to work with anxiety, both directly and indirectly that can help with what you are dealing with.Do you think you may be experiencing a panic attack?  Sounds like you are feeling some dread about what will happen to you and physical symptoms common with attacks.  Panic attacks are the body's way of trying to alert you to danger, whether that is real or perceived.  It's not something your body does against you, but instead to keep you safe by keeping you in a state where you could react quickly (run, fight, etc.).  This can happen even if there aren't any real threats and you logically know you are safe.  Even if you aren't having panic attacks, that heightened anxiety can still feel really awful and exhausting.What have you done so far that is not working?  When the brain is in that "danger" mode, talking it down tends to be unsuccessful--this is very evident in bounds of research we have on how the brain functions.  The part of the brain that senses threats and triggers anxiety responses reacts more effectively to body signals to relax---such as controlled breathing.  Mindfulness breathing techniques have a lot of value for this reason and there are many options available (apps like Calm and Headspace, youtube guided videos, etc).  Try to keep in mind that having anxiety doesn't mean that you are actually in any danger, and mindfulness is not meant to be an escape.  It does help to regulate and make you feel more in control of your body.  Your anxiety will always come back down--you can even track it to see the real-time changes that happen.  It's normal for it to rise and fall a few times during a panic attack, so if you notice a rise, it has no meaning other than that you're body is normally going through it's anxiety response.I think seeing a doctor is a great idea to rule out any other issues happening within the body.  Some medical issues can materialize as anxiety and depression.  Depending on your symptoms, they may even suggest a medication developed for these issues.Anxiety is one of the top researched symptoms, so we do have tons of research available on what works and what's less effective.  We know that talking alone doesn't reduce the body's fear response, unless talking is the method of exposure (talking about a traumatic experience, talking within a group if you have social anxiety, etc.).  For the brain to learn you are safe, it takes experience via exposure while riding the wave of anxiety.  For example, if you fear vomiting, you would expose yourself to things that remind you of vomiting and breathe through the anxiety you feel without avoiding the triggers.  That would teach your brain that those triggers are actually benign, and would no longer  create that panicky response. To address your depression and social anxiety, there are several therapeutic approaches that may be helpful for you. One effective approach is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). By working with a therapist, you can develop healthier perspectives and coping skills to improve your overall mood and reduce the impact of social anxiety.

Another beneficial therapeutic approach is interpersonal therapy (IPT). IPT focuses on improving interpersonal relationships and resolving any difficulties related to them. In addition to therapy, it's important to consider self-care practices as part of your journey towards cultivating healthier patterns of connection. Alongside journaling, self-care activities, and gratitude exercises, you might want to try mindfulness techniques such as meditation or deep breathing exercises. These practices can help you become more present in the moment and reduce anxiety.

You could also consider joining support groups or seeking out social activities where you can meet people who share similar interests. This will provide opportunities for you to connect with others who understand what you're going through and create potential for new, fulfilling relationships to develop.

It can be helpful to set small goals for yourself, such as engaging in one social activity per week or reaching out to an old friend for a catch-up conversation. Celebrate each step forward and recognize that progress may come in waves.

I was the one who ended it, and I'm so glad I did. It was the best decision I made in my life. But how do I stop the nightmares and flashbacks? It is creating a wall in my current relationship.

Ending an abusive relationship is often very difficult, especially if you were very close initially without the presence of abuse.  If the abuse included verbal or psychological condemnation, you will often have a negative self-image that you may "know" is not true but often feels very true. This negative self-image and fear of being abused again can activate protections in you that were needed at the time you were abused but now create a "wall" in your current relationship.  The fact that you were able to end the relationship and know that you made the right decision is a great acknowledgement that you have solid internal resources to draw upon in healing from the abuse.  Good for you!Nightmares and flashbacks are a strong sign of memories, including associated beliefs, emotions, and physical sensations, that have remained unprocessed and therefore unhealed.  There are likely reminders (called triggers) of the past abuse that are being activated in your current relationship that are allowing these unhealed memories to come to the surface and affect both your sleep and your waking experiences.  This is certainly not something you are purposefully doing but is the result of what happened to you.  However, you likely feel as if you are not in control.    The goal is protect your current relationship, evaluate your self-image for flaws in beliefs and feelings, and begin working on healing your memories of abuse. In many cases, my use of EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) would be helpful in reducing the emotional strength of your abuse memories, reduce or eliminate triggers, bring healing, and allow you to enjoy being in the present with your current relationship.  I would recommend discussing with your current partner your harmful past experiences, your decision to pursue counseling, and your strong desire to be healthy for your current relationship.  With a good support network in place, healing is very possible.

To begin addressing this concern, effective time management strategies can make a significant difference. Prioritizing tasks based on urgency and importance can help create more structure in your day. Consider creating a schedule or routine that allows for dedicated quality time with your child. This could involve setting aside specific hours each day solely dedicated to activities together, such as reading, playing, or having conversations. Utilizing technology, like setting reminders or alarms, may also assist in staying organized and managing time effectively throughout the day.

While balancing work and parenting responsibilities, it's crucial not to neglect self-care practices. Taking care of yourself emotionally, physically, and mentally is essential, as it will directly impact your ability to be present and provide support for your child. Find small pockets of time throughout your day to engage in activities that bring you joy or help you relax. It could be exercising, practicing mindfulness or meditation, engaging in hobbies, connecting with supportive friends, or even just taking short breaks to recharge and refocus.

Take advantage of any available resources, such as local parenting groups, online communities, or social services, which can offer additional guidance, reassurance, and practical advice. Building relationships with other parents who are experiencing or have experienced similar challenges can provide valuable insights and a sense of solidarity.

Hello, and thank you for your question. Guilt is one of those things that nearly everyone has experienced at one time or another, and it can feel like a huge weight around your neck. Unfortunately, it is unlikely that we can give you some words of wisdom that will make it all go away. However, I will give you some ideas and hopefully this will help.One of the things that we know about guilt is that it doesn't usually do much to help us in the long-run. People may make changes for a short-term period of time because they feel guilty about something they did, but usually they will go back to their old behaviors if they don't have something else to help them change permanently, such as a new skill. So, guilt doesn't necessarily help us. In fact, as I write this someone out there is eating an entire key lime pie because they feel guilty about falling off their diet. Someone may be drinking alcohol because they feel guilty about drinking alcohol. For whatever reason, this is just a common thing that we do. Now accountability is different than guilt. Accountability can actually be constructive.  When you hold yourself accountable you can admit that you have done something wrong. That it hurt others and you deeply regret it. That you are prepared to take steps to make sure it doesn't happen again. That you have done what you can to make amends, if necessary. That you are sorry. And then you move on. Why is moving on necessary? Well, for one thing, it doesn't usually help the people who you hurt. In fact, someone's guilty behavior may serve to remind the people who were hurt, over and over again, about what happened. Guilt is usually 100% about us, and not about those we hurt. Also, guilt can lead us to behave in ways that may even hurt people more. Having said all of that, guilt is a normal human emotion. Sometimes we experience it for a while and it goes away. Sometimes we need help to work through it. There are many self-help books about forgiving yourself. You can try Amazon to find some, or consider getting help from a counselor. Be well,Robin Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

The question about identifying the right therapist is a compelling one to be sure.  The therapeutic relationship is based on trust and confidentiality is the cornerstone of the profession. Therefore, it is essential to seek a therapist who practices ethically, is empathetic, and has the capacity to be objective as well as non-judgmental. It is also important to seek a therapist who specializes in your particular issue and has clinical  experience as well as a passion in striving for toward the best outcome. You will not need to train your therapist as a competent therapist will help you explore the sources of your distress, or limitations in your belief system and so forth. A competent therapist will be able to suggest a variety of treatment approaches and together you will decide which approach is best for you. However, you also have to decide what kind of therapist you envision being comfortable with. Some clients prefer a more directive approach and others a more collaborative one.Most therapists offer a consultation which is a good opportunity to ask questions and get a sense of the therapist's treatment approaches, training, credentials,  style, ideas and so forth. I have questions regarding the therapeutic process. How long does grief usually last? Will I ever truly move on? And what techniques can you teach me to honor his memory while still finding happiness amidst the sorrow?

Grief is indeed an overwhelming experience, especially when faced with the loss of a loved one like your father. It's completely understandable that you're seeking solace and hoping to better manage your emotions through counseling.

The mix of sadness, guilt, and anger you feel is common during the grieving process. Blaming yourself for not spending enough time with your dad and feeling angry at the world are natural reactions to such a profound loss. It's important to remember that these emotions are valid and part of your healing journey.

Visiting your childhood home must have been an incredibly triggering event for you. Seeing your dad's belongings untouched can make the reality of his absence hit even harder. The flood of memories and intense crying afterwards are all normal responses to the grief you're experiencing.

Remember, grief comes in waves, sometimes unexpectedly. Those waves may be more frequent when encountering photographs or videos of your dad. This ebb and flow of emotions is a testament to the deep connection and love you shared. Allow yourself to feel those moments fully, even if they catch you off guard.

It's unfortunate to hear that your relationship with your family has become strained since your loss. Understandably, your mom may be blaming herself, adding further tension. Arguments over trivial matters can often arise as everyone in the family navigates their own grief and tries to cope. Remember to practice patience and understanding with each other during this difficult time.

Isolating oneself from friends is also common due to the fear of burdening others with personal sorrow. However, reaching out to close friends who have experienced similar losses can offer a source of support and understanding. Sharing your feelings with them can provide relief and give you a sense of community.

Journaling your emotions is an excellent coping tool, allowing you to express and process your thoughts and feelings effectively. Talking to others who share similar experiences can also create a sense of connection and validation. Engaging in self-care activities, such as exercising, provides a temporary distraction from the pain and can contribute to your overall well-being.

In terms of the therapeutic process, the duration of grief varies for each individual. There isn't a set timeline that applies to everyone. It's important to remember that healing takes time, and it's a unique journey for each person. Moving on doesn't mean forgetting or getting over the loss; rather, it involves finding ways to integrate your loved one's memory into your life while still pursuing happiness.

Therapeutic techniques will largely depend on your specific needs and preferences. Some approaches therapists often use when working with individuals who are grieving include validating your emotions, exploring coping strategies, facilitating self-compassion, providing validation, helping you navigate through guilt, anger, and sadness, and assisting you in finding ways to honor your dad's memory.

Remember, patience and self-compassion are vital during this process. Every step you take towards healing is significant. You're not alone in this journey, and by seeking support and guidance, you're already taking an active role in finding solace and managing your emotions.

I know this fear doesn't make sense. How can I overcome it?

Your fear may not seem "rational" but that doesn't mean it doesn't make sense!  There's 100% a reason for why this fear happens for you.  Most everyone has this fear because we are social animals and need to care what others think of us sometimes.  When it becomes a bigger issue is when it keeps you from enjoying your life or interferes with your functioning.Do you think it may have to do with uncertainty of what others may be thinking of you? Or that people will ultimately reject you? Sometimes when we don't know what others think, we assume they judge.  This is especially true if you've experienced direct judgment or bullying in your past, or if a significant parent or caregiver in your life made you feel shame.When I have a client that often fears others are judging them, I have them list out the evidence they see to support that.  What evidence is there to tell you that someone is judging you?  If you take something as evidence, also ask yourself if they behave the same with other people.  When we fear judgment, we often micro-analyze and misinterpret people's body language to mean something it doesn't.  It can also help to make a mental or actual list of other possibilities.  Most people are concerned about what others are thinking of them, so it's possible people you interact with are wondering what you think of them.  It's also possible they are judging you positively--what are some things in this category that people have told you about how they see you?  Sometimes taking feedback from people closest to you whom you trust can be the most accurate representation of how others may see you.  Counseling could be a great option as well because I guarantee these fears will show up in sessions and that's GOOD.  It gives you a chance to process them with someone who will help you understand these fears and may even give you genuine feedback about how they perceive you (at the right time).  It can be very healing!

I'm a teenager, and while I’ve never been to any kind of therapist, I noticed I experience several anxiety symptoms. I frequently find myself not going out and following my parent around the house. I can't go into stores (grocery stores specifically) on my own, and when I do, I have to be on the phone with my dad the whole time. I also forget things a lot.

With the way you described your anxiety, it sounds like you have different types of anxiety. I'm not sure whether you have anxiety of public places, large crowds, being alone  (sometimes called separation anxiety), or some combination thereof.One thing that would be helpful would be to track your anxiety and see how anxious you are (on a scale of 1 to 10) in different situations. Also, if you know what leads up to your anxiety, it would be good to know this as well so you can look for patterns.As for forgetting things, you could be anxious because you are forgetting things or you could be forgetting things because you are anxious. When you are having anxiety, certain parts of your brain are overactive because you are in a kind of protective mode. It's also possible that forgetting things and anxiety are not related.Something else to try would be to notice where you feel your anxiety in your body and put your hand there is a way of giving yourself comfort.Another thing about anxiety is that having anxiety can lead to more worry about having more anxiety. One thing that helps for some people is to go to the regular primary care doctor to make sure that there are no physical problems (just for the regular physical) so they know that there are no physical problems and that the anxiety will lessen in a few minutes.Also, if you are able to notice your feet on the floor or your hips in the chair, this is helping you to be mindful of your body and connecting you to your surroundings. During this in combination with naming your emotions can be soothing as well. For example, in the grocery store, if you are feeling anxious, you could say to yourself "I'm anxious right now and I'm okay" while gently shifting your weight from one foot to the other. No one around you would notice what you were doing and the motion may be soothing to you.Anxiety can have a lot of different causes and things that trigger it. If it is difficult for you to work it out on your own (which is very common), consider talking with a local therapist so you can have more specific ideas.Also consider making a list of people who you trust and what it is about them that makes you feel comfortable.

Explain me the concept of "Karma" in Buddhism.

Karma is one of the most misunderstood aspects of Buddhism. In simple terms, Karma is the law of action and reactions. Our actions, both physical and thoughts, are the acts that are put in the world. Reactions can be referred to as their manifestations in the actor's life, i.e. our own life. For example, suppose your mind is filled with greed, evil thoughts like harming another person, and jealousy. In that case, it reflects restlessness as we will never be satisfied, punishments for harming another person, and stress to become like someone else, respectively. For a positive example, a life lived with generosity, righteousness, kindness, and genuinely putting good out there will lead to respect in society and a fulfilled life. Furthermore, Buddhism believes in reincarnation. So the good acts and deeds that one puts in this life, one also reaps the benefits in the next life. Therefore, the equation of Karma is relatively straightforward. Do good and work for the betterment of society and oneself.
