Depression has left me feeling hopeless, and I want to find a way out of this darkness. Lately, I've been struggling with persistent feelings of guilt and worthlessness. It's as if a heavy cloud follows me everywhere, making it difficult to enjoy anything or see any positive aspects of my life. For example, when I achieved a long-term goal recently, instead of feeling proud, I convinced myself that it was just luck and that I didn't deserve the success.

It can be incredibly challenging when depression leaves you feeling hopeless and trapped in a dark place. The persistent feelings of guilt and worthlessness that you've been experiencing must be weighing heavily on you, making it difficult to find joy or see the positive aspects of your life. It's understandable how achieving a long-term goal recently didn't bring you the sense of pride you expected, as you convinced yourself it was merely luck and not something you deserved.

In times like these, it might be helpful to remind yourself that depression often distorts our perception of ourselves and our accomplishments. It can make us believe negative thoughts that aren't necessarily true. Recognizing this distortion is an important step towards regaining control over your emotions and finding a way out of the darkness.

One strategy you could try is challenging those negative thoughts by asking yourself for evidence that supports them. Are there any objective facts that prove you are truly worthless or undeserving of success? Often, we realize that these thoughts are based on subjective interpretations rather than concrete reality.

Additionally, it may be beneficial to practice self-compassion and kindness towards yourself. Treat yourself with the same understanding and support you would offer to a close friend going through a tough time. Remind yourself that everyone makes mistakes and experiences setbacks, but that doesn't diminish your worth as a person.

Engaging in activities that bring you even a small amount of pleasure or satisfaction can also help lift your mood gradually. Start by identifying things you used to enjoy or exploring new hobbies that pique your interest. While it may feel challenging at first, taking small steps towards engaging in these activities can contribute to a sense of accomplishment and provide moments of respite from the heaviness you're experiencing.

Remember, healing takes time, and it's essential to be patient with yourself throughout this process. If possible, consider reaching out to trusted friends or loved ones who can offer support and encouragement along the way. They may not have all the answers, but having someone to listen and validate your feelings can make a significant difference.

What are some ways to care for a new tree

There are many ways to care for a young tree to ensure its future health and success.  Some ways you may want to care for a young tree include:
 - Frequent watering.  The amount of water and frequency will vary depending on the tree and climate but frequent, deep watering is essential for early development.
 - Nutrients.  Fertilizers may aid in the early stages.  Be sure to read the manufacturers label and instructions before application.
 - Mulch.  Applying mulch to the base of the tree aids in weeds suppression and moisture retention. 
 - Remove nearby weeds/plants.  Weeds and plants can provide competition to your tree for important resources.  Remove any near the root system of your tree.

These are just some ways you can ensure a healthy start to your tree!

What is the difference in the US between a stop sign and a traffic light?

A stop sign is a red, eight-sided metal sign that requires a driver to stop and then proceed when it is safe to do so. Many intersections have either two or four stop signs. When more than one car arrives at the intersection, the car that arrived first has the right of way. If more than one car arrives at the same time, then the car to the right has the right of way. An electric traffic light typically has three different signals: red indicates drivers should stop until the light changes; a yellow light indicates that the driver should stop if it is safe to do so because the signal is changing from red to green; and a green light means that drivers may proceed through the intersection without stopping.

A failed suicide attempt is commonly thought of as a “cry for help,” however it can also be a serious attempt to find a permanent solution to depression, hopelessness or other feelings a person feels are unbearable. It’s wonderful that you want to support your husband, but If your husband is feeling depressed and hopeless, you can best help him by getting him to a mental health professional. Feelings of hopelessness and depression, and previous attempts at suicide are all risk factors for future suicide attempts. With a mental health professional, or in the emergency room of a hospital, your husband should be evaluated for suicidal thoughts, intent and plan, and if he is a danger to himself he should probably be hospitalized again until he is stable. Without knowing the particulars, your husband may suffer from Major Depressive Disorder or some other illness on the depressive spectrum. In that case medication could help him immensely, at which point you can offer your support and encouragement him to practice gentle self-care. And do not forget to practice it for yourself.  Remember: a suicide attempt not only affects the person, but it is an immense stressor for his or her loved ones as well. As they say, “put your oxygen mask on first.” Then you will be better able to provide your husband with calm and loving care and attention.Kayla Schwartz, LMSWkayla@nyccounseling.com

Hey there, therapist. My anxiety has been worsening, particularly in social situations. Last week, I attended a party where I felt a constant sense of dread and discomfort. This intense apprehension made it challenging for me to engage in conversations and prevented me from enjoying myself. I want to work on managing this social anxiety so I can feel more at ease and confident in social settings.

It may help to start by acknowledging and accepting your anxiety in social situations. Recognize that it is a common experience for many people and that you are not alone in feeling this way. Take some time to reflect on the specific triggers or thoughts that contribute to your anxiety in these situations. Are there certain situations, topics, or types of interactions that tend to make you more anxious? Identifying these triggers can help you better understand your anxiety and develop strategies to manage it.

One effective technique for managing social anxiety is gradual exposure. Start by gradually exposing yourself to social situations that make you anxious, but in a controlled and manageable way. For example, you could begin by attending small gatherings with close friends or engaging in group activities where conversation is not the main focus. As you become more comfortable, gradually increase the size of the events or try engaging in conversations with new people.

Practice deep breathing exercises or other relaxation techniques to help calm your body and mind during moments of heightened anxiety. Diaphragmatic breathing, where you breathe deeply into your belly rather than shallow chest breaths, can be particularly helpful in reducing physical symptoms of anxiety.

Challenging negative thoughts and replacing them with more realistic and positive ones can also be beneficial. Try to identify any negative thought patterns or self-doubt that often arise in social situations. Ask yourself if there is evidence to support these thoughts and consider alternative perspectives. Remind yourself of times when you have successfully navigated social situations or received positive feedback from others. This can help build confidence and alleviate feelings of dread.

Consider seeking support from trusted friends or loved ones who can provide encouragement and understanding. Sharing your experiences and fears with others can be empowering and remind you that you are not alone. Building a strong support network can also help boost your confidence in social settings.

Lastly, remember to be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. Overcoming social anxiety takes time and effort, but with consistent practice and self-compassion, you can gradually improve your comfort level in social situations.

Additionally, therapy can provide a safe space for you to process and heal from any past traumatic events you've experienced. Trauma can have a lasting effect on mental health, and addressing it in therapy can help you develop new coping skills and find greater resilience.

Whenever I have to speak up in front of others, my mind goes blank, my hands tremble, and I feel like everyone is judging me. My goal is to gain more confidence in these situations and stop the constant worrying beforehand.
I think the anxiety stems from past negative experiences where I felt embarrassed or humiliated while speaking publicly. Now, even imagining presenting in a meeting makes me extremely nervous.
For instance, in my last team meeting, I was asked to give a presentation on our latest project. As soon as I stood up, my heart raced, and my voice shook uncontrollably. I stumbled over my words and couldn't concentrate.
These symptoms have been persistent for about a year now, and they occur every time I have to speak in front of others. The intensity increases depending on the size of the audience and the importance of the event.
To cope with this anxiety, I've tried practicing my presentations repeatedly, but it only helps to a certain extent. Before big events, I sometimes take anti-anxiety medication prescribed by my doctor as a last resort.
I wanted to ask if there are any techniques or exercises that can help me overcome these symptoms, specifically in situations where I need to speak publicly. Are there any relaxation techniques I could try beforehand?

When it comes to speaking in front of others and experiencing anxiety, it's important to remember that you're not alone. Many people struggle with similar feelings, so please know that there are strategies and techniques that can help.

One technique that may be helpful for you is deep breathing exercises. Taking slow, deep breaths can have a calming effect on both your mind and body. You can try inhaling deeply through your nose, holding the breath for a few seconds, and then exhaling slowly through your mouth. Repeat this a few times before speaking publicly to help relax your nerves.

Another technique you can try is visualization. Before an event or presentation, visualize yourself delivering a successful speech or presentation. Imagine the audience being engaged and supportive, and see yourself speaking confidently and fluently. This practice can help build positive associations with public speaking and reduce anxiety.

Additionally, it may be beneficial to gradually expose yourself to speaking in front of others. Start by practicing in low-pressure situations, such as in front of friends or family members. As you become more comfortable, gradually increase the challenge level by speaking in front of small groups or joining organizations where you can practice public speaking regularly.

Preparing thoroughly for your presentations can also boost your confidence. Make sure you know your material well and practice your delivery. Rehearse out loud, imagining you're addressing an audience. By doing this, you'll become more familiar and comfortable with the content, which can help reduce anxiety.

It might also be helpful to reach out to a support system. Talking to trusted friends, family members, or even finding a mentor who has experience with public speaking can provide guidance, encouragement, and perspective.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself and acknowledge your progress along the way. While these suggestions can be helpful, if your symptoms persist or worsen, seeking professional help from a mental health expert could offer additional strategies tailored specifically to your needs.

Anxiety has made decision-making incredibly difficult for me. Even simple choices like what to eat for dinner can send me into a spiral of doubt and worry. I second-guess myself constantly and fear making the wrong choice. I would appreciate guidance on how to navigate decision-making with less anxiety.

Navigating decision-making with less anxiety can be challenging, but there are strategies that may help you feel more confident and at ease. Here are some suggestions to consider:

1. Recognize the impact of anxiety: Acknowledge that anxiety is influencing your decision-making process. By understanding this, you can start to separate your anxious thoughts from your true preferences and values.

2. Break decisions into smaller steps: Sometimes, the weight of making a big decision can feel overwhelming. Try breaking it down into smaller, manageable steps. Focus on one aspect at a time, allowing yourself to make progress without feeling overwhelmed.

3. Gather information: Decision-making becomes easier when you have all the necessary information. Take the time to research and gather relevant facts about the choices you're considering. This will provide you with a clearer picture and help alleviate uncertainty.

4. Consider pros and cons: Make a list of the potential advantages and disadvantages of each option. Evaluating the positives and negatives can bring clarity and assist in weighing the different factors involved.

5. Trust your instincts: While it's important to gather information and weigh options, don't underestimate the power of your intuition. Pay attention to your gut feelings and what resonates with you personally. Trusting yourself can help reduce anxiety around decision-making.

6. Set realistic expectations: Understand that not every decision will yield perfect outcomes. Embrace the idea that mistakes or unforeseen challenges are part of life. Instead of striving for perfection, focus on making choices that align with your values and goals.

7. Practice self-compassion: Be kind to yourself throughout the decision-making process. Remember that everyone makes imperfect choices at times, and that's okay. Treat yourself with compassion and remind yourself that you're doing the best you can.

8. Seek support if needed: If decision-making continues to cause significant distress, consider reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or mental health professional. They can provide an outside perspective and offer guidance tailored to your specific situation.

Remember, decision-making is a skill that can be developed over time. By implementing these strategies and being patient with yourself, you can gradually reduce anxiety and make choices that align with your values and well-being.

Depression has consumed me completely. Simple tasks that were once enjoyable now seem unbearable. I struggle to focus on anything for more than a few minutes without losing interest. Negative thoughts seem to control my mind, whispering that I'm not good enough, that everyone would be better off without me. Even watching my favorite TV shows or listening to music doesn't bring me pleasure anymore. To overcome this deep sadness and seek a path towards recovery is what I aim for.

It sounds like you are experiencing a deep sense of sadness and despair, which is impacting your ability to enjoy daily activities and maintain positive thoughts about yourself. It's important to remember that you are not alone in feeling this way and there is hope for recovery.

One suggestion I have is to reach out to someone you trust and let them know what you're going through. Sharing your feelings with a supportive friend or family member can provide emotional support and potentially help ease the burden that depression has placed on you. They may be able to offer encouragement, validate your emotions, and assist you in finding additional resources.

Engaging in self-care activities can also be helpful. While it may feel challenging right now, try to engage in small acts of self-care each day. This could be as simple as taking a walk outside, practicing deep breathing exercises, journaling, listening to soothing music, or engaging in hobbies or activities that bring you some joy. Taking care of your physical health by getting enough sleep, eating nourishing meals, and exercising regularly can also contribute to overall well-being.

Consider reaching out to online mental health communities or forums where individuals with similar experiences can provide support and understanding. Connecting with others who have gone through or are going through similar struggles can help combat feelings of isolation and provide valuable insights into coping strategies and techniques.

In addition, if you haven't done so already, consider consulting a healthcare professional. A doctor or therapist can assess your situation more comprehensively and discuss potential treatment options tailored to your specific needs. They may suggest therapy, medication, or a combination of both.

Remember, recovery takes time and everyone's journey is unique. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. Keep seeking support, setting small achievable goals, and celebrating even the smallest victories along the way. You deserve happiness and well-being, and with time and support, I believe you can find your path towards recovery.

Good day, counselor. Anxiety has controlled my life for far too long. It stops me from pursuing opportunities and living authentically. I want to break free from its grip and gain confidence in myself. How do we start addressing my anxiety in our sessions, and what approach will you take to help me overcome it?

In order to address your anxiety and help you overcome it, we can start by exploring the root causes of your anxiety and identifying any triggers that may be contributing to its hold on you. This process allows us to gain a deeper understanding of the factors at play in your experience.

One approach we could use is called cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). It focuses on examining the thoughts and beliefs that contribute to your anxiety, as well as the behaviors and actions influenced by those thoughts. Together, we can identify any negative or unhelpful thought patterns and work on replacing them with more positive and constructive ones. Additionally, we would also aim to gradually expose you to situations that provoke anxiety in order to help you gradually build confidence and reduce the fear associated with those situations.

Another helpful technique we can incorporate into our sessions is mindfulness. Mindfulness involves bringing your attention to the present moment without judgment. By practicing mindfulness exercises, you can learn to observe your anxious thoughts and feelings without getting caught up in them. This can provide some distance and control over your anxiety, helping to lessen its impact on your daily life.

Furthermore, it might be beneficial to explore relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided imagery. These techniques can help you calm your body and mind when anxiety arises. They can serve as valuable tools for managing anxiety both within and outside of our sessions.

As we progress in our sessions, we will work collaboratively to tailor our approach to your individual needs and goals. It's important to keep in mind that overcoming anxiety takes time and perseverance. Utilizing the strategies mentioned here consistently and actively engaging in our therapy sessions will contribute greatly to your progress.

Remember, you have the power to break free from the grip of anxiety and regain confidence in yourself. I am here to support you throughout this journey and guide you towards a more fulfilling and authentic life.

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

The right therapist can sometimes be tricky especially if this is your first experience seeking mental health services or assistance. Finding the right therapist means considering what issues you would like to address and which therapists has specialities in what you are seeking. When searching for a therapist reach out to those in your support system who have had experiences with a therapist and find out their likes and dislikes. Use some time looking via search engines for therapists in your area and allow your curiosity to lead you to therapists directories where therapists are displaying their philosophy of how they help client's heal. Consider whether gender and race/ethnicity is a preference and who you would feel the most comfortable with sharing your concerns that "gets you." Also do not hesitate to ask about free-consultation calling services that further allow you the opportunity to provide a bit of information about yourself and allows you the benefit of asking additional questions about the therapist, their services and offerings and whether you are ready for treatment or rather search for other options.In regards to "training" your therapist, remember that therapy is a collaborative approach involving both client and counselor. This will depend on your needs, goals for therapy and the overall objectives. A licensed therapist that is trained will be knowledgeable to assist you in your journey through treatment. As a trained therapist, one will assist in clarifying of your current situation(s), work out past experiences that may hinder your improvement and provide the necessary skills to assist in your progress throughout. If you believe that you are not receiving these things voice your concerns with your therapist, ask for recommendations and/or referrals for a better fit. That's perfectly okay!

One of the sometimes difficult things about being in a relationship is the fact that you can make goals for yourself, but you can't make goals for your partner. If your fiancé wants to learn to live more in the present and learn to let go of the past or move in a different direction, you can certainly assist him, but you can't independently make it happen.I wonder if both of you would be willing to have a discussion where he is able to explain to you what he is experiencing and you are able to listen for five, 10, 15 minutes in a way that is not blaming or pointing fingers or asking him to change, but just listening (kind of like an investigative reporter) so you can have more details and ask questions that you may have about what certain things mean, when it feels like to to him when this is discussed, etc. At that point, maybe he would willing to listen to your thoughts on the subject as well.Also, if he wants to make a change, it may be helpful to see a therapist who specializes in working with couples. Sometimes changes such as these require a great deal of personal awareness and there can be quite a bit of emotions attached, so it is often helpful to have someone there to assist.It may also be nice to have a discussion where you consider what makes you feel valued, appreciated, special, or loved, and also consider what makes your fiancé feel that way.

On the day of the presentation, I was so stressed that I stumbled over my words and struggled to convey my message effectively.

Symptoms of stress manifest as muscle tension, difficulty concentrating, and frequent headaches. It feels as though I am always on edge, awaiting the next challenge. These symptoms occur almost every day, sometimes lasting for hours on end.

Given recent changes in my personal life such as moving to a new city and adjusting to a different job, the added uncertainty contributes significantly to my overall stress level. Additionally, strained family relationships further compound my stress and affect my ability to cope effectively.

I am interested in understanding how therapy can assist individuals with managing chronic stress effectively. What techniques or coping mechanisms do you recommend for dealing with high levels of stress? Could counseling help me develop long-lasting strategies to find balance in my life?

Managing chronic stress is indeed a common concern that many individuals face. It's great to see that you're open to exploring therapy as a way to find healthier ways to cope with your stress levels.

To start, one technique that may be helpful is mindfulness. Mindfulness involves focusing your attention on the present moment without judgment. By practicing mindfulness regularly, you can train your mind to become more aware of patterns of negative thinking and learn to let go of thoughts that contribute to your stress. There are various mindfulness exercises such as deep breathing or body scans that you can incorporate into your daily routine for short moments of relaxation.

Another coping mechanism worth exploring is cognitive restructuring. This approach focuses on identifying and challenging unrealistic or negative thoughts that contribute to stress. By questioning these thoughts and reframing them in a more positive or realistic light, you can gradually change how you perceive stressful situations and reduce their impact on your well-being.

Additionally, it might be helpful to establish a structured routine that allows for regular self-care activities and downtime. By setting aside specific times for relaxation, exercise, hobbies, or spending time with loved ones, you create opportunities to recharge and engage in activities that bring you joy and fulfillment. Building this structure into your daily life can help provide a sense of balance and prevent overwhelming feelings from taking over.

Support networks are valuable resources in managing stress as well. Seeking out individuals who can offer understanding, encouragement, and guidance can make a significant difference in your journey toward finding balance. Consider reaching out to trusted friends, family members, or support groups to share your experiences and gain perspective from others who have faced similar challenges.

Lastly, counseling can certainly assist in developing long-lasting strategies to manage not only chronic stress but also other aspects of life that may contribute to your overall well-being. A therapist can work with you to explore your unique circumstances, identify triggers, and develop personalized coping mechanisms. They can help you navigate through the difficulties related to your recent changes in life and strained family relationships, providing guidance and support throughout the process.

Remember that managing stress is an ongoing journey, and it may take time to find what works best for you. Be patient with yourself and open to trying different techniques until you discover a combination of strategies that has a positive impact on your well-being.
How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

To be able to identify a clear ending to a counseling relationship, we must have a clear understanding of the goals and limitations of treatment.  Usually, during the initial evaluation, I identify my client’s short term and long term therapy goals.  As therapy progress, we verify goals on a monthly to a quarterly basis, depending on the frequency of the appointments.  Once the therapy goals have been met, there is a closing session, the counseling relationship is ended, and the client can stop attending sessions.  In some cases, the client can also establish new goals and determine if I am a good fit for their therapy needs or if they need a new provider, in which case I provide multiple referrals.The counseling relationship could also end due to other factors like noncompliance= when a client is not committed to the agreed treatment process, or when the client’s or a counselor violates the counseling relationship.  Either the counselor or the client is able to end counseling.  Although, as mental health providers we need to provide a reason for terminating our therapeutic relationship and referral options, as a client no explanation is needed, a closing session is highly recommended.  ¿Cómo termina la terapia?¿Cómo un consejero decide cuando terminar las sesiones de consejería o terminar de trabajar con un paciente?Para poder determinar el final de la relación del consejero, debemos comprender las metas y parámetros de la terapia.  Usualmente durante la evaluación inicial se identifican metas a corto y largo plazo con el cliente, y se discute con el cliente como esas metas serán alcanzadas.  Durante el proceso de terapia el consejero revisa las metas mensual o trimestralmente dependiendo de la frecuencia de las citas.  Ya que las metas de terapia son alcanzadas, hay una sesión de cierre y el cliente puede terminar la terapia.   En algunos casos el cliente puede identificar nuevas metas para la terapia y determinar si el mismo consejero u otro consejero le pueden asistir. 
La relación de consejería también puede terminar por no conformar o violentar los parámetros  establecidos para la terapia.   Tanto el consejero como el cliente pueden terminar la relación de terapia.  Como proveedores de salud mental los consejeros estamos obligados a proveer un razón para la conclusión del tratamiento y proveer referidos según aplique, los clientes no necesitan proveer una explicación, aunque es recomendable discutirlo en una sesión de cierre.

Lately, stress has taken hold of my life and I need guidance on how to manage it effectively. My goal today is to learn coping strategies to reduce the impact of stress on my well-being.

I constantly feel overwhelmed by the demands of work, family responsibilities, and personal expectations. There never seems to be enough time in the day to accomplish everything on my to-do list. This pressure leads to physical and emotional exhaustion, which further hinders my ability to handle stress effectively.

One specific situation that triggers immense stress for me is public speaking. Whenever I have to give a presentation or speak in front of a group, I experience intense anxiety leading up to the event. I worry about forgetting my lines or being judged by others. These anxious thoughts increase my stress levels exponentially, making it challenging for me to perform at my best.

When it comes to managing stress and reducing its impact on your well-being, developing effective coping strategies is crucial. It's understandable that feeling overwhelmed by work, family responsibilities, and personal expectations can take a toll on you. To address this, I suggest exploring some practical techniques that may help alleviate stress in your daily life.

One potential strategy could be prioritizing and organizing your tasks. By establishing clear priorities and breaking down larger tasks into smaller, more manageable steps, you might find it easier to navigate through your busy schedule. Consider creating a to-do list or using a planner to keep track of both professional and personal obligations. Additionally, allocating specific time blocks for various activities could help create structure and provide a sense of control over your day.

When it comes to the anxiety triggered by public speaking, there are several methods worth exploring. One technique you might find helpful is deep breathing exercises. Taking slow, deep breaths can activate your body's relaxation response and help reduce anxiety. Before a presentation or speaking engagement, try taking a few moments to focus on your breath. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold for a few seconds, then exhale slowly through your mouth. Repeat this a few times until you feel more centered.

Another approach to consider is visualization. Take some time beforehand to visualize yourself successfully delivering your speech or presentation. Imagine the details: the confident tone of your voice, maintaining eye contact with the audience, and receiving positive feedback afterward. This kind of mental rehearsal can help build confidence and reduce anticipatory anxiety.

If these techniques don't prove sufficient, you may want to explore seeking support from a trusted friend, partner, or mentor who can offer encouragement and reassurance. Talking about your fears and concerns with someone understanding can often alleviate some of the stress associated with public speaking.

While implementing these suggestions, it's important to remember that everyone's journey is unique, and what works for one person may not work for another. Be patient with yourself as you experiment with different strategies and find the combination that works best for you. In time, by proactively addressing stress and incorporating these coping techniques into your routine, you may experience a noticeable improvement in your overall well-being.

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

Hi there, There are a number of reasons why a therapeutic relationship might end including, but not limited to the client reaching their goals, the client reaching a place of acceptance where they wish to remain or even a breach within the relationship.  The last aspect should likely be taken to supervision in order to be fully processed.  All of these things could happen, and usually happen organically (again, except for the last example). Your question, however, was about the counselor ending treatment. This is a bit more difficult and can be very nerve-wracking.  It may be beneficial to take this with you to supervision, as well.  It's important to understand why you feel the need to end or terminate with the client, as well. Do you feel that they would be better suited for another therapist, have they achieved their goals or is it something else?In regular, open-ended sessions, I try to make a point of checking in with the clients fairly frequently. In these check-ins, I use the time to ask the client how they feel about the sessions and if there is anything they wish to focus on more astutely.  I also ask if they have any immediate goals that they would like to prioritize.  In goal-oriented sessions, I check in more frequently to ensure that both the client and I remain focused and, should they wish to shift their focus, that they recognize it is part of my responsibilities to make sure we move back to the desired goal. Often, especially in longer term therapeutic relationships, we as clinicians can see that the client has reached their goal, however they are apprehensive about ending therapy.  This is actually a great place to go with them; why would they feel unable to handle issues in their external or internal environment without you? Often, having this open discussion can increase empowerment and mastery. That said, it could also highlight other issues which the client may have been apprehensive about going into within therapy and now, as the relationship seems to be ending, feels more confident in bringing these up. In the case where the relationship is a toxic one, terminating with a client may be the best option for both of you. It's a difficult conversation, but recall that part of the role of the therapist is to model that these discomforts can be managed. I hope that this brief response can assist you going forward!

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

There are typically three reasons why therapy is terminated:1) Client has met therapy goals2) Client is not progressing 3) Therapist is not a good fit for clientIn order to properly assess whether therapy is helping and what progress is being made, the therapist needs to have ways of consistently checking in with clients sessions-by-session to determine what is helping, what isn't, and where the client is at in relation to their original therapy goals. When a client has met their goals, that is a good time to end counselling sessions unless the client has new goals or simply wants to check-in periodically to make sure that they are still on track (sometimes referred to as relapse prevention). When a client is not progressing, and feedback has been taken and attempts have been made to make the therapy more helpful for the client but to no avail, than it is considered unethical to continue to work with the client. In these circumstances, referring out to another therapist who may be a better fit is a good idea.

Hello, therapist. Anxiety has taken control of my life in unpredictable ways. I can't escape the racing heart, sweaty palms, and intrusive thoughts that flood my mind. Even seemingly harmless situations become sources of immense distress. It all started after surviving a traumatizing incident where I feared for my life. Through counseling, I hope to address the underlying trauma and gain tools to navigate my anxiety more efficiently, enabling me to live a fulfilling life once again.

It sounds like anxiety has been significantly impacting your daily life, and I understand the distress it is causing you. It's positive to hear that you're seeking counseling to address the underlying trauma and learn effective tools to manage your anxiety.

First off, it's important to recognize that healing takes time and everyone's journey is unique. Trauma can affect us in different ways, but with therapy, progress can be made. Your counselor will work with you to explore the traumatic incident and its impact on your anxiety. Together, you'll gradually uncover coping mechanisms specific to your needs.

One approach often beneficial for addressing trauma-related anxiety is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). CBT helps examine and challenge negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety symptoms. By identifying cognitive distortions and replacing them with more realistic thoughts, you can reduce the intensity of your anxious feelings.

Another helpful technique you may explore with your therapist is grounding exercises. These exercises involve focusing on your senses or engaging in calming activities to bring your attention back to the present moment. Examples include deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or using sensory objects such as a stress ball.

In addition to therapy, self-care practices can enhance your overall well-being and support anxiety management. Engaging in regular physical exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, getting adequate sleep, and setting aside time for activities you enjoy can positively impact your mental health.

Connecting with a support system can also be beneficial. Sharing your experiences and concerns with trusted loved ones allows them to provide emotional support and understanding. Isolation can intensify anxiety, so opening up to someone you trust might help alleviate some of the distress.

Lastly, consider exploring mindfulness and meditation techniques. Practicing mindfulness involves being fully present in the current moment without judgment. Engaging in regular meditation sessions can help you develop an increased awareness of your emotions and cultivate a sense of calmness.

Remember, this journey will have ups and downs, but with proper guidance and support, you will gradually regain control over your anxiety. Keep communicating openly with your counselor about your progress and any challenges you may face along the way.

Does counseling really do anything that can help people?

I love this question! Some people shy away from counseling because they think since they already talk about how they feel to their relatives or friends they shouldn't need a counselor. However, if you are having a difficult time, counseling can be beneficial in helping you move forward and get your life back on track. Counseling is not like the kind of talking we do to people we know. For one, your counselor does not have a history with you and has no expectations of how you will act and what you will do. In that way, counselors come to a session without judgement and expectation. This gives you the platform to truly explore your thoughts and feelings. A counselor can also help you understand your motivation and help you integrate your past experiences and recommend coping skills that can help you if you are feeling overwhelmed by your emotions. Over time, as you work with a counselor you will get feedback and also be able to share new insights. The work you do is based on you and where you are at. Oftentimes, when we talk to friends they bring their own agenda to a conversation, and while they mean well they may offer solutions that work for them and not you. A counselor will help you uncover the solutions that work best for you and help you find the motivation to follow through with your plan.Best of luck to you!

I've noticed a pattern where I experience deep sadness, lack of motivation, and a general feeling of emptiness for prolonged periods. It significantly affects my ability to function on a day-to-day basis. My objective is to get to the root cause of these depressive episodes and develop tools to better cope with them.

It's difficult to experience deep sadness, lack of motivation, and a general feeling of emptiness for prolonged periods. I can hear that it significantly affects your ability to function on a day-to-day basis. Your objective of getting to the root cause of these depressive episodes and developing tools to better cope with them is a great step towards improving your well-being. Here are some suggestions and guidance:

1. Self-reflection: Take some time to reflect on any possible triggers or patterns that may be contributing to your depressive episodes. Are there certain situations, events, or thoughts that seem to precede these episodes? Journaling your feelings and experiences can help you gain insights.

2. Support system: Reach out to trusted friends or family members who can provide emotional support during challenging times. Remember, you don't have to go through this alone. Sometimes, talking about your feelings with someone who cares and understands can make a significant difference.

3. Healthy lifestyle: Engage in activities that promote physical and mental well-being. Regular exercise, proper nutrition, and sufficient sleep can positively impact your overall mood. Additionally, consider incorporating relaxation techniques such as mindfulness or meditation into your routine.

4. Cognitive reframing: Notice any negative thought patterns or self-talk that might be perpetuating your depressive episodes. Practice challenging those thoughts and replacing them with more realistic and positive ones. It takes time and effort, but this shift in mindset can lead to improved coping mechanisms.

5. Professional help: If your symptoms persist or worsen despite your efforts, seeking professional help from a mental health expert could be beneficial. They can provide you with personalized guidance, therapy options like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), or even medication if necessary. However, remember that taking this step is ultimately up to you and should be done at your own pace.

6. Hobbies and interests: Engage in activities that bring you joy and fulfillment. Pursue hobbies or interests that you enjoy, as these can provide a sense of purpose and distraction from negative thoughts.

7. Gratitude practice: Cultivate gratitude by focusing on the positive aspects of your life. Take some time each day to reflect on things you are thankful for, no matter how small. This practice can help shift your focus towards optimism and improve your overall mood.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, so find what works best for you. It may take some trial and error to discover which coping strategies and support systems resonate most with you. Be patient with yourself and know that progress takes time.

I've been caring for my father at home for years, but he's becoming weaker, and I'm worried I won't be able to take care of him much longer. He refuses to go to a nursing home or adult care facility, insisting he'd rather stay at home.

Your concern is a common one faced by many family caregivers. It's natural to feel overwhelmed and uncertain about the future, especially when it comes to the well-being of a loved one. I can see how much you care for your father and how deeply you want to ensure his comfort and safety. However, it's essential to consider the long-term implications of continuing to provide care at home.

Your father's insistence on staying at home is understandable, but it's crucial to weigh the potential risks and challenges that come with this decision. Caregiving can be physically and emotionally demanding, and the financial burden can be significant. It's essential to explore alternative care options that can help alleviate some of the pressures you're facing.

One potential solution is adult day care programs, which can provide your father with socialization, medical care, and therapeutic activities while giving you a much-needed break. Home health services can also be an option, allowing professional caregivers to assist with daily tasks and provide medical care as needed. Respite care is another valuable resource, offering temporary relief for caregivers through short-term stays at care facilities or the hiring of temporary caregivers.

Involving other family members or friends in the caregiving process can also be helpful, as can seeking support from community resources and professional organizations. Remember, making the decision to seek outside help doesn't mean you're failing as a caregiver; it's an act of self-care and a way to ensure that your father receives the best possible care.

It's important to approach this decision-making process with a clear understanding of your father's needs, your own limitations, and the available resources. I encourage you to take the time to research these options, discuss them with your family, and consult with healthcare professionals to determine the best course of action for your situation. Remember, your well-being is just as important as your father's, and taking care of yourself will ultimately enable you to provide the best care possible for him.

I've been bullied for years and the teachers have done nothing about it. I haven't been diagnosed with depression, but i have been extremely sad for years.
   How can I deal with being bullied at school when the teachers won't help?

I used to do sessions in the middle school where I live and it's an epidemic.  Many schools struggle to address these problems and leave people like you feeling alone and lost.  I'm so sorry you have to go through that.Do they physically hurt you?  Not that emotional pain isn't just as worse, but sometimes adults act quicker when someone is assaulting you.  You can also report them if you feel comfortable (enough) to.  Police involvement may be suitable if you fear for your physical safety.No matter what you choose, there are some things you can do.  One is very hard but also really effective long-term---don't react to them at all.  I don't know if this is one person or a number of people, but they are getting a reward every time they bully you--your reaction.  That does not mean their actions are your fault or that you share any of the responsibility for how they treat you.  Their actions are their poor choice, never yours...that's why you are reaching out for help!  When you stop giving them a reaction, "comeback", etc., they may try to step it up in order to get a response from you.  If you continue to ignore them, after a time bullies tend to stop the behavior because they are no longer being rewarded for being mean.  If they start physically hurting you or hurt you worse than before, I would really challenge you to talk to someone so you are at least safe.If you don't feel like that's possible or it turns out to be unhelpful, reaching out to people you trust or asking your parents for help with finding a counselor could be beneficial for you.  Being bullied can make you feel really alone, so it's very important to have someone to talk to that you trust.  Sounds like you have been needing this for a long time.I'm not sure if you are in middle school or high school, but some schools offer activities or clubs that focus on building certain skills or interests.  Sometimes this can help you find your people when you feel like you don't belong anywhere.  It can also help to make you more confident in something you do, which can reflect as confidence to others.It's also important to ask yourself when you have felt strong in the past or recently.  What gives you strength?  Is it a hobby, a friend, a pet?  Or is it what you know about yourself, like a value you have or your morals?  Even turning your awful experiences into something meaningful (e.g., creating an anti-bullying group, standing up for others, etc.) can contribute to the feeling of strength or resilience.  You are already seeking help at a young age, which is amazing and also hard.  There's some part of you that is fighting for yourself, so whatever you do next know that that exists in you!

I'm in my late teens and live with my dad. The only time I go out is for my college classes. Sometimes when I see my friends I want to talk with them, but sometimes I won't want to talk to them for days or even weeks.    Sometimes I feel i'm not worth knowing or i'm never going to do anything right.
   Are they right, am I depressed?

Hello. Being a teenager in our society today can cause depression quite easily. We look at the world in which we live, and the doubts we have about being able to make a contribution, or to have value and worth with the people around us, and we begin to internalize those messages of self-worth. If that alone were not enough, you are trying to figure out where you want to go in life, and who you are supposed to be in the world. Teens are faced with pressures of being judged by your peers for how you present yourself; following current fashions; possessing the trendy things; and hanging out with the "in crowd." Here's a "secret" that might help with most of those issues: Not much of those problems I've just described will really matter as they might seem to right now, in the real world. If you are feeling depression because you feel you lack some of those things that are seen as important by others (like your peers), I can assure you that being someone who is kind; compassionate; understanding of another person's suffering; and the effort you make to be the best person you can become in the world, will far outweigh anything you experienced in your teen years.When we are young, we judge everything based on what our peers have, what they say, the way they dress, who's popular, who's not popular, and for the most of it, all of that is external. So the question becomes, are you trying to fix the feelings on the inside (the internal stuff), with the trappings of all the stuff on the outside (the internal)? That is to say, do you feel that if you had what your friends have, you would be happy and less depressed? Depression is usually a symptom of something much bigger, it is not typically a problem by itself (just as a person who experiences a high temperature may likely have a cold). So fixing the symptom requires looking at the possible causes. In your post, you mentioned that you live with your dad. Are your parents divorced or separated, or has your mom passed away? Either of these circumstances could certainly cause depression. Finding out when you started feeling depressed, might be able to pinpoint the trigger that caused it, which requires looking at when you last felt really happy. It is also important to keep in mind, that as a teenager, your emotions are often being experienced very randomly, and sometimes without cause. It is part of your emotional development, but as you grow older can learn how to manage those emotions better and practice doing things that help you feel better (without causing harm to yourself).Have you tried talking to your dad about your feelings, or maybe another relative if you feel safer doing so? Do you have a friend who is your best friend...someone who is there for you no matter what? If not, there is a service you can use that is a national number for teens to talk with teen peer counselors. They are teens like yourself, but they have some insights that might be helpful. Its called Teen Line (https://teenlineonline.org/). It helped me when I was in my teens, and has helped lots of other teens as well. You might find a place to get some referrals to other local services in your area. If you want are in Washington state and would like to connect with me directly, you call link to me via my profile page. Or perhaps finding a counselor in your local area might be useful. Most towns and cities have some form of low cost counseling. You might also check with your school for assistance.Don't be afraid of not always knowing how you are supposed to feel. Adults don't always have a handle on it either. Being a teenager carries a lot stress, fear, and uncertainty. But you are not alone, and there is help if you reach out for it. I wish for you the very best, and bright future.

It's important to remember that caregiving is a complex and multifaceted role, and it's natural to feel a range of emotions as the needs of your loved one change. You've been an essential partner in your husband's care for a long time, and it's only natural that you're feeling a sense of loss as you relinquish some control.

I encourage you to continue reaching out to your nurse and hospice team for support. They are there to help you navigate this new phase and ensure that you have the resources and knowledge you need to continue caring for your husband effectively. It's also essential to prioritize your own self-care and well-being during this time. Caregiving can be emotionally and physically taxing, and it's crucial that you have the support and resources you need to maintain your own health and well-being.

By focusing on the role that each team member plays, you may find that you feel more connected and supported during this time.

Additionally, it may be helpful to explore the concept of self-compassion. Caregiving can be a demanding and emotionally taxing role, and it's essential to be kind to yourself during this time. Allow yourself to feel your emotions, and remember that it's okay to ask for help and delegate tasks when needed. You're doing the best you can with the resources you have, and that's enough.

Have you asked your daughter why she's doing the behaviors you describe?Often the best way to find out why someone does something is to simply ask them their reason.Her answer will give you some guidance as to next possible steps.If she's pretending to be a fantasy figure or trying to find out how being taller feels, or walking on high heels or some other image then knowing this rules out that she has some unbearable pain in her arch which may require more practical answers such as new shoes or even indicate a medical problem.Ask if she's noticed any change in the way she walks.   Maybe she doesn't know she's doing this and maybe she feels embarrassed to tell you she's doing something a bit odd.Since usually 12 year olds don't color, is it new that she started coloring?Maybe given the fact of messy handwriting, she's in a phase of pretending or reflecting on good times as a young child.Then this becomes the topic of examination.Does she feel insecure about being on the cusp of adolescence?Some of these questions can be asked directly and some are for you to first decide based on what you know of your daughter, which questions and what direction to take in understanding your daughter's motivation.

Hello and thank you for your question. I worked for a number of years with people who have been both abused in their relationships and those who have been abusive. Being involved in a relationship with a partner who does the behaviors you describe can be incredibly difficult, and many would argue is even harder than overcoming actual physical violence. I was a little confused about whether you're are still broken up with this person or if you are still thinking about it. I am going to assume you are still undecided. Some of the things you are describing sound like emotional abuse. Even without physical abuse, being emotionally abused can still be traumatizing. When partners question and accuse, they are often trying to exercise power and control over their partners by hurting them with unfounded accusations.  The accusations serve to make someone feel guilty and to manipulate them. For example, if your partner accuses you of cheating when you go out bowling with friends, you may elect not to go bowling just to satisfy your partner and prevent a fight from occurring. The person being accused or questioned often tries to prove over and over again that they have done nothing wrong, but it doesn't matter. And that brings me to the point of what some people who experience these behaviors do in order to start feeling like they have some power again. Here are just a few things:1. They realize there is no right answer. Trying to be logical with someone who doesn't want to be logical doesn't work. Many people simply stop trying to defend themselves against false accusations because there was no answer that would satisfy their partner anyway. In addition, the rules of the relationship seem to change on a daily basis, and what may be okay with your partner one day may make them angry the next. And this can leave people constantly feeling like they are on eggshells.  2. The find support. Finding a support group or a group of people who remind you on a daily basis that you are a decent person is always a good idea. One of the things that can happen when we are with someone who does emotionally abusive things is begin to have a negative concept of ourselves. Surrounding yourself with people who remind you that you are a good person is a great idea. 3. They reinvest in themselves. Try to find some time for yourself. This couldn't possibly sound more cliché, but it is actually true. Whether that is taking up a new hobby or doing an old one. One thing that can happen when emotional abuse takes place in a relationship is the person being abused can begin to isolate and not do the things that make them enjoy life. Taking some time for the self can sometimes bring things into perspective.I don't know if you are still in counseling, but if you are and you are getting what you need then that is great. If not, there are others you can try. It's important to find the right fit. As for the question of whether or not you should leave your partner, that is a question that can only be answered by you. But you could ask yourself some questions  like these to help you decide:1. What are some of my values about relationships? Do I want Trust? Honesty? Ask yourself if you have these things in your relationship.2. Do I feel like this relationship brings out the best in me, or does it seem to bring me down?3. If I want to stay in this relationship, what are some specific things that need to change? Hope some of these suggestions help. Good luck to you. Be well.Robin Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

I feel as though I'm suffering severe abandonment issues stemming from childhood. I convince myself I'm not worthy of happiness, and I’m always afraid I'm doing something wrong. It's as if I create little scenarios in my mind, and I start to believe them.

This is an understandable response to early childhood trauma and loss.  Oftentimes when we have overwhelming or difficult experiences as a child including poor caregiving, the ways we managed and the feelings we had then show up in our lives as adults.  Especially when we get close to someone, it mirrors our early experiences with caregivers in early life.  So....our body, nervous system, and emotions respond in the same way.  They feel as if what we experienced when we were little is happening now and they go into full force to manage and protect us.  Sometimes the ways that happens can feel pretty bad and we can stuck in these loops of old beliefs about ourselves.  Therapy is a great way to interrupt these patterns, process the early experiences, and be able to be in the present with your current relationships.  It is very possible to shift this cycle and also have meaningful healing from the experiences that caused so much hurt and distress from childhood.

Hi Pocahontas, This is a painful situation. When you're in a relationship, you assume that you will continue to receive warmth and affection. When it dries up, it's a very lonely place. It's possible that there is an unaddressed issue in the relationship. It's also possible that your partner has hormonal issues, pain issues,  sexual dysfunction or is asexual. There is no one answer here. Only you can decide what is right for you. But let me ask some questions to help you explore next steps:Aside from the sex, is your wife loving and supportive? What are the other ways in which you feel loved? Does your wife talk to you? Does she communicate her needs and desires? Does she articulate what gets in the way of having sex? If your wife is generally a loving, open partner, you use this to see that her behaviours aren't personal. Whether she resolves this or not, it can help you to cope with the rejection. This is your wife's issue, and the "ball" is in her court.In my opinion, if couple's therapy hasn't helped, it's time for your wife to own whatever is blocking her and address it with her physician and therapist. Let her be in charge of the sex for a while, to take the pressure off, and she can have the time to figure out what gets in the way of having regular sexual intimacy in your relationship. If you think of this as "my wife is in crisis and needs support in figuring this out", it can help you manage your own emotions. Pressure to have sex might push her further away. Did the couple therapist help you to see the dynamic in your relationship? Has your partner identified something she feels she is lacking in the relationship? One good way to make sure you "get" is to "give" (and I mean give what she wants, not sex). It's appropriate to say to her now "I cannot live in a relationship with so little intimacy. I need for you to be honest with me about what you want for us sexually. If this is all you want, I'm not sure I can do it. If you want us to be more sexual, I need you to address what gets in the way for you."  Give her some time, help her in any way you can, and then see where you are. See if she does seek help to address an issue that is hers. Then...you have a decision to make. I encourage you to make it looking at the big picture, not just the sex.

Feelings of anxiety can be scary and sometimes we're not aware of the triggers that lead up to moments of anxiety, i. e., heart racing, sweaty palms, sweating, shortness of breath. It's important to realize that in moments of anxiety our body & mind are experiencing a reaction from our primal or reptilian brain that is signaling the flight or fight response within us, which kicks the hypothalamus into action flooding our body with chemicals, like adrenaline or cortisol.  So, one way to work with anxiety is to find out what the triggers are that lead to anxiety, such as fear, stress. negative thought patterns, not enough food or sleep. Keeping a daily journal can help you track the patterns and triggers and once you identify the triggers you can ameliorate them by learning new skills & techniques and by reducing stress and getting enough sleep. One quick way to reduce anxiety is by taking deeper breathes, sometimes this is called belly breathing. When you breath in make sure your belly rises and expands and as you breath out the belly deflates. Many of us do shallow breathing up in our chest which does not allow for a full breath, and getting a full breath is so important as a tool to help relax us in times of stress & anxiety .

What is a “knock knock joke”?

It’s a joke with a specific format that requires interaction between two people. The person saying the joke begins with the phrase “knock knock” and the other person responds with “who’s there?” The person asking the joke then gives the setup, and the other person repeats back the setup verbatim and adds the word “who” at the end. The person asking the joke then delivers the punchline. An example of a knock knock joke is: 
Knock knock
Who’s there?
Orange
Orange who?

What is the Taylor rule?

The Taylor rule is a monetary policy targeting rule. The rule was proposed in 1992 by American economist John B. Taylor for central banks to use to stabilize economic activity by appropriately setting short-term interest rates. The rule considers the federal funds rate, the price level and changes in real income. The Taylor rule computes the optimal federal funds rate based on the gap between the desired (targeted) inflation rate and the actual inflation rate; and the output gap between the actual and natural output level. According to Taylor, monetary policy is stabilizing when the nominal interest rate is higher/lower than the increase/decrease in inflation. Thus the Taylor rule prescribes a relatively high interest rate when actual inflation is higher than the inflation target.

 "My siblings and I constantly clash when it comes to handling our parents' needs. We argue about the best approach, and it feels like no one is willing to compromise. The tension between us is affecting our relationships."

Navigating family conflict can be difficult, especially when it involves addressing the needs of our aging parents. It's understandable that you and your siblings may have different perspectives on how to handle things, which can lead to arguments and a lack of compromise.

Here are some suggestions that might help in resolving these conflicts:

1. Communication: Open and honest communication is key. Create a safe space where each sibling feels comfortable expressing their thoughts and concerns. Encourage active listening and try to understand each other's points of view without judgment.

2. Family Meetings: Schedule regular family meetings to discuss your parents' needs and concerns. This allows everyone to come together and share their ideas, thoughts, and concerns in a structured environment. Establishing an agenda beforehand can keep the discussion focused and productive.

3. Empathy and Understanding: Remember that each person has their own perspective based on their unique experiences. Try to put yourself in each other's shoes and empathize with their feelings and viewpoints. Showing understanding can go a long way towards finding common ground and fostering compromise.

4. Mediation: If conversations become particularly heated or unproductive, consider involving a neutral third party as a mediator. This could be a trusted friend, relative, or even a professional mediator if necessary. A mediator can provide an unbiased perspective and help guide the conversation towards resolution.

5. Seek Professional Advice: While I'm not a mental health expert, seeking guidance from professionals such as therapists or counselors who specialize in family dynamics might be beneficial. They can offer strategies and techniques to navigate these conflicts more effectively.

Remember, patience and understanding are essential when dealing with family conflict. Finding a solution may take time, but by promoting open communication, empathy, and seeking support when needed, there is hope for improving relationships within your family.

Hello, and thank you for your question. This is one of those times when you wish you could assure someone that everything will go perfectly, but unfortunately I can't do that. There is no way of knowing how parents might respond until you tell them. The truth is that people have come out to their parents in many different ways. Some have told their parents directly, some drop hints, some have had others tell their parents, etc. The only "right" way to come out is the one that you choose. The one that feels right to you. That is the best way. Some people decide not to come out, and some wait for a very long time. Both of these things are okay. Coming out is deeply personal, and there can be real consequences to someone's emotional health and safety if they tell the wrong person. That is why it should only be done when you are ready. When you feel that you have the emotional and personal support that you need to take the risk. Sometimes people can feel pressured to come out, but I encourage you to do it in your own time. The truth is, there is a spectrum of how people's parents react to this kind of news. On one end, you may have the parents who shut a person out and are abusive, and on the opposite side you may have parents that are totally okay with it and throw you a "Coming Out" party. Most parents are going to fall somewhere in the middle. It is important to remember that their feelings may change over time. Many parents struggle at first, but they love their kids and get better with it over time. If you decide to tell them, consider taking someone along to support you. Plan ahead on what you want to say. It can be an emotional time, so do what you need to do to take care of yourself. If you need to, leave. You don't have to stay anywhere where someone is being cruel to you. I wish you well, and good luck.Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Hello, stress seems to be an omnipresent force in my life lately, and it's taking a toll on both my physical and mental health. Today, I hope to learn tools to manage stress effectively and prevent it from negatively impacting my well-being. One specific situation that triggers my stress levels is when I receive unexpected workload demands at the office. Last week, my manager assigned me a high-priority project with a tight deadline, which left me feeling overwhelmed and anxious. I experience frequent headaches as well as irritability during these periods of stress. Can you help me find ways to reduce and cope with this constant pressure?

Managing stress can be challenging, but there are strategies you can use to effectively reduce and cope with the constant pressure you're experiencing. It's great that you're seeking tools to manage stress in order to prevent it from negatively impacting your well-being. Let's explore some ways to address your specific situation of receiving unexpected workload demands at the office.

1. Prioritize and Delegate: When faced with a high-priority project and tight deadline, it can feel overwhelming. Start by breaking down the tasks involved and prioritize them based on urgency and importance. If possible, delegate some tasks to colleagues or ask for support when needed. This can help lighten your workload and reduce the stress associated with managing everything alone.

2. Effective Time Management: Managing your time efficiently is key to reducing stress levels. Consider using techniques like setting clear goals, creating a schedule, and breaking larger tasks into smaller, manageable steps. By setting realistic deadlines and allocating specific time slots for each task, you can work more steadily towards completing your projects without feeling overwhelmed.

3. Communication and Boundaries: Open communication with your manager or supervisor is crucial during times of increased workload. Share your concerns about feeling overwhelmed, and together, explore potential solutions such as prioritizing tasks, adjusting timelines, or redistributing responsibilities. Clearly defining your boundaries and advocating for yourself can contribute to a healthier work environment and reduce stress levels.

4. Self-Care Practices: Taking care of your physical and mental well-being is essential to coping with stress. Engage in activities that promote relaxation, such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or mindfulness practices. Physical exercise, getting enough sleep, and maintaining a healthy diet also play an important role in managing stress by supporting your overall resilience.

5. Seek Support: Connecting with others who may be going through similar experiences can provide valuable support. Consider joining professional networking groups or seeking mentorship opportunities within your field. Additionally, confiding in trusted friends, family, or loved ones about your stress can offer an outlet for emotional support.

Remember that everyone's journey is unique, so it may take time to find the strategies that work best for you. Be patient with yourself as you explore different tools and coping mechanisms. If stress continues to significantly impact your daily life and well-being, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Are there any treatment options besides medication that could be beneficial for someone with depression? I would prefer exploring non-pharmacological approaches if possible.

There are indeed various treatment options that can be beneficial for individuals with depression, aside from medication. Exploring non-pharmacological approaches is a great idea, as it allows you to consider different avenues for managing your symptoms. Here are some suggestions:

1. Therapy: Engaging in therapy can provide significant support and guidance in managing depression. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is particularly effective in helping individuals identify negative thought patterns and develop healthier coping strategies. Other types of therapy, such as interpersonal therapy or psychodynamic therapy, may also be worth exploring.

2. Exercise: Regular physical activity has been shown to have positive effects on mental health, including reducing symptoms of depression. Consider incorporating activities you enjoy into your routine, whether it's going for walks, practicing yoga, or participating in team sports. Start small and gradually increase the intensity and duration of your workouts.

3. Mindfulness and meditation: These practices can help cultivate a sense of calm and improve overall well-being. By focusing on the present moment and observing your thoughts without judgment, you may find relief from depressive symptoms. There are numerous apps and online resources available to guide you through mindfulness exercises and meditation techniques.

4. Social support: Building and maintaining a strong support network can make a significant difference in managing depression. Reach out to trusted friends or family members who can offer understanding and encouragement. Consider joining support groups where you can connect with others who may be experiencing similar challenges.

5. Sleep hygiene: Prioritizing good sleep habits can positively impact your mood and energy levels. Establish a consistent sleep schedule, create a relaxing bedtime routine, and ensure your sleeping environment is comfortable and conducive to restful sleep. Avoiding stimulants like caffeine close to bedtime can also be helpful.

6. Nutrition: While diet alone cannot cure depression, adopting a balanced and nutritious eating plan can contribute to overall well-being. Focus on consuming whole foods, including fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains. Limiting processed foods, sugary snacks, and excessive alcohol intake can also be beneficial.

Remember, everyone's journey with depression is unique, so it may take some trial and error to find the combination of approaches that works best for you. It can be helpful to consult with a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support throughout your treatment process.

Could you tell me more about cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and if it's suitable for individuals with generalized anxiety disorder? Are there any other therapeutic approaches that may be helpful for managing anxiety?

Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is a therapeutic approach that focuses on the connection between our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. It can be very effective in treating generalized anxiety disorder.

In CBT, you'll work collaboratively with a therapist to identify and challenge negative or distorted thought patterns that contribute to your anxiety. By gaining insight into these thoughts and developing more realistic perspectives, you can begin to change your responses and reduce anxiety symptoms.

CBT often includes specific techniques and exercises to help you manage anxiety more effectively. For example, you might learn relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation to calm your physical symptoms. You may also practice exposure therapy, gradually facing and confronting the situations that trigger anxiety in order to build resilience and confidence.

While CBT is a widely-used and evidence-based therapy for anxiety disorders, there are other approaches that may also be helpful. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), for instance, focuses on accepting difficult emotions rather than trying to control them. This approach empowers individuals to align their actions with their values, even in the presence of anxiety.

Mindfulness-based therapies, such as Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), can also be beneficial. These therapies teach you to cultivate present-moment awareness and non-judgmental acceptance of your thoughts and feelings. With regular practice, mindfulness can help you develop a greater sense of control over your anxiety and reduce rumination.

It's important to remember that everyone responds differently to different therapeutic approaches, so finding the right fit may require some exploration. I encourage you to seek out a mental health professional who can assess your unique situation and provide personalized guidance. They can help determine which approach is most suitable for you based on your individual needs and preferences.

In the meantime, it's great to hear that you're already utilizing grounding techniques, exercise, and journaling to manage your anxiety. These self-care practices can be complementary to therapy and may continue to support your overall well-being. Keep exploring different strategies, try new things, and remember to be patient with yourself as you navigate this journey towards managing your anxiety more effectively.
