For the past few weeks, I have been feeling extremely down and hopeless. I struggle to find motivation to do basic tasks, even getting dressed seems like an overwhelming challenge. This depression has impacted my ability to function at work, and I've withdrawn from social activities. Understanding why I feel this way and exploring possible treatment options are important goals for me in therapy.

It sounds like you have been dealing with a lot lately, and I commend you for reaching out for help. Feeling down and hopeless can be very challenging, but remember that you are not alone in this journey. Here are some suggestions and guidance to consider:

1. Acknowledge your feelings: Start by recognizing and accepting the fact that it's okay to feel this way. Be kind to yourself and understand that experiencing depression is not a sign of weakness or failure. Give yourself permission to feel what you're feeling.

2. Seek support: Talking about your emotions can provide immense relief. Consider reaching out to friends, family members, or even online support groups where you can share your experiences and receive understanding and empathy from others who may have gone through similar situations.

3. Establish a routine: Depression often makes it difficult to find motivation. However, establishing a daily routine can create a sense of stability and structure in your life. Start small by setting achievable goals for each day, such as getting dressed, engaging in activities that bring you joy, and taking care of your basic needs.

4. Engage in self-care: Prioritize self-care activities like exercise, nutritious meals, and sufficient sleep. Engaging in activities that you enjoy and that make you feel good, such as hobbies or practicing mindfulness, can also contribute positively to your well-being.

5. Explore therapy options: As you mentioned, therapy can play a vital role in addressing your concerns. Different types of therapy, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) or psychotherapy, can help you explore the root causes of your depression and develop coping mechanisms. It would be beneficial to find a therapist who specializes in treating depression or mood disorders.

6. Challenge negative thoughts: Depression often distorts our thinking patterns, leading us to believe negative thoughts that may not be true. Practice identifying and challenging these negative thoughts by looking for evidence that supports or contradicts them. Replace unhelpful thoughts with more positive and realistic ones.

7. Stay connected: Although you mentioned withdrawing from social activities, maintaining connections with others is essential for your well-being. Reach out to supportive friends or family members, even if it feels challenging at first. Engaging in social interactions, even on a small scale, can improve your mood and provide a sense of belonging.

8. Consider lifestyle changes: Reflect on any areas of your life that may be contributing to your depression. Are there any toxic relationships, unhealthy habits, or stressful environments that could be influencing how you feel? Making gradual changes in these areas might positively impact your mental health.

Remember, everyone's journey with depression is different, so what works for one person may not work for another. It may take time, patience, and exploration to find the right tools and strategies that will support your recovery. You're taking an important step towards understanding why you feel this way and exploring treatment options by seeking therapy. Keep up the effort, and remember that healing takes time and progress often happens in small steps.

I have been living with anxiety for as long as I can remember. Even the smallest things trigger intense worry and panic within me. For example, going to crowded places or even answering phone calls makes my heart race uncontrollably. These anxious feelings are affecting my relationships and limiting the experiences I can fully enjoy. I want to break free from this cycle of fear and develop healthier coping mechanisms. How can therapy help me challenge my anxious thoughts and alleviate the physical manifestations of anxiety?

You mentioned that you have been dealing with anxiety for a long time, and it seems to be impacting various areas of your life. It's understandable that even small things can trigger intense worry and panic within you, such as going to crowded places or answering phone calls. These anxious feelings are affecting your relationships and limiting the experiences you want to fully enjoy.

Therapy can definitely be beneficial in helping you challenge your anxious thoughts and alleviate the physical manifestations of anxiety. One approach that therapists often use is Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT). In CBT, you work with a therapist to identify and challenge negative thought patterns that contribute to your anxiety. By examining these thoughts and looking for evidence to support or contradict them, you can start to develop more balanced and realistic ways of thinking.

Another aspect of therapy that can be helpful is learning and practicing relaxation techniques. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness meditation are just a few examples of techniques that can help reduce the physical symptoms of anxiety. Your therapist can guide you through these techniques and help you find ones that work best for you.

Additionally, therapy can provide a supportive space for you to explore the root causes of your anxiety. Sometimes past experiences or underlying beliefs contribute to our anxious feelings. Through therapy, you can gain insight into these factors and work towards resolving any unresolved issues or traumas that may be contributing to your anxiety.

I've noticed that I have a tendency to catastrophize situations and always expect the worst outcome. For example, if I make a mistake at work, I immediately assume I'll be fired and lose everything. This negative thinking pattern fuels my anxiety and prevents me from taking risks or trying new things. I would like to challenge these irrational thoughts and develop a more positive mindset.

It's great that you've recognized this tendency to catastrophize situations and expect the worst outcome. This negative thinking pattern can indeed fuel anxiety and hinder your ability to take risks or try new things. Challenging these irrational thoughts and developing a more positive mindset is definitely possible. Here are some suggestions and guidance for you:

1. Identify and challenge negative thoughts: Start by becoming aware of your negative thoughts when they arise. Notice the patterns and themes in your thinking. When you catch yourself catastrophizing, ask yourself if there is any evidence to support this extreme outcome. Challenge these thoughts by considering alternative, more realistic possibilities.

2. Practice reframing: Once you've identified negative thoughts, work on reframing them into more balanced and realistic perspectives. For example, instead of assuming you'll be fired and lose everything after making a mistake at work, remind yourself that everyone makes mistakes and it doesn't necessarily lead to such drastic consequences. Focus on the lessons learned and potential opportunities for growth.

3. Cultivate self-compassion: Be kind and understanding towards yourself when facing challenges or setbacks. Acknowledge that nobody is perfect and that making mistakes is a natural part of life. Treat yourself with the same compassion and understanding you would offer to a friend in a similar situation.

4. Seek evidence and gather perspective: When faced with a potentially catastrophic thought, actively seek evidence to support or refute it. Consider seeking input from trusted friends, family members, or colleagues who can provide a different perspective on the situation. Sometimes, an outside viewpoint can help us see things more realistically.

5. Practice gratitude and positivity: Incorporate gratitude exercises into your daily routine. Take a few moments each day to reflect on the things you're grateful for. This practice can help shift your focus towards the positive aspects of your life and counterbalance the tendency to always expect the worst.

6. Set realistic goals and celebrate progress: Break down larger goals into smaller, achievable steps. By setting realistic expectations for yourself and acknowledging your progress along the way, you can build confidence and reinforce a positive mindset.

7. Consider professional support: If you find it challenging to challenge these negative thoughts on your own or if they significantly impact your daily life, consider seeking support from a mental health professional. They can provide additional guidance and techniques tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, changing long-standing thinking patterns takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself as you work towards developing a more positive mindset. With consistent practice and self-reflection, you can gradually shift away from catastrophizing and embrace a more balanced perspective.

What are monsoons in India?

Monsoons in India typically refer to the rainy season, which is generally between June and September. It follows the summer season. Monsoons also refer to the seasonal weather pattern that causes rains in India due to the changing direction of winds. The hot summers cause the air over the land to heat up and rise causing low pressure, which the moisture-filled air from the ocean rushes to fill. As this air rises over the mountains, it cools and brings rain to many parts of the Indian subcontinent.

The fear of rejection holds me back from initiating conversations or making plans. Building and maintaining meaningful social relationships can indeed be challenging, but it's great that you're recognizing your desire for genuine connections and are willing to take steps towards overcoming your fears. Here are some suggestions and guidance for improving your social skills and cultivating lasting relationships:

1. Start small: Begin by joining activities or groups that align with your interests or hobbies. This will allow you to meet like-minded individuals who share common ground and make initiating conversations easier.

2. Practice active listening: Show genuine interest in others by actively listening to what they have to say. Maintaining eye contact, nodding, and asking follow-up questions can demonstrate your engagement in the conversation and help establish a deeper connection.

3. Open up gradually: It's okay to feel hesitant about opening up to people initially. Instead of divulging personal information right away, start with sharing thoughts or opinions on various topics. As trust builds over time, you can gradually reveal more about yourself.

4. Be positive and non-judgmental: Foster an environment of positivity and acceptance by refraining from judging others. Everyone has their own unique experiences and perspectives, so try to embrace diversity and learn from different viewpoints.

5. Nurture existing relationships: Remember to invest time and effort into maintaining the friendships you already have. Organize social gatherings or simply reach out to friends regularly to show them that you value their presence in your life.

6. Seek opportunities for connection: Attend local events, workshops, or volunteer activities where you can interact with new people and expand your social circle. Engaging in shared experiences can lay the foundation for stronger connections.

7. Embrace vulnerability: Overcoming the fear of rejection often involves embracing vulnerability. Understand that not every relationship will work out, but remind yourself that each interaction is an opportunity for growth and learning.

8. Set realistic expectations: Building deep connections takes time and effort. It may not happen overnight, but persevering through challenging moments will eventually lead to meaningful relationships.

9. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of your mental and emotional well-being is crucial in establishing healthy relationships. Practice self-compassion, engage in activities that bring you joy, and seek support from trusted individuals when needed.

10. Consider therapy or counseling: If your fear of rejection significantly hinders your ability to connect with others, seeking professional help from a therapist can provide additional guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, building social relationships is a skill that can improve with practice and patience. Be kind to yourself through this process and celebrate the small victories along the way.

I'm currently struggling with diagnosed depression, anxiety, and Misophonia. Also, I am 99% sure I have Borderline Personality Disorder and Avoidant Personality Disorder. I read the DSM-IV, taken college psychology, etc. I know it in my heart I have them. Is self-diagnosing okay with the right research?

Sounds like you are really concerned about the things you are feeling and the way you are interacting with others.  Self-diagnosing is not typically recommended since there could be a misinterpretation of the criteria even if you do seem to "fit the mold".  How you interpret how you feel or how you behave can be distorted, no matter who you are.  I actually did this to myself when I was in graduate school and it turned out to be wrong!With that being said, I believe people are the experts on their lives and know best what is happening for them.  What is telling you that you have these diagnoses?  What does it mean about you if you do?  I don't give a ton of weight to diagnoses in the sense of treatment because a lot of diagnoses share the same underlying themes and origins.  Both Borderline Personality Disorder and Avoidant Personality Disorder can be a result of childhood trauma, so treating one may not look that different from treating the other one---and the most important factor will always be the relationship you have with your therapist otherwise treatment won't work.I do give a lot of weight to diagnoses in terms of emotional relief.  It can be really stressful to feel like there's something "wrong" with you and not be able to give it a category.  It can reduce stigma as well to know that what's happening to you is normal for what you've been through, and that others are going through it, too.  And it definitely helps to know that there are ways to help and people that know how to help you.Either way, kudos to you for noticing something in your life that you want to change!  It seems like relationships are important to you and you maybe worry you are pushing people away that are important to you?  Even if you do have these disorders, you can totally learn how to change your life.

"Hi there, I have been struggling with low self-esteem and negative self-image lately. My goal through counseling is to develop a healthier self-perception, boost my confidence, and cultivate positive self-worth. The way I view myself affects every aspect of my life, and I want to change that."

"I've been feeling extremely unhappy, insecure, and overly self-critical. It seems like every decision I make or action I take is followed by a barrage of negative thoughts about myself. This constant inner criticism blocks me from appreciating my own achievements and strengths."

"Numerous situations have triggered these feelings, but one example that stands out is when I was overlooked for a promotion at work despite putting in the effort and skill required. Instead of focusing on the potential external factors leading to this outcome, I immediately blamed myself and questioned my capabilities."

"The symptoms I experience include persistent feelings of inadequacy, comparing myself to others constantly, avoiding new challenges due to fear of failure, and struggling to accept compliments. These symptoms persist daily and significantly impact my overall well-being."

"In terms of significant life events, I experienced bullying during high school, which left deep emotional scars and further contributed to my lack of self-esteem. This past trauma continues to influence the way I perceive myself and interact with the world around me."

"To cope with these challenges, I have tried practicing positive affirmations, surrounding myself with supportive individuals, and engaging in activities I enjoy. While they provide temporary relief, they don't address the root causes of my low self-esteem."

"I'm interested to know how counseling can help me develop a more positive self-image. Are there specific techniques or exercises you employ to target low self-esteem? Additionally, what strategies can I practice outside of sessions to strengthen my self-worth?"

Developing a healthier self-perception and boosting your confidence are indeed important goals, and it's great that you recognize the impact of your self-view on various aspects of your life. It's also fantastic that you've been taking proactive steps such as practicing positive affirmations, surrounding yourself with supportive individuals, and engaging in enjoyable activities.

To address your low self-esteem, counseling can be beneficial in many ways. One technique commonly used is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). This approach focuses on identifying and challenging negative thoughts and beliefs about yourself. By examining evidence and considering alternative perspectives, this process helps to replace negative self-talk with more balanced and realistic thinking patterns. Your counselor might provide exercises for you to practice outside of sessions, such as thought records or journaling, to further reinforce these positive changes.

Another helpful technique is called self-compassion. This involves treating oneself with kindness, understanding, and acceptance, just as you would treat a close friend. Self-compassion encourages acknowledging and embracing your imperfections while recognizing that everyone makes mistakes and experiences setbacks. Engaging in self-care activities like relaxation exercises, mindfulness meditation, or pursuing hobbies that bring you joy can also contribute to cultivating self-compassion and improving self-worth.

Building assertiveness skills may also benefit you. Learning effective communication techniques and setting healthy boundaries can help boost your self-esteem by allowing you to express your needs and opinions confidently. Assertiveness training often involves practicing specific scenarios and responses, which can empower you to advocate for yourself and feel more secure in your interactions with others.

Additionally, addressing past trauma, such as the bullying you experienced during high school, could be an essential part of your journey towards improving self-esteem. Exploring these emotional scars with a counselor can aid in reframing negative beliefs associated with those events and finding healing and closure.

Remember that progress takes time and effort, so be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. Celebrate even small victories and achievements along the way, as this can boost your self-confidence. Consistency in attending counseling sessions, actively participating in exercises provided by your counselor and integrating them into your daily routine will be key to making lasting changes.

Keep in mind that every individual's therapeutic journey is unique, so these suggestions may not cover everything you'll experience in counseling. However, your therapist will work collaboratively with you to tailor their approach to your specific needs and goals.

Overall, counseling offers a supportive space for exploring the root causes of low self-esteem and developing strategies to improve your self-worth. With dedication, patience, and an open mind, you can foster positive self-image and regain confidence in yourself.

"I'm having difficulties maintaining healthy relationships with friends and family. I often feel misunderstood and neglected. Sometimes it feels like people take advantage of me, which hurts a lot. I want to understand why this keeps happening and develop better boundaries so that I can build more fulfilling connections."

Building and maintaining healthy relationships can be challenging, but it's great that you're recognizing the difficulties you're facing and wanting to make a positive change. It's important to remember that developing better boundaries is an ongoing process, so be patient with yourself as you navigate this journey. Here are some suggestions and guidance to help you understand why this keeps happening and develop those stronger boundaries:

1. Reflect on your past experiences: Take some time to reflect on your past relationships and interactions with others. Do you notice any patterns or recurring themes? Identifying these patterns can provide valuable insights into why you may feel misunderstood or neglected.

2. Understand your own needs and values: Sometimes we unknowingly attract people who may not align with our core values or meet our emotional needs. Spend some time reflecting on what you truly value in relationships and consider whether your current connections fulfill those needs. By understanding your own needs and values, you can identify red flags and make more informed choices about who you let into your life.

3. Communicate assertively: Effective communication plays a crucial role in establishing and maintaining healthy boundaries. Practice expressing your feelings, thoughts, and expectations openly and honestly, while also actively listening to others. Be assertive in setting clear boundaries by letting others know your limits and what you're comfortable with. Having open and respectful conversations can prevent misunderstandings and help build fulfilling connections.

4. Learn to say 'no': Many times, feeling taken advantage of stems from difficulty saying 'no' when necessary. Remember that prioritizing your own well-being and setting healthy boundaries are essential for your mental health. Practice assertiveness when it comes to declining requests or situations that don't align with your values or personal boundaries.

5. Seek support if needed: If you find it hard to implement these suggestions or if you're struggling with deeper emotional issues related to your relationships, seeking support from a trusted friend, family member, or even a professional can be beneficial. Sometimes, an outside perspective can help provide guidance and support as you navigate through these challenges.

Remember, developing healthy boundaries takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself as you embark on this journey of building more fulfilling connections. Celebrate your progress along the way, and remember that it's okay to step back from toxic relationships in order to prioritize your own well-being. I have been struggling with panic attacks recently, and it's becoming increasingly distressing. The panic attacks typically start with a sudden wave of intense fear and impending doom accompanied by physical symptoms like chest pain, dizziness, and trembling. These attacks usually come out of nowhere and happen at least once a week. I want to understand how to manage these panic attacks better and prevent them from controlling my life.

Managing panic attacks can be challenging, but there are steps you can take to better cope with them and reduce their impact on your life. Here are some suggestions:

1. Take slow, deep breaths: When a panic attack starts, focus on taking slow, deep breaths. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold it for a few seconds, then exhale slowly through your mouth. This can help regulate your breathing and decrease the intensity of the physical symptoms.

2. Challenge your thoughts: Panic attacks are often triggered by negative or catastrophic thoughts. Learn to challenge these thoughts by asking yourself if they are rational or based on evidence. Remind yourself that panic attacks are temporary and not life-threatening. Try replacing negative thoughts with more realistic and positive ones.

3. Practice relaxation techniques: Engaging in relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation, meditation, or guided imagery can help calm your mind and body. These practices can be learned through online resources or mobile apps designed for stress reduction.

4. Identify triggers: Pay attention to situations, activities, or even specific thoughts that tend to provoke your panic attacks. Keeping a journal can be helpful in identifying patterns and triggers. Once you know what triggers your panic attacks, you can work on finding ways to avoid or manage those triggers effectively.

5. Seek support: Consider reaching out to friends, family, or support groups to share your experiences and emotions. Talking about your feelings can provide relief and help you gain different perspectives on managing panic attacks. You may find comfort in knowing that others have experienced similar challenges.

6. Adopt healthy lifestyle habits: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle can contribute positively to managing panic attacks. Ensure you prioritize getting enough sleep, eating balanced meals, exercising regularly, and avoiding excessive caffeine and alcohol consumption. Taking care of your physical health can also have a positive impact on your mental well-being.

7. Consult with a healthcare professional: While these self-help strategies can be beneficial, it's important to consult with a healthcare professional who can assess your situation and provide personalized guidance. They may recommend additional interventions such as therapy or medication if necessary.

Remember that managing panic attacks takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself throughout the process and celebrate even small victories. You are not alone in this journey, and there is support available to help you through.

I'm so sorry you've been hurt.  It's very normal to stop feeling emotions as a way to protect yourself after experiencing a traumatic event.  You can think of it as emotional shock-- you experienced something that was so awful that you have numbed yourself (mind and body) as a way to stop the emotional and physical pain of the event.  It's actually pretty amazing that our selves know how to do this automatically.  And, I hear you saying that you'd like to get some feeling back now.So here are some ideas for how you can change this:I think it would be a great idea to find an experienced therapist you like and trust and/or a good support group so that you can have some allies as you go through this process.  You also could try journaling.  If you're not sure what to write then check out this list of prompts to get you started (it's for teachers, but I really like it).  There's also art journaling.  Pinterest has lots of suggestions.Meditation could be useful.  There are lots of apps available that offer guided meditations.Yoga, tai chi, or chi gong might also help.I have lots of other ideas, but without knowing more about you I'm reluctant to make suggestions that could accidentally make you feel worse.  IThis protective mechanism of numbing yourself kicked in for a good reason and as you get your feelings back, you may find some pretty challenging reactions coming up.  I guess my final piece of advice to is encourage you to trust yourself and gently go at your own pace in your healing.  I hope this was helpful.

Social situations trigger intense anxiety for me. Whether it's attending parties, speaking in public, or even meeting new people, I become overwhelmed by self-consciousness and fear of judgment. These anxious feelings often lead me to avoid socializing altogether. I hope therapy can provide me with tools to overcome social anxiety and feel more comfortable in social settings.

It's great that you're seeking therapy to help with your social anxiety. Social situations can indeed be challenging and trigger intense anxiety for many people. It's important to remember that you're not alone in feeling this way, as social anxiety is a common issue that many individuals face.

In therapy, there are various tools and techniques that can be helpful in managing social anxiety and increasing comfort in social settings. One approach that therapists often use is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and behaviors that contribute to anxiety. By working with a therapist, you can learn strategies to challenge and reframe anxious thoughts, as well as gradually expose yourself to social situations in a controlled and supportive manner.

Another technique that may be beneficial is relaxation exercises. Deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness practices can help reduce anxiety symptoms and promote a sense of calmness. These techniques can be practiced both during therapy sessions and in daily life to manage anxiety when it arises.

Additionally, setting small, achievable goals can be helpful in overcoming social anxiety. Start by exposing yourself to low-pressure social situations, such as joining a small group activity or attending a gathering with close friends. As you become more comfortable, gradually increase the level of challenge by participating in larger events or engaging in public speaking opportunities. Remember to celebrate each step forward, no matter how small, as progress is progress.

Lastly, it can be beneficial to build a support system outside of therapy. Surrounding yourself with understanding and supportive individuals who accept you for who you are can provide a sense of safety and encouragement. Consider reaching out to trusted friends or family members who can offer guidance and companionship as you navigate social situations.

Remember, therapy is a collaborative process, and your therapist will work with you to tailor an approach that suits your specific needs and goals. With time, patience, and consistent effort, it is possible to overcome social anxiety and feel more comfortable in social settings.

It seems like I struggle to connect deeply with others or establish lasting friendships. Although I enjoy being around people and crave connections, I often find it challenging to trust and open up. Building healthy and fulfilling social relationships can indeed be challenging, Olivia. It's not uncommon to experience difficulty connecting deeply with others or establishing lasting friendships. Trusting and opening up can be especially challenging, but it's great that you're seeking guidance to address these barriers.

First, self-reflection is key. Take some time to understand what may be contributing to your struggle in trusting and opening up. Reflect on any past experiences or traumas that might have impacted your ability to form close bonds. Being aware of these factors can help you better navigate your emotions and reactions in future social interactions.

Once you have a better understanding of yourself, practice self-care. Taking care of your own well-being is crucial for building meaningful relationships. Explore activities that bring you joy and make you feel fulfilled. Engage in hobbies or sports groups where you can meet like-minded individuals who share similar interests and values.

In social settings, take small steps towards building connections. Start by engaging in casual conversations with acquaintances or colleagues, gradually transitioning into deeper topics as you become more comfortable. Show genuine interest in the lives and feelings of others, actively listening and validating their experiences.

Remember that building trust takes time. Be patient with yourself and others. Allow relationships to develop naturally, without placing unnecessary pressure on yourself or them. Give people the chance to earn your trust gradually and observe if they reciprocate your efforts in building a connection.

Additionally, consider joining social clubs, volunteer organizations, or support groups centered around your interests or personal growth. These environments provide opportunities to meet new people who are also looking for meaningful connections.

Lastly, therapy can be immensely helpful in exploring and addressing the barriers you mentioned. A therapist can guide you through developing strategies specific to your needs and goals. They can offer insights, tools, and techniques to improve communication, trust-building, and establishing closer bonds.

Remember, Olivia, building strong connections takes time and effort. Focus on self-reflection, practicing self-care, taking small steps, and being patient with the process. With time and dedication, you can develop meaningful relationships that provide the support and understanding you long for.

How does a person start the counseling process?

Great question. Too often people search for the help they need via a phone book or a basic internet search. When looking for a new person to add to your team, whether it be a Counselor, Plumber, or Mechanic, it is important to know as much as you reasonably can about the person. I generally take the following steps: 1.) Know what is important to me in finding help. 2.) Ask for referrals from my trusted friends, family, and colleagues. 3.) Search for online reputation (Better Business Bureau, Yelp, etc). The absence of an online reputation is not necessarily a bar to consideration. However, a predominantly negative review may warrant further research. 4.) Finally call the Counselor and ask a few questions. Let the Counselor know what you are looking for. Trust your gut. For example, if you feel rushed or do not receive thorough answer, move on to the next. Taking the time to defining and conveying your requirements about what you are looking for in counseling can save you a lot of work down the road.

Symptom description: During episodes of anxiety, I experience shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat, sweating, and shaking. The duration typically ranges from several minutes to an hour or longer.
Discussion of significant events: Anxiety runs in my family, and I grew up around high expectations and critical judgments. Additionally, being bullied during my school years has deeply impacted my confidence levels, contributing to my chronic anxiety.
Coping strategies: I attempt to practice relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing exercises and progressive muscle relaxation, when anxiety becomes overwhelming. Questions for the mental health professional: What types of therapeutic interventions are available for individuals struggling with severe anxiety? Are there any specific coping mechanisms you recommend for managing intense fears and worries on a day-to-day basis? How can counseling help someone overcome their fear of judgment and build self-confidence?

It can be incredibly challenging to deal with constant fear and worry. It's understandable that these feelings make it difficult for you to relax or enjoy anything. However, there are therapeutic interventions available to help individuals struggling with severe anxiety.

One approach that may be helpful is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on understanding the connection between our thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. By identifying and challenging unhelpful thought patterns, you can learn new ways of thinking that decrease anxiety. A therapist trained in CBT can work with you to develop personalized strategies for managing your fears and worries more effectively.

Additionally, exposure therapy might be beneficial for overcoming your fear of judgment and building self-confidence. This type of therapy involves gradually facing situations that trigger anxiety, helping you become desensitized over time. Working with a skilled therapist, you can develop a step-by-step plan to confront your fears, allowing you to regain control and build confidence.

In terms of day-to-day coping mechanisms, mindfulness practices can be valuable. Mindfulness involves grounding yourself in the present moment, observing your thoughts and sensations without judgment. Recognizing when anxiety arises and consciously shifting your attention to the present can provide some relief from overwhelming thoughts. You could try incorporating short mindfulness exercises into your daily routine, such as taking a few minutes to focus on your breath and notice any physical sensations without getting caught up in them.

Another suggestion is practicing self-care regularly. Engaging in activities that bring you joy, relaxation, or a sense of accomplishment can help alleviate anxiety. Consider finding a hobby or creative outlet that allows you to express yourself and find temporary relief from anxious thoughts. Remember, though, that coping mechanisms alone may not address the root causes of your anxiety. Seeking professional support can assist you in exploring those underlying factors and working towards long-lasting solutions.

Counseling provides a safe space for you to explore your fear of judgment, low self-confidence, and other related issues. A therapist can help you develop self-compassion, challenge negative beliefs, and build healthier coping mechanisms. They will work collaboratively with you to create a treatment plan that meets your specific needs.

Keep in mind that everyone's journey is unique, so it may take time and experimentation to find the strategies that work best for you. It might be helpful to reach out to a mental health professional who specializes in anxiety disorders to guide you through this process and support you along the way. Remember, you have the strength and resilience to overcome these challenges and live a more fulfilling life.

I am currently suffering from erectile dysfunction and have tried Viagra, Cialis, etc. Nothing seemed to work. My girlfriend of 3 years is very sexually frustrated. I told her that it is okay for her to have sex with other men. Is that really okay?

Hi, First and foremost, I want to acknowledge your efforts to gain (your) ideal erectile function. If the medications are not working and you have taken them as prescribed, I would encourage you to seek the help of a sex therapist as the dysfunction may be due to a psychological and/or relational issue rather than a physical/medical one. As for your question, only you can answer this. Is it OK? Are you OK with her sleeping with others? Have you thought through what this may look like, feel like, become for you and her? Opening up a relationship is a choice only the people in the relationship can answer. Even then, the answer may change at any point by either of you. I encourage you to also determine what the intention is underneath your telling your girlfriend she could sleep with others. Be clear with the intention and then together have continuous conversations about the expectations of opening up (i.e.: are there any kinds of sex that is off limits, areas of the body where touch or intimacy is not allowed, are uses of safer sex required or not, do you want to know the details or not, so forth). An excellent resource would be the book "Opening Up" by Tristan Taormino. I wish you the best of luck!Dr. Lily Zehner, MFT-C
What should I not do if I see a bear?

Everyone knows that bears are not fluffy friends, and are unfortunately likely to maul humans. There is clear guidance on what to do depending on what type of bear you see: if it’s a black bear, make yourself loud and fight if necessary. If it’s a brown bear, lay down and cover your head. If it’s a polar bear, hope you updated your will recently. However, there is very little guidance on what not to do if you see a bear. Thankfully it is easy to provide guidance that applies to all bear types. First, do not attempt to hug the bear. While they do look fluffy and very much in need of a hug, bears highly value consent and will attempt to eat you if you ignore that. Next, do not invite a bear over for dinner. While some bears, black bears especially, may look like good dinner guests they are known for extremely rude eating habits and will likely dirty your house. Further, some types of bears might think that you are the menu. It is also not a good idea to challenge a bear to a game of basketball. Most bears are actually extremely adept at basketball, and this would likely hurt your ego considerably as they would dunk on you and then eat you as a celebration for winning. While this is not an exhaustive list of what not to do if you see a bear, it covers the most common questions.

What should I look for when looking for a used car?

Items to look for when looking to purchase a used car:

* First of all, ask about any major work done to the car like engine, suspension, body work. If it's been in any accidents that may have impacted it's chassis at all. Later on when we're examining the car we may find evidence of damage or repair work, and it's good to know if the seller is lying to cover up any issues before we start negotiating price with them. Pulling the carfax can also be a good way to check if the seller is lying since it often contains detailed information about repair that has been performed to the car. If you notice that the seller is lying either after pulling the carfax or after inspecting the body, it's best not to purchase the car.

* Ask the owner if they have any maintenance records. If they do, that not only means that the car has received the proper care but it also illustrates that the buyer is the kind of person that is very organized and likes to keep their processions in good condition, which is super important. That's the kind of person you want to be buying a car from. Also note that if the owner has been taking the car to the dealership or to an independent shop it's very easy to obtain these service records using the VIN number either online or by calling the mechanic directly.

* Cars having a timing belt needs to be replaced every 70,000-100,000 miles. You can easily check if the car you're planning on purchasing has a timing belt or timing chain. Typically timing chains do not need to be replaced for the life of the car, so finding a car with a timing chain means that you have to worry less about this aspect. Depending on the car replacing the timing belt can be from 1,000 to 6,000 dollars so it's a pretty significant expense that you should take into account.

* Ask how frequently the owner has been changing the oil. In most cases changing it every 3,000 to 6,000 or every year (whichever comes first) is ideal. Many owner manuals mention that you can go over this mileage. In some cases manuals mention oil change intervals of 10,000 or 20,000 miles. Personally, I would not consider a car that has its oil replaced this infrequently. In many cases, these longer intervals are an attempt by the manufacturer's marketing department  to make the car more appealing to buyers if it requires less maintenance. Also ask if they've been using synthetic oil. Typically synthetic oil doesn't break down over time so longer intervals might be ok.

* Ask when was the last time brake pads and rotors have been replaced. Typically brake pads need to be replaced every 50000-100000 miles. Brake rotors can be trickier because whether or not needs replacing depends on its thickness, however if during the test drive you notice vibration when braking, it's likely due to the brake rotors. If the owner hasn't replaced the brakes recently there might be a good opportunity for negotiating the price.

* If the car is a manual ask if the clutch has been replaced. This is a wear item and the time to replace it depends on the usage (cars driven in cities with a lot of stop and go traffic will need a replacement more frequently than cars driving long distances on the freeway).

* For automatics ask when was the last time the transmission fluid was changed. Typically this needs to be replaced every 50-60k miles. Again many service manuals mention that the transmission fluid does not need to be replaced at all, but that's arguably again due to marketing reasons.

* Examine the tires and note how much tread is on the tires. If you were to imagine putting a penny into the tire's tread, a new tire would take up 1/3 - 1/2 of the penny. Also tires need to be replaced every 5 years. The tire sidewall has a 4 digit number which shows the week and year it was manufactured, so it's easy to check if it's due for a replacement. Lastly check if the tires (especially the front) are worn evenly. If the interior part is more worn compared to the exterior, they might indicate suspension or alignment issues. So these issues will need to be addressed and the tires will need to be replaced to fix that problem.

* Ask for and look for any interior problems, bulbs, gauges, AC, power windows not working, stuff like that.

* Check for rust in the wheel wells and rocker panels. Stand back from the car and look for any slight differences in color between it's exterior panels that may indicate they were replaced, also look for dents. The best and easiest indication that a car was repaired or in an accident is if the gaps between body panels is uneven. A good way to identify body panel issues is by running your finger across a body panel, if you feel that one part of the body is lower than the other or if that gap is not consistent, this might mean that the car has been in an accident.

* Look for any signs of fluids, greasy stains on metal, anything that would indicate that it's leaked something. Oil leaks would look dark and greasy. Battery leaks look white and powdery. Coolant leaks look dark and smell sweet. Look at the bottom of the hood, if there are any leak stains there too. Also looks underneath the engine for any greasy spots, because fluids always drip down.

* Do some parts on the car look newer/cleaner than others? A new radiator could mean that the car was recently in a frontal collision.

* Listen to the engine. Does it sound like it's keeping a constant RPM? You may hear some ticking caused by piston slapping or poorly lubricated valves. These are signs that the engine is old, but isn't that big of a deal. Grinding noises are very bad and expensive to fix. Older engines can be pretty noisy until they warm up which is normal.

* Ask the owner to rev the engine while you look at it. Does the engine hop violently when it's revved? This might mean that the engine mounts might need to be replaced.

* Again, ask the owner to rev the engine, this time look at the exhaust. If any blue smoke comes out, or (if it's a warm day outside) any dense white smoke comes out it may indicate that the engine is burning oil, and unless you like adding oil to your engine as often as you fill up your gas tank, it'll be expensive to fix.

Time to take it for a test drive!

* Look at the gauge cluster, is the check engine light on? Keep an eye on the temperature gauge during your trip, does it fluctuate at all? A good car's temperature stays constant during it's trip.

* Take some sharp turns at speed and listen to any thumping or squeeking noises that may come from the suspension or drive train.

* Does the steering wheel shake at all? (when driving it could mean bad alignment or bad steering, when braking it could mean warped rotors)

* Make sure you take the car in and out of all it's gears.

* Listen for funny noises, rattles, squeeks, clanks, vibrations, etc. It's inevitable that older cars will have some interior panels rattle.

* Accelerate hard and brake hard. If the car has ABS does it activate or do you feel that the wheels stop moving?

* Go over some speed bumps, or go on a bumpy road. The car shouldn't be bouncy when recovering from a bump, and neither should it feel like riding over a bump in a shopping cart. It should absorb the bump in a firm but smooth manner.

* After driving for a while, pull over to the side of the road and turn off the car. Pop the hood and look at the coolant resevoir (DON'T OPEN IT!!!) and check if the fluid inside is bubbling or boiling. If it is then the headgasket is blown.

* Remember when we asked the owner when they changed their oil? New oil should look like honey, old oil should have the same color as dark coffee (dark coffee color is a good thing). If the oil is brown or any other funky colors or smells funny something might be wrong with the engine.

* Once you let the car rest for a few minutes check the oil level by using the dipstick if it's not all the way to full, it might be burning or leaking oil.

Anxiety has been plaguing me in various aspects of my life. A specific event that triggered intense anxiety was when I had to travel alone for the first time. The fear of getting lost, missing flights, or encountering dangerous situations consumed my thoughts leading up to the trip. This resulted in sleepless nights, irritability, and panic attacks.

It's understandable that anxiety has been impacting different areas of your life. The specific event you mentioned, traveling alone for the first time, seems to have triggered intense anxiety for you. It's common to feel fearful about getting lost, missing flights, or encountering dangerous situations when embarking on a new experience like this.

To address these concerns and manage your anxiety, here are some suggestions:

1. Preparation: Plan ahead and gather as much information as possible about your travel arrangements. This can include researching transportation options, mapping out routes, and familiarizing yourself with the airport layout. Having a clear plan in place can help alleviate some of the uncertainty and reduce anxiety.

2. Practice relaxation techniques: Engaging in relaxation exercises such as deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation can be helpful in calming your mind and body. These techniques can be practiced both before and during your trip to help manage anxiety symptoms.

3. Challenge negative thoughts: Anxiety often stems from negative thinking patterns. When anxious thoughts arise, try to challenge them by asking yourself if there is any evidence supporting those thoughts. Consider alternative perspectives or more realistic possibilities. Remind yourself that although it's natural to feel nervous, the likelihood of something catastrophic happening is usually very low.

4. Gradual exposure: If possible, consider exposing yourself gradually to similar situations that trigger anxiety. Start with smaller steps, such as taking short trips closer to home, and gradually work your way up to longer journeys. Each successful experience will build confidence and decrease anxiety over time.

5. Seek support: Talking to someone you trust about your fears and anxieties can provide emotional support. They may offer reassurance, share their own experiences, or simply lend a listening ear. Additionally, joining support groups or online communities where others discuss their travel experiences can help normalize your feelings and provide valuable tips.

Remember, managing anxiety takes time and patience. It's important to celebrate small victories along the way and be kind to yourself throughout the process. If your anxiety continues to significantly impact your daily life, it may be beneficial to seek professional help from a mental health therapist who can provide personalized guidance and support.

As a single parent, I often feel overwhelmed and exhausted. Balancing work, household responsibilities, and taking care of my children feels like an impossible task. I wish I had more support or knew better ways to manage my time and energy. How can I take care of myself while also being there for my kids?

I can imagine how challenging it must be for you as a single parent to juggle all the responsibilities and still find time for yourself. It's important to prioritize self-care in order to maintain your well-being while also being there for your children. Here are some suggestions that might help:

1. Establish a routine: Creating a consistent daily schedule can provide structure and make tasks more manageable. This way, you can allocate specific times for work, household chores, and quality time with your kids.

2. Delegate tasks: Don't hesitate to ask for help from family members, friends, or even your children if they're old enough. Delegating certain responsibilities can lighten your load and give you some much-needed breathing space.

3. Seek out support networks: Look for local community groups, online forums, or parenting organizations where you can connect with other single parents who may have valuable insights and advice to share. Building a support network can make you feel less alone and provide a sense of camaraderie.

4. Prioritize self-care: Carving out time for yourself is crucial. Find activities that recharge and relax you, whether it's reading a book, taking a bath, going for a walk, or pursuing a hobby. Remember, taking care of yourself enables you to better care for your children.

5. Simplify tasks: Explore ways to simplify your daily routines. For example, meal planning and preparing meals in advance can save time and energy during busy weekdays. Additionally, creating organized systems for managing household chores can help streamline those responsibilities.

6. Communicate openly with your children: Let your kids know about your challenges and involve them in age-appropriate discussions about sharing responsibilities. This not only teaches them valuable life skills but also fosters a sense of teamwork within the family.

7. Celebrate small victories: Recognize and celebrate your accomplishments, no matter how small they may seem. Give yourself credit for the effort you put into balancing work, household tasks, and parenting. Remember that every step forward is a step in the right direction.

I hope these suggestions provide some guidance and support as you navigate your role as a single parent. You're doing an incredible job, and it's important to remember that taking care of yourself is just as vital as caring for your children.

Anxiety has been consuming me lately, especially when it comes to social situations. Just last week, I was invited to a friend's party and even though I initially felt excited, as the day approached, I began overthinking. Thoughts like "What if no one talks to me?" or "What if I embarrass myself?" flooded my mind, causing intense feelings of unease.

It can be really overwhelming when anxiety starts to consume you, especially in social situations. It's completely normal to have those thoughts and worries about what might happen or how you'll be perceived by others. One thing that may help is to challenge those negative thoughts with more positive and realistic ones. Instead of focusing on the "what if's," try reminding yourself of times when things went well in social situations or times when people did talk to you and showed interest in what you had to say.

Taking slow, deep breaths and practicing relaxation techniques can also be helpful in managing anxiety symptoms. When you feel those anxious thoughts starting to flood your mind, try to take a moment to focus on your breathing and bring yourself back into the present moment. Engaging in activities that you enjoy and that make you feel calm can also help redirect your attention away from anxious thoughts.

Another approach to dealing with anxiety in social situations is gradual exposure. Start by putting yourself in easier, less intense social situations and gradually work your way up to more challenging ones. This allows you to build confidence and become more comfortable over time.

Remember to be kind to yourself and give yourself credit for even small victories. It takes courage to face your fears and push through anxiety, so acknowledge and celebrate your efforts.

Lastly, seeking support from loved ones can make a big difference. Sharing your feelings with someone you trust can provide comfort and understanding. They may even be able to offer suggestions or join you in navigating challenging social situations.

Keep in mind that everyone's journey with anxiety is unique, so it's important to find strategies and coping mechanisms that resonate with you personally. If you continue to struggle with anxiety and it significantly impacts your daily life, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide further guidance and support tailored specifically to your needs.

My boyfriend won't touch me intimately, he won't kiss me while we are having sex and he won't have oral sex with me. I know he has done this things with other women in the past. I don't know why he won't do them with me. What should I do?

First off, don't blame yourself or be too quick to jump to any scary conclusions.  Human sexuality can be incredibly complex at times (e.g., what turns us on at one time may not be what turns us on the next time). There could actually be a number of things going on including him having performance anxiety...maybe he had a bad experience with a previous partner that's left him scared to try again (we call this operant conditioning).  It could also be that he puts you in a different category than previous lovers.  Sometimes I refer to this as the "hooker-housewife mentality" where a partner somehow gets the idea that when we truly fall in love, we treat that one differently; almost up on a pedestal.  Drives many partners crazy until they're aware that this is going on and give their boyfriend/ girlfriend permission to enjoy both the naughty and the nice with them. It could also be that he's not even aware that he's not doing these things. If you haven't asked him yet, you might try gently approaching the subject when you're not already in the bedroom or trying to get in on and inquire what he most enjoys about sex with you (or has enjoyed in the past, or thinks he might enjoy).  You can also share your favorite highlights of sex with him.  Give him an ego boost and tell him what he does well while then asking him if he'd be down to go downtown.  "Baby, it REALLY turns me on when you kiss me during sex."If you continue to get the impression that it's somehow only about YOU or that he's just really hesitant to talk about sex in general, you might see if he'd be cool to chat with a counselor who specializes in sexual intimacy.

We might encourage you to put words to the tears as well, to help you expand on your experience and begin to make more sense of it.As a therapist, our job is help you open up and feel comfortable enough doing so. I sincerely hope no therapist would ever shame you for whatever experience you are having in the room.

Hey, I'm hoping you can assist me with my anxiety issues. Lately, I've been experiencing frequent panic attacks that come out of nowhere. These episodes leave me feeling completely out of control and terrified that something terrible is going to happen. My heart pounds so hard it feels like it might burst out of my chest, and I struggle to catch my breath. The fear of having another panic attack creates a vicious cycle of constant anticipation, which further enhances my anxiety. I'm desperate for some strategies to regain a sense of calm during these overwhelming moments.

One helpful strategy for managing anxiety and panic attacks is deep breathing exercises. When you feel a panic attack coming on, try taking slow, deep breaths in through your nose and exhaling slowly through your mouth. This can help regulate your breathing and slow down your heart rate, promoting a sense of calm.

Another technique that may be beneficial is grounding yourself in the present moment. Focus on your senses by identifying five things you see, four things you can touch or feel, three things you hear, two things you smell, and one thing you taste. Engaging your senses can bring your attention away from anxious thoughts and back to the present reality.

Additionally, consider exploring relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation or guided imagery. Progressive muscle relaxation involves tensing and then releasing different muscle groups throughout your body, which can release physical tension associated with anxiety. Guided imagery involves visualizing a peaceful, calming place or scenario, which can shift your mindset away from fear and towards relaxation.

It could also be helpful to establish a routine that promotes overall well-being. Consistent exercise, balanced meals, adequate sleep, and regular self-care activities like hobbies or spending time outdoors can contribute to reducing anxiety symptoms. Taking care of your physical health can have a positive impact on your mental health as well.

Lastly, seek support from trusted friends, family members, or a support group who can provide encouragement and understanding during difficult moments. Sometimes just talking about your fears and experiences with someone empathetic can alleviate some of the anxiety you are feeling.

Remember, it's important to practice these strategies consistently and give yourself grace as you learn to cope with anxiety. While these suggestions offer guidance, remember that everyone's experience with anxiety is unique. If your symptoms persist or worsen, don't hesitate to reach out to a mental health professional for further assistance tailored to your specific situation.

The most important agent of change in therapy is your relationship with your therapist. It is so important for you to find a therapist that you trust and feel comfortable enough to just lay everything out there and be vulnerable with. Therapy is really building a safe and healthy relationship with a professional that can then help guide you in some of the most intimate and emotional parts of your life. This relationship does take time to build, but usually you can get a sense of a therapist's personality and approach from their bio and website. Once you have found someone that you think you could really connect with, then it's about looking at do they have the expertise you need. Do they have training in relationship counseling or in working with anxiety, depression, or trauma? It is important to find an expert in the field so you are getting the best care possible...just like if you were to go to a general family doctor versus a specialist. I hope that is helpful!

I'm depressed often, and my mind goes a million miles a minute. Every once in a while, things are okay for a few days. After a bit, I start noticing that I am picking at my skin profusely. Hello, and thank you for your question. I am very sorry that you are struggling. I have a few thoughts and perhaps some of my colleagues will add something else. Depression and anxiety can both be chronic conditions, as you have experienced. This means that they may always require treatment in order to have some kind of relief from them. Treatment could mean medication or some kind of counseling. Some people may take medication for the rest of their lives. Some people may go to counseling at times when the depression and anxiety worsens. As you mentioned, sometimes the symptoms improve for a little while, but they can also come back. When they do, it is important to talk to your medical provider if you are getting medication, and/or to go back to your counselor and talk to them about the symptoms that have returned. Skin picking and some other behaviors are not uncommon for people who are experiencing something like anxiety. Many people report that they do this when they feel anxious, and some say it calms them down. It is not really a surprise that you are constantly trying to change things and even starting fights to do so. These are ways to try to avoid, escape and distract yourself from the feelings of anxiety and depression. That is a very normal thing to do. Nobody likes these feelings, and so distraction is something we naturally try in order to get rid of them. The problem is that things like distraction and escape do not work as a long-term solution. In fact, they usually make things worse for many different reasons. Depression and anxiety can  be treated, but it is likely something you will need some help with. I would recommend finding a counselor who has experience with anxiety and depression. Medication can be helpful, but I still recommend counseling. The reason for this is that the medication can help with symptoms, while the counseling can address the symptoms and provide you with very helpful skills. Be well,Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPCC, NCC

I struggle with constant worry and need support in dealing with my anxiety.
 To alleviate excessive worrying caused by anxiety.

Lately, I've noticed that I tend to overthink everything and constantly worry about what could go wrong. The smallest things can set off my anxiety spiral, such as receiving an email from my boss or hearing unexpected noises. These worries keep me up at night, and it feels like my mind never takes a break. Just yesterday, I couldn't sleep because I kept replaying scenarios in my head where I make mistakes and fail at work.

Could you please guide me on how to stop these racing thoughts and find some peace of mind?

It can be really challenging when your mind is constantly consumed with worries and anxieties. The good news is that there are some strategies you can try to help alleviate these racing thoughts and find some peace of mind.

First, it might be helpful to practice mindfulness techniques. Mindfulness involves being fully present in the current moment and observing any thoughts or feelings without judgment. One technique you could try is deep breathing exercises. Take slow, deep breaths in through your nose, hold for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. Focusing on your breath can help anchor your attention to the present and calm your racing thoughts.

Another strategy you could consider is challenging your anxious thoughts. When you notice yourself getting caught up in worry, ask yourself if there is any evidence to support these thoughts. Often, our anxieties are based on irrational or exaggerated thinking patterns. By questioning the validity of your anxious thoughts, you may be able to shift your perspective and reduce their intensity.

It can also be helpful to engage in activities that distract and relax your mind. Find hobbies or activities that you enjoy and that help take your focus away from worry. This might include reading, exercising, listening to music, or practicing relaxation techniques such as yoga or meditation. These activities can provide a much-needed break for your mind and provide some relief from constant worrying.

Additionally, establishing a consistent self-care routine can be beneficial. Prioritize activities that promote overall well-being, such as getting enough sleep, eating balanced meals, and engaging in regular physical activity. Taking care of your physical health can have a positive impact on your mental well-being and help reduce anxiety.

Lastly, seeking support from trusted friends or loved ones can be valuable. Talking about your worries and fears with someone you trust can provide emotional support and different perspectives on your situation. Sometimes simply verbalizing your concerns can help bring them into perspective and lessen their grip on your mind.

Remember, finding the right strategies to alleviate excessive worrying caused by anxiety may take time and experimentation. Be patient with yourself as you explore these techniques, and don't hesitate to reach out for additional support if needed.

Assuming there are no medical explanations for this issue, many men I've worked with on this come to see it as essentially a form of Anxiety. There is a phenomenon called the Yerkes Dodson Law (see below; source: Wikipedia), which basically states that if we feel either too much or too little stress, pressure, or nervousness about a task, it will adversely impact our ability to do carry it out successfully. The ideal amount of stress/arousal is right in the middle - not too little and not too much. This applies to more things than we might often realize - from giving a presentation, to ordering food, to making a free throw, to driving, to sexual intimacy as in this case. A common suggestion that many men find helpful is initiating open and honest conversations with their partners about this issue, and for a temporary period of time, agreeing to physical intimacy and sexual pleasure in other forms, and without the expectation of intercourse. There are many ways to go about that (which are outside the scope of this blog article), but this can be a path to connecting intimately and renewing physical bonding without unhelpful anxiety - and over time, can lead back to intimacy in all the ways that have become elusive. The first thing I usually recommend to clients that are coming in for these issues in addition to stress management is visiting their doctor.  We really don't know if it's something psychological that's influencing your symptoms, or if there's other issues happening within the body.  Pancreas or thyroid issues can perpetuate anxiety and depression symptoms pretty intensely--these are things your doctor knows more about and can help test for (and maybe rule out).As you probably already know, lack of sleep is a giant contributor to an increase in symptoms.  We don't know too much about sleep in the research, but we do know it's necessary to function and function well.  Some suggestions here from the research we do have: creating a calming routine at night can help with your body's relationship to sleep.  This can be your normal nightly hygiene paired with some relaxing videos or soundscapes (there are apps for this--Calm, Headspace, PanicShield).  Practicing these for a few weeks can help your brain pair your routine with sleeping.  Another suggestion directly from the research is not to take naps.  Yes, your brain needs sleep, but napping messes with our circadian rhythm and our quality/quantity of nightly sleep.  When we sleep, we go through sleep stages--but when we nap, those stages aren't completed like they would be during a full night of sleep where we go through those stages multiple times.  Both deep sleep and REM sleep (typically when we dream) seems to be especially important for feeling rested.  Napping usually only offers us a small dose of that, whereas a full night can offer as many more completed cycles including both these stages.  If you are waking into a panic attack, this site may give you some info on what that means: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/panic-attacks/expert-answers/panic-attacks/faq-20057984.  Here's a great information website that has tons of resources, including support groups: https://washingtoncenterforcognitivetherapy.com/problems-treated/panic-disorder/panic-disorder-organizations/.Glad you reached out here!

It can be challenging to feel anxious and uncomfortable in social settings, especially when it affects your ability to start conversations and causes worry about saying the wrong thing. The avoidance of social gatherings seems like a way to cope with these feelings, but it also limits your opportunities for connection and growth.

Here are some suggestions that might help you navigate these difficulties:

1. Start small: Instead of overwhelming yourself with large social gatherings, try starting with smaller, more intimate settings where you feel more comfortable. This could be meeting up with a close friend or attending a small gathering with people you trust.

2. Prepare beforehand: If initiating conversations feels daunting, consider preparing some topics or questions in advance. Knowing what you can talk about may alleviate some anxiety and give you more confidence during interactions.

3. Practice active listening: Engage in active listening by paying attention to what others say and responding with interest and empathy. By focusing on the conversation rather than worrying about how you're perceived, you might find it easier to participate without feeling overwhelmed.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Recognize that your worries about saying the wrong thing are often based on unfounded assumptions or judgments. Try questioning those thoughts and replacing them with more realistic ones. Remember, nobody is perfect, and making mistakes is a normal part of social interaction.

5. Seek support from friends or loved ones: Sharing your struggles with someone you trust can provide comfort and understanding. They might offer helpful insights or even accompany you to social events, providing a sense of reassurance.

6. Consider seeking professional help: If your anxiety continues to significantly impact your daily life despite trying self-help strategies, it may be beneficial to consult with a mental health professional who specializes in anxiety disorders. They can provide personalized guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, building social confidence takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself throughout this journey, celebrate small victories, and don't hesitate to ask for support when needed.

Lately, I've been struggling with my self-esteem. I constantly compare myself to others and feel inadequate in various aspects of my life. This negative self-image is affecting my confidence and enjoyment of daily activities. I want to develop a more positive self-perception and learn how to build genuine self-esteem.

It can be really challenging when we find ourselves constantly comparing ourselves to others and feeling inadequate in different areas of life. Developing a more positive self-perception and building genuine self-esteem is definitely possible with some effort and self-reflection. Here are a few suggestions that may help you along this journey:

1. Practice self-compassion: Treat yourself with kindness and understanding, just as you would treat a close friend. Accept your imperfections and remind yourself that nobody is perfect. Focus on your strengths and achievements rather than dwelling on perceived shortcomings.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: When you catch yourself engaging in negative self-talk or comparing yourself unfavorably to others, make an effort to challenge those thoughts. Ask yourself if there's evidence to support them or if they're simply based on assumptions or unrealistic expectations. Try replacing them with more balanced and positive thoughts.

3. Set realistic goals: Break down larger goals into smaller, achievable steps. Celebrate each accomplishment along the way, no matter how small. This will help build confidence and reinforce a sense of competence.

4. Cultivate self-care practices: Engage in activities that bring you joy, relaxation, and fulfillment. Take care of your physical and mental health by eating well-balanced meals, exercising regularly, getting adequate sleep, and practicing stress management techniques such as meditation or journaling.

5. Surround yourself with positivity: Connect with supportive individuals who uplift you, inspire you, and genuinely care about your well-being. Limit exposure to toxic relationships or social media platforms that trigger comparison and self-doubt.

6. Appreciate your uniqueness: Remember that everyone has their own unique journey and strengths. Embrace your individuality and focus on personal growth instead of comparing yourself to others. Recognize and value the qualities that make you who you are.

7. Seek professional help if needed: Consider reaching out to a mental health professional if you continue to struggle with low self-esteem despite your efforts. They can provide customized guidance and support to help you overcome these challenges.

Remember, building self-esteem is a gradual process, so be patient and kind to yourself along the way. You deserve to feel confident and comfortable in your own skin. Keep striving for personal growth and focus on developing a positive self-perception.

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

As a therapist who believes in client self-determination above most other elements of the process, I want to as much as possible leave it up to the client to determine when they are finished. In the case of a termination because a client's distress has resolved, I might periodically check in with the client about how therapy has been going, and if we want to re-evaluate where we are.The more unfortunate situation would come about if I felt that I wasn't the best fit for the client. I would offer that in words, and ideas of therapists (with names) of who I thought might be a better fit and why. It still is up to the client whether to continue, however should they want to keep seeing me, a part of the work would be about that want (to see someone who professionally doesn't believe they can help as much as someone else.)I also find it perplexing when I hear a client (or on a personal level) tell me that their therapist said they "didn't need therapy." I don't know that I buy into that scenario all that much, because I do believe that yes, not everyone NEEDS therapy, but that everyone CAN benefit from therapy and I don't believe it is the therapist's job to deter someone from ever seeking out help of any kind.
