Stress has taken over my life, and I'm desperate to find ways to alleviate its effects. One significant trigger for my stress is financial instability. I constantly worry about money, struggling to make ends meet and feeling overwhelmed by debt. For example, I have trouble paying bills on time, which adds to my anxiety and feelings of incompetence. The intensity of my stress increases when unexpected expenses arise, leaving me feeling helpless and trapped. These financial stressors affect my sleep, appetite, and ability to concentrate. They also strain my relationships as I become irritable and withdrawn. To cope, I've tried budgeting and seeking additional sources of income, but the stress persists. Are there any strategies or resources available to help me manage my financial stress and regain a sense of stability?

Managing financial stress can be challenging, but there are strategies and resources available to help you alleviate its effects and regain a sense of stability. Here are some suggestions:

1. Prioritize and budget: Start by prioritizing your expenses and creating a realistic budget. Identify essential expenses such as rent, utilities, and groceries, and allocate funds accordingly. This will give you a clearer picture of your financial situation and help reduce anxiety about making ends meet.

2. Seek professional advice: Consider reaching out to a financial advisor or counselor who can provide guidance tailored to your specific circumstances. They can help you develop a personalized plan to manage debt, create savings goals, and explore options for additional sources of income. Their expertise can offer valuable insights and support in navigating your financial challenges.

3. Explore community resources: Look into local organizations or non-profit agencies that offer assistance with financial matters. These resources may include financial education programs, workshops on money management, or even emergency financial aid. Connecting with these resources can provide you with the necessary tools and support to overcome your financial difficulties.

4. Practice self-care: It's important to prioritize self-care during times of stress. Engage in activities that promote relaxation and well-being, such as exercise, meditation, or hobbies that bring you joy. Taking care of yourself physically and emotionally can help reduce the impact of stress on your sleep, appetite, and concentration.

5. Communicate with loved ones: Share your concerns and struggles with trusted friends or family members. Opening up about your financial stress can not only relieve some of the emotional burden but also allow others to offer support and understanding. Additionally, maintaining open lines of communication can help prevent strain on your relationships caused by irritability and withdrawal.

Remember, managing financial stress takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself as you navigate through this process. By implementing these strategies and utilizing available resources, you can gradually work towards alleviating the effects of stress and regaining a sense of stability in your life.

My husband and I had our first threesome recently. Everyone was drinking and he was on her more then me. 

He and I talked about it afterwards and it made me feel better, and now I'm craving more of it. But before it gets close to happening I get this empty feeling. Why am I feeling this way?

Hello, and thank you for your question. Nervousness, when doing something new, especially something sexual that can feel so personal, is very common. Indeed, despite the fact that nervousness can be uncomfortable, it is also part of the excitement of trying something new. Many people who engage in open, polyamorous, and/or other-type relationships, will tell you that difficult feelings, such as jealousy and anger, do show up sometimes. This doesn't prove that there is something wrong with the relationship, it just shows that you retain normal human emotions while in one. And many people who are in polyamorous relationships have written about the work it sometimes takes to make such relationships work. Of course, all relationships take work, so polyamorous and other types of relationships are simply not an exception. There could be several reasons why you are feeling the way you do. One reason could be that you are simply not as comfortable with the idea as you think you are. Some time and good communication with your husband may help you with this. Another reason this may be bothering you is because, on some level, you are aware of the messages society gives us about marriages. They are supposed to be monogamous, heterosexual, etc. etc. Just because you may not agree with these beliefs doesn't mean that you haven't been influenced by them. We all have. Another reason this may be upsetting you is because it may feel a little frightening. Perhaps there are a lot of "What ifs" going on in your mind. When you get the "empty" feeling, it may be helpful to try to really nail down the emotions that are attached to that feeling. One thing that I do think is very important is that you communicate these feelings to your husband. It may even be a good idea to talk about expectations or "ground rules", if you will. It is important that you are both on the same page about what this is, and why you are doing it. If you continue to struggle, I suggest finding a counselor who has experience in sex and sexuality.  I wish you well.Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPCC, NCC

It sounds like you've been experiencing a significant amount of anxiety and stress lately. I can understand how challenging it must be for you to navigate these emotions and cope with them in the best way possible.

When it comes to feeling anxious and on edge, it is important to remember that what you are going through is valid and understandable given your circumstances. It's common for stressors at work and daily life demands to compound and exacerbate these feelings.

In terms of managing your reactions and finding relief during high-stress moments, here are a few techniques you can try:

1. Grounding techniques: Engage your senses by focusing on things around you. For example, you could take a moment to notice five objects you can see, four things you can touch, three sounds you can hear, two scents you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This exercise helps redirect your attention away from the overwhelming thoughts and brings you into the present moment.

2. Progressive muscle relaxation: Start by tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body, progressively moving from your toes all the way up to your head. This technique promotes relaxation and helps reduce physical tension associated with stress.

3. Journaling: Expressing your thoughts and emotions on paper can provide catharsis and clarity. Try writing down your worries, fears, and frustrations without judgment. Additionally, you can also jot down positive experiences or things you're grateful for to help shift your focus towards more positive aspects of your life.

4. Physical activity: Engaging in regular exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Consider incorporating activities such as walking, jogging, yoga, or dancing into your routine. Even short bursts of movement throughout the day can have a positive impact on your mental well-being.

5. Social support: Reach out to loved ones who can offer a listening ear or lend a helping hand. Sharing your feelings with someone you trust can provide support and a sense of relief. Sometimes, simply expressing your emotions out loud can help alleviate some of the built-up tension.

Remember that finding the techniques that work best for you may involve some trial and error. It's important to be patient with yourself as you explore different strategies and give them time to see their effects. If none of these suggestions seem sufficient in managing your stress levels, consider reaching out to a professional mental health therapist who can offer tailored guidance.

I hope these suggestions provide you with some additional relief during those high-stress moments. Take care of yourself and know that you have the strength to navigate through this challenging time.

I love this question! Some people shy away from counseling because they think since they already talk about how they feel to their relatives or friends they shouldn't need a counselor. However, if you are having a difficult time, counseling can be beneficial in helping you move forward and get your life back on track. Counseling is not like the kind of talking we do to people we know. For one, your counselor does not have a history with you and has no expectations of how you will act and what you will do. In that way, counselors come to a session without judgement and expectation. This gives you the platform to truly explore your thoughts and feelings. A counselor can also help you understand your motivation and help you integrate your past experiences and recommend coping skills that can help you if you are feeling overwhelmed by your emotions. Over time, as you work with a counselor you will get feedback and also be able to share new insights. The work you do is based on you and where you are at. Oftentimes, when we talk to friends they bring their own agenda to a conversation, and while they mean well they may offer solutions that work for them and not you. Furthermore, self-care plays an essential role in navigating depression. Prioritizing activities that bring you joy, peace, and relaxation can go a long way in improving your overall well-being. Even small bursts of movement throughout the day, such as taking short walks or stretching breaks, can make a difference.

Lastly, if you find that negative thoughts and rumination persist despite your efforts, consider exploring cognitive behavioral therapy techniques. These methods focus on challenging and reframing negative thought patterns, allowing for more positive and realistic thinking.

It sounds like you've been experiencing a lot of anxiety recently, and it's become challenging for you to manage. I'm here to provide some guidance and suggestions to help you understand why this might be happening.

Firstly, it's important to remember that anxiety can arise from various factors, such as stress, life changes, or underlying emotional issues. Reflecting on any recent events or changes in your life may help shed light on potential triggers for your anxiety. Consider if there have been any significant life events, work-related pressures, relationship changes, or other stressful situations that could be contributing to your current state.

In addition, it might be helpful to explore any patterns or recurring thoughts that accompany your anxious feelings. Are there specific worries or fears that tend to surface? Identifying these thought patterns and understanding their origins can offer insights into the root causes of your anxiety.

Engaging in self-care activities is another essential aspect of managing anxiety. Is there something that brings you joy and helps you relax? It could be spending time with loved ones, practicing mindfulness or meditation, pursuing hobbies, exercising, or anything else that offers a sense of peace and calm. Prioritizing self-care can significantly contribute to reducing anxiety levels.

Consider reaching out to someone you trust, such as a friend or family member, to talk about what you're going through. Sometimes, verbalizing our emotions and concerns can alleviate some of the weight we feel. Explaining how you've been feeling to others can also provide them with an opportunity to support you during this difficult time.

If your anxiety continues to interfere with your daily life and well-being, seeking professional help may be beneficial. A mental health professional, such as a counselor or therapist, can provide you with additional tools and strategies to manage your anxiety effectively. They will work with you to explore the underlying causes, develop coping mechanisms, and create a personalized treatment plan tailored to your needs.

Remember, you don't have to face this alone. Take the necessary steps to prioritize your mental health and seek the support that is available to you. You deserve it, and with time and effort, I believe you can overcome these challenges and regain a sense of well-being.

We've been in a long distance relationship for two and a half years. I recently saw his phone and saw the people he texts the most and one of them was a female coworker. I don't know how to approach this situation. How do I ask him about it?.

I agree with Sherry that in a close intimate relationship, you are entitled to ask questions about his relationship with significant others. These questions help couples to build connection and trust. It's based on the idea that if you reach out to him for whatever reason (support, openess, understanding, empathy), you can count on him and can expect him to be responsive. How he responds to your question will give you an idea whether he helps you to feel more emotionally secure and builds trust or if you feel that you cannot be open with him. If your partner responds in an open and understanding manner, it usually indicates that he cares about your feelings and values your importance. If he responds in a defensive manner, it could mean that he does not like that you are questioning your trust in him or that he has something to hide. Either way, you may wish to explain that building trust is something that is very important to you in a relationship and that talking to him openly helps to foster that. If he continues to be defensive or evasive, then there might be some bigger issues at stake and the two of you may benefit from couples counselling or having a discussion about the values that are important to you in the relationship and how the two of you will go about supporting those values with actions.Dr. Virginia Chowwww.PsychologyResource.ca
Does counseling really do anything that can help people?

Counseling is a collaborative process which involves the development of a confidential, unique, therapeutic, helping relationship. This relationship is unlike any other as the counselor will act as a facilitator in helping you better understand yourself, the world around you, your feelings, and your behaviors.As is the case with most things in life, there are both benefits and risks while participating in counseling. Counseling may improve your ability to relate with others, provide a clearer understanding of yourself, your values, and your goals, and it often helps relieve stress immediately.Along with these benefits, counseling will also involve discussing the unpleasant parts of your life, and you may experience uncomfortable feelings during these moments. It sounds like you have been experiencing a lot of anxiety that is impacting your daily life. Dealing with racing thoughts and constant worry can be incredibly challenging, but there are strategies that might help you manage your anxiety more effectively.

One approach that may be beneficial is practicing relaxation techniques. This could include deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation. These techniques can help you calm your mind when it feels overwhelmed, and provide some reprieve from the racing thoughts.

Another helpful strategy might be to challenge your anxious thoughts. Often, our worries are based on irrational or exaggerated beliefs. Whenever you catch yourself thinking negatively or catastrophizing, try to question those thoughts and look for evidence that contradicts them. Remind yourself that just because you feel anxious, it doesn't mean something bad will actually happen.

Additionally, maintaining a consistent sleep routine can work wonders for managing anxiety. Prioritize good sleep hygiene by creating a relaxing bedtime routine, avoiding stimulating activities before bed, and ensuring your sleeping environment is comfortable and conducive to restful sleep. Making sleep a priority can help minimize racing thoughts that keep you awake at night.

Engaging in regular physical exercise has also been shown to reduce anxiety symptoms. Physical activity releases endorphins, which are natural mood lifters. Finding an exercise routine that suits your preferences and abilities, whether it's walking, yoga, dancing, or any other form of movement, can help regulate your emotions and ease anxiety levels.

Lastly, consider seeking support from trusted individuals in your life who can listen to your concerns and offer compassion. Friends, family members, or even support groups can provide comfort and understanding during difficult times. Sharing your feelings with others may alleviate some of the burdens of anxiety.

Remember, finding ways to manage anxiety takes time and perseverance. It's important to be patient with yourself throughout this process. If your symptoms persist or worsen, reaching out to a mental health professional or counselor may prove beneficial in obtaining further guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Lately, my anxiety has been out of control. I worry excessively about things that might go wrong, even in situations where there is no real threat. These anxious thoughts consume me and prevent me from fully enjoying life. My goal for this session is to learn effective techniques to manage my anxiety.

Managing anxiety can be a challenge, but there are definitely steps you can take to help alleviate your symptoms and regain control over your thoughts and emotions. Here are some techniques that may assist you in managing your anxiety:

1. Deep breathing exercises: Practice taking slow, deep breaths whenever you feel overwhelmed by anxious thoughts. Focus on your breath as it goes in and out, allowing it to calm your body and mind.

2. Progressive muscle relaxation: This technique involves tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body, starting from your toes all the way up to your head. By doing so, you can promote physical relaxation that helps reduce anxiety.

3. Grounding techniques: When you find yourself caught up in worries about future events, try grounding yourself in the present moment. Pay attention to your senses - what you can see, hear, touch, smell, and taste. Engage with the environment around you to distract yourself from anxious thoughts.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Often, anxiety is fueled by irrational or exaggerated thinking patterns. Take a step back and question the validity of your anxious thoughts. Ask yourself if there is concrete evidence supporting them. Consider alternative perspectives and challenge the pessimistic assumptions you might be making.

5. Create a worry time: Instead of letting anxious thoughts consume your entire day, set aside a specific time block for worrying. During this designated period, allow yourself to fully explore and address your concerns. Once the time is up, let go of those worries and focus on other activities.

6. Incorporate regular exercise: Physical activity has been shown to have a positive impact on mental health. Engaging in activities such as walking, jogging, or yoga can help release tension, boost your mood, and reduce anxiety levels.

7. Prioritize self-care: Make sure you're practicing good self-care habits like getting enough sleep, eating well-balanced meals, and incorporating activities you enjoy into your daily routine. Taking care of yourself overall can contribute to a more stable mental state.

Remember, it may take time and practice before you see significant improvements. Be patient with yourself as you learn these techniques and discover what works best for you. If your anxiety continues to interfere with your ability to enjoy life and function day-to-day, consider reaching out to a mental health professional for additional support tailored to your specific needs.

This is a common issue. You grow up gradually, and parents often forget to shift their habitual responses according to your newfound level of maturity and growing need for freedom and independance. I'm all for helping you find new ways to cope and interact with your mom. Ultimately, you only have control over yourself, so that's the place to start. You can remind yourself that Mom's behaviours don't mean that she doesn't trust you or love you; it's just that she has habitual ways of talking to you that seem stuck in the fourteen year old range. If you can see her responses as habits, rather than a reflection of how she feels about you, then you can keep yourself calm. The more calm you are, the more she will buy into it when you invite her into a different sort of relationship. Take a look at the picture from her perspective. She may feel overwhelmed with finances (are you in college?), and feel burdened by the mundane tasks in life that she doesn't know how to recruit help for. I bet your mom spends a lot of time picking up after you, cleaning, cooking, doing laundry...all those thankless mom tasks. Take a look at how she talks to you... is she nagging about chores? Can you see that underneath the nagging there's a pretty overwhelmed and powerless person who needs assistance?  Okay, so my guess is that you both have a legitimate beef. She wants help. You want respect. Let's talk about how you get both.I propose that you sit down with mom and negotiate out a different sort of dynamic. "Mom...I see us as stuck in how we interacted when I was fourteen. Can we do this differently in a way that we both get what we want?" Sell it as "win-win". Then you write down some things that end up forming a contract. The first part is stuff that's your business and your business alone: things you want your mom to respect, like your room, your school, your job, your personal relationships and hygiene.... Mom's voice has no place in these arenas, unless you are storing food in your room and it's a health hazard. This is a "Mom says nothing about" list. The second part is about what Mom needs from you. What are her expectations about your role in the home as an adult. Does she want you to contribute to rent? Buy your own food? Do your own laundry? What items can we put in your control that would take some burden off of Mom? How will these things be enforced? What will happen if you don't follow through? Write it all down so it's really clear. It has to all be mutually agreed upon.The third part of the conversation is about how she talks to you, and how you talk to her. You can let her know that you don't want to be told what to do or when to do it; that doesn't work when you're 20 years old. Listen to what she wants too. Beyond the contract you've just written up, anything else you want from each other is a request, it's optional, and whether and when you do it is at your discretion. My guess is that if she spoke to you with more respect, you'd be more willing to help out. AND, I think if you participated a bit more she would nag at you less. Go for the win-win. I wish you well as you negotiate a new relationship with Mom. :)

"I recently went through a breakup and it has been taking a toll on me emotionally. It feels like my world has turned upside down, and I'm struggling with feelings of sadness, anger, and confusion. I find myself constantly questioning what went wrong and blaming myself for the relationship dissolving."

Breakups can be incredibly difficult and can have a significant impact on our emotions. It's natural to feel a range of emotions, including sadness, anger, and confusion after going through a breakup. During this challenging time, it's important to prioritize self-care and allow yourself to process these feelings.

One helpful approach is to practice self-compassion. Rather than blaming yourself for the end of the relationship, try to treat yourself with kindness and understanding. Remind yourself that relationships involve two people, and it's rarely just one person's fault when things don't work out. Give yourself permission to grieve the loss of the relationship and acknowledge that it's okay to be sad.

Another strategy that may be useful is examining your expectations. Reflect on what you had hoped for in the relationship and compare it to the reality of what was happening. It's common to idealize past relationships or focus on the positive aspects while downplaying the negative. Taking a more balanced perspective can help you understand that the end of the relationship might have been necessary for both parties' well-being.

Engaging in healthy coping mechanisms can also support your emotional healing. This might include activities like journaling, exercising, spending time with loved ones, or pursuing hobbies that bring you joy. Engaging in these activities can help distract your mind from repetitive thoughts and give you a sense of accomplishment and fulfillment.

It might be beneficial to seek support from friends, family, or a supportive community group during this time. Talking about your feelings and experiences can help you process them in a healthy way. Remember, it's okay to ask for support and lean on others when needed.

Lastly, consider seeking professional help if you find that your emotions are overwhelming or interfering with your daily functioning. A mental health therapist can offer guidance and provide you with additional tools to cope with the challenges you're facing.

In a way, self-harm can present somewhat like an addiction.  According to new research within the field of neuroscience there is a valid explanation for this.  When a person cuts or uses other forms of self harm, the body produces endorphins to help make a person feel better.  If a person was dealing with depression or high anxiety, that might be misinterpreted by the brain as a way to help oneself feel better and a new neural network or map might form (addiction) that would utilize this new behavior.  Another way to look at it would be thru a behavioral lens, a positive reward for a behavior, even though the behavior has other long term negative consequences.  Consider working with someone who can both have you work on and address those items that trigger your behavior and the root causes, in this case sadness or depression, and second find someone who can help give you alternatives that take into account the neurological requirement by replacing the behavior with another behavior (such as snapping a rubber band on the wrist) and working to extinguish the unwanted behavior.   Someone who is trained in Dialectic Behavior Therapy and/or Interpersonal Neurobiology would most likely have the skills and means available to address this with you.

I've been having trouble falling asleep and staying asleep lately. My goal for this counseling session is to find ways to improve my sleep quality and develop a healthier sleep routine. These sleep issues have been affecting my daily functioning and overall well-being.

These thoughts constantly race through my mind, making it nearly impossible to relax and unwind before bed.

One specific example that triggers my sleep concerns is when I have an important presentation or meeting the next day. The fear of not performing well or facing judgment from others keeps me awake for hours on end, even if I'm physically exhausted.

The frequency of these symptoms varies, but on average I struggle with falling asleep at least three nights a week. Once I do fall asleep, I often wake up in the middle of the night and find it extremely difficult to go back to sleep. As a result, I feel tired throughout the day and lack focus and concentration.

In terms of coping strategies, I've tried experimenting with relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises or listening to calming music before bedtime. While these methods may help temporarily, they haven't provided a consistent solution for my sleep issues.

Could you offer any advice on how to establish a healthier sleep routine? What are some effective strategies for managing stress and anxiety to promote better sleep?

To improve your sleep quality and establish a healthier sleep routine, here are some suggestions you can consider:

1. Establish a consistent bedtime routine: Develop a relaxing routine before bed that signals to your body it's time to wind down. This could include activities such as reading a book, taking a warm bath, or practicing gentle stretching exercises.

2. Create a comfortable sleep environment: Ensure that your bedroom is optimized for sleep. Make sure the temperature, lighting, and noise levels in your room are conducive to a restful night's sleep. Consider using earplugs, eye masks, or white noise machines if necessary.

3. Set boundaries with technology: Avoid looking at screens, such as smartphones or laptops, for at least an hour before bed. The blue light emitted by these devices can interfere with your sleep patterns. Instead, engage in calming activities that promote relaxation.

4. Manage stress and anxiety: Practice stress management techniques during the day to help calm your mind before bed. Engage in activities like yoga, meditation, journaling, or talking to someone you trust about your concerns. These strategies can help reduce the impact of work-related pressure, financial worries, and relationship conflicts on your sleep.

5. Challenge negative thoughts: When specific events trigger your sleep concerns, try challenging any negative thoughts that arise. Ask yourself if there is evidence supporting these thoughts and if there are alternative perspectives. By questioning and reframing negative thoughts, you may be able to decrease their power over your ability to fall asleep.

6. Create a worry journal: Before going to bed, spend 10-15 minutes jotting down any recurring thoughts, worries, or tasks that need to be addressed. By writing them down, you can temporarily set them aside until the next day, helping to clear your mind and alleviate racing thoughts.

7. Stay physically active: Regular exercise can positively impact both your physical and mental well-being, leading to better sleep. Engage in activities you enjoy, such as walking, cycling, or dancing, for at least 30 minutes most days of the week. Just ensure that you finish exercising at least a couple of hours before bedtime to allow your body time to wind down.

8. Avoid stimulants: Limit your intake of caffeine and nicotine, especially later in the day. They can interfere with falling asleep and staying asleep. Be aware of hidden sources of caffeine, such as certain medications and chocolate, which might affect your sleep as well.

It's important to remember that improving your sleep routine takes time and experimentation. You may need to try different strategies to find what works best for you. If these suggestions don't bring about sufficient improvement over time, it could be beneficial to seek additional support from a mental health professional who specializes in sleep disorders or anxiety management.

Ive been in an on an off relationship with a this man for almost 3 years. Even though I care about him, he continues to hurt me.    He and his wife were separated when we met. Now he's going through a really difficult divorce from her and is taking it really hard. I want to end this relationship, but I don't feel like I can. How can I let go?

Hello, and thank you for your question. Boy, ending relationships is tough, isn't it? Sometimes it's tough even when we are 100% sure that it is the right thing to do!I am going to give you some of my thoughts, and hopefully some colleagues will add some others. One of the things that I want to point out is that "letting go" is not really a thing. In other words, it's not really something you can reach out and grab. It's more of a process. This is good news, because you don't necessarily have to be at the end of the process to end an unhealthy relationship. We just have to accept that there will be feelings that come up even after the relationship is over. For example, someone can end an unhealthy relationship today, but then be reminded of the good times on what would have been their "anniversary." This could make the person very sad. They may even regret ending the relationship for a little while. It would important, then, for the person to remind themselves why the relationship needed to end, and that they are healthier because of it. This is relevant for you. It's hard to walk away from a relationship. We fear all kinds of things, including being single! Sometimes it's helpful to compare what you are getting out of the relationship to what you want from a relationship. It's helpful to be honest about what we have given up for an unhealthy relationship. It's fine to admit uncertainly about ending things. It's okay to be afraid. It's okay to have moments of doubt and sadness along with a dash of guilt. And even with all of that, someone can still leave if it is the healthiest thing for them. As for techniques and approaches used in counseling sessions, there are various therapeutic modalities that counselors may draw from based on your specific needs. Some common ones include cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns; psychodynamic therapy, which explores unconscious influences on behavior and relationships; and person-centered therapy, which emphasizes empathy and understanding.

However, it's important to note that each counselor may have their own individual style and approach. It might be helpful to ask potential counselors about their preferred methods during the initial session or when researching different therapists.

Ultimately, the goal of counseling is to help you gain insight into your challenges, develop coping strategies, and work towards positive change. Your counselor will collaborate with you to tailor the therapy to your specific needs and goals. Hi, thank you for seeing me today. I wanted to discuss my anxiety issues that have recently worsened. Specifically, I've noticed recurring panic attacks. These episodes are highly distressing as they come out of nowhere and make me feel like I'm losing control. They often start with shortness of breath, chest tightness, and an overwhelming sense of fear. One incident happened just last week while driving on the highway. Suddenly, it felt like everything was closing in on me, and it became increasingly difficult to breathe. This lasted for several minutes, leaving me emotionally and physically drained afterwards. Frequency-wise, the panic attacks occur now every two weeks, which makes my everyday life challenging. Considering these symptoms, I'd appreciate your guidance on how to manage and reduce my anxiety levels.

Recurring panic attacks can indeed be distressing and make you feel like you're losing control. It's important to remember that you are not alone in dealing with anxiety, as many people experience similar symptoms.

To start managing and reducing your anxiety levels, there are several strategies you can try:

1. Deep Breathing: When you notice the onset of a panic attack, focus on slowing down your breathing. Take slow, deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth. This can help reduce the intensity of your symptoms by slowing down your heart rate and promoting relaxation.

2. Grounding Techniques: During a panic attack, it can be helpful to bring yourself back to the present moment. Try grounding techniques such as focusing on your senses. Look around and name five things you see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This technique can divert your attention away from anxious thoughts and bring you back to reality.

3. Progressive Muscle Relaxation: Tension often accompanies anxiety, so practicing progressive muscle relaxation can be beneficial. Start by tensing and then relaxing each muscle group in your body, one at a time. This exercise promotes physical relaxation and helps alleviate some of the physical symptoms associated with anxiety.

4. Self-Care Routine: Developing a self-care routine can contribute to overall emotional well-being. Prioritize activities that help you relax and destress, such as taking baths, reading, or engaging in creative outlets. Regular exercise, a balanced diet, and sufficient sleep also play a crucial role in managing anxiety.

5. Journaling: Keeping a journal can provide an opportunity for self-reflection and expression. Write down your feelings and thoughts when you experience anxiety or after a panic attack. Not only does this serve as a way to process emotions, but it may also help identify triggers or patterns related to your anxiety.

6. Seek Support: Don't hesitate to reach out to friends, loved ones, or support groups who can provide understanding and encouragement. Sometimes it can be helpful just to talk about your experiences with someone you trust.

Remember, everyone's journey in managing anxiety is unique, so feel free to explore these strategies and find what works best for you. If your symptoms persist or worsen, it may be beneficial to seek professional help from a mental health expert who can tailor treatment specifically for you.

Every time I experience a minor physical symptom like a headache or stomachache, my mind immediately jumps to catastrophic conclusions. Last week, I felt a sharp pain in my side and immediately became convinced that I had a serious medical condition. This triggered a full-blown panic attack where I experienced shortness of breath, racing heart, and trembling hands. It lasted for almost an hour before I could regain control. These episodes are becoming more frequent and impacting my ability to enjoy life without constant worry.

I wanted to discuss different treatment options for health anxiety specifically. How can I address the irrational thoughts and fears that seem to dominate my mind? It can be challenging to cope with severe anxiety, especially when it is triggered by health-related concerns. I want to assure you that there are treatment options and strategies available to help address your irrational thoughts and fears.

One approach that may be helpful for you is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). In CBT, the focus is on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. By recognizing and questioning these thoughts, you can begin to develop more realistic and balanced perspectives. As a start, try to pay attention to the specific catastrophic conclusions your mind jumps to when experiencing minor physical symptoms, like headaches or stomachaches. Consider whether there is any concrete evidence supporting those conclusions, or if they are based solely on fear and assumptions.

Relaxation techniques and mindfulness exercises can also play a valuable role in managing anxiety symptoms. Deep breathing exercises, such as diaphragmatic breathing or box breathing, can help regulate your breath and promote feelings of calmness. When practicing deep breathing, focus on inhaling deeply through your nose, allowing your abdomen to rise, and exhaling slowly through your mouth. You might find it helpful to set aside a few minutes each day to practice deep breathing or engage in activities that promote relaxation, such as listening to calming music or taking a warm bath.

Mindfulness exercises involve paying attention to the present moment without judgment. This can help redirect your thoughts away from worrying about potential health problems. One simple mindfulness exercise you can try is mindful observation. Find a quiet space, choose an object in front of you, and intentionally observe it, noticing its colors, textures, and shapes without analyzing or judging them. If your mind begins to wander back to anxious thoughts, gently bring your focus back to the object. Over time, mindfulness exercises can help you become more aware of your thoughts and emotions while reducing their ability to overwhelm you.

In addition to these self-help strategies, don't hesitate to consider seeking support from professionals who specialize in anxiety. They can provide personalized guidance and help tailor a treatment plan that fits your specific needs.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and practice, so be patient with yourself throughout this journey. By actively engaging in these techniques and exploring treatment options, you are taking an important step towards managing your health anxiety and regaining control over your life.

I've experienced a traumatic event recently that has left me feeling overwhelmed and anxious. Every time I close my eyes, I can vividly recall the details of what happened. It's affecting my sleep and concentration, and I'm having frequent nightmares. I want to heal from this trauma and find strategies to cope with the distressing memories.

Allow yourself time and space to process the traumatic event you experienced. It is normal to feel overwhelmed and anxious after such an experience. Here are some strategies that may help you cope with the distressing memories:

1. Create a calming routine before bedtime: Establish a relaxing routine before going to sleep, such as taking a warm bath, practicing deep breathing exercises, or listening to soothing music. This can help prepare your mind for restful sleep.

2. Engage in relaxation techniques: Practice mindfulness or meditation exercises during the day to help ground yourself and reduce anxiety. These techniques can also assist in managing intrusive thoughts when they arise.

3. Express your emotions: Find healthy outlets for your emotions. Consider keeping a journal where you can freely express your feelings about the trauma. Alternatively, talk to trusted friends or family members who can provide support and understanding.

4. Seek distractions: Engaging in activities that bring you joy or divert your attention can be helpful. Find hobbies, interests, or projects that capture your focus and give you moments of respite from the distressing memories.

5. Consider professional support: If the distressing memories persist and affect your daily functioning significantly, it might be beneficial to seek support from a mental health professional. They can provide specialized guidance and develop personalized coping strategies tailored to your needs.

6. Explore grounding techniques: When you find yourself overwhelmed by the vivid recall of the traumatic event, try grounding techniques. Focus on your senses by noticing five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This exercise can help shift your attention away from the distressing memories and bring you back to the present moment.

7. Take care of your physical well-being: Prioritize self-care activities like maintaining a balanced diet, getting regular exercise, and ensuring sufficient sleep. Physical well-being plays a crucial role in mental health recovery.

Remember, healing from trauma takes time and patience. It can be a challenging journey, but with consistent effort, you can gradually find ways to cope with the distressing memories and experience a sense of relief.

I'm going to reframe this and you can decide if this is helpful!What I'm reading based on what you gave is that you are actually doing your best to manage intense feelings of internal dysregulation.  Anger is something that is generally a protective emotion that quickly arises to keep us safe in some way, whether or not the situation is truly a threat.  The part of our brain that perceives this is not controllable to us, so we don't get to decide what emotion(s) we respond with.It does also sound like you are experiencing some significant anxiety, maybe even underlying the anger?  Without knowing the context, it's hard to say what would help on an individual level but working through those triggers and what is really influencing them deep down could be beneficial.  There's many different ways to do that in therapy if you so choose that as your path.If you do decide to see a therapist, most will tell you that the goal is not necessarily to control your anxiety or anger.  Sometimes there's a strong set of beliefs that, when activated, are catalysts to strong emotions that influence behavior.  Trying to control an emotion on its own is usually unsuccessful for people because it leaves out all the other powerful elements at play.  Emotions are information and the brain sends that information out because it believes we need it at that time.  Therapists can help unravel that with you in whatever way you need, whether that's with somatic work, work at the level of belief (or schemas), or otherwise---hitting it at these deeper layers can unpair and/or decrease emotional responses.  It all takes work and time, so don't get down on yourself if the process is complicated or slower than you expected or hoped for.What we know though is that the brain is very capable of change (even if it's painful).   Hope this gives you a helpful place to start from!

Our family has been going through constant conflicts and arguments lately. There is tension among everyone and it feels like we are walking on eggshells around each other. I don't understand why there is so much conflict and I feel stuck in the middle. I hope to gain some insights into the dynamics within my family and find ways to improve communication and resolve conflicts peacefully.

It can be challenging when there is constant conflict and tension within the family. Finding ways to improve communication and resolve conflicts peacefully is a common goal for many people in similar situations. Here are some suggestions that may help you gain insights into the dynamics within your family and work towards resolving these conflicts:

1. Take a step back and observe: Try to objectively observe the interactions and dynamics within your family. Look for patterns, triggers, and underlying issues that may contribute to the conflicts. By gaining a better understanding of these dynamics, you can start addressing them more effectively.

2. Identify emotions and needs: Conflict often arises from unmet emotional needs or misunderstandings. Encourage open and honest communication within your family, where everyone has an opportunity to express their feelings and needs without judgment. This can foster empathy and understanding among family members.

3. Active listening: When conflicts arise, it's important to actively listen to each other. Practice giving your full attention, maintaining eye contact, and reflecting back what the speaker is saying to ensure accurate understanding. This helps create a safe space for open dialogue and demonstrates respect for one another's perspectives.

4. Use "I" statements: During discussions or arguments, using "I" statements can promote better communication. Instead of blaming or accusing others, focus on expressing how you feel and how certain actions impact you personally. This approach reduces defensiveness and encourages constructive conversations.

5. Seek compromises and solutions: Encourage problem-solving as a family. Together, brainstorm potential solutions and encourage each member to voice their ideas and concerns. Strive for win-win outcomes by finding compromises that take everyone's needs into account.

6. Practice self-care: Coping with family conflicts can take a toll on your mental well-being. Make sure to prioritize self-care activities that help manage stress, such as engaging in hobbies, exercise, spending time with supportive friends, or seeking professional support if needed.

7. Consider family therapy: Family therapy can be a valuable resource for navigating conflicts and improving communication. A trained therapist can facilitate discussions, provide additional insights, and offer specific strategies tailored to your unique family dynamics.

Remember, every family is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all approach to resolving conflicts. The above suggestions are meant as general guidance, but it's important to adapt them to your own situation and consider what works best for you and your family.

The stress I experience on a daily basis has started to impact my physical health. I've noticed an increase in blood pressure and difficulty sleeping. My body constantly feels tense, and I struggle to relax even during moments of rest. I'm interested in exploring relaxation techniques that can help me alleviate these physical symptoms associated with stress.

It's great that you're interested in exploring relaxation techniques to alleviate the physical symptoms associated with stress. Here are a few suggestions that may help:

1. Deep breathing exercises: Taking slow, deep breaths can activate your body's relaxation response and help reduce tension. Try inhaling deeply through your nose for a count of four, holding your breath for a count of four, and exhaling slowly through your mouth for a count of four. Repeat this several times whenever you feel stressed.

2. Progressive muscle relaxation: This technique involves tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body, one at a time. Start with your toes and work your way up to your head, focusing on the sensations of tension and relaxation. This exercise can help promote overall relaxation and relieve muscle tension.

3. Mindfulness meditation: By practicing mindfulness, you can learn to focus your attention on the present moment without judgment. Find a quiet space, sit comfortably, and bring your awareness to your breath or any other sensation in your body. Whenever your mind starts to wander, gently guide it back to the present moment. Regular practice can help reduce stress and increase relaxation.

4. Guided imagery: Close your eyes and imagine yourself in a peaceful and calming environment, such as a beach or a forest. Engage all your senses by visualizing the sights, sounds, smells, and textures of this place. Allow yourself to fully immerse in this mental image, letting go of any tension or stress.

5. Physical activity: Engaging in regular exercise can be an effective way to manage stress and improve overall well-being. Whether it's going for a walk, practicing yoga, or participating in a sport you enjoy, physical activity releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters.

Remember, these techniques may not provide instant relief, but with consistent practice, they can gradually help reduce stress and its impact on your physical health. It's important to find what works best for you and incorporate these techniques into your daily routine. If you have any concerns or questions, don't hesitate to reach out.

"Within romantic relationships, I struggle with trust due to past experiences of infidelity and betrayal. For instance, in my previous relationship, my partner cheated on me, leading to deep emotional pain and insecurities. It's challenging for me to believe that future partners won't hurt me in the same way."

Building trust in romantic relationships after experiencing infidelity and betrayal can be a difficult journey, but it's not impossible. Here are some suggestions to help you navigate through this challenging situation:

1. Reflect on your past experiences: Take the time to acknowledge and process the pain and insecurities caused by your previous partner's actions. Understand that these emotions are valid, and it's natural to feel apprehensive about future relationships.

2. Work on self-healing: Prioritize self-care and nurturing your own emotional well-being. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help rebuild your self-esteem. Seek support from trusted friends or family members who can offer a listening ear and understanding during this healing process.

3. Practice effective communication: Openly communicate your concerns and fears with potential partners when you're ready to build a new relationship. Honest conversations about your past experiences can increase understanding and pave the way for empathy and reassurance from them.

4. Set healthy boundaries: Establishing clear boundaries within your romantic relationships can help create a sense of safety. Clearly express what behaviors are unacceptable to you and make sure to respect yourself enough to enforce those boundaries if they are crossed.

5. Take things at your own pace: It's essential to move forward at a pace that feels comfortable for you. Building trust takes time, so allow yourself to proceed gradually as you develop confidence in your new partner's trustworthiness.

6. Recognize the difference between past and present: While it is understandable to worry about history repeating itself, it's important to remember that each person and relationship is unique. Try not to let past experiences overshadow your ability to see new partners for who they truly are.

7. Focus on building a strong foundation: Instead of dwelling solely on the fear of being hurt again, concentrate on cultivating a mutually respectful and supportive relationship. Invest time in getting to know your partner deeply, building trust through open communication, shared experiences, and consistent actions over time.

8. Seek professional support if needed: If your struggles with trust continue to significantly impact your well-being and ability to form connections, consider seeking the guidance of a mental health professional who can provide additional tools and techniques tailored to your specific circumstances.

Remember that rebuilding trust is a gradual process, so be kind to yourself along the way. Healing takes time, but with patience, self-care, effective communication, and appropriate boundaries, it's possible to regain a sense of trust in romantic relationships.

Piggybacking on the other respondent's suggestions, I also agree that most couples could use more frequent and more bonding communication in their relationships, and this is a GREAT place to get the ball rolling towards reconnecting.Surveying the demographical data on long-term relationships, it's pretty common for couples to start to struggle around the 7-10 year mark and in fact, that's often when first time divorces happen. And for lots of reasons...most of them having something to do with beginning to take one another for granted and no longer doing the little things that nourish the relationship and light our partners up.  Seems like you've encountered this in your own relationship...where he appears to be neglecting your need for emotional connection with him.Doesn't have to be this way though. And from my own personal clinical experience, I can tell you that when even ONE partner is willing to make some small but powerful changes, they can often ripple outward to the other partner and bring about miraculous outcomes! So my encouragement to you is this - if you're still in love with him...even a little bit...and you're down to try something new, there's hope!  As hard as it may be, I would ask you to try and focus on YOUR own side of the street when approaching him. Use an open and curious approach with him. Ask him what he thinks he needs in a marriage. What is it about you he fell in love with? What helps him feel more fulfilled as a man and as a husband? What little things that you have done over the years does he appreciate? Like Sherry said, if you can get him talking, there'll be plenty to work with. We only need a spark to kindle a fire. If he can give you a list, you'll have a blueprint for getting him to reconnect with you and it opens the door for you to offer him little suggestions as well.By the time a couple reaches the point where you're at, there's usually very little fun going on. We've stopped enjoying one another's company. Try and think creatively about some shared experiences he might be willing to do. A picnic? Happy hour? Concerts, museums, cooking class, new sexual behaviors...the list is as infinite as you want it to be! Some of my favorite suggestions for couples looking to understand how they got here and how to build their way out are:"The Secret to Desire in a Long-Term Relationship" (Ted Talk) by Esther Perel"Getting Together & Staying Together: Solving the Mystery of Marriage" by William & Carleen Glasser"Divorce Busting - A Step By Step Approach to Making Your Marriage Loving Again" by Michelle Weiner-Davis"The Relationship Cure: a 5 step Guide to Strengthening your Marriage, Family, and Friendships" by John Gottman & Joan DeClaire"The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work" by John Gottman & Nan Silver"The Five Love Languages" by Gary ChapmanAnd of course, I'd be remiss if I didn't suggest that if you're open to the idea, maybe some individual and/ or couples counseling could be helpful too.My very warmest regards to you,Tamara Powell, LMHC

Begin by describing the situation itself, detailing the emotions and thoughts you had during this period. Aim for around 500 words, incorporating concrete examples to provide clarity.

Reflecting on a recent experience with stress can be helpful in gaining insight into our emotions and thought patterns. It's important to remember that stress is a normal part of life, and we all go through it at different times.

One situation that comes to mind where stress played a significant role was when I had to give a presentation at work. The mere thought of speaking in front of a large audience made me feel anxious and overwhelmed. Leading up to the presentation, my mind was filled with thoughts like "What if I mess up?", "Will people judge me?", and "I'm not good enough for this."

As the day approached, my emotions intensified. I started feeling physically tense, experiencing knots in my stomach and sweaty palms. Fear of failure consumed me, and I found it difficult to focus on anything else. Negative self-talk became a constant companion, fueling my doubts and insecurities.

On the day of the presentation, my nerves were at an all-time high. My heart raced, and I could feel the adrenaline pumping through my veins. Walking into the room, I noticed how crowded it was, which added to my anxieties. As I began speaking, my voice trembled, and I struggled to maintain eye contact with the audience. Thoughts of being judged and criticized flooded my mind, making it hard to express myself clearly.

Despite the challenges, there were a few moments during the presentation where I felt a glimmer of confidence. When I saw some nodding heads and engaged expressions from the listeners, it reassured me that perhaps I wasn't as inadequate as I believed. These positive moments helped alleviate some of the stress momentarily.

Looking back on this experience, it's clear that stress impacted both my emotional and cognitive well-being. Emotionally, I experienced fear, anxiety, and insecurity. Cognitively, my thoughts were predominantly negative and self-doubting. In hindsight, I realize that my self-critical thinking worsened the level of stress I experienced.

To manage stress in similar situations, there are a few strategies that could be helpful. Firstly, practicing relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation can help calm the body and mind before facing a stressful event. Additionally, challenging negative thoughts with more realistic ones can mitigate some of the anxiety and self-doubt.

Preparing thoroughly and visualizing success can also boost confidence while reducing stress. By rehearsing the presentation, seeking feedback from trusted colleagues, and mentally picturing a positive outcome, we can increase our chances of performing well. Moreover, establishing a support system of friends or mentors who can provide encouragement and reassurance can make a significant difference during stressful times.

Lastly, it's important to remember that mistakes happen, and they don't define our worth. Accepting that imperfections are part of being human can alleviate unnecessary pressure and reduce stress levels. Embracing a growth mindset where learning and improvement are valued over perfection can create a healthier perspective on stressful situations.

In conclusion, reflecting on this recent experience has shed light on how stress can impact us emotionally and cognitively. By implementing relaxation techniques, challenging negative thoughts, preparing thoroughly, building a support network, and embracing imperfection, we can better navigate future stressful experiences. Remember, you're not alone in experiencing stress, and developing effective coping mechanisms takes time and practice.

Managing work-related stress can be challenging, but there are effective techniques that can help you cope. Let's explore some strategies together:

1. Prioritize and set boundaries: It's important to prioritize your tasks and set realistic deadlines for yourself. Identify the most crucial tasks and focus on completing them first. Learn to say no when necessary, and establish clear boundaries with your colleagues to avoid feeling overwhelmed.

2. Break tasks into smaller parts: Instead of looking at a project as a whole, break it down into manageable tasks. This can make it feel less daunting and more achievable. Celebrate small victories along the way, as they can boost your motivation and reduce the sense of being overwhelmed.

3. Practice time management: Effective time management can help reduce stress. Consider using techniques like Pomodoro Technique or time blocking to allocate specific periods for work and breaks. Remember to schedule regular breaks to rest and recharge.

4. Develop healthy coping mechanisms: Find healthy ways to relieve stress outside of work. Engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as exercise, hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or practicing mindfulness and deep breathing exercises. These activities can help distract your mind from work-related stressors.

5. Improve sleep hygiene: Establish a relaxing bedtime routine and create an optimal sleep environment. Avoid screens before bed, keep your bedroom quiet and dark, and maintain a consistent sleep schedule. If insomnia persists, consider speaking with a healthcare professional who can provide appropriate guidance.

6. Incorporate physical activity: Regular exercise has been shown to significantly reduce stress levels. Find time each week to engage in activities that get your body moving, whether it's walking, jogging, dancing, or participating in a sport. Physical activity releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters and can alleviate tension headaches and muscle soreness.

7. Seek support: Talking about your job-related stress with trusted friends, family members, or colleagues can provide emotional support. Sometimes, sharing your experiences and concerns with others who understand and empathize can be helpful.

Remember, it's important to take care of yourself both mentally and physically. If you find that work-related stress continues to impact your well-being despite trying these techniques, it may be beneficial to consult with a mental health professional for further guidance tailored to your specific situation.

I have a panic attack at least once a week and suffer from severe anxiety.

I'm sorry you're going through that.  Panic attacks are terrifying.One thing to start with is knowing that panic attacks are not going to hurt you and your anxiety will come down with time.  Fighting that process can sometimes heighten symptoms because your brain wants the message of panic to be heard.  Some of the best ways to counter that message is through focusing on the present moment through sensations or breathing.  Taking deep breaths allows your body and brain to slow down, sending the message that there's no present danger.  Focusing on the present can also send the same message, as anxiety typically throws us into the "what ifs" of the future.  If you search google or pinterest, there are tons of methods you can use for this---some people prefer to focus on colors, shapes, smells, textures, etc., while other prefer to pay attention to internal sensations.  There are also apps that can help with these techniques, such as Calm and Headspace.  They work best when you aren't in a panic attack or when you feel one coming on.  If you are already at the peak of an attack, they can still help, it just may take a bit longer.  Some clients I have like to track their anxiety with a scale system.  Let's say you scale your anxiety at an 8 out of 10, do some breathing exercises for 5 minutes, then scale it again.  It's likely the anxiety decreased, at least to a 7 or 7.5.  Doing this can give you some physical proof that you have some control over your body.  You can also scale it without the breathing to see how it just fluctuates on its own.  Anxiety will always go down and you can see that happening via numbers.  This method will let you see the light at the end of the tunnel.There are other ways that might work for you via a quick google search, or through therapy.  Keep trying new things until you find what works best for you!

When it comes to trauma, especially in the event that it has caused you to develop PTSD, there can be a lot of difficulty in attempting to resolve these issues on your own simply because of how strong your urge to avoid it whenever thoughts of the traumatic experience come up. PTSD is best treated with the help of a mental health professional and if using the Cognitive Processing Approach can be treated in as few as 17 weeks. As for your other concerns, many of these can be treated independently if you have the motivation to manage your way through. Panic attacks and depression, specifically, often respond well to self-help treatment manuals. The Centre for Clinical Interventions is a great online resource for workbooks to help you learn to manage the depression and panic attacks. Whether you decide to work through these concerns on your own or in professional therapy, just know that your panic attacks must be managed prior to addressing your trauma. Hope this is helpful and if you have any other questions don't hesitate to ask.

I've hit my head on walls and floors ever since I was young. I sometimes still do it but I don't exactly know why,    I have anxiety and I had a rough childhood but now I'll start to hit my head and sometimes not realize it but I don't know how to stop or even why I'm doing it.    How can I help myself to change my behavior?

Hello. I have to wonder from a behavioral perspective if what you are doing is useful for you. In other words, does it serve a purpose in some way when you find yourself doing it. Yes, this could well be an expression of anxiety, or maybe some type of coping skill you have developed over the years to deal with stressful situations. Yet it sounds like you have developed a sort of knee-jerk behavioral conditioning that causes you to do this behavior during specific (or perhaps even non-specific) circumstances. Do you think it is a self-soothing behavior? Do you feel good after you have done it? The behavior itself is likely causing some form of slow physical damage, so I would recommend you have yourself checked by a doctor, to rule out any injury. If none exists, this obviously doesn't excuse the behavior, it just says that for the moment luck is on your side.When we do any behavior of any kind, it is good to ask if what we are doing has merit or value. Is the behavior helping us to solve our problem, or is it merely creating yet another problem by doing the behavior in the first place. In the same way that a person might drink excessively because they are stressed and need to cope with some unresolved issue, when they are done drinking the original problem will still likely be there, but now they are intoxicated. No closer to solving the issue. When we deal with things like anxiety or depression, we need to do things that work on dealing with the symptoms, but also get to the root issue that created those feelings and find effective solutions. So the things we do to cope with life events need to not be ones that cause us harm, but rather support us as we move forward and work to deal with what life throws at us.Sometimes seeking support from a friend or a counselor is a good idea. Being given the opportunity to express your feelings about what is going on around you and getting feedback and insight from others is much more effective than actions of self-harm, wouldn't you agree? So I would encourage you to find a counselor or a trusted friend who can help you find positive behaviors you can take to deal with your feelings, as you also work to find the answers to the day to day issues of living a life filled with promise and opportunity.Reach out if you need help...there will likely be a hand there waiting for you.

One suggestion is to start by exploring new activities or hobbies that you haven't tried before. Sometimes, trying something different can help break the cycle of emptiness and bring a sense of fulfillment. It doesn't have to be anything grand or expensive; even small, simple activities can make a difference. For example, going for a walk in nature, trying out a new recipe, or picking up a creative outlet like painting or writing could provide a fresh perspective and potentially ignite a spark of joy.

In social settings, I experience intense anxiety symptoms like sweating, trembling, and a racing heart. It's embarrassing and makes me want to avoid any situation where others might notice my anxiety. How can I manage these physical symptoms?

It can be really challenging to navigate social settings when you experience intense anxiety symptoms like sweating, trembling, and a racing heart. These physical symptoms can indeed feel embarrassing and make you want to avoid situations where others might notice your anxiety. However, there are some strategies that may help you manage these symptoms:

1. Deep breathing exercises: When you start experiencing these physical symptoms, try taking slow, deep breaths. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold it for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This can help regulate your breathing and calm your body down.

2. Progressive muscle relaxation: Tense and relax each muscle group in your body, starting from your toes and working your way up to your head. This technique can help release tension and reduce the physical symptoms of anxiety.

3. Grounding techniques: Focus on your senses to bring yourself back to the present moment. For example, you can name five things you see around you, four things you can touch, three things you hear, two things you smell, and one thing you taste. This can help shift your attention away from the anxiety symptoms and onto your surroundings.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Anxiety often comes with negative thoughts and assumptions about how others perceive us. Take a step back and question the evidence supporting these thoughts. Are there alternative explanations? Challenging and reframing these thoughts can help alleviate some of the anxiety associated with social situations.

5. Gradual exposure: Consider gradually exposing yourself to social situations that trigger your anxiety. Start with smaller, less intimidating gatherings and work your way up at your own pace. Over time, this can help desensitize you to the anxiety-provoking situations.

Remember, managing anxiety symptoms takes time and practice. It's important to be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. If you find that these strategies aren't providing enough relief, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide additional guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

What is the best way to file California State Tax for Spouse Abroad in community property jurisdiction countries like China? The goal is to minimize the tax for community property income.

For resident spouse in California (CA) and non-resident spouse living and working in China, you can file Federal tax jointly and California state tax separately to minimize the community property income. But since both the California state and China are community property jurisdiction, only 50% of the non-resident spouse's income can be exempt from CA state tax, i.e. 100% of the resident spouse's California source income needs to be filed (50% in resident's form 540, and another 50% in non-resident's form 540NR), and 50% of non-resident spouse's foreign income needs to be filed in resident's Form 540. 

Note that Foreign Tax Credit or Exemption cannot be applied to state tax like federal tax.

I hear that you have been struggling with forming and maintaining relationships, both romantic and platonic. It can be difficult when it feels like you are always the one getting left behind or forgotten by the people in your life. This has led you to question if there's something wrong with you or if it's just bad luck. Understandably, you would like to gain more self-confidence and learn how to build healthy relationships that last.

Building and maintaining relationships can indeed be challenging, but it is definitely possible to improve these skills. Here are a few suggestions to help you on this journey:

1. Focus on self-reflection: Take some time to reflect on yourself and your past experiences. Identify any patterns or behaviors that may contribute to relationship challenges. Are there certain communication styles or coping mechanisms that could be affecting your connections with others? Self-awareness can provide valuable insights to work on improving your relationships.

2. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of yourself is crucial for building healthy relationships. Make sure you are setting aside time for activities that bring you joy, practicing self-compassion, and managing stress effectively. When you feel good about yourself, it becomes easier to engage authentically with others.

3. Work on communication skills: Effective communication is key to building strong relationships. Practice active listening, empathy, and expressing your needs and emotions clearly. It may also be helpful to understand non-verbal cues and body language to enhance your interactions with others.

4. Seek common interests: Look for opportunities to connect with others who share similar interests or hobbies. Join clubs, classes, or groups where you can meet people who enjoy the same activities as you do. Shared passions often lay the foundation for meaningful friendships.

5. Set realistic expectations: It's important to recognize that not all relationships will last forever. Some friendships naturally evolve over time, while others come and go. Avoid putting external pressure on yourself to maintain every relationship indefinitely. Instead, focus on nurturing the connections that bring joy and fulfillment to your life.

6. Practice vulnerability: Building lasting relationships often involves being vulnerable with others. While it can feel uncomfortable, opening up and sharing your thoughts and feelings can deepen connections and foster trust. Start by taking small steps in gradually revealing more about yourself to those you trust.

Remember, building healthy relationships is a process that takes time and effort. It's okay to seek support from friends, family, or even online communities along the way. Also, keep in mind that everyone faces challenges in their relationships at times - it doesn't necessarily mean there's something wrong with you. Be patient with yourself and celebrate each step forward on your journey towards forming meaningful and lasting connections.

What is the best way to get from one place to another?

The term "best" is relative to your individual preferences and circumstances. 

In general, how to get from one place to another depends on several key factors, such as the distance between these two places, available methods of transportations, and the amount of money that you are willing to spend. Additional factors to consider are whether you have a preferred method of transportation and how much time you are willing to spend on this trip. Cheaper transportation options may take a longer time. 

The methods of transportation include airplanes, trains, ships or ferries, busses, and cars, but not all locations have all these transportation methods available.

Usually, if the two places are relatively close to each other, a bus or a train may be a good option. If public transportation between these two places is not well established, then a personal car may be a reasonable alternative.

In some circumstances, when the distance between the two place is very short, less than three miles or so, walking may be your best option. This, of course, depends on your ability and willingness to walk that distance.

If the two places are relatively far, usually more than a couple hundred miles, an airplane may be a good option to consider.
Why should people consider going on holiday in Henley on Thames, UK?

Henley on Thames is a village in England 45 minutes west of London by train. Whether you're an avid walker, ale enthusiast, or history buff this small sanctuary on the Thames will surely hold something for you. Touted as one of the oldest market towns in England, Henley has a lively high street and village center. The storefronts include cafes, restaurants, clothing boutiques, art galleries, and antique shops - many are locally owned small businesses. Be sure to check out the award winning butcher, Gabriel Machin, located right on the town square. 

A stroll along the Thames is the perfect after lunch activity. If you head west along the village side of the river, you'll pass the River and Rowing museum. This is an excellent museum showcasing the history of the significance of the Thames in this region, as well as a Wind and the Willows exhibit for children. You can also choose to cross the bridge and walk the historic regatta path along the Thames heading east. This is where university rowing teams congregate every year for the annual regatta in July; this brings in thousands of visitors to the village during the summer months. 

You won't struggle for choice of the towns many historic pubs and restaurants. Enjoy a pint outside on the river deck at the Angel on the Bridge before making you way to one of the towns many restaurant and food options.
