How does a person start the counseling process?

Hello. Counseling often begins way before the client ever actually calls the local therapist. There is often a tipping point in the internal struggle that the client experiences, where they can no longer deal with the issues on their own and thus giving the motivation to seek external help. That said, clients usually go seeking therapists based on what their insurance will cover, or what is likely to be more and more the case in the near future...what they are able to pay for out of pocket. That first phone call to a prospective counselor can often feel like torture, but it doesn't have to stay that way. Counselors are well trained to acknowledge the inherent goodness of all clients, and should be able to see and hear the sense of fear in the client of being judged or put down in some way. The counselor you select should be compassionate, caring, able to join with you on your journey to resolving your issues or concerns, and to do so without negative judgment of you as a person of worth.Once you have found a counselor you want to work with, you would then schedule an appointment to meet. That first session is often very low key. There might be some forms for you to complete, which will help the counselor address your concerns and learn a bit more about you. The counselor will typically provide you with what we generally call in the profession a professional disclosure or practice statement. This document (which may be several pages long) usually outlines the counselor's credentials; practice rules; forms of payment; office hours; emergency contact details; and confidentiality guidelines under state and federal law, among other details. All of this benefits you as the client, so that you are well informed and can focus your attention on why you are meeting with the counselor.In the first session, it is absolutely okay to be nervous. Here's a really big secret (which is important to keep in mind as counseling begins): Counselors are often as nervous (if not more) to meet a new client, as the client is to meet their new counselor. It's true. We as professionals are trying to put our best foot forward to impress you with our awesome counseling skills. While simultaneously hiding all the troubling unwanted issues that we ourselves have in our life too, and being worried that we might not know if we can help the client sitting in front of us. What makes it even more challenging, is that counselors are often put on a giant pedestal of perfection by clients (all while we as counselors tend to look at it like we're standing on a three legged stool). This is normal for us when seen from the eyes of the client. Counselors and clients are both human, and we both make mistakes. Coming from that place of understanding, might bring a sense of ease to both the client and the therapist as they seek to work together. Part of this perception of perfection held by clients toward counselors, is that the skills of the counselor might look like they have all the answers. We honestly do not, plain and simple. Counselors come from life experiences (where they might be farther down on life's road than you); they hold completion of various forms of training; and have advanced education. Yet we are in the end, imperfect beings struggling to help imperfect people. This makes it easier to be compassionate to new clients walking through our door with the hope that we will receive that same compassion in return. Very often, we can find ourselves reflected in our clients' lives with their struggles and can become more effective at helping if we have resolved similar issues in our own life. So as you begin to seek out a therapist, try looking for one who is aware of their own life issues and is actively working on them too. Someone who can meet you where you are at emotionally and can understand your sense of your struggle that you are facing at the present moment. That counselor may be a good example for you as you enter into therapy and build your own strength, and thus begin dealing with the issues more effectively you bring up in therapy.

I'm having relationship problems and I want to fix them to make things right before I lose her. How can I learn how to listen and get myself together?

Thanks for your question. Becoming a good listener is an essential piece in being a better communicator. Being an effective communicator will almost always improve the quality of your relationships. What stands in your way of listening to her? Do you find yourself becoming defensive when she brings up issues? Do you often find yourself thinking of what you want to say next? Do you take her words personally, preventing you from having the ability to problem solve?Here are some tips that may help you with being a better listener:1. Concentrate on what you are hearing, not on what you will say next.2. Ask questions if you need clarification or don't understand.3. Summarize what you're hearing after every couple of minutes to make sure that you're not missing anything.4. Ask your partner what she needs from you. Is she expecting advice or does she simply need to vent?5. Keep eye contact and avoid using non-verbal cues that demonstrate defensiveness or irritation such as eye rolling or crossing your arms.6. Remember that it's okay to disagree and, if this is the case, then decide as a team, how you want to move forward.I hope this helps. Good luck to you!

My brother has been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and has not been taking his medication. He's been using methamphetamine and alcohol and was found sleeping naked in my step mom driveway in 12 degree weather.
   I was adopted in by his dad (who just passed) and his mother will not Get involved because she's afraid of financial responsibility.    Do I have the rights to be able to sign my brother into mentalhealth facility?

Hello, My heart goes out to you, your brother, and your family, dealing with a very painful and difficult situation. In New York, you can't institutionalize someone else directly. You can, however, call the police or EMS. If they agree that he would benefit from hospitalization (and it sounds like they would), he can be held in the hospital for up to 72 hours, whether he agrees or not. Some hospitals will not hold a person that long, in spite of what we might want. I have seen many patients in and out of hospitals countless times, and it has been my experience that it can be extremely difficult to hold a person long enough to achieve good stability and an appropriate after-care plan. Hospitals in NYC tend to take a "patch and release" approach more often than I would like. It's been my experience that family makes a difference. Assertive, knowledgeable, persistent family can improve the quality of your loved one's care. Hospitals are highly pressured to discharge people quickly but they can not discharge a homeless person without someplace to go. If your family is willing to accept your brother, that will be the path of least resistance for the hospital. If the family refuses, they will be forced to find another path for him. You can also pressure the hospital to refer to rehab after psychiatrically stablized (which may only take a few days) and that may give your brother more time to begin making clear-headed decisions. If your brother has a psychiatrist, that person should be actively involved. I had a patient patched-and-released three times, in spite of my advocacy and him literally begging to remain and stop his voices. We finally got a 90 day hospitalization because I strong-armed his psychiatrist into demanding that the hospital stabilize his patient.  If your brother has a history of non--compliance with oral medications, you can push the hospital for injection, which again will help your brother stay stable for longer. Best wishes to you and your family.

First off, it is great that you recognize that some changes need to be made. It is also really good that you understand where the source of your anxiety and stress comes from. Fortunately there are many self help books and internet sources that provide free tools to help you cope with life's obstacles, including anger management. There are several strategies that you can try to help control your anger, but the ones that I would recomend first are the following:1. Try a different way of communicating with your parents. Since arguing with them is a great source of anger for you, learning more effective ways of communicating with them will likely be of great benefit. Choose a time to talk with them about "heated issues" when everyone is calm and emotions are not heightened. Use "I phrases" by telling them how the arguments effect you, as opposed to placing blame on them. Validate what you hear your parents say in order to allow them to know that you understand their point of view.2. When you feel yourself becoming angry, take a break. Simply excuse yourself from the situation, find a quiet place to be by yourself, and do some deep breathing. Close your eyes, slowly count to four as you inhale, and exhale even slower, counting to 6. Focus on nothing except for your breathing and do this for 5 minutes.3. Stop any negative thoughts in their tracks. Often times when we get upset, we catastrophize and do not see things clearly. When you catch yourself thinking negatively stop the thoughts and ask yourself if your thinking is logical and rational. If you cannot find much or any evidence that your thoughts are valid, then let them go and replace them with realistic, logical thoughts.4. Finally, find a friend or someone to talk to and/or keep a journal. Keeping your emotions to yourself will not help you. It's important to hear that you've been experiencing severe anxiety lately and that it's impacting various areas of your life. Your main goal for counseling is to identify the triggers of your anxiety and develop coping mechanisms to regain control. Let's explore some recommendations and approaches for reducing anxiety symptoms.

To begin, the physical sensations you described, like a pit in your stomach, trembling, dizziness, and nausea are common manifestations of anxiety. Many people can relate to these experiences, so know that you're not alone. Identifying triggers is an excellent first step towards managing anxiety effectively.

Based on what you shared, situations involving public speaking, tight deadlines, and social gatherings tend to heighten your anxiety levels significantly. It's valuable insight to recognize these specific triggers. During our sessions, we can work together to delve deeper into each trigger, understanding any underlying beliefs or thoughts associated with them.

Regarding your childhood environment and past traumatic event, it seems plausible that they have contributed to your current feelings of unease. We will explore these factors further to gain a better understanding of how they may be impacting your anxiety. By identifying any negative thought patterns that developed as a result, we can then work on challenging and replacing them with more positive and realistic ones.

In terms of therapy techniques for individuals struggling with anxiety, there are several evidence-based approaches we can consider. Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is often effective in treating anxiety by examining and modifying unhelpful thinking patterns and behaviors associated with anxiety. I've always been a bit of a worrier, but lately, my anxiety has taken over everything. My mind constantly races with irrational thoughts and worries. For example, last week I was supposed to meet friends for dinner, but I couldn't stop thinking that something awful will happen on the way there. I ended up canceling plans because I couldn't shake off the intense fear. These worrying thoughts seem to be taking control of my life, and I don't know how to make them stop. I really need help managing my anxiety.

One approach that can be helpful in managing anxiety is through cognitive-behavioral techniques. These are strategies that focus on the connection between our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. It seems like you're experiencing a lot of anxious thoughts, which may be contributing to your intense fear and the impact it has on your daily life.

To start addressing this, one technique you can try is called cognitive restructuring. This involves challenging and reframing irrational thoughts or worries. When you catch yourself thinking something negative or catastrophic, take a moment to pause and ask yourself if there is any evidence supporting these thoughts. Often, we realize that our worries are not based on facts but rather on fears and assumptions. By actively questioning and replacing these irrational beliefs with more rational ones, it can help reduce the power of those worrying thoughts.

Another useful strategy is relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation. These practices can help calm your mind and body when you start feeling overwhelmed by anxiety. Incorporating them into your daily routine, even for just a few minutes a day, can have a positive impact on managing anxiety overall.

Additionally, engaging in regular physical exercise can play a significant role in reducing anxiety symptoms. Exercise releases endorphins, which act as natural mood boosters and stress relievers. Finding an activity you enjoy, whether it's walking, yoga, dancing, or anything else that gets you moving, can serve as a healthy outlet for releasing tension and improving your overall well-being.

It may also be helpful to establish a consistent sleep schedule and prioritize quality rest. Lack of sleep can worsen anxiety symptoms, making it harder to cope with worrisome thoughts. Set a bedtime routine that promotes relaxation and creates a conducive environment for sleep.

Lastly, consider seeking support from trusted friends, family members, or even online communities who may be going through similar experiences. Talking about your anxieties and worries with others can provide a sense of validation and understanding. Sometimes, simply venting or receiving an outside perspective can offer relief and potentially open up new ways of managing your anxiety.

Remember, it takes time and patience to develop effective coping mechanisms for anxiety. Be kind to yourself during this process and celebrate small victories along the way. If you find that these techniques are not bringing the desired results, don't hesitate to reach out to a mental health professional who can provide further guidance tailored to your specific needs.

Hello, and thank you for your question. The question about
whether or not to cheat is based on personal values that can only be answered
by you. However, here are a few things to consider and questions to ask
yourself to help you find your answer:
1.    
Do you feel like you are violating your own
values or morals? This is important, because we all have different values and
morals surrounding sex, love, and monogamy. If you value monogamous
relationships and find yourself cheating on your partner, then you may feel
like you are living in contradiction to your values, and most people are not
happy when they do that. However, if monogamy is not something you value, then
perhaps it is time to re-evaluate the relationship and determine if it is still
right for you. Not all people want monogamous relationships, and that
is alright. Finally, if you value your husband’s feelings and know that the
affairs would hurt him, then your behaviors may again be in contrast to your
own values. That can only be determined by you. 
2.      Based on how you describe your relationship, it
sounds like you are not very satisfied with the way it is.  From the outside, it looks like the affairs
are a way to “get even” with your husband or to feel better after an argument. This
is something that can happen when mutual respect starts to fade in a
relationship and gets replaced with contempt. We can simply stop caring about
how our actions hurt each other, or potentially hurt each other. Perhaps the
question to ask here is, when you look out toward the future with your husband,
is this the pattern that you want to keep? The pattern of very little sex,
argument, and then satisfying the pain or dissatisfaction with affairs. 
 3.      What are your goals for this relationship? If we
start to become disconnected in a relationship, we can begin to do things on
autopilot. Get up, get the kids up, go to work, come home, and go to bed. None
of which requires any intimacy at all. Are you still able to see the hopes and
dreams you once had for this relationship?
 4.     
Have you considered seeking marital counseling? Not
having affairs won’t actually fix the part of the relationship that is leading
you to have them. If there is something broken, it sometimes requires some help
to get it fixed. 
 Hopefully these questions and thoughts will help you come to
some kind of conclusion about what is right for you and your relationship. I certainly
wish you well. 
 Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

When faced with uncertainty or change, my anxiety tends to skyrocket. It's as if my mind gets stuck in an endless loop of "what ifs" and catastrophic thinking. This makes decision-making incredibly difficult, as I fear making the wrong choice and facing dire consequences. I'd like to develop strategies to navigate these situations more effectively.

It can be challenging when anxiety takes over and makes decision-making difficult. The good news is that there are strategies you can develop to navigate these situations more effectively. Here are some suggestions:

1. Start by acknowledging your anxiety: Recognize that it's normal to feel anxious in uncertain or changing circumstances. Instead of trying to suppress or ignore your anxiety, acknowledge its presence and accept it as a natural response.

2. Challenge catastrophic thinking: When your mind gets stuck in a loop of "what ifs" and worst-case scenarios, try to challenge those thoughts. Ask yourself if there is any evidence to support these catastrophic outcomes. Often, our fears exaggerate the potential negative consequences. Remind yourself that uncertainty doesn't always lead to disaster.

3. Practice mindfulness: Mindfulness techniques can help ground you in the present moment and reduce anxiety. Take a few minutes each day to focus on your breath or engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation. This can help break the cycle of rumination and allow for clearer thinking.

4. Break decisions into smaller steps: Sometimes, making big decisions can feel overwhelming. To make the process more manageable, break it down into smaller steps. Focus on one aspect at a time and gather information or seek advice before moving forward. This approach can alleviate some of the pressure and give you a sense of control.

5. Seek support from trusted individuals: It can be helpful to discuss your concerns with someone you trust, such as a friend, family member, or mentor. Sharing your thoughts and getting an outside perspective can provide valuable insights and reassurance.

6. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of your physical and emotional well-being is crucial during times of uncertainty. Make sure to prioritize self-care activities that help you relax and recharge. This may include exercise, hobbies, spending time in nature, or engaging in activities that bring you joy.

Remember, developing new strategies takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself as you navigate through these challenging moments. With persistence and the right tools, you can learn to manage your anxiety and make decisions more effectively.

One of the most difficult challenges we face is not being heard! It is incredibly frustrating and hurtful when others, especially parents, do not listen. While your parents surely love you and want to understand you, it may be difficult for them to fully understand your feelings and experiences. They are quite a bit older and have likely not dealt with some of the struggles that you face. I would suggest communicating your feelings to them about not being heard. Talk to them during a non-emotional moment when the discussion is not already heated. In other words, do not wait until an argument ensues to have an open discussion with them about how you are feeling. Prepare them by asking them what time is good for them to talk. Let them know you have something important to get off your chest. Try and avoid using exaggerated or extreme language such as "you NEVER listen," "you ALWAYS say..." and stray away from placing blame. Instead of beginning your statements with "you" try using "I" by letting them know how their behavior effects you. Finally, let them know that they are important to you and that having their trust and support would mean a lot to you. Perhaps giving them suggestions as to what you wish for and would like to see change would help them to better understand.I would also suggest that you seek guidance from a therapist, teacher, or school counselor if possible. Most schools have counseling resources on sight in which a trained professional is available to talk with students looking for help.Best of luck to you.

Anxiety has been paralyzing me lately, preventing me from living a fulfilling life. Through counseling, I want to address the root causes of my anxiety and learn coping techniques to reduce its intensity and frequency.

It sounds like anxiety has been having a significant impact on your life lately, making it difficult for you to engage in activities and find fulfillment. It's great that you're considering counseling as a way to address the root causes of your anxiety and learn coping techniques.

To start addressing the root causes, therapy can provide a safe space for exploration and understanding. A therapist can help you identify any underlying issues or past experiences that may contribute to your anxiety. Through open and honest discussions, you can gain insights into your thoughts, emotions, and behaviors, which can be helpful in identifying patterns and triggers.

In addition, therapy can help you develop effective coping techniques to reduce the intensity and frequency of your anxiety. These techniques can vary depending on what works best for you, but some commonly used strategies include deep breathing exercises, mindfulness practices, progressive muscle relaxation, and reframing negative thoughts. Your therapist can work with you to tailor these techniques to fit your specific needs.

It's important to remember that progress takes time, so be patient with yourself throughout this journey. It can also be helpful to communicate openly with your therapist about your goals and expectations to ensure they align with yours.

Outside of therapy, self-care is crucial when managing anxiety. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as hobbies, exercise, spending time in nature, or practicing meditation, can help promote overall well-being and reduce stress levels. Additionally, maintaining a healthy lifestyle by getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and managing caffeine intake can positively affect your emotional well-being.

Remember, everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, and what works for one person may not work for another. Keep an open mind and be willing to try different strategies until you find what helps you manage your anxiety effectively.

I hope this guidance and suggestions are beneficial to you as you embark on your journey towards reducing the impact of anxiety on your life. Take small steps each day, and with time, you can find relief and live a more fulfilling life.

1. Recognize and acknowledge your stress: Start by acknowledging the impact that losing your job has had on your life and how it has contributed to your stress levels. Understanding the sources of your stress can be an essential first step in effectively managing it.

2. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to prioritize self-care activities and establish routines that promote physical and mental well-being. In a way, yes, you have separation anxiety. It's normal in a relationship for us to slow down a bit with the attachment behaviours that establish and deepen love and connection. So, just because your boyfriend isn't talking as much or keeping you up-to-date doesn't necessarily mean what you fear it means...that he's forgotten about you or loves you less. It could mean quite the opposite...that he's focused on being successful in his new job and impressing you. He may think he's loving you more, but you feel loved less. You have two jobs to do here. The first is to manage your anxiety by "talking back" to the thoughts it puts into your head. It sounds like "It's normal to be insecure, but I have tons of evidence that he loves me and that I mean the world to him..." Find that evidence that helps you refute what anxiety is trying to claim. The second part of your job is to let him know what you need. You need more affection and connection during this period when he's away (more texts, phone calls, information). It's okay to want that, and I am sure he will be relieved to know exactly what he can do to help you feel secure and calm when he's away.

In terms of treatment options, I'm curious about whether cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) could be beneficial for managing my anxiety. How does CBT work, and what strategies does it involve? I'm also interested in exploring any potential side effects of medication for anxiety if that becomes a consideration.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) can indeed be beneficial for managing anxiety. It is a type of therapy that focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and behaviors that contribute to anxiety. CBT works by helping you develop healthier coping mechanisms and more positive ways of thinking.

In terms of strategies, CBT typically involves several components. One common technique is called cognitive restructuring, where you learn to challenge and replace negative thoughts with more realistic and balanced ones. This can help reduce anxiety by shifting your perspective and reducing the power of anxious thoughts.

Another strategy often used in CBT is exposure therapy. This involves gradually facing feared situations or triggers in a safe and controlled manner, allowing you to build confidence and reduce anxiety over time. By repeatedly exposing yourself to these situations, you can learn that they are not as threatening as you initially believed.

Additionally, CBT may involve teaching relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises or progressive muscle relaxation. These techniques can help you manage physical symptoms of anxiety, such as rapid heartbeat or tense muscles.

Regarding medication for anxiety, it's important to consult with a healthcare professional who can provide personalized advice based on your specific situation. They will consider factors such as the severity of your anxiety, any underlying conditions, and potential side effects of medications. Medication can be an option if other treatments like therapy alone aren't sufficient, but it's crucial to have a thorough discussion with a medical expert to weigh the benefits and risks.

Remember, everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, so what works for one person may not work for another. It's essential to find the right treatment approach that suits your individual needs. If you're considering CBT or medication, I encourage you to reach out to a mental health professional who can guide you through the process and help determine the best course of action for you.

Stress has been weighing me down heavily and I can't seem to catch a break. Work demands are increasing by the day, leaving me drained physically and mentally. The long hours and high pressure take a toll on my well-being. To add to it, I've been having trouble juggling my personal life and responsibilities. It feels like everything is collapsing around me, and I need someone to guide me through managing stress effectively.

Finding ways to manage stress effectively can be crucial for maintaining your well-being, especially when facing increasing work demands and struggling to balance personal responsibilities. Here are some suggestions that may help:

1. Prioritize self-care: Set aside time each day to engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation. This could include hobbies, exercise, or simply taking a break to unwind.

2. Establish boundaries: It's important to set clear limits in both your personal and professional life. Communicate openly with your colleagues and loved ones about your needs and limitations, and don't hesitate to say no if you feel overwhelmed.

3. Break tasks into manageable steps: When faced with mounting responsibilities, it can be helpful to break them down into smaller, actionable tasks. This can make them feel more achievable and prevent overwhelm.

4. Seek support: Remember that you don't have to face everything alone. Reach out to friends, family, or trusted individuals who can provide a listening ear, emotional support, or practical assistance.

5. Practice stress management techniques: Explore different techniques such as deep breathing exercises, mindfulness meditation, or progressive muscle relaxation. These practices can help reduce anxiety and promote overall well-being.

6. Time management strategies: Consider implementing effective time management techniques, such as creating schedules or using productivity apps, to better prioritize tasks and allocate time efficiently.

7. Take breaks during the workday: Even short breaks throughout the day can help recharge your energy and enhance focus. Use these moments to step away from your workstation, engage in physical activity, or practice relaxation techniques.

8. Stay connected with loved ones: Maintaining social connections is important for emotional well-being. Make an effort to nurture relationships with friends and family, whether through regular phone calls, video chats, or meeting up in person when possible.

9. Unplug and disconnect: Limit exposure to stressful stimuli by setting boundaries around technology use. Create designated screen-free times or spaces to allow for mental detox and rest.

10. Consider professional support: If stress continues to feel overwhelming or is affecting your daily functioning, it can be beneficial to seek guidance from a qualified mental health professional who can provide personalized strategies and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember that managing stress effectively takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself as you explore different techniques and find what works best for you.

What is EFTPOS?

Electronic funds transfer at point of sale, or EFTPOS, is an electronic payment system involving electronic funds transfers based on the use of payment cards, such as debit or credit cards, at payment terminals located at points of sale. EFTPOS technology was developed during the 1980s. In Australia and New Zealand, it is also the brand name of a specific system used for such payments; these systems are mainly country-specific and do not interconnect. In Singapore, it is known as NETS.

Debit and credit cards are embossed plastic cards complying with ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 standard. The cards have an embossed bank card number conforming with the ISO/IEC 7812 numbering standard.

I've been feeling really overwhelmed and stressed lately. It seems like everything is happening all at once, and I'm struggling to keep up with my responsibilities. I hope to find ways to manage this stress and prevent it from taking over my life.

Feeling overwhelmed and stressed can be tough to handle, especially when it seems like everything is piling up all at once. However, there are ways you can manage your stress and regain control over your life. Here are a few suggestions that might help:

1. Prioritize and set realistic goals: Make a list of your responsibilities and prioritize them based on their importance. Break down larger tasks into smaller, more manageable ones. Setting achievable goals will give you a sense of accomplishment and ease some of the pressure.

2. Practice self-care: Taking care of yourself physically, mentally, and emotionally is crucial during times of stress. Make sure to engage in activities that bring you joy, such as hobbies or spending time with loved ones. Additionally, try incorporating relaxation techniques into your routine, such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or practicing mindfulness.

3. Establish boundaries: It's essential to set boundaries and learn to say no when necessary. Overcommitting yourself can lead to increased stress and a feeling of being overwhelmed. Learn to prioritize your own well-being by recognizing your limits and giving yourself permission to decline certain obligations or delegate tasks to others.

4. Seek support: Connecting with others who may be experiencing similar feelings can provide reassurance and perspective. Reach out to trusted friends or family members and share your concerns with them. Sometimes, simply talking about what we're going through can alleviate stress.

5. Take breaks: Remember to take regular breaks throughout the day, even if just for a few minutes. Stepping away from your responsibilities allows you to recharge and clear your mind. Engaging in activities like going for a short walk, listening to music, or practicing deep breathing exercises can help you relax and refocus.

6. Practice time management: Creating a schedule or a daily routine can help you stay organized and ensure you allocate enough time for each task without feeling overwhelmed. Prioritize important commitments, but also make sure to include time for self-care and relaxation.

7. Challenge negative thoughts: During times of stress, it's common to have negative thoughts that contribute to feeling overwhelmed. Try to identify any negative or unrealistic thinking patterns you may be experiencing. Replace them with more positive and realistic thoughts. Reframing your mindset can help reduce stress levels and improve your overall well-being.

Remember, managing stress is an ongoing process, and it may take some trial and error to find what works best for you. If your stress continues to persist or intensify despite these strategies, don't hesitate to reach out to a mental health professional who can provide additional support tailored to your needs.

Crying is a natural process when you talk about upsetting things especially in therapy when you are opening up and being so vulnerable. I suggest that you consider how you would feel/respond to someone that was confiding to you and they began to cry. If you felt concerned, supportive and empathetic then you know exactly how us therapists feel when our clients are emotional in sessions. I suggest that you think of times where you have cried and how you felt at that time in public and what would have helped to make you feel less uncomfortable during your tears. I think of crying like any other natural reaction of our body such as sneezing, laughing, coughing. You can't help but do those things and most people won't really judge negatively if you do it in public. Similarly, crying is our body's reaction when we are emotional whether it is tears of joy, from a hilarious joke or from being upset. If you are very uncomfortable about crying but willing to start therapy perhaps you can ask the therapist if you can turn your chair around if you begin crying. Every time I have to speak in public or present something at work, I experience extreme anxiety. My heart pounds, my hands shake, and my mind goes blank. This fear of public speaking has held me back in my career and prevents me from pursuing opportunities for growth. I want to overcome this anxiety and gain the confidence to express myself without fear.

It can be challenging to experience extreme anxiety when speaking in public or presenting at work. The physical symptoms you described, such as a pounding heart, shaking hands, and a blank mind, are common reactions to fear and stress. It's understandable that this fear of public speaking has had an impact on your career and prevented you from pursuing opportunities for growth.

To overcome this anxiety and gain confidence in expressing yourself without fear, there are several strategies you can try:

1. Preparation: One effective way to reduce anxiety is through thorough preparation. Take the time to research and gather information about the topic you will be speaking about. Practice your presentation multiple times, both alone and in front of trusted friends or family members. This will help you become more familiar with the material and increase your confidence.

2. Deep breathing exercises: When you feel anxious, take slow, deep breaths. Focus on inhaling deeply through your nose and exhaling slowly through your mouth. Deep breathing can help calm your nervous system and reduce physical symptoms of anxiety.

3. Positive self-talk: Replace negative thoughts with positive affirmations. Remind yourself that you are capable and prepared. Repeat phrases like "I am confident" or "I have valuable insights to share." By shifting your mindset to a more positive one, you can build self-assurance and reduce anxiety.

4. Gradual exposure: Consider starting small by practicing public speaking in low-pressure situations. For example, you could join a local Toastmasters group or participate in small group discussions where you gradually increase your comfort level. With each successful experience, your confidence will grow, making it easier to tackle larger speaking engagements.

5. Seek support: Don't hesitate to reach out to supportive friends, family members, or colleagues who can provide encouragement and constructive feedback. Sometimes having someone in your corner can make all the difference in boosting your confidence.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself and celebrate even the smallest victories along the way. With consistent effort and these strategies, you can gradually overcome your fear of public speaking and gain the confidence to express yourself without fear.

Managing overwhelming feelings of anxiety can be challenging, but there are strategies you can learn to help cope with them. Taking a step-by-step approach may be helpful:

1. Deep breathing exercises: When you notice your heart racing or feeling overwhelmed, try taking slow, deep breaths. Focus on your breath as it enters and leaves your body. This technique can help calm your nervous system.

2. Grounding techniques: Engaging your senses can bring your attention back to the present moment. Try focusing on something around you, like the texture of an object, the sound of birds chirping, or the taste of something pleasant. This can redirect your mind from worrying about what might happen in the future.

3. Progressive muscle relaxation: Tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body can promote relaxation and reduce physical tension. Start at your toes and work your way up to your head, tensing and releasing each area for a few seconds.

4. Self-care activities: Incorporate regular self-care activities into your routine. Engaging in hobbies, exercise, mindfulness practices, or spending time with loved ones can help reduce anxiety levels over time.

5. Identifying triggers and challenging negative thoughts: Take note of situations or thoughts that trigger your anxiety. When these arise, challenge any irrational or negative thoughts by questioning their validity or considering alternative perspectives.

6. Seeking support: It's important to have a solid support system. Reach out to friends, family, or online communities who understand what you're going through. Sharing your experiences and receiving support can provide comfort and reassurance.

7. Establishing a routine: Creating structure in your daily life can help manage anxiety. Setting small goals, prioritizing tasks, and maintaining a consistent sleep schedule can contribute positively to your overall well-being.

2. Set realistic goals: It's important to set achievable goals for yourself. Don't put too much pressure on yourself to immediately jump back into all the activities you once enjoyed. Start with something you feel comfortable with and gradually increase the level of difficulty as you start feeling better.

3. Seek support: Reach out to someone you trust, such as a close friend or family member, and let them know what you're going through. Having someone who understands and supports you can make a big difference. They may also be able to offer assistance or accompany you during activities until you regain your confidence.

4. Prioritize self-care: Take care of yourself physically and emotionally. Make sure you're getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and engaging in activities that promote relaxation and well-being. This could include things like taking walks in nature, practicing mindfulness or meditation, or pursuing hobbies that bring you peace and happiness.

5. Consider professional help: If your depression symptoms persist or worsen, it might be beneficial to seek professional help from a mental health therapist or counselor. They can provide guidance tailored to your specific situation and help you develop coping strategies to manage your depression more effectively.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, and recovery takes time. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. You deserve support and understanding as you navigate through these challenges.

How does a person start the counseling process?

Great question. The decision to pursue therapy can be a very difficult one and the fact that there seem to be so many profiles that you have to wade through can be particularly daunting. Here's what I suggest to make the process a bit easier: 1) Narrow down your preferred geographical area. Are you in a rural, suburban, or urban environment? If it's either of the latter two, you'll probably have a mental health professional close by. Decide now if it's important to you that their office be within walking or short driving distance. 2) Decide if you need it to be covered by your insurance. You'll have more options if you're willing to pay out of pocket and get reimbursed by your insurance, but more and more people are accepting insurance these days. 3) Find someone whose profile has the key words that you're looking for. If you're struggling with traumatic flashbacks, make sure they have "trauma" or something along those lines in their profile.4) Make sure they have a friendly and professional picture. This is small, but this detail shows that they really care about how they present to the world. 5) Come up with a list of about 3 people and rank them from most appealing to least. Set up an appointment with the person who seems like the best fit and give it a try for the first session. You'll know by the end of it if it's a good fit.It can be scary, but finding the perfect fit makes it so worth it. Good luck!

I've been experiencing a lot of stress and anxiety in relation to my upcoming exams. My main goal for this counseling session is to learn effective stress management techniques to help me cope with the pressure and perform better academically. The thoughts of failure and disappointing my parents have been consuming me, leaving me feeling overwhelmed and unable to concentrate. Just yesterday, I had a panic attack while studying where my heart raced, I felt shortness of breath, and experienced trembling hands. It lasted for about 30 minutes until I was able to calm down. These symptoms occur frequently during stressful situations and really hinder my ability to focus and retain information. Furthermore, the constant need to achieve perfection has left me feeling exhausted, leading to difficulty sleeping and loss of appetite. 

I would like to know if you have any strategies for managing test anxiety specifically. How can I break the cycle of negative thoughts and replace them with more positive ones? Can counseling help me improve my performance and overall well-being during such stressful periods?

When it comes to managing test anxiety and the stress that comes with upcoming exams, there are some effective strategies that might help you cope better. One technique you could try is deep breathing exercises. When you notice yourself starting to feel overwhelmed or anxious, take a moment to focus on your breath. Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of four, hold your breath for a count of four, and then exhale through your mouth for a count of four. Repeat this several times until you start to feel more calm and centered.

Another strategy that can be helpful is to challenge negative thoughts and replace them with more positive ones. Whenever you catch yourself thinking that you will fail or disappoint your parents, try to counter those thoughts with more realistic and supportive statements. For example, remind yourself of previous successes or think about specific steps you can take to prepare for the exam. It may also be helpful to write down these positive affirmations or repeat them out loud to reinforce their impact.

In addition to these techniques, it's important to establish a structured study routine that includes regular breaks. Studying for long periods without taking breaks can actually lead to decreased concentration and retention. Consider breaking your study sessions into smaller chunks and incorporating enjoyable activities during your breaks, such as going for a walk or engaging in a hobby you love.

Regarding your question about whether counseling can help improve your performance and overall well-being during stressful periods like this, counseling can definitely be beneficial. A counselor can provide support, guidance, and assistance in developing personalized coping strategies tailored to your unique situation. They can help you explore any underlying factors contributing to your stress and anxiety, and work with you to develop healthier patterns of thinking and behavior.

I was raped a couple months ago, Since then, along with other unfortunately events that have occurred, I have been having trouble feeling emotions. It's almost as if I'm a sociopath lacking any feeling. What can I do to change this?

I'm so sorry you've been hurt.  It's very normal to stop feeling emotions as a way to protect yourself after experiencing a traumatic event.  You can think of it as emotional shock-- you experienced something that was so awful that you have numbed yourself (mind and body) as a way to stop the emotional and physical pain of the event.  It's actually pretty amazing that our selves know how to do this automatically.  And, I hear you saying that you'd like to get some feeling back now.So here are some ideas for how you can change this:I think it would be a great idea to find an experienced therapist you like and trust and/or a good support group so that you can have some allies as you go through this process.  You also could try journaling.  If you're not sure what to write then check out this list of prompts to get you started (it's for teachers, but I really like it).  There's also art journaling.  Pinterest has lots of suggestions.Meditation could be useful.  There are lots of apps available that offer guided meditations.Yoga, tai chi, or chi gong might also help.I have lots of other ideas, but without knowing more about you I'm reluctant to make suggestions that could accidentally make you feel worse.  IThis protective mechanism of numbing yourself kicked in for a good reason and as you get your feelings back, you may find some pretty challenging reactions coming up.  I guess my final piece of advice to is encourage you to trust yourself and gently go at your own pace in your healing.  I hope this was helpful.

I need help dealing with stress. How can I handle it all and feel less stressed out?

There are many causes for feeling stressed out. Between a demanding job, family responsibilities, and everything else that can come up, stress becomes more and more part of our everyday life. One of the best ways to combat the toxic effects of stress on our bodies, social lives, and overall well being is to engage in self-care. But not the self-care that most people think of like vacations or massages. The best self-care is the kind that helps you live the life that you already have rather than escape it. You see, the reason why vacations and massages don't work long term in reducing stress is that they allow you to escape from what is causing the stress without truly fixing it so you just return to what already stressed you out. So, instead you need to find ways to help live with the stressors that you already have. They can be things like creating a more manageable schedule, introducing healthy eating or exercising, financial planning, and even learning a few simple relaxation skills. The key to combatting stress is to make small but consistent changes to your life so that it becomes more manageable and more enjoyable.

My friend is abusing her prescription medicine. Even though she told me she didn't have any more pills, I found she has prescriptions for anxiety medications.

Hello! Thank you for your question. I have a worked with many people who have become addicted to benzodiazepines, like Clonazepam. It is a difficult road for people who are trying to become clean. It is also a very difficult road for those who love the person and are trying to be supportive. During those times, it is important to remember to take care of yourself, too. As for taking your friend's pills, my concern would be the legal ramifications that you could face should you ever be caught with someone else's prescription medication, and especially these types of medications. Our laws have become much more strict surrounding prescription drug sales and possession due to the increase in prescription drug abuse. In addition, people who are in active addiction are likely to find some other means to get their drug, so it would do little to help the overall problem. I don't know about your friend's family situation, but they may be a better route to take if you are concerned about your friend. They may already be involved, but with your help you may be able to convince your friend to go to treatment willingly. That is usually better. In many states, there are also involuntary committal processes where a person's family may be able to convince a court to force the person into treatment. This varies from state to state. If your friend's family is not aware of this option, it may be something to look into. It usually does take a relative, or a medical provider, to begin this process if it is available. I hope this was helpful, and I wish you and your friend well. Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

There are several reasons for a counselor to decide to end counseling.  A major reason to end counseling is if the counselor feels that he or she does not have the skills or experience to work with the client.  This may happen during the intake process or after working with the client for some time.  If the clinician feels that the client is not benefitting from the therapy, it is ethical to suggest that the client terminate the therapy.  The process of termination must not injure the client and, if necessary, the clinician may need to refer the client to other treatment modalities.  Another reason to terminate working with a client is if the client needs a higher level of care.  If the client has a crisis or is at risk of hurting himself or someone else, he or she may need a higher level of care.  In this circumstance, the clinician may need to involve outside services such as a crisis unit.  A third reason to terminate with a client is if the clinician feels that he or she cannot remain professional with the client relationship.  For example, if the issues that the client is working on bring up something significant for the clinician and the clinician feels that he is unable to separate that from the professional relationship.  In this instance, the clinician should refer the client to another therapist.  Finally, if the client has reached her goals for therapy and no longer needs treatment, the clinician and client should terminate treatment.

The pain associated with this decision is immense, both emotionally and logistically. I want assistance in navigating this process as smoothly as possible while prioritizing everyone's well-being.

Navigating the end of a long-term relationship can indeed be challenging, both emotionally and logistically. It's understandable that you're experiencing significant pain during this difficult time. In order to support yourself and prioritize everyone's well-being, here are some guidance and suggestions:

1. Take time to process your emotions: Acknowledge and allow yourself to feel the range of emotions that may come up, such as sadness, anger, or confusion. It's important to give yourself permission to grieve the loss of the relationship.

2. Seek support from loved ones: Surround yourself with understanding and empathetic friends or family members who can provide emotional support. Sharing your thoughts and feelings with them may help alleviate some of the burdens you're carrying.

3. Consider professional counseling: Connecting with a licensed therapist can offer valuable assistance throughout this process. They can provide a safe space for you to express your feelings, gain insights, and develop coping strategies specific to your situation.

4. Create a supportive environment: Establishing healthy boundaries and open communication with your partner might contribute to a smoother transition. Setting realistic expectations and discussing how you both can navigate this process together could minimize conflict and promote everyone's well-being.

5. Seek legal advice if necessary: If there are logistical challenges involved in dissolving the relationship, consulting with a lawyer specializing in family law could help ensure a fair and smooth separation. They can guide you through matters like asset division, child custody, or other legal implications.

6. Focus on self-care: Divorce or separation can disrupt routines and negatively impact one's well-being. Prioritize self-care activities that nurture your physical, mental, and emotional health—such as exercise, maintaining regular sleep patterns, connecting with hobbies, practicing mindfulness or relaxation techniques, and seeking solace in nature.

7. Explore personal growth opportunities: Although endings often bring pain, they can also pave the way for new beginnings. Consider utilizing this period of transition as an opportunity for personal growth and self-reflection. Engaging in activities that bring you joy, exploring new interests or passions, or even seeking a support group centered around similar experiences can provide a sense of optimism and renewal.

Remember, every individual's situation is unique, so it's essential to trust your instincts when selecting the most appropriate steps forward. By prioritizing emotional well-being, fostering open communication, seeking appropriate support, and practicing self-care, you can navigate this process with resilience and compassion for all involved.

Instead of enjoying moments of relaxation, my mind constantly jumps to worst-case scenarios and irrational fears. It sounds like you're going through a difficult time with anxiety. Experiencing excessive worry and fear throughout the day can be exhausting and overwhelming. It's great that you want to regain control over your thoughts and emotions. Here are some suggestions that may help:

1. Deep breathing exercises: When you notice yourself getting caught up in anxious thoughts, take a moment to focus on your breath. Take slow, deep breaths in and out, counting to four for each inhale and exhale. This can help activate your body's relaxation response and bring you into the present moment.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: Anxiety often feeds off of negative thinking patterns. Pay attention to the thoughts that fuel your anxiety and ask yourself if there is evidence to support them. Try reframing those thoughts by replacing them with more realistic or positive alternatives. For example, instead of "Everything will go wrong," remind yourself "I have successfully handled similar situations before."

3. Practice self-care: Taking care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally can make a big difference in managing anxiety. Make sure you're getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and engaging in regular physical activity. Also, find activities that bring you joy and help you relax, such as hobbies or spending time in nature.

4. Establish a routine: Having a structured daily routine can provide a sense of stability and reduce anxiety levels. Plan your days ahead, including specific times for work, breaks, leisure activities, and self-care. Prioritize tasks and break them down into smaller, manageable steps so they feel less overwhelming.

5. Seek support: Consider reaching out to trusted friends, family members, or support groups who can offer a listening ear or share their own experiences. Sometimes talking about our worries and fears can provide relief and perspective. You don't have to face this alone, and it's okay to ask for help.

Remember, these suggestions may not magically eliminate your anxiety, but they can be helpful tools in managing and reducing its impact on your daily life. It might also be beneficial to explore professional guidance with a mental health expert who can provide personalized strategies and support tailored to your needs.

I'm having relationship problems and I want to fix them to make things right before I lose her. How can I learn how to listen and get myself together?

The first step for making this sort of change is being motivated to change and it sounds like you have that, so you are already on the right track.As far as learning how to listen, try some of these steps:Ask whether a certain time is a good time for your girlfriend to have an important conversationIf she has a subject that she would like to discuss, consider listening to her as an investigative reporter and asking questions that help you to gain more understanding of her experience. These questions usually begin with words like who, what, where, when. Questions starting with the word why can sometimes make people very uncomfortable because they may not explicitly know why they are asking for something or feeling a certain way. You can try communicating this way for just five minutes or so on until you feel as though you can restate what your girlfriend is saying and have her agree that you are recapturing the essence of what she is trying to communicateThen you can switch so she is listening to you trying to understand your experience. You could also start by talking about something that is important to you.Remember that stating that you follow or hear something that she is saying doesn't mean that you agreeAlso, try sticking to one subject at a time. It's difficult to really understand one topic if you are on to the next within just a minute or twoTry to use the word want or wish instead of need. Saying that you need something (or if your girlfriend would say that) that is not a need for safety or something like that can make whatever you are asking for sound like an obligation. That takes away from that whole motivation to change from inside the partner who is agreeing to change or try to changeSomething else to try would be using some sort of timeout. Consider this:Discuss the idea of using timeout before you actually need it and before the discussion starts. Timeout is a way to give each of you a way to calm down for five, 10, 15 minutes, or maybe even an hour. When there are a lot of emotions happening, each person gets wrapped up in protecting themselves from the emotions they are feeling and can lose track of what is actually going on in the conversation as compared to what they are perceiving.When using timeout, say to your girlfriend (or she can say to you) "I need an hour before we can go back to this." Then actually come back to the discussion.Some people are very afraid to use this technique because in the past not talking about something right away meant that it never was returned to and was never resolved in any way. This is why the agreement is important before you need it.While it may be helpful to ask your girlfriend what it is she may want from you, it is you that would be in charge of deciding whether you want to make that change and putting it into practice.Try to remember that part of being in a couple is holding onto your own wants, wishes, and desires while recognizing those of your partner.As one final idea, consider spending about 15 minutes a week together where you are not problem-solving about anything, just connecting with one another.I encourage you to see a therapist who specializes in couples if you would like some more specific ideas for what is happening within each of you and between you.Best wishes!

There's a lot of conflict within my family, and it's taking a toll on my mental health. The fighting and tension are constant, making it hard for me to feel safe and secure at home. I would like to explore ways to navigate these family conflicts and establish healthier communication patterns.

Navigating family conflicts and establishing healthier communication patterns can certainly be challenging, but there are steps you can take to improve your situation. Here are some suggestions:

1. Take care of yourself: Prioritize self-care to support your mental well-being during this difficult time. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help reduce stress. This could include physical exercise, hobbies, spending time with supportive friends, or practicing relaxation techniques like deep breathing or meditation.

2. Communicate openly and calmly: When discussing sensitive topics with your family members, try to remain calm and approach the conversation with an open mind. Use "I" statements to express your feelings and needs, focusing on how their actions impact you personally. Active listening is also important - genuinely listen to their perspective without interrupting, judging, or attacking them.

3. Choose the right time and place: Timing is crucial when addressing family conflicts. Find a quiet and neutral environment where everyone can feel comfortable expressing themselves. Avoid bringing up contentious issues during times of heightened emotions or distractions. Instead, choose a moment when everyone is more likely to be receptive and attentive.

4. Seek understanding: Remember that each person involved has their own thoughts, feelings, and perspectives. Try to understand where they're coming from, even if you disagree. Empathy and compassion can go a long way in diffusing tensions and finding common ground. Ask questions to gain insight into their point of view and show genuine interest in understanding their experiences.

5. Set boundaries: If certain behaviors or discussions consistently trigger negative emotions or worsen conflicts, it may be necessary to establish clear boundaries. Let your family know what you consider acceptable behavior and communicate any consequences for crossing those boundaries. However, ensure these boundaries are reasonable and respectful of others' autonomy as well.

6. Consider mediation: In some cases, involving a mediator or impartial third party can help facilitate healthier communication and conflict resolution within the family. They can provide guidance, promote understanding, and offer constructive suggestions for moving forward. This can be a trusted friend, counselor, or community mediator.

7. Practice self-reflection: Take time to reflect on your own reactions and patterns of communication during conflicts. Are there changes you could make to contribute to more productive conversations? Consider working on personal growth and finding healthier ways to express yourself within the family dynamic.

8. Seek support outside the family: It can also be helpful to have someone outside of the family to confide in, such as a close friend, mentor, or support group. They can provide an empathetic ear and help you process your emotions, providing valuable perspective and support.

Remember, these suggestions may not completely resolve all conflicts overnight, but they serve as tools to help you navigate and cope with the situation more effectively. Keep in mind that change takes time and effort from everyone involved. Patience and persistence are key as you work towards establishing healthier communication patterns and creating a more harmonious family environment.

1. Set realistic goals: Make sure the goals you set for yourself are achievable and specific. Break them down into smaller steps so they feel more manageable. Celebrate each small success along the way to keep yourself motivated.

3. Create a routine: Establishing a consistent routine can make it easier to stick to your new behaviors. Plan out your exercise sessions, meals, and mindfulness practices ahead of time. Having a schedule can provide structure and make it less likely for you to slip back into old habits.

One recurring theme in my life is anxiety surrounding change and uncertainty. Whenever faced with an unpredictable situation, even if it's relatively minor, I feel anxious to the point where it consumes me. Thoughts race through my mind, creating catastrophic scenarios that drive up my fear. These moments paralyze me, preventing me from taking risks or moving forward. It can be challenging to face anxiety surrounding change and uncertainty. It's important to remember that everyone experiences some level of anxiety when confronted with unpredictable situations. One way to begin addressing this is by acknowledging and accepting your feelings of fear and anxiety as a normal response.

One strategy that may help you manage these anxious thoughts is practicing mindfulness. Mindfulness involves paying attention to the present moment without judgment or trying to control it. When you notice thoughts racing through your mind and creating catastrophic scenarios, try to bring your focus back to the present moment. Engaging in deep breathing exercises can also aid in grounding yourself and calming your mind during these moments of paralysis.

Additionally, reframing your perspective on change and uncertainty might help reduce your anxiety. Instead of viewing them as threats, try to perceive them as opportunities for growth and self-discovery. Remind yourself that change is a natural part of life and can lead to new experiences and possibilities. It may also be helpful to make a list of all the previous instances where you successfully adapted to change, highlighting your resilience and ability to overcome challenges.

To build courage and embrace new opportunities, start small. Set achievable goals that involve gradually exposing yourself to uncertain situations. As you take small risks and realize that you can handle the outcomes, your confidence will grow over time. Remember to celebrate even the smallest successes along the way, as this can reinforce your belief in your abilities.

Engaging in self-care activities is crucial in managing anxiety. Prioritize activities that promote relaxation and stress reduction, such as exercise, engaging hobbies, spending time in nature, or practicing meditation. Taking care of your physical health through proper nutrition and sleep can also have a positive impact on your overall well-being and resilience to anxiety.

Lastly, consider seeking support from trusted friends, family members, or support groups who can provide emotional encouragement and understanding throughout your journey. Remember, overcoming anxiety is a process that takes time and effort, so be patient and kind to yourself along the way.

I hope you find these suggestions helpful as you work towards overcoming anxiety and embracing new opportunities in your life.

First I think we have to acknowledge that you are doing something amazing.  You are putting yourself out there and becoming a Water Safety Instructor.   We often times will focus on the negative and forget about the positive.  Next, you had an incident where someone pointed something out which may have caused embarrassment.  Whether or not it was malicious on his part I think the important thing to focus on is what is called "Common Humanity".  Common Humanity is one of the three elements of self-compassion.  Common humanity essentially recognizes that suffering and personal inadequacy is part of the shared human experience.  While you may have had this embarrassing moment at this time, that boy may have had an embarrassing moment another day.  We all have embarrassing moments.  When we recognize that we do not suffer in isolation then we are able to move past that suffering.  Additionally another element to self-compassion is self-kindness.  My question is why must you forgive yourself?  Rather, be kind to yourself for learning an amazing new talent.

I've recently started counseling, and while I understand the importance of opening up and being honest, I find it incredibly difficult to trust someone with my deepest thoughts and emotions. It's hard for me to let my guard down and share my vulnerabilities. How can I build a trusting relationship with my therapist and overcome these barriers?

It's great that you've started counseling and recognize the importance of being open and honest. Building trust with your therapist can take time, but there are steps you can take to help overcome these barriers.

Firstly, it might be helpful to remind yourself that therapists are trained professionals who have experience working with individuals like yourself. They are there to provide support and guidance without judgment. Remembering this can help alleviate some of the anxiety or fear associated with sharing your deepest thoughts and emotions.

Another way to build trust is by starting slowly. You don't have to dive into the most vulnerable aspects of your life right away. Take your time and gradually share what feels comfortable for you. As you see that your therapist is supportive and understanding, it may become easier to open up further.

Communication is key in any therapeutic relationship. If you're finding it difficult to trust, it could be helpful to express this concern to your therapist. Let them know about your struggles and fears regarding vulnerability. This will allow them to better understand where you're coming from and tailor their approach to meet your needs.

Additionally, consider discussing your goals and expectations for therapy with your therapist. By having a clear understanding of what you hope to achieve, both you and your therapist can work together towards those goals. This collaborative approach can foster trust and create a safe space for exploration and growth.

Lastly, remember that building trust takes time and patience. It's okay to have ups and downs along the way. Celebrate the small victories when you do feel comfortable opening up, and be gentle with yourself during the times when it feels more challenging.

I believe in your ability to develop a trusting relationship with your therapist. Keep taking those brave steps forward, and know that they are there to support you on your journey.

Good day! Today, I would like to discuss my struggles with anticipatory anxiety and obsessive thoughts, which are affecting my daily life. My goal through this counseling session is to learn techniques to manage these symptoms effectively and gain control over my mind.

Anticipatory anxiety often consumes me before events or activities that I perceive as challenging or demanding. These feelings emerge even when there may not be a rational basis for worry. It feels as if my mind fixates on every possible negative outcome and won't allow me to see the situation from a more balanced perspective.

A recent example of this was before an upcoming job interview. Despite being fairly well-prepared, my anxiety began to spiral out of control days in advance. The night before the interview, I experienced trouble sleeping due to repetitive thoughts about all the things that could go wrong. On the day itself, I felt physically unwell, shaky, and unable to focus during the process. The anticipatory anxiety had impacted my performance negatively.

The frequency and intensity of these episodes vary depending on the importance I attach to the event. They range from mild unease to severe distress, causing a significant disruption in my overall functioning. The duration can last anywhere from a few days leading up to an event to several hours during the event itself.

In my family dynamic, there has been a history of high expectations and pressure to succeed academically and professionally. This environment cultivated a need for perfectionism within me and fostered self-doubt. Additionally, I experienced a traumatic incident during adolescence that heightened my vigilance and tendency towards obsessiveness.

I have tried various coping strategies such as journaling, practicing mindfulness, and engaging in physical exercise. While they provide temporary relief, I hope to explore more adaptive strategies that can address the root causes of my anticipatory anxiety.

During our session, I would like to know more about how cognitive restructuring techniques could be employed to challenge and reframe negative thoughts effectively. Additionally, it would be beneficial to discuss any available resources for ongoing support outside of therapy sessions.

It's great that you're reaching out for support with your struggles around anticipatory anxiety and obsessive thoughts. These challenges can definitely have a significant impact on your daily life, so I appreciate your willingness to address them.

Anticipatory anxiety is a common experience, where our minds tend to focus on possible negative outcomes before events or activities. It often occurs even when there may not be a rational basis for worry, leading us to fixate on these negative possibilities rather than seeing the situation from a more balanced perspective.

I understand how distressing this can be, especially when it starts affecting your performance in important situations like job interviews. The physical symptoms like trouble sleeping, feeling unwell, shakiness, and inability to focus are all manifestations of the intense anxiety you're experiencing.

The fact that the frequency and intensity of these episodes vary depending on the importance you attach to the event shows that it's deeply linked to your own expectations and pressures surrounding success. Growing up in an environment with high expectations and pressure to succeed academically and professionally can contribute to the development of perfectionism and self-doubt within yourself.

Additionally, experiencing a traumatic incident during adolescence further heightened your vigilance and tendency towards obsessiveness. Traumatic incidents can have a long-lasting impact on our mental health, and it's understandable that they have influenced the way you approach challenging situations.

You've already taken some positive steps by trying coping strategies such as journaling, practicing mindfulness, and engaging in physical exercise. While they provide temporary relief, exploring more adaptive strategies that address the root causes of your anticipatory anxiety could be beneficial.

Cognitive restructuring techniques can indeed be effective in challenging and reframing negative thoughts. By identifying any cognitive distortions (such as catastrophizing or black-and-white thinking) and actively replacing them with more realistic and balanced thoughts, you can gradually shift your mindset toward a healthier perspective. This process takes practice, but over time it can help reduce anticipatory anxiety.

In terms of available resources for ongoing support outside therapy sessions, there are a few options worth considering. Self-help books or online resources that focus on cognitive-behavioral techniques could provide additional guidance and exercises to practice between sessions. Support groups or forums where individuals with similar experiences share their strategies and offer support might also be helpful for you.

Remember, this is just an overview of some possible approaches, and it's important to continue discussing your specific needs and concerns in our counseling sessions. Together, we can work on developing personalized coping strategies and explore further techniques that align with your goals of effectively managing these symptoms and gaining control over your mind.

Define Part of Speech

In grammar, a part of speech or part-of-speech (abbreviated as POS or PoS, also known as word class or grammatical category) is a category of words (or, more generally, of lexical items) that have similar grammatical properties. Words that are assigned to the same part of speech generally display similar syntactic behavior (they play similar roles within the grammatical structure of sentences), sometimes similar morphological behavior in that they undergo inflection for similar properties and even similar semantic behavior. Commonly listed English parts of speech are noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition, conjunction, interjection, numeral, article, and determiner.

Almost all languages have the word classes noun and verb, but beyond these two there are significant variations among different languages. For example:

Japanese has as many as three classes of adjectives, where English has one.
Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese have a class of nominal classifiers.
Many languages do not distinguish between adjectives and adverbs, or between adjectives and verbs.
Because of such variation in the number of categories and their identifying properties, analysis of parts of speech must be done for each individual language. Nevertheless, the labels for each category are assigned on the basis of universal criteria
What is deafblindness

Deafblindness is the condition of little or no useful hearing and little or no useful sight. Different degrees of vision loss and auditory loss occur within each individual. Because of this inherent diversity, each deafblind individual's needs regarding lifestyle, communication, education, and work need to be addressed based on their degree of dual-modality deprivation, to improve their ability to live independently. In 1994, an estimated 35,000–40,000 United States residents were medically deafblind. Helen Keller was a well-known example of a deafblind individual. To further her lifelong mission to help the deafblind community to expand its horizons and gain opportunities, the Helen Keller National Center for Deaf-Blind Youths and Adults (also called the Helen Keller National Center or HKNC), with a residential training program in Sands Point, New York, was established in 1967 by an act of Congress.

The deafblind community has its own culture, comparable to those of the deaf community and the blind community. Members of the deafblind community have diverse backgrounds but are united by similar experiences and a shared, homogeneous understanding of what it means to be deafblind. Some deafblind individuals view their condition as a part of their identity.
