How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

Hello. The end of the counselor/client relationship is one of mutual respect and engagement. Counseling sessions can end for any number of reasons. Among them are the client's inability to make forward progress in therapy; the clinician's inability to help the client (for a variety of reasons); a mutually agreed upon time frame for a number of sessions to be provided; or the financial challenges of the client who decides that they need to put their resources elsewhere. In this last case, a counselor should never cancel sessions with a client simply on the basis of the client's inability to pay. That is traditionally seen as an unethical practice. Other arrangements can be made to provide care to the client, which in itself should be paramount.When the client and therapist decide that services are done, it is best if there is at least one or two more sessions to allow a case file review to occur, and to bring an appropriate psychological sense of closure to the client (and vicariously to the clinician as well, those this is perhaps not as important). This transition gives both a sense of having reached the end of a journey...rather than some abrupt departure from it. (An abrupt ending in therapy can have a varying level of impact both emotionally and psychologically on the client and therapist). Sometimes the closure of therapy is the result of a program of therapy being formally completed, in which there is a mutually known (albeit perhaps approximate) date of when that program will be finished. In this case, the client is likely feeling that impending closure and has time to prepare mentally and emotionally from a place of being the client in therapy, to a place of healing, growth and situational resolution.I have always worked in therapy with the following slogan (if you will), that I learned years ago during graduate school: "Not every therapist is good for every client, and not every client is good for every therapist." It is perhaps one of the most important guiding views I hold in working with clients. The therapeutic relationship is driven by mutuality - the desire of the client to get better at living life, and the therapist's desire to truly see the client heal and grow. When there is a block in this process from either side that prevents that synergy from occurring, the relationship that should be established may not be able to form. Or, if already formed, may at some point be unable to move forward. In these instances, referring the client to another type of service or clinician is appropriate. Usually, this can be seen pretty quickly by either party, though sometimes it is not always clear.Ultimately, the client and counselor need to work together to discover if the needs of the client (which is paramount) are being met in the therapeutic engagement with their current counselor, or if other arrangements need to be made to go elsewhere. If both are observant in this process, they can work together to maintain that sacred space and continue to reach the goals that have been set. Eventually, therapy will end, but hopefully based on the client's successful journey to the place where they wanted to go, and thus opening the next chapters of their life to a space that is more whole and brighter.

You can try grounding techniques, such as paying attention to your senses or engaging in a simple activity that brings you into the present moment. It may also be beneficial for you to challenge and reframe your negative thoughts about failing and embarrassing yourself. Instead of automatically assuming the worst outcome, ask yourself if there is any evidence supporting these thoughts. In addition to these self-help strategies, seeking support from friends, family, or a support group can provide valuable emotional assistance. They can offer encouragement, reassurance, and serve as a sounding board for your concerns. Sometimes, talking through your fears with someone who understands can give you a fresh perspective and alleviate some of the pressure.

If your anxiety continues to impact your daily life significantly, it might be worth considering professional help. Dealing with severe anxiety can be incredibly challenging, but it's great that you're seeking therapy as a way to address and manage it. It's important to remember that uncovering the root causes of anxiety may take time and patience, so try not to put too much pressure on yourself to find instant answers. Instead, focus on gradually exploring your thoughts, feelings, and experiences in therapy to gain insight into what might be triggering your anxiety.

In terms of developing strategies to calm yourself during anxious moments, there are several techniques you can try. Deep breathing exercises, for example, can help regulate your breathing and activate your body's relaxation response. You can start by inhaling deeply through your nose, counting to four, then exhaling slowly through your mouth, also counting to four. Repeat this process several times until you begin to feel more centered.

Another helpful technique is grounding yourself in the present moment. You can do this by using your senses to anchor yourself in reality. For instance, focus on the sensation of your feet making contact with the ground or pay close attention to the sounds around you. By shifting your attention away from anxious thoughts, you can create some mental distance from them.

Additionally, incorporating regular physical exercise into your routine can have a positive impact on reducing anxiety levels. Engaging in activities like walking, jogging, dancing, or yoga can release endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Find an activity that you enjoy, and aim to incorporate it into your schedule consistently.

Lastly, consider practicing self-care techniques that promote relaxation and stress reduction. This can include engaging in hobbies you enjoy, spending time in nature, journaling, listening to calming music or podcasts, taking warm baths, or practicing mindfulness meditation. Experiment with different activities and find ones that resonate with you personally.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, and what works best for one person may not necessarily work for another. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process, and don't hesitate to discuss your progress and any challenges with your therapist. They will be able to provide personalized guidance and support as you navigate through uncovering the root causes of your anxiety and developing strategies to calm yourself during those moments.

Developing emotional intimacy and the ability to open up can often be a challenging process, but with dedication and self-awareness, it is possible to cultivate more meaningful connections. Here are some suggestions that may help you along this journey:

1. Reflect on your past experiences: Take the time to explore any past events or relationships that might have influenced your difficulty in opening up emotionally. Identifying patterns or triggers from your past can provide valuable insight into why you struggle with vulnerability.

2. Practice self-compassion: It's important to remember that building emotional intimacy takes time and patience. Be kind to yourself throughout this process and acknowledge that everyone has their own unique timeline for growth. Cultivating self-compassion will allow you to approach these challenges with greater understanding and acceptance.

3. Start small: Begin by slowly sharing your thoughts and feelings with trusted friends or family members. Choose individuals who have demonstrated support and understanding in the past. Opening up gradually can help you build confidence and create a safe space for emotional expression.

4. Explore your emotions: Pay attention to your emotions and try to identify what you're feeling in different situations. Journaling or practicing mindfulness exercises can be helpful in increasing your awareness of emotions. Understanding your emotional landscape better can assist you in expressing yourself authentically when engaging with others.

5. Communicate your needs: Learning how to express your emotional needs and boundaries is crucial for fostering intimacy. Experiment with assertive communication techniques to clearly convey your desires, thoughts, and feelings. Being honest about your needs allows others to understand and support you in creating deeper connections.

6. Seek professional guidance if needed: While counseling may not be an option at the moment, reaching out to a mental health professional can provide additional insights and strategies specifically tailored to your circumstances. They can offer guidance, support, and resources to assist you in developing emotional intimacy.

Remember, building emotional intimacy is a gradual process and there isn't a one-size-fits-all approach. Be patient with yourself, celebrate small victories, and embrace vulnerability as an opportunity for personal growth. It all started when I was in high school, constantly comparing myself to the thin models I saw on social media. I wanted to look like them, so I started restricting my calorie intake and obsessively tracking every bite that went into my mouth.

There have been numerous triggering situations in my life that have increased my symptoms. One major event was being bullied in college for my appearance. The constant criticism made me believe that I needed to punish myself by further restricting my food intake. Additionally, whenever I feel stressed or anxious about something, my thoughts immediately turn to controlling what I eat as a form of comfort.

These disordered eating patterns have led to various symptoms. I often experience intense guilt after eating certain foods and engage in excessive exercising to compensate for any perceived overindulgences. Sometimes, the desire to lose weight takes over my mind completely, causing significant distress and negatively impacting my daily functioning.

In terms of coping strategies, I occasionally try to distract myself from negative body image thoughts by engaging in hobbies I enjoy or spending time with supportive friends. However, these methods are not always effective, and I frequently find myself falling back into old habits.

As we begin this counseling journey, I would like to discuss ways to challenge my negative thoughts and beliefs surrounding food and body image. Moreover, I am curious to learn more about different treatment options available for individuals with eating disorders and how the therapeutic process can support me in my recovery.

Developing a healthier mindset towards eating is an important goal, and I'm here to support you in this counseling journey. It takes courage to recognize the impact that negative thoughts and beliefs about food and body image have on our well-being. 

It's understandable how the constant exposure to thin models on social media during high school influenced your relationship with food. Comparing ourselves to others can be challenging, especially when it comes to appearance. Restricting your calorie intake and obsessively tracking what you eat became ways for you to strive for that idealized image.

Experiencing bullying in college based on your appearance must have been incredibly difficult for you. It's not uncommon for such experiences to reinforce negative feelings and the belief that punishing yourself by further restricting your food intake is necessary. And when stress or anxiety arise, it makes sense that your thoughts turn to controlling what you eat as a way to find comfort.

The disordered eating patterns you described have had significant impacts on your daily life. Experiencing intense guilt after eating certain foods and engaging in excessive exercise are common behaviors associated with these patterns. The desire to lose weight becomes all-consuming at times, affecting your overall well-being.

You've already made some positive attempts to cope with negative body image thoughts by distracting yourself with hobbies and seeking support from friends. These strategies can indeed provide temporary relief. However, breaking free from old habits isn't always easy, and it's normal to find yourself falling back into them periodically.

Together, we can challenge those negative thoughts and beliefs surrounding food and body image. One approach is exploring self-compassion and practicing kindness toward yourself. This means actively recognizing and accepting that everyone has unique bodies and our worth shouldn't be solely determined by our appearance. Another strategy is to focus on intuitive eating, which involves paying attention to internal cues of hunger and fullness rather than strict external rules.

Regarding treatment options, there are various approaches available depending on your specific needs and goals. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has shown effectiveness in helping individuals with eating disorders. CBT can help you identify and modify the negative thoughts and behaviors that contribute to disordered eating patterns. Another potential option is dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), which focuses on developing skills for emotional regulation and distress tolerance.

In therapy, we will work collaboratively to develop a personalized treatment plan that suits your needs. Therapy can support you by providing a safe space to explore underlying concerns, build self-esteem, and enhance coping skills. It's important to remember that everyone's journey is unique, so progress may take time.

As we continue this counseling process, I encourage you to communicate openly about any concerns or questions you have. Together, we can navigate towards a healthier relationship with food and body image, and make progress in your recovery.

To alleviate your symptoms and regain control over your life, here are a few suggestions:

1. Deep breathing exercises: When you start feeling anxious, focus on taking slow, deep breaths. This can help activate your body's relaxation response and reduce physical symptoms.

2. Progressive muscle relaxation: Tense each muscle group in your body one at a time, then release the tension slowly. This technique helps promote relaxation and ease bodily discomfort associated with anxiety.

3. Mindfulness meditation: Engaging in mindfulness techniques can help you become more aware of your thoughts and sensations without judgment. Regular practice may improve your ability to handle anxiety-inducing situations.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Notice the thoughts of danger or impending doom that accompany your physical symptoms. Try questioning their validity and replacing them with more realistic and positive thoughts.

6. Reach out for support: Share your experiences with trusted friends or family members. Their understanding and encouragement can provide emotional support during moments of anxiety.

7. Exercise regularly: Physical activity releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Find an exercise routine that suits you, such as walking, swimming, or yoga, and integrate it into your weekly schedule.

8. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to allocate time for activities that help you relax and unwind. This could include reading, listening to music, taking baths, or practicing hobbies that bring you joy.

Depression can indeed make it challenging to experience enjoyment and interest in activities that used to bring you joy. Here are some suggestions and guidance to help you on this journey:

1. Start by exploring self-care practices: Engaging in activities that promote self-care can be a helpful way to manage depression symptoms. This could include things like getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, exercising regularly, and practicing relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or meditation.

2. Consider setting small, achievable goals: When dealing with depression, it can be overwhelming to think about finding immediate happiness and fulfillment. Instead, focus on setting small, realistic goals that you can work towards. These goals can be related to personal interests, hobbies, or even daily routines. 3. Reach out for support: It's important to remember that you don't have to face depression alone. Consider reaching out to trusted friends, family members, or support groups who can provide understanding and encouragement. It can be challenging to experience intense anxiety in certain situations and have it impact your ability to engage in activities you once enjoyed. To regain control over your life, I suggest exploring some coping strategies that may help you overcome these anxieties.

One effective technique is deep breathing exercises. When faced with triggering situations, focus on taking slow, deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth. This can help relieve feelings of fear and worry by activating your body's relaxation response.

Another helpful strategy is gradually exposing yourself to the situations that cause anxiety, also known as exposure therapy. Start by exposing yourself to mildly anxiety-inducing situations and then work your way up to more challenging ones. By repeatedly facing your fears in a controlled manner, you can build resilience and reduce the intensity of your anxiety over time.

Additionally, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can provide valuable tools for managing anxious thoughts. CBT helps identify and challenge negative thinking patterns or irrational beliefs, replacing them with more realistic and positive thoughts. You could try reframing your perception of social events and public outings, focusing on potential positive experiences instead of dwelling on the fears.

Mindfulness techniques are also worth exploring. These involve being fully present in the moment, without judgment or attachment. Mindfulness exercises can help ground you during moments of anxiety and bring your attention back to the present rather than worrying about future scenarios.

Regarding treatment options, medication is a possibility, but it's important to discuss this with a healthcare professional who can evaluate if it aligns with your needs. They will consider factors such as severity, persistence, and other relevant considerations when determining whether medication may be appropriate in your case.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, so finding the right combination of coping strategies and support takes time and experimentation. Consider consulting with a mental health expert for personalized guidance and ongoing assistance in navigating through this process.

I'm in my late teens and live with my dad.  The only time I go out is for my college classes. Sometimes when I see my friends I want to talk with them, but sometimes I won't want to talk to them for days or even weeks. 

Sometimes I feel i'm not worth knowing or i'm never going to do anything right.

Are they right, am I depressed?

Hello. Being a teenager in our society today can cause depression quite easily. We look at the world in which we live, and the doubts we have about being able to make a contribution, or to have value and worth with the people around us, and we begin to internalize those messages of self-worth. If that alone were not enough, you are trying to figure out where you want to go in life, and who you are supposed to be in the world. Teens are faced with pressures of being judged by your peers for how you present yourself; following current fashions; possessing the trendy things; and hanging out with the "in crowd." Here's a "secret" that might help with most of those issues: Not much of those problems I've just described will really matter as they might seem to right now, in the real world. If you are feeling depression because you feel you lack some of those things that are seen as important by others (like your peers), I can assure you that being someone who is kind; compassionate; understanding of another person's suffering; and the effort you make to be the best person you can become in the world, will far outweigh anything you experienced in your teen years.When we are young, we judge everything based on what our peers have, what they say, the way they dress, who's popular, who's not popular, and for the most of it, all of that is external. So the question becomes, are you trying to fix the feelings on the inside (the internal stuff), with the trappings of all the stuff on the outside (the internal)? That is to say, do you feel that if you had what your friends have, you would be happy and less depressed? Depression is usually a symptom of something much bigger, it is not typically a problem by itself (just as a person who experiences a high temperature may likely have a cold). So fixing the symptom requires looking at the possible causes. In your post, you mentioned that you live with your dad. Are your parents divorced or separated, or has your mom passed away? Either of these circumstances could certainly cause depression. Finding out when you started feeling depressed, might be able to pinpoint the trigger that caused it, which requires looking at when you last felt really happy. It is also important to keep in mind, that as a teenager, your emotions are often being experienced very randomly, and sometimes without cause. It is part of your emotional development, but as you grow older can learn how to manage those emotions better and practice doing things that help you feel better (without causing harm to yourself).Have you tried talking to your dad about your feelings, or maybe another relative if you feel safer doing so? Do you have a friend who is your best friend...someone who is there for you no matter what? If not, there is a service you can use that is a national number for teens to talk with teen peer counselors. They are teens like yourself, but they have some insights that might be helpful. Its called Teen Line (https://teenlineonline.org/). It helped me when I was in my teens, and has helped lots of other teens as well. You might find a place to get some referrals to other local services in your area. If you want are in Washington state and would like to connect with me directly, you call link to me via my profile page. Or perhaps finding a counselor in your local area might be useful. Most towns and cities have some form of low cost counseling. You might also check with your school for assistance.Don't be afraid of not always knowing how you are supposed to feel. Adults don't always have a handle on it either. Being a teenager carries a lot stress, fear, and uncertainty. But you are not alone, and there is help if you reach out for it. I wish for you the very best, and bright future.

Hi there, I have noticed that during periods of high stress, I tend to become irritable and easily agitated. Little things that wouldn't usually bother me suddenly provoke strong emotional reactions. This not only strains my relationships but also exacerbates my already elevated stress levels. Is there any way to prevent this heightened irritability and better cope with stressful situations?

It's great that you've recognized this pattern in yourself! Irritability and heightened emotional reactions during times of stress can definitely put a strain on your relationships and overall well-being. Here are a few suggestions to consider:

1. Take note of triggers: Pay attention to the situations or events that tend to provoke strong emotional reactions. Identifying these triggers can help you better anticipate and prepare for them in the future.

2. Practice self-care: Taking care of yourself is crucial during periods of high stress. Make sure to prioritize activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as exercise, getting enough sleep, engaging in hobbies, or spending time with loved ones. These activities can help reduce stress levels and promote emotional balance.

3. Learn and use coping strategies: Explore different coping mechanisms that work well for you. This could include deep breathing exercises, journaling, practicing mindfulness or meditation, engaging in creative outlets, or seeking support from friends and family. Experiment with various techniques to find what helps you relax and de-stress.

4. Communicate your needs: It's important to let those close to you know about your struggles with irritability and emotional reactivity. By expressing your needs, they may be more understanding and supportive when you're feeling overwhelmed. Healthy communication can also prevent conflicts and misunderstandings in your relationships.

5. Seek professional support if needed: If your difficulties with irritability and emotional reactivity persist or worsen over time, it might be beneficial to seek guidance from a mental health professional. They can provide individualized tools, techniques, and strategies to help cope with stress and manage emotions.

Remember, managing irritability and reacting less strongly to stressful situations takes practice and patience. Be kind to yourself throughout the process, and don't hesitate to reach out for support when necessary.

How do therapists classify the type of personality their clients have?  What characteristics do they look at to decide what type of personality the client has? I've read about this online, but I'd like to understand this from a therapist's point of view.

This is a great question, and I am happy to have the opportunity to explain my approach. When I am determining what type of personality a client has, I take my time and really absorb their lens/ point of view to themselves and others. Determining a personality type takes some time getting to know the person, and building rapport. After taking time to get to know them, and learning about their view they have of themselves and others, it is important to pick-up on more specific personality traits, which comprehensively contribute to a personality type. Clinicians, including myself, often witness certain traits that are enduring and consistent, which indicate a type of personality. For example, if a therapist is noticing that a client is exhibiting traits of organization, needing to be on time, planning, and perfectionism, these traits contribute to the "type A personality". In addition to utilizing clinical judgment, clinicians often use personality assessments and follow the guidelines of the DSM-5/ ICD-10.
I'm constantly in a bad mood and I have no energy. Is that depression?

Depression has many different signs and symptoms and looks different for every person.  Often times people think depression is more about feeling "sad," but depression can, in fact, express itself through irritability (or bad mood as you say) and lack of energy.  According to the DSM-V (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), depression includes the following symptoms:-Depressed mood-Irritable mood-Decreased interest or pleasure in activities you usually participate in or enjoy-Significant weight change or change in appetite-Change in sleep (insomnia or hypersomnia)-Psychomotor aggitation or retardation-Fatigue or loss in energy -Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt-Diminished ability to concentrate or indecisiveness-Thoughts of suicide or plan The great news is that there are many ways to improve depressive symptoms.  If you are up for it, perhaps the best place to start is by seeing a physician or a therapist who can help determine how severe the depression is and can suggest methods of addressing the depression that fit your lifestyle, values, and capabilities.  Good luck!

Why is it so hard now to name a favorite musician?

Compared to 10 years ago, this question has grown a lot harder to answer. In the old days, songs were indexed by song-writers. Prior to the digital age, the most popular media was physical cassettes, and it’s natural to group the cassettes by artists. Moreover, artists used to be the primary mechanism to discover new music. The cost of listening to new songs was usually high, since there were few ways to try new music, so fans tended to buy music from the same artists for quality (and taste) assurance.

With the evolution of music streaming and the decline of the recording industry, the granularity of “listening to music” has refined significantly. Listeners no longer need to buy whole cassettes, but can pick songs individually. Moreover, recommendation algorithms allow fans to discover music by popularity, genre or even mood.  As a result, music fans now sample from such a wide range of artists that it’s hard to name a single favorite. And due to the insane number of accessible songs, Even if you listen to a specific artist most frequently among your collection, you may still only like a small percentage of all the songs he/she wrote, which leads to the shaky conviction that you actually have a “favorite musician”.

On the other hand, I believe the palette for music depends a lot on “environment”. It could be a physical environment (eg. beach or gym), an action (eg. working or cooking), or a mood (eg. chill or psyched). The like or dislike towards a certain piece of music changes drastically when these variables change. To some extent, I view music more as a tool than as an art form, in that I seek certain utility from music at different times. However, music judgment for me is also not 100% a rational or utilitarian process. It still very much comes from intuition, though that intuition is heavily biased by environmental factors.

Food insecurity can lead to less expensive, less healthy food choices that are limited in variety. In addition, children who do not have a consistent source of food may overeat when food is available. Low-income families often must choose high-fat, energy-dense, inexpensive food to maximize their calories per dollar spent. I experienced a traumatic event a few years ago and ever since then, I haven't been able to move on from it. The memories haunt me and I have nightmares almost every night. I constantly feel on edge and anxious, always anticipating something terrible might happen again. I isolate myself from others because I don't trust anyone anymore. I hope that through counseling, I can find healing and learn how to cope with these overwhelming emotions.

It sounds like you have been carrying a heavy burden from the traumatic event you experienced, and it's understandable that it has had a lasting impact on you. The memories and nightmares must feel overwhelming and make it difficult to move forward. It takes courage to recognize the need for healing and seek support.

Firstly, know that you are not alone in this journey. Many others have faced similar challenges and found ways to cope with their emotions. Counseling can indeed provide a safe space for you to explore and process these overwhelming feelings. A professional counselor can guide you through various therapeutic techniques that may help reduce the intensity of nightmares and alleviate anxiety.

One effective approach often used in therapy is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT aims to identify and challenge negative thought patterns associated with the trauma, allowing more balanced and realistic thinking. This can result in a reduction in anxiety symptoms and increased ability to handle distressing memories. Additionally, therapists may teach grounding techniques to help manage moments of heightened anxiety or flashbacks.

Another potential technique that could be beneficial for you is eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR). EMDR focuses on processing distressing memories by pairing them with bilateral stimulation, such as eye movements or tapping. Gradually, this technique can help diminish the emotional charge connected to the traumatic event and potentially reduce nightmares and anxiety.

While therapy is helpful, there are also practices you can incorporate into your daily life to support your healing process. Engaging in regular physical exercise, such as jogging or yoga, can promote overall well-being and assist with managing anxiety. Creating a self-care routine that includes activities you enjoy, like reading, painting, or spending time in nature, can provide an outlet for relaxation and escapism. Consider reaching out to trusted friends or joining support groups online to gradually rebuild trust and connection with others.

Remember, healing is a gradual process, and everyone's journey is unique. Be patient and kind to yourself as you navigate through this difficult time. If possible, try not to put pressure on the pace of your recovery. Stay committed to therapy and utilize the tools and techniques recommended by your counselor consistently.

You have taken an important step in acknowledging your need for healing and being open to counseling. With persistence and support, there is hope for finding relief from the overwhelming emotions tied to your traumatic experience.

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

It is usually time to end counseling sessions when it is clear to both the client and the counselor that therapeutic goals have been reached and enough improvement has been made that the client can continue without that support. There are exceptions to this rule, but for the most part this is when counselors begin termination. For some clients, this is an easy process that marks the achievements they have made in working through their emotions and difficulties. For some other clients, however, this is a difficult process in which they are losing a valuable support and are understandably anxious about what life will be like without the frequent meetings. Ultimately, termination is different for everyone, and there are many ways that termination can be healthy and helpful.

Stress has taken a toll on both my physical and mental health. With deadlines looming and constant pressure, I often feel overwhelmed and unable to cope. Through this counseling session, I aim to gain insights into stress reduction strategies so that I can regain balance in my life.

It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of stress that is impacting both your physical and mental health. This can definitely be challenging, but there are strategies you can try to help reduce stress and regain balance in your life. Here are some suggestions:

1. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of yourself is crucial during times of stress. Make sure you are getting enough sleep, eating well-balanced meals, and engaging in regular exercise. Additionally, find activities that you enjoy and make time for them regularly.

2. Practice relaxation techniques: Incorporate relaxation techniques into your daily routine to help manage stress. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation can all be effective ways to calm the mind and body.

3. Set realistic goals and boundaries: It's important to set realistic expectations for yourself and establish boundaries to prevent becoming overwhelmed. Break tasks down into smaller, manageable steps and prioritize them based on importance. Learn to say no when necessary and delegate tasks when possible.

4. Time management: Develop effective time management skills by creating a schedule or to-do list. Prioritize tasks based on urgency and importance, and try to avoid multitasking as it can increase stress levels. Remember to include breaks in your schedule to give yourself time to rest and recharge.

5. Social support: Reach out to friends, family, or support groups who can provide a listening ear or offer assistance. Sometimes sharing your thoughts and feelings with someone who understands can help alleviate stress. Consider joining a community group or participating in activities that align with your interests and values.

6. Seek healthy outlets for stress relief: Engage in activities that help you relax and unwind. This could be anything from reading, writing, painting, or playing music, to going for walks in nature or practicing yoga. Find what works best for you and make it a priority to incorporate those activities into your routine.

Remember, managing stress is an ongoing process, so be patient and kind to yourself as you work towards regaining balance. If your stress levels continue to be overwhelming, it may be beneficial to seek professional help from a mental health therapist who can provide additional support and guidance tailored specifically to your needs.

It could be really helpful to see a counselor/therapist about your increasing depression/panic symptoms. Finding out the cause of depression/anxiety isn't always as straightforward as it seems, since both issues tend to become patterns we engage in rather than solely related to a specific trigger/reason. For example, if I am feeling down about a particular circumstance in my life, then I start seeing life through this lens of feeling down, and typically I'll start to see a lot more that I get down about, and it can really build very quickly on itself. Same with anxiety. Obviously, this is a very simplified example and it can be very difficult to see how the pattern is maintained, but that's where working with a counselor/therapist comes in. I would be curious about whether you can start to notice the initial sensations of panic, and if you can (through the panic attack) continue to maintain awareness of the actual physical sensations. Even better if you can talk yourself through the sensations you're feeling - such as saying to yourself "Okay, I'm breathing really rapidly, and my heart is racing, now my palms are sweaty and my chest is feeling really tight..." Reminding yourself that it's just your body's reaction to stress, and while it might be overreacting right now, you're okay and eventually it will go away. I highly recommend the SAM for Anxiety Management app for the anxiety piece, and I wouldn't be surprised if addressing the anxiety helped to address some of the depression too.

Every winter I find myself getting sad because of the weather. How can I fight this?

Cold climate is often accompanied by grey skies, snow and
ice. The elements along with wind, windchill and severely cold temperatures may
lead to feelings of sadness, anxiety, and low energy. For some people these
symptoms occur each year from late fall to early spring and may be suffering
from a condition known as Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD). Whether you have
been diagnosed with SAD or are finding yourself struggling with the “winter
blues” for the first time here are some suggestions for feeling better and
staying healthy.1. Nutrition Most likely you have
heard the term “comfort food.” These foods and snacks are high in
carbohydrates, sugar and fat. Avoid overeating cookies, cakes and candy. Chose
vegetables, fruit and protein for snacks and plan balanced meals. If you find
yourself wanting to eat or snack throughout the day, ask yourself why you are
eating. Are you hungry? Or Are you eating because you are bored?2. AlcoholKeep in mind that alcohol is a depressant so consuming wine,
beer or liquor when already feeling sad, anxious or depressed will only add to
your symptoms. Do not consume alcohol while engaging in outdoor activities such
as snow removal, skiing, or ice fishing. If you find yourself reaching for an
additional glass of wine or beer be mindful and ask whether you are doing it
due to boredom. Instead of mindlessly taking another glass of alcohol, drink a
glass of water. 3. SunlightGet
out in the sunlight or brightly lit spaces, especially early in the day.4. Be activeIf you are unable to go to your favorite gym, exercise class
or go for a run, find a way to stay active in your home. There are a lot of
short, instructional programs available on YouTube that you can follow to do
some gently yoga, dance, or do strengthening exercises using only your body
weight.5.  Reach out for help
Confide in someone you trust about how you are feeling. Do
not hesitate to contact a counselor if you feel that you are becoming more
depressed and anxious. If you experience thoughts of suicide call the National
Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-8255.
My mom is always bossy and treats me like a child even though I'm in my 20s. She argues with me over stupid stuff.

This is a common issue. You grow up gradually, and parents often forget to shift their habitual responses according to your newfound level of maturity and growing need for freedom and independance. I'm all for helping you find new ways to cope and interact with your mom. Ultimately, you only have control over yourself, so that's the place to start. You can remind yourself that Mom's behaviours don't mean that she doesn't trust you or love you; it's just that she has habitual ways of talking to you that seem stuck in the fourteen year old range. If you can see her responses as habits, rather than a reflection of how she feels about you, then you can keep yourself calm. The more calm you are, the more she will buy into it when you invite her into a different sort of relationship. Take a look at the picture from her perspective. She may feel overwhelmed with finances (are you in college?), and feel burdened by the mundane tasks in life that she doesn't know how to recruit help for. I bet your mom spends a lot of time picking up after you, cleaning, cooking, doing laundry...all those thankless mom tasks. Take a look at how she talks to you... is she nagging about chores? Can you see that underneath the nagging there's a pretty overwhelmed and powerless person who needs assistance?  Okay, so my guess is that you both have a legitimate beef. She wants help. You want respect. Let's talk about how you get both.I propose that you sit down with mom and negotiate out a different sort of dynamic. "Mom...I see us as stuck in how we interacted when I was fourteen. Can we do this differently in a way that we both get what we want?" Sell it as "win-win". Then you write down some things that end up forming a contract. The first part is stuff that's your business and your business alone: things you want your mom to respect, like your room, your school, your job, your personal relationships and hygiene.... Mom's voice has no place in these arenas, unless you are storing food in your room and it's a health hazard. This is a "Mom says nothing about" list. The second part is about what Mom needs from you. What are her expectations about your role in the home as an adult. Does she want you to contribute to rent? Buy your own food? Do your own laundry? What items can we put in your control that would take some burden off of Mom? How will these things be enforced? What will happen if you don't follow through? Write it all down so it's really clear. It has to all be mutually agreed upon.The third part of the conversation is about how she talks to you, and how you talk to her. You can let her know that you don't want to be told what to do or when to do it; that doesn't work when you're 20 years old. Listen to what she wants too. Beyond the contract you've just written up, anything else you want from each other is a request, it's optional, and whether and when you do it is at your discretion. My guess is that if she spoke to you with more respect, you'd be more willing to help out. AND, I think if you participated a bit more she would nag at you less. Go for the win-win. I wish you well as you negotiate a new relationship with Mom. :)

I'm really sorry to hear that you went through a traumatic event recently. It sounds like it has had a significant impact on your well-being, leaving you feeling shaken and overwhelmed. Processing trauma can be a challenging journey, but I want you to know that you don't have to face it alone.

Firstly, it's important to acknowledge the emotions you are experiencing right now. Traumatic events can stir up a range of feelings such as fear, anger, sadness, or even confusion. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed by these emotions. Remember to be patient with yourself during this process and allow yourself the time and space to heal.

Finding healthy coping mechanisms is an essential step towards healing. Everyone copes differently, so it might take some trial and error to discover what works best for you. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation can help provide a sense of comfort and relief. This could include things like spending time in nature, practicing mindfulness or meditation, journaling, engaging in creative outlets, or seeking support from loved ones.

In addition to finding healthy coping mechanisms, processing the trauma itself may also be beneficial. Talking about your experience with someone you trust, such as a close friend or family member, can offer a sense of validation and support. If you're comfortable, sharing your thoughts and feelings with them might help lighten the emotional burden you're carrying.

Remember that healing takes time, and there is no set timeline for recovery. It's okay to have good days and bad days throughout this process. If at any point you find that your symptoms worsen or become unmanageable, it may be helpful to seek professional guidance from a mental health expert who can provide specialized support tailored to your needs.

Please know that I am here to support you along your healing journey. You've taken an important step by reaching out, and I commend your strength and resilience. "Relationships"

"I've been feeling really down lately, and I think a lot of it has to do with my relationship issues. I'm constantly arguing with my partner, and we can't seem to see eye to eye on anything. It's affecting my mood and overall happiness. My goal for this counseling session is to understand why we're having these conflicts and how to improve our communication."

One aspect that may be helpful to consider when it comes to relationship conflicts and communication is the importance of active listening. When we engage in arguments or disagreements, we often focus on getting our own point across rather than truly listening to what the other person is saying. This can lead to misunderstandings and further escalate the conflict.

Instead, try actively listening to your partner's perspective without interrupting or formulating a response in your head. Really make an effort to understand their feelings and point of view. Reflect back to them what you heard to ensure that you've understood correctly. This can help create an atmosphere of understanding and empathy.

Another suggestion would be to practice effective communication techniques such as "I" statements. Using "I" statements allows you to express your thoughts and emotions without sounding accusatory or confrontational. For example, instead of saying "You always ignore me," you could say "I feel hurt when I perceive that my needs are being ignored." This approach helps avoid placing blame on your partner and encourages open dialogue.

Furthermore, it can be beneficial to establish regular times for open and honest conversations where you both have an opportunity to share your thoughts and concerns. Setting aside dedicated time for communication allows for greater focus and ensures that both parties feel heard.

Additionally, take some time to reflect on your own needs and desires within the relationship. Understanding your own values and boundaries can provide clarity in expressing yourself effectively and assertively. It's essential to communicate these needs with your partner so they fully understand what is important to you.

Lastly, seeking support from trusted friends or family members who can offer objective perspectives can also be valuable. Sometimes an outside viewpoint can shed light on dynamics that may not be immediately apparent to those directly involved.

Remember, improving communication takes time and effort from both partners. Patience, understanding, and the willingness to work together will greatly contribute to resolving conflicts and fostering a healthier relationship overall.

"Hello, I would like to discuss my struggles with intimacy and their impact on my romantic relationship. My objective through counseling is to improve my ability to connect emotionally and establish stronger bonds with my partner. Lately, I have noticed that I struggle with being vulnerable and opening up about my deepest emotions. As a result, my partner feels distant and unappreciated, which leads to frequent disagreements and arguments. For example, when asked about my feelings, I often deflect the question or respond superficially. This pattern has caused tension between us for quite some time now. How can I create a safe space for vulnerability and enhance emotional intimacy within myself and in my relationship?"

Building emotional intimacy and fostering vulnerability in a relationship can be challenging, but with dedication and effort, it is absolutely possible. Here are some suggestions that may help you create a safe space for vulnerability and enhance emotional intimacy within yourself and your relationship:

1. Reflect on your fears: Take some time to understand why you struggle with being vulnerable. Are there past experiences or traumas that have influenced your ability to open up? Acknowledging and addressing these fears can help you gradually overcome them.

2. Start small: Instead of trying to immediately share your deepest emotions, begin by expressing thoughts or feelings that are slightly more personal than what you usually share. This gradual approach will help both you and your partner feel more comfortable with the process.

3. Practice self-compassion: Remember that opening up and being vulnerable requires courage. Be kind and patient with yourself as you navigate this journey. Celebrate each step forward and acknowledge that change takes time.

4. Set aside dedicated time for communication: Create regular opportunities to connect with your partner in an intentional and meaningful way. For example, schedule weekly "check-ins" where you both have the opportunity to discuss your feelings and concerns.

5. Active listening: When your partner opens up about their emotions, make a conscious effort to actively listen without interruption or judgment. Show empathy and validate their feelings, letting them know that you appreciate their vulnerability.

6. Seek understanding: Openly communicate with your partner about your intent to improve emotional intimacy and establish stronger bonds. Share your struggles with vulnerability and ask for their support and patience as you work through this together.

7. Consider couple's therapy: If the tension and disagreements persist despite your efforts, it might be helpful to seek professional guidance through couple's therapy. A therapist can provide you with additional tools and techniques tailored specifically to your relationship, facilitating deeper emotional connection.

Remember, building emotional intimacy is a journey that requires ongoing commitment from both partners. Be patient with yourself and your partner as you work towards creating a safe space for vulnerability, ultimately enhancing the emotional connection between you.

As you know (probably very well), those types of thinking patterns are energy suckers.  I'm assuming you are often tired and don't sleep as well as you could, especially as our thoughts tend to creep up on us when we are trying to fall asleep.One thing to know is that those thought patterns are a protective mechanism.  Ruminating on what could happen and how we will respond is how we feel prepared for what's to come.  In a logical sense, there's so much uncertainty in life that trying to plan all that out is nearly impossible.  Although not a bad idea to have a game plan or rehearse how you are going to respond to conflict, endlessly revisiting those things tend to take away from why we want to be prepared in the first place--to protect our well-being (in any aspect).  The trick is how to calm the brain which is so much easier said than done!  To start, take the time to write your thoughts down.  You can do that via journaling, or by splitting a piece of paper into two categories (one side is helpful planning and other side unhelpful planning).  The brain is a spectacular organ, but sometimes we really need to see things externally to be able to process them effectively.  Excessive worry is really a result of pretty significant fears--whether those fears come from not feeling like you can handle situations, that other people can't handle things, that you will lose something important to you, or that you will fail.  Writing about those fears could help you understand where those thoughts are coming from, or you could even talk those out with a friend or counselor.  Sometimes someone else's feedback about our situations can change how we see things since we tend to get perpetually stuck in the same perspectives.My last suggestion is to work on trying to stay in the present via mindfulness, at least 5 minutes a day.  It's probably going to feel foreign and weird, maybe even scary, since you live more in the future vs the present moment.  It's common for the brain to respond by trying to push back into those thinking patterns, but mindfulness actually increases your ability to problem-solve and see things more clearly.  Constant anxiety clouds us.  Mindfulness clears that out.  And I'm sure you really could use a brain break!

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

There are different reasons why a counselor may seek to terminate with a client and these will each have different processes by which the counselor will come to that decision. Here are a few examples. The counselor may determine that the client's needs are outside what the counselor is competent to be able to work with. A person may have come to the counselor talking about a particular issue but either when they first met or as counseling progressed, it may become clear that the issue is in fact something different or that there is an additional related issue. If that issue is outside the competence of the counselor, the counselor should look for alternatives, the most common of which would be to terminate and refer. Beyond clinical issues, this could also come up around particular other related facts, such as the culture of the client or linguistic issues. This could also be the choice of the counselor if they know someone that they feel would be a better match for the client's issues. Another reason for discharge (and possible referral) would be if the relationship does not seem to be a good fit. No counselor is the right person to work with everyone. If the right level of connection is not happening, the counselor will often look first at what they are doing, might talk about it with the client and ultimately will admit that things don't seem to be working to allow the desired therapeutic process to work. A similar process would be followed if the counselor determined that the client might not yet be ready for counseling as evidenced by lack of engagement such as frequent cancellations, not doing any agreed on work between sessions, showing up late or being really guarded in session. The easiest situation to decide on is when a person has met their counseling goals and have nothing new that they are working on. While this is the easiest one to determine, it is also probably the hardest one for the counselor as they may be like the client in not wanting the relationship to come to an end. However, counselors know that this is part of the process. They will also determine this by regularly reviewing the treatment plan or by sending in the sessions that the work has come to an end. This type of termination maybe final or may be with the intent that the client will return later to address other things that have been identified but for which they are not ready to move into. All of these (and other) situations involves the counselor being open to the relationship ending, to monitoring how things are going, then engaging in self reflection, possibly talking with the client and then coming to a conclusion on which the counselor  follows through.

These anxiety symptoms are not limited to specific situations. Every day, I struggle with feelings of restlessness, feeling on edge, and always expecting something bad to happen. To start addressing your anxiety, it might be helpful to explore some specific techniques and strategies. Besides breathing exercises and grounding techniques, mindfulness practices can also be beneficial. This involves focusing on the present moment without judgment, allowing you to observe your thoughts and emotions without becoming overwhelmed by them. You can find guided meditation apps or online resources that offer mindfulness exercises tailored for anxiety.

Additionally, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based technique used to help individuals identify and modify unhelpful thought patterns contributing to anxiety. It can teach you how to challenge negative thoughts, reframe them in a more positive or realistic light, and develop healthier coping mechanisms.

Regarding the impact of childhood experiences on anxiety levels, it can certainly be worth exploring. Childhood experiences can shape our beliefs and expectations about ourselves and the world, which may contribute to anxiety later in life. You might consider discussing these experiences with a therapist who specializes in trauma or childhood issues, as they can provide you with guidance and support.

In terms of medication, it's important to consult with a healthcare professional who can assess your needs and make personalized recommendations. Medication can be effective for managing anxiety symptoms, but whether it would be appropriate or necessary for you specifically depends on various factors that should be evaluated by a medical expert. They can discuss the potential benefits, side effects, and alternatives with you, providing a comprehensive understanding of medication options.

Remember, everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, so don't hesitate to reach out to mental health professionals who can provide you with individualized treatment and support.

I went through a traumatic experience that still haunts me. The flashbacks and nightmares make it hard for me to function normally. I hope therapy can help me process my trauma and find ways to cope with the lingering effects.

Processing trauma and finding ways to cope with its lingering effects can be a challenging journey, but it's important to know that you're not alone in this. I commend you for reaching out and seeking therapy as a potential avenue for healing.

It might be helpful to start therapy by building a trusting relationship with your therapist. This will provide a safe space where you can freely express your emotions and experiences without judgment. Developing this trust may take time, so be patient with yourself throughout the process.

When it comes to processing your trauma, therapy can offer various techniques and approaches tailored to your needs. One commonly used method is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), which can help identify negative thoughts and beliefs related to the trauma and work on reframing them into more positive and realistic ones.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) is another approach that targets traumatic memories by utilizing rapid eye movements to desensitize their emotional impact. EMDR has shown promising results in reducing distress associated with traumatic experiences.

Moreover, exploring relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises, mindful meditation, or progressive muscle relaxation could alleviate anxiety symptoms like flashbacks and nightmares. These methods aim to ground you in the present moment, providing relief from overwhelming emotions.

Engaging in self-care activities can also contribute positively to your healing process. Pay attention to things that bring you joy, whether it's spending time in nature, practicing hobbies, or connecting with loved ones. Engaging in activities that make you feel good can replenish your energy and boost your overall well-being.

Remember, progress might not happen overnight, but each step forward counts. Throughout this journey, please be compassionate with yourself and celebrate small victories along the way. And if at any point you feel overwhelmed, don't hesitate to reach out for support from friends, family, or other trusted individuals.

Therapy can play a significant role in helping you navigate through the challenges of processing trauma and finding healthy coping strategies. By committing to the process and being open to exploring different techniques, you can gradually regain a sense of normalcy and find new ways to thrive despite the lingering effects of your past experiences.

After years of ups and downs, my partner and I have reached a point where we're considering ending our relationship. We've tried everything we can, but the love between us has faded, and resentment seems to be taking its place. Our goal for this counseling session is to explore all possible options before making any final decisions. One situation that triggered significant concern was when we realized we were living more like roommates than romantic partners. The emotional connection we once had is barely recognizable now. Sleepless nights filled with arguments and feelings of loneliness have become the norm. Emotionally, we feel drained and exhausted. How can we navigate through this difficult phase and determine if we can salvage our relationship or if dissolution is the best option?

Navigating through a difficult phase in a relationship can be challenging, but it's great that you and your partner are open to exploring all possible options before making any final decisions. It's understandable that the fading love and increasing resentment have raised concerns for both of you.

One way to start navigating this difficult time is by having open and honest communication with each other. Create a safe space where you can both express your feelings without judgment or defensiveness. Take turns listening to each other's perspectives and try to understand where the challenges are stemming from.

It could also be helpful to reflect on what initially brought you together and the positive aspects of your relationship. Sometimes reconnecting with shared interests, memories, and experiences can help reignite the emotional connection. Consider engaging in activities you used to enjoy as a couple or finding new hobbies or adventures together.

Additionally, seeking professional guidance from a couples therapist may provide valuable insight and support. A trained therapist can facilitate conversations that uncover underlying issues and help develop strategies to address them. They can offer tools and techniques to improve communication, intimacy, and overall relationship satisfaction.

Taking care of yourselves individually is equally important during this difficult phase. Find healthy ways to manage stress, such as engaging in self-care activities like exercise, meditation, or pursuing personal hobbies. This can contribute to your overall well-being and reduce feelings of exhaustion and drain.

Lastly, remember that there is no one-size-fits-all answer when it comes to determining if a relationship can be salvaged or if dissolution is the best option. Ultimately, trust your instincts and prioritize your own happiness and emotional well-being. 

Remember, only you and your partner can decide what is best for your future. I encourage you to keep an open mind, remain patient, and continue to communicate openly as you navigate through this challenging phase.

My boyfriend’s sneaky and puts his friends before me. He fights just to leave. One day, he's happy. The next, he's mean and blames me for everything. He can't admit faults. He thinks he's perfect and does no wrong.

Hi, Ontario. I live in the other Ontario; in Canada. I'll try to help you sort this out. You have a long list of complaints about your boyfriend! It sounds like he's maybe a bit immature and moody, and these things affect you, for sure. I get it. It's got me curious, and if I was working with you, I'd want to know a lot more about how long you've been together and what's actually working well between you two. I would also ask a lot of questions about the details of your description. What tells you he's 'sneaky'? Does he lie? How do you know he lies to you? Also, are you wanting to make things better with him, do you just want an ear to vent to, are you looking for validation, or do you hope someone will help you wake up to an unhappy situation?  It helps me if I know what you want.Whenever I meet someone who has a lot of complaints about their partner or boyfriend, I encourage them first to look at the language they're using. Some of your words tell me that you think you know what he's thinking (that he wants to fight so he can leave, that he thinks he's perfect). It's always tricky when we assume what someone's thinking, and in an argument or dialogue, these kinds of statements tend to lead to defensiveness and an escalated argument. I'd encourage you to focus on his actual behaviours and how they affect you, rather than the motives or beliefs you think are behind the behaviours (because you really can't know what he's thinking unless he tells you). As a general rule, the "When you do X, I feel Y" sentence goes far in helping others understand what we feel.So, it's fair to say "when you lie to me, I can't trust you", or "when you end our date early to hang with your friends I feel like I'm not important to you", or "your mood swings are difficult for me", or "I don't seem to get apologies from you". Try to focus on his actual behaviour when you talk to him about this stuff. A relationship counsellor can help you each understand the other better beyond the surface behaviours if you want to improve the relationship.That said, I have to ask...if you haven't been with Mr. Not So Great for very long, is it maybe time to rethink the relationship? Unless there is a balance of really loving and positive behaviours that you're leaving out, you don't seem happy. A good therapist can help you understand why you are stuck in an unhappy relationship, if that is what's happening. There's a lot to sort out here...how to communicate about your needs, how to know when to call it quits if something doesn't feel good... I wish you the best as you continue to examine these questions with assistance from friends or professionals.

Hi there, I've been struggling with anxiety for quite some time now and I'm hoping this counseling session will provide me with tools to manage it better. The main cause of my anxiety is social situations. Whenever I am faced with meeting new people or speaking in public, my heart races, my hands shake, and I have trouble catching my breath. Even just the thought of upcoming social events triggers intense worry and dread. For instance, last week I had a job interview, and the days leading up to it were filled with constant worry and fear of failure. During the actual interview, I felt extremely self-conscious, stumbled over my words, and couldn't focus on answering questions effectively. These anxiety symptoms are frequent and impactful, making it challenging for me to fully engage in social interactions.

I'm curious about the most effective treatment options for social anxiety disorder. Are there any specific techniques or exercises that can help alleviate the physical symptoms during anxiety attacks? Can therapy help improve my overall confidence and reduce the frequency of these episodes?

Managing anxiety can be challenging, but there are effective techniques and strategies that can help you navigate social situations with greater ease. It's great that you're seeking counseling to find tools to manage your anxiety better.

When it comes to social anxiety disorder, therapy can certainly be beneficial in improving your overall confidence and reducing the frequency of these episodes. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is often recommended as a first-line treatment for social anxiety disorder. This type of therapy focuses on helping you identify and challenge negative thought patterns and beliefs that contribute to your anxiety. Through CBT, you can learn coping skills, relaxation techniques, and problem-solving strategies to address the physical symptoms and fears associated with social situations.

One specific technique you can try is called deep breathing or diaphragmatic breathing. When you feel your heart racing or have trouble catching your breath, take slow, deep breaths from your abdomen rather than shallow breaths from your chest. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold the breath for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. Deep breathing can help calm your body and reduce the physical symptoms of anxiety.

Another helpful exercise is progressive muscle relaxation. This technique involves tensing and relaxing different muscle groups in your body, starting from your toes and working your way up to your head. By systematically releasing tension, you can promote a sense of relaxation and decrease feelings of anxiety.

Therapy can also provide a safe environment for you to practice facing your fears gradually through exposure therapy. This involves engaging in social situations that make you anxious while using the coping techniques you've learned. Over time, this can help desensitize you to the fear and discomfort associated with social interactions.

Alongside therapy, self-care activities such as regular exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and practicing stress-management techniques like mindfulness or meditation can also support your overall well-being and help reduce anxiety symptoms.

Remember, everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, and it may take some time to find the strategies that work best for you. Be patient with yourself as you embark on this journey of managing your anxiety, and remember that therapy can be a valuable resource in helping you develop effective coping mechanisms.

First, let me express my support and compassion for what you're going through. Hearing voices can be incredibly difficult and can feel like you can't get a moment's peace, even in the privacy of your own mind. And not everyone will necessarily understand what you're dealing with, so I imagine you may also be feeling isolated or somehow different. Atta girl/boy on reaching out for help! Many people find benefit to taking medications, such as risperdal, seroquel, and so on. These should be prescribed by a nurse practitioner or psychiatrist -- I do not recommend a primary care doctor venture into this area, as a general rule. Discuss the options thoroughly and insist on a good rapport with your prescriber, if you decide to go this route. Some people are having results with a talk-therapist to develop coping strategies. There is a new and somewhat less conventional approach to challenging voices with a professional to assist you, rather than to suppress the voices, which medication will do. There is peer-run organization and a general approach that attempts to live with voices in a different way.  You can read about it in Living With Voices by Marius Romme. I have heard interviews but have not read the book(s) and can't speak to its efficacy. No matter what steps you decide to try, managing your stress, sleep, exercise, healthy food is essential -- in other words, just the daily care and feeding of yourself should be included in all of your efforts and bears surprising benefits to your brain and emotional health. Best wishes to you,Karen Keys, LMHC, CASAC

I don't know what's with me. I'm almost constantly angry. Even when I'm happy, I still feel anger inside me. When I acknowledge it, it ruins my mood and takes over. I get angry at the littlest things. Even if I think someone said something they didn't, it infuriates me. Something perfectly normal can make me go off. When my anger flares up, I get a terrible pain in my chest that lasts for a while. It's like there is a fire constantly burning in my body, and anger is gasoline.

Hi Nashville, I'm glad you want this to be different. It doesn't feel good to be angry all the time, and it's stealing your energy as well as affecting relationships, I'm sure.Working with a therapist, you can learn to recognise the deep emotions that lie underneath the anger. It's likely to be either powerlessness or worthlessness, and what happens is this... a small moment in the present touches on an old, tender, bruised emotion that we've simply felt too much of or too strongly in the past. We develop ways of avoiding these vulnerable emotions, and anger is one way of doing that. So, when someone looks at you in a certain way, or says something, you'd rather be angry than feel powerless, or unimportant (or whatever your kryptonite feeling is). In that moment, your instinct is to blame whatever happened, no matter how small, because that's the thing that happened just before you got mad. You fail to recognise that the problem is not the look on that person's face, or the shoe that someone left in front of the door...it's that you can't stand feeling something and you want to avoid it like you want to stamp your foot out if it's on fire.I suggest finding a therapist to work with. You can learn to take responsibility for your old emotions and find new ways to manage them. :)

Lately, I've been struggling with depression, and it feels like everything is an uphill battle. There are days when I struggle to get out of bed and even simple tasks seem overwhelming. It all started after losing my job unexpectedly. Since then, I've felt a deep sense of worthlessness and lack of motivation. This depressive episode has lasted for months now, with persistent feelings of sadness, fatigue, and loss of interest in activities I once enjoyed. My main goal in counseling is to create a roadmap towards recovery and learn techniques to manage my depression effectively.

It's unfortunate to hear that you've been experiencing such difficulty lately, especially with your depression making everything feel like an uphill battle. Losing a job unexpectedly can certainly be a challenging situation to navigate. Feeling a deep sense of worthlessness and lack of motivation afterwards is something many people struggle with. It sounds like this depressive episode has persisted for quite some time now, with feelings of sadness, fatigue, and loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed.

Creating a roadmap towards recovery and learning techniques to effectively manage your depression are excellent goals for counseling. There are several strategies that may be helpful in addressing these concerns. One potential approach is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns that contribute to your depressive symptoms. This can help alleviate the feelings of worthlessness and lack of motivation by challenging distorted thinking and replacing it with more realistic and positive beliefs.

In addition to CBT, incorporating self-care practices into your routine can also make a significant difference. Engaging in activities that bring you joy or relaxation, such as exercise, hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or practicing mindfulness and meditation, can help improve your mood and overall well-being. Setting small achievable goals for yourself each day can provide a sense of accomplishment and gradually increase your motivation.

Another important aspect of managing depression effectively is ensuring a healthy lifestyle. This includes getting regular sleep, maintaining a balanced diet, and avoiding excessive alcohol or drug use, as they can exacerbate depressive symptoms. Physical activity, even in the form of short walks or light exercises, has proven to have positive effects on mood.

Lastly, building a support system can be invaluable during times like these. Sharing your thoughts and experiences with trusted friends or family members who are willing to listen and offer support can provide comfort and reassurance. If possible, consider reaching out to community resources or local support groups where individuals facing similar challenges can come together to share their experiences and coping strategies.

Remember, recovery takes time and progress may feel slow at times. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this journey. It's important to recognize that seeking counseling is a proactive step towards better managing your depression. I hope these suggestions provide you with some guidance and support as you work towards creating your roadmap for recovery.

"My stress levels have reached a point where it's affecting my physical health. I constantly feel tense, my muscles are often sore, and I experience frequent headaches. It's becoming difficult for me to perform daily tasks without discomfort. Through counseling, I hope to discover ways to manage my stress-related physical symptoms."

Managing stress-related physical symptoms can be challenging, but there are steps you can take to find relief. Here are some suggestions for you:

1. Deep Breathing Exercises: Incorporating deep breathing exercises into your daily routine can help reduce tension and promote relaxation. Try taking slow, deep breaths in through your nose, holding it for a few seconds, and then exhaling slowly through your mouth.

2. Physical Activity: Engaging in regular physical activity can help relieve stress and improve overall well-being. Find an exercise that you enjoy, such as walking, swimming, or yoga, and aim to incorporate it into your routine several times per week.

3. Relaxation Techniques: Explore different relaxation techniques, such as progressive muscle relaxation or guided imagery. These practices can help relax your body and mind, reducing the physical symptoms associated with stress.

4. Healthy Lifestyle Habits: Pay attention to your lifestyle habits, including sleep, nutrition, and hydration. Prioritize getting enough restful sleep each night, eating balanced meals, and staying hydrated throughout the day. These factors can have a significant impact on your overall well-being and help alleviate stress.

5. Time Management: Consider evaluating how you manage your time and make adjustments if necessary. Prioritizing tasks, setting realistic goals, and delegating when possible can help reduce feelings of overwhelm and minimize stress.

6. Self-Care Activities: Dedicate time to engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation. This could include hobbies, spending time in nature, practicing mindfulness or meditation, or enjoying quality time with loved ones.

7. Social Support: Reach out to trusted friends, family members, or support groups who can provide a listening ear and emotional support. Sharing your experiences and feelings with others can help lighten the burden of stress and improve your overall well-being.

Remember, managing stress is a process and it may take time to find what works best for you. It's important to be patient and kind to yourself as you explore different strategies. If your symptoms persist or worsen, consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide additional guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.
