It can be really challenging when you're experiencing a deep sadness that seems to linger. It's important to acknowledge and address these feelings, so I'm glad you reached out for support. Here are some suggestions that may help provide relief from this constant state of sadness:

1. Engage in activities that used to bring you joy: Even though it might feel difficult at the moment, try to engage in activities that used to bring you pleasure or interest. Start small and gradually increase your involvement. This could include hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or exploring new experiences.

2. Seek social support: Reach out to trusted friends or family members who can offer a listening ear and emotional support. Sometimes talking about our feelings can help alleviate some of the burden we carry. If you feel comfortable, consider sharing your experience with someone close to you.

3. Prioritize self-care: Take care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally. Make sure you're getting enough sleep, eating well-balanced meals, and engaging in regular exercise. Additionally, incorporate activities that promote relaxation and stress reduction into your routine, such as meditation, deep breathing exercises, or taking walks in nature.

4. Consider professional help: If your symptoms persist or worsen over time, it may be beneficial to seek professional help from a mental health therapist. They can provide guidance tailored to your specific needs and help you develop coping strategies to manage your sadness more effectively.

5. Challenge negative thoughts: Depression often involves negative thinking patterns. Practice identifying and challenging negative thoughts by questioning their validity and replacing them with more positive or realistic alternatives. This process takes time and practice but can contribute to a shift in mindset.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, and what works for one person may not work for another. Be patient with yourself and give yourself permission to prioritize your well-being. You deserve support and relief from this constant state of sadness.

Another situation that heightens my anxiety is traveling. Whether it's taking a flight or even just driving on the highway, I experience intense fear and panic. My heart races, my palms sweat, and I can't shake the feeling that something terrible will happen. This fear has prevented me from going on vacations or visiting loved ones who live far away.

It can be challenging when anxiety starts to interfere with your ability to travel and enjoy experiences like vacations or visiting loved ones. It's important to remember that you are not alone in feeling this way, as many people struggle with anxiety related to traveling.

One suggestion I have is to start by gradually exposing yourself to the situations that trigger your anxiety. For example, if flying causes intense fear and panic, you could try taking small steps such as watching videos about flying, reading books or articles on aviation safety, or even visiting an airport without actually boarding a plane. These gradual exposures can help desensitize your mind and body to the fears associated with traveling.

Another technique that may be helpful is deep breathing exercises. When you notice your heart racing and palms sweating, take slow, deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth. Focusing on your breath can help calm your nervous system and reduce feelings of panic.

Additionally, it might be beneficial to explore relaxation techniques such as meditation or mindfulness. These practices can help train your mind to stay present in the moment and let go of anxious thoughts. There are plenty of apps and online resources available that offer guided meditations or mindfulness exercises specifically designed for anxiety.

If these self-help strategies don't provide enough relief, it could be worth considering seeking support from a mental health professional who specializes in anxiety disorders. They can work with you to develop personalized coping mechanisms and potentially explore other treatment options, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) or medication.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and patience. Be kind to yourself throughout this process and celebrate each small step forward. With persistence and the right support, it is possible to manage your anxiety and regain the freedom to travel and visit loved ones without overwhelming fear.

My toddler defies everything I say and doesn’t see me as authoritative, so she says no about everything. I'd like to hear some ways I can work on not needing to feel so much in control all the time.

Hi Biddeford,This is a super goal. Feeling powerless is something parents are wise to get used to; there's a creature in the home whose job it is to find and use their power in the family and in the world. Of course your toddler defies you, and that's healthy. I worry more about the overly compliant ones. She is wanting to know what the rules are, and all you have to do is show her clearly where the lines are. I'll give you some tips.First, remind yourself that it's her job to learn what the rules are, and where her power is. Don't be so surprised when she wants it her way. If we go through our days being ready and prepared for these beautiful creatures to have minds of their own, we're less caught off guard when it happens. Avoid situations that invite power struggles. Any time you tell your daughter "do this now", you set up a power struggle. The good thing is that she's young enough you can pick her up; now is the time to teach her that mom's (or dad's) word means something. So, if you say "let's get you dressed", then be prepared to pick her up right away and show her that when you say something will happen, you can make it happen. And I'm talking about gently picking her up here...not roughly. Pick your battles; only give instructions when you have the power to make it happen.Give her choices, so she can see her power. Instead of opening her drawer and asking what she wants to wear, give her two choices. Here's an example...she's on the ipad and you say ipad time is over. She says "no". You can say "ipad time is over. If you put it down, you can play later. If I have to take it away, you don't play it later." The choice is hers. Then follow through."When...then" statements are really helpful. Your child asks for something. Instead of saying no, try "as soon as the toys are picked up, we can have a snack". You're simply a pleasant parent who wants the same thing they do...but they have to earn it. Staying calm yourself is the key, because then at least you will feel in control of yourself, which is the ultimate goal. Use self-talk to calm yourself. Remind yourself her behaviour is normal and healthy. Breathe through a moment in which you would have reacted, and it will be over by the time the breath is done. You can give yourself time to think before you make parenting decisions. Time is a useful tool not enough parents use. Good luck!

Anxiety has taken over my life. I'm constantly worried about everything, from the smallest tasks to major life decisions. It's like there's a never-ending loop of "what ifs" playing in my head. It's physically exhausting and mentally draining. I want to learn how to quiet this constant anxiety and find peace within myself.

Learning to quiet constant anxiety and finding peace within yourself can be a gradual process, but it is definitely attainable. Here are some suggestions and strategies that may help:

1. Practice mindfulness: Mindfulness involves bringing your attention fully to the present moment without judgment. Engaging in activities such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or yoga can help you cultivate awareness of your thoughts and physical sensations, allowing you to let go of anxious thoughts.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: Becoming aware of negative thought patterns and actively challenging them can help break the cycle of anxiety. When an anxious thought arises, ask yourself if there is evidence to support it or if there might be alternative explanations for what you're experiencing.

3. Create a worry journal: Consider writing down your anxious thoughts in a journal. Not only does this provide an outlet for expressing your worries, but it also allows you to identify recurring themes and triggers. Writing can help bring clarity and provide insights into your anxiety.

4. Establish a self-care routine: Prioritize self-care activities that promote relaxation and reduce stress. This could include regular exercise, getting enough sleep, eating nourishing foods, spending time in nature, engaging in hobbies, or practicing relaxation techniques like progressive muscle relaxation.

5. Set realistic goals and break them down: It's common for anxiety to escalate when we feel overwhelmed by tasks or decisions. Break down larger goals into smaller, manageable steps. By taking things one step at a time, you can alleviate some of the pressure and make progress towards your goals.

6. Seek social support: Reach out to trusted friends or loved ones who can provide a listening ear or offer support. Sharing your experiences with others can often provide relief, reassurance, and different perspectives on your situation.

7. Limit exposure to triggers: Identify any external factors that contribute to your anxiety and find ways to limit your exposure to them. For example, if certain news topics or social media platforms induce anxiety, consider setting boundaries around when and how often you engage with them.

8. Consider professional help if needed: While the suggestions mentioned above can be helpful, it's important to recognize that everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, and different approaches work for different people. If your anxiety persists or significantly impacts your daily life, considering reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide guidance tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, managing anxiety takes time and patience. Be gentle with yourself throughout this process and celebrate each small step forward.

How do you replace a hole in the drywall?

First you start by locating the nearest wooden studs and cut a square, larger than the hole and exposing up to one inch of each wooden stud.  Each wooden stud is typically sixteen inches apart - center to center.  And each wooden stud is typically two inches in width.  Second step is to carefully measure the open space after you've cut the square.  Take your time and measure as close to the existing drywall as possible.  Take 4 measurements of 2 in length and 2 in width to ensure accuracy.  Cut that square from your replacement drywall.  Shave sides with sandpaper for tight fit.  Once your replacement square fits, insert drywall screws into the sides of the drywall that will also go through the previously exposed wooden studs.  Once the new square is secure, you can layer ontop the drywall paste to let dry.  Sand the drywall paste over the seams of the square, and repeat as necessary until you have a uniform, smooth surface.  Apply paint over the entire workspace and let dry.

Hi Anaheim,Relationships with therapists have some things in common with other relationships; they work best if there is dialogue about what your hopes, thoughts, emotions and needs are. Are you letting your therapist know what your goals are? It's okay to say "I'd really like us to focus on this piece", or "I'm looking for specific direction about how to manage this part". Your therapist is wise if they ask questions that determine what your needs are, but they can't read your mind. Not every therapist will be a good fit for you. I know I'm not a good fit for everyone I meet. We have different styles; some are more  passive and focus on listening. This might be the type of therapist you have. For some people this is what they want, but maybe it's not for you. Maybe you want someone who digs at you more, asks more questions, gives you strategies, lets you know what they think... someone more active. If this is the case, it doesn't mean s/he's a bad therapist...it's just not what you're looking for. Sometimes people think they can't end sessions with their therapist; they might be worried about hurt feelings. But, in the end, you don't owe your therapist anything if you feel it's not working or it's not a good match. Just move on and try someone new. Maybe ask them questions first about their style, even. Best of luck!

Anxiety has taken control of my life. I constantly worry about everything, from minor tasks to major life events. It affects my ability to concentrate and enjoy daily activities. By discussing my thoughts and emotions related to anxiety in this counseling session, I hope to learn coping mechanisms and techniques to manage it effectively.

It's great that you're seeking strategies to manage your anxiety and regain control of your life. Here are some suggestions and techniques that may help:

1. Practice deep breathing exercises: Deep breaths can help activate your body's relaxation response and reduce anxiety. Try inhaling deeply through your nose, holding it for a few seconds, and then exhaling slowly through your mouth. Repeat this several times whenever you feel overwhelmed.

2. Challenge anxious thoughts: When you find yourself worrying excessively, question the validity of those thoughts. Are they based on facts or are they distorted? Try focusing on evidence that supports or disproves your worries. This process can help you gain a more balanced perspective.

3. Engage in regular physical activity: Regular exercise has been shown to alleviate symptoms of anxiety by releasing endorphins, improving mood, and reducing stress levels. Find activities you enjoy, such as walking, yoga, or dancing, and incorporate them into your routine.

4. Establish a consistent sleep schedule: Lack of proper sleep can intensify feelings of anxiety. Aim for a consistent sleep schedule that includes enough hours of quality sleep each night. Create a relaxing bedtime routine and avoid screens before bed to promote better sleep.

5. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of yourself is crucial when dealing with anxiety. Make time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation, whether it's reading, taking baths, spending time in nature, or engaging in hobbies. Remember to nurture both your physical and emotional well-being.

6. Practice mindfulness and grounding techniques: Mindfulness involves bringing your attention to the present moment without judgment. You can try deepening your awareness by observing your surroundings, focusing on your senses, or practicing meditation. Grounding techniques like describing objects around you or noticing sensations in your body can also help anchor you in the present moment.

7. Seek support from loved ones: Sharing your experiences and feelings with trusted friends or family members can be incredibly helpful. They may provide a listening ear, emotional support, or even suggestions based on their own experiences. Connecting with others who understand and validate your feelings can make a big difference.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, so it might take some time and experimentation to find what works best for you in managing anxiety. Stay patient and compassionate with yourself as you explore these different techniques. If needed, consider reaching out to mental health professionals for additional guidance.

Wishing you all the best in your counseling session and on your path towards effectively managing your anxiety.

I am in a high stress position for a tech company. I am being overworked and underpaid for my contributions and it is not only giving me anxiety, but also demoralizing.
   What can I do to manage my stress?

Ugh!  We spend so many hours at work, so if it's a tough environment it can really drag you down.  Is this your "dream job" gone sour or a "just pay the bills" deal that has gotten stale?  It makes a big difference in terms of next steps.For example, if this job is a step on the way to a bigger goal, it might be time to assess whether you need to be moving along to then next phase.  Have you learned what you needed to learn to make this a helpful experience?  Or do you sense there is more to learn, but you feel stuck in some way? If this current job is part of a bigger plan, then you need to practice some good self care, set up ways to remind yourself why you are doing what you are doing, and make sure you are including some "carrots" along the way.  That might mean spending some time each week networking (preferably live but online works well too) with peers in similar situations (entrepreneur groups, skill building trainings, etc).  Big dreams require small steps, but we all need support along the way.If , however, this is "just a job", then you really have to reassess your situation.  If you are burned out and not getting paid your worth then  look around for other opportunities.  You are employed, not owned.  You mentioned anxiety, and while I don't want to minimize the very real issues anxiety presents, is it possible that some of your anxiety can be seen as "revving your engine"  and readying you to move on?  Or is it that pervasive feeling  of never being able to finish your work, feeling like you will be "in trouble", or dreading every single moment of your workday?  The first is a potentially positive motivator, the second is just bad for you.   See the difference?In order to feel any satisfaction with your job, it needs to be financially rewarding (to a level that makes sense), be a good atmosphere to learn, be supportive and/or be a step on the way to a bigger plan you have.  If your job isn't fulfilling any of those criteria, you need to move on.  And finally, if the only reason you have this job is to pay the bills, and you truly see no way around keeping your current position for now, remember why you are there - this is a job, not a family.  You rent your brain and body to your employer, not your heart and soul.  Those belong to you and you are responsible for feeding them.  That means good self-care, making sure you have social engagement (face-to-face, not just online), move your body, feel the sun on your face daily, creating ways to refresh your body and mind and generally taking care of your whole being.Discomfort exists for a reason - it primes us for change, gives us the necessary motivation to take reasonable risks, and pesters us until we do so.  The first step is to figure out what change is realistic, and take action.

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

As a therapist who believes in client self-determination above most other elements of the process, I want to as much as possible leave it up to the client to determine when they are finished. In the case of a termination because a client's distress has resolved, I might periodically check in with the client about how therapy has been going, and if we want to re-evaluate where we are.The more unfortunate situation would come about if I felt that I wasn't the best fit for the client. I would offer that in words, and ideas of therapists (with names) of who I thought might be a better fit and why. It still is up to the client whether to continue, however should they want to keep seeing me, a part of the work would be about that want (to see someone who professionally doesn't believe they can help as much as someone else.)I also find it perplexing when I hear a client (or on a personal level) tell me that their therapist said they "didn't need therapy." I don't know that I buy into that scenario all that much, because I do believe that yes, not everyone NEEDS therapy, but that everyone CAN benefit from therapy and I don't believe it is the therapist's job to deter someone from ever seeking out help of any kind.

My anxiety often manifests as physical symptoms such as racing heart, shortness of breath, and trembling hands. These episodes occur frequently throughout the day and can be quite intense. I would like to discuss strategies to reduce the frequency and intensity of these symptoms.

It seems like you're experiencing a lot of physical symptoms related to your anxiety, such as a racing heart, shortness of breath, and trembling hands. These episodes can be quite intense and happen frequently throughout the day. I understand that you would like to find strategies to reduce both the frequency and intensity of these symptoms.

One technique that might help is deep breathing exercises. When you start feeling anxious, try taking slow, deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth. This can help calm your body down and regulate your breathing. You could also consider practicing mindfulness or meditation, which can help you become more aware of your thoughts and sensations in the present moment, allowing you to better manage your anxiety.

Another strategy to explore is identifying triggers for your anxiety. Pay attention to situations, people, or thoughts that tend to make your symptoms worse. Once you've identified these triggers, you can work on finding ways to either avoid them or cope with them more effectively. It may be helpful to keep a journal where you record your experiences and note any patterns you notice.

Engaging in regular physical activity can also be beneficial for managing anxiety symptoms. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Find an activity that you enjoy, whether it's going for a walk, dancing, or playing a sport, and aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days of the week.

Additionally, incorporating relaxation techniques into your daily routine can provide relief from anxiety symptoms. This could include activities such as listening to calming music, taking warm baths, practicing progressive muscle relaxation, or engaging in hobbies that bring you joy and help you unwind.

Lastly, don't hesitate to reach out to supportive friends or family members who can offer a listening ear or provide distractions when you're feeling overwhelmed. Sometimes talking about our worries and fears can help alleviate some of the anxiety we experience.

Remember, everyone's journey with anxiety is unique, so it may take some trial and error to find the strategies that work best for you. It could be helpful to consult with a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support as you navigate through this process.

Hello, and thank you for your question. When faced with these kinds of difficult challenges, I usually encourage people to look to their values for help in determining what their behavior should be. Indeed, it is usually when our behaviors conflict with our values that we don't feel very content with our lives. Perhaps you can take some time to think through a couple of these questions: What kind of person do I want to be deep in my heart? What kind of character do I want to have when in public and in my private world when nobody is watching? How would I want others to describe me? Let's say that you want others to see you as being authentic, and YOU also value authenticity as something you want to live by. You may feel like this value is currently at odds with the behaviors you are engaging in right now. That you are not being the person that you really are deep in your heart. This is not an unusual struggle when it comes to sexual behavior and sexual orientation. So please, try not to feel alone. We all know quite well how unacceptable it may be to be seen as gay, lesbian, bisexual, etc. And I am not just talking about being unaccepted by others, but a person may have a VERY hard time accepting themselves. Thinking about your values and living a life based on them can bring a lot of freedom, but I won't lie, it can also bring a lot of pain at the same time. For example, someone with the value of living authentically may decide they have to tell others who they are and what they stand for, even if that means people may disapprove. That may cause a lot of pain, but it may also come with a sense of freedom to live a life based on honesty and authenticity. It may be helpful to find a counselor who is trained in affirmative therapy, which is recommended for people who are navigating their sexual behaviors and figuring out what is right for them. I would also sit down and think through some of the questions above and consider what your values are... both as an individual and as someone's fiancé.Above all, I wish you well in this journey. Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

E-readers also give the ability to read in the dark without using other lighting that may disturb those around you.

To cope with my anxiety, I usually try deep breathing exercises when I start feeling overwhelmed. However, they don't seem very effective in reducing the intensity of my symptoms. In this counseling session, I would like to know more about different coping mechanisms that could help me manage my anxiety better. Is medication something we should consider? How does therapy typically address anxiety-related issues?

It can be challenging to navigate through moments of extreme anxiety, especially when it affects your daily life. The stress and pressure you're experiencing at work seem to be contributing to the intensity of your symptoms. It's important to create strategies to manage your anxiety and reduce its impact on your well-being.

One approach that may be helpful is identifying specific triggers or situations that tend to heighten your anxiety. By recognizing these triggers, you can start preparing yourself mentally and emotionally ahead of time. This might involve breaking down overwhelming tasks into smaller, more manageable steps. Prioritizing and creating a schedule could also help in alleviating some of the pressure associated with deadlines.

In addition to deep breathing exercises, you may want to explore other relaxation techniques that are more effective for you personally. For example, progressive muscle relaxation involves consciously tensing and then relaxing different muscle groups to promote physical relaxation. Visualization exercises, such as imagining yourself in a peaceful setting, can also help calm your mind.

Since you mentioned that even activities like walking or practicing yoga have become less effective lately, it could be beneficial to incorporate new hobbies or interests into your routine. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is a commonly used approach that focuses on identifying unhelpful thought patterns and replacing them with more constructive ones. I’ve been on 0.5 mg of Xanax twice a day for the past month. It hasn't been helping me at all, but when I take 1 mg during a big anxiety attack, it calms me down. Hello, and thank you for your question. While counselors work closely with medical providers, and sometimes have discussions about medications with people, we rarely make recommendations about how much or what type of medication a person should be taking. This is because prescribing and advising on medication is out of our scope of practice. The only exception would be if a counselor is also a physician, nurse practitioner, physician's assistant, etc. Having said that, I certainly understand that anxiety is a real serious problem that many folks struggle with. If you are currently not in therapy to help you with these panic attacks, you should consider it. Medications can be helpful for anxiety, and medications like Xanax may help for immediate relief, but they do nothing to deal with the root of anxiety and may not help with anxiety long-term. Therapists who have experience in exposure therapies would be good people to start with. Exposure therapy has good outcomes for people with anxiety disorders and panic attacks. If you are interested in speaking with your provider about the Xanax, I think explaining it the way you did on here is just fine. The provider will then decide if they feel comfortable increasing your medication. Please remember that medical providers are not trying to give people a hard time. Medications like Xanax really are highly addictive. The more you take, the more you may feel you need. The more often you may feel you need to use it. Depending on the frequency and amount of use, some people suffer serious withdrawal symptoms when they do not take the medication. It is a good idea to talk to medical provider about all of those things so that you can partner on right course of action to manage this anxiety. I certainly hope that you get some relief.... I know anxiety is awful.Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Building and maintaining social relationships can indeed be challenging at times, but I want to assure you that there are strategies and techniques that can help. 

Firstly, it's important to acknowledge and validate the mix of emotions you've been experiencing - loneliness, frustration, and self-doubt. Instead of trying to engage in superficial conversations with many people, seek out opportunities for more meaningful interactions with individuals who share similar interests or values. Anxiety is constantly present in my life. It affects even simple tasks such as grocery shopping. Just yesterday, when I entered the crowded supermarket, I noticed my heart racing, dizziness, and difficulty breathing. The large number of people triggered this feeling of being trapped and overwhelmed. Talking about it during sessions would provide immense support in managing anxiety's grip on my daily activities.

One approach that may help you manage your anxiety during grocery shopping is to practice some relaxation techniques beforehand. Deep breathing exercises can be particularly helpful in calming down your body's response to stress and reducing physical symptoms like racing heart, dizziness, and difficulty breathing. Before entering the supermarket, take a few minutes to find a quiet space where you can focus on your breath. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold your breath for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. Repeat this process several times until you start feeling more relaxed.

Another technique you could try is progressive muscle relaxation. This involves tensing and releasing different muscle groups in your body to promote overall relaxation. Start with your toes, tensing them for a few seconds and then releasing the tension. Move up to your calves, thighs, abdomen, chest, arms, and so on, progressively working your way through each muscle group. By becoming more attuned to the sensations of tension and relaxation in your body, you may find it easier to recognize and alleviate any physical discomfort that arises in anxiety-provoking situations.

Additionally, it might be beneficial to challenge any negative thoughts or beliefs that contribute to your anxiety. When you notice yourself thinking things like "I'm trapped" or "I'm overwhelmed", pause for a moment and examine whether these thoughts are really accurate or if they're just anxious interpretations. Consider alternative perspectives or more balanced thoughts that acknowledge your ability to cope with crowded places and convey reassurance and self-confidence. Remember, these new ways of thinking will take time and practice, but gradually replacing negative thought patterns with positive ones can have a significant impact on how you experience anxiety.

Incorporating regular exercise into your routine can also be instrumental in managing anxiety. Engaging in activities such as walking, jogging, swimming, or even yoga can help reduce overall stress levels and increase feelings of well-being. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood-boosting chemicals in the brain, and can also serve as a healthy distraction from anxious thoughts.

Lastly, if talking about your experiences with anxiety during therapy sessions provides immense support for you, it's important to communicate this need to your therapist. Discussing specific situations or triggers that increase your anxiety levels, like crowded spaces or feeling overwhelmed, can help your therapist tailor their guidance and strategies specifically to your needs. They may suggest further techniques, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy exercises or exposure therapy, to gradually desensitize yourself to overwhelming environments.

Remember, managing anxiety is an ongoing process, and finding what works best for you may take time and experimentation. It's also okay to seek professional help from a mental health expert, counselor, or therapist who can provide additional support and guidance tailored to your unique situation.

Absolutely not. It's actually quite rare for someone to come in to therapy for "just one thing." More often than not, even people who seek out therapy "just for anxiety" often find a host of other related things when they start peeling back the layers in therapy.When clients come to me with a list of things like this, our first step is to put it all out there and THEN to work on finding the "constellation." All of these things tie together to form a more complete picture of who you are and how your experiences have impacted you and have led to other experiences. For example, many clients find it helpful to understand how a history of sexual abuse can increase the likelihood of developing insomnia. Seeing how everything ties together often helps people to slow down and take a step back from the tendency to take each of these struggles as a personal flaw or failure and to see how the whole picture fits. Plus, on the upside, once you've started to piece together the larger picture, you can use that to decide where to begin. Once you begin learning skills you can apply to one area, often times those same skills can be applied to other concerns with just a little variation. For example, the skills required to process through the beliefs you developed as a result of sexual abuse so that you can start shifting your mindset to more helpful perspectives is actually the same skills you can use to change the thought processes that maintain insomnia. So the skills can be generalized relatively easily!As long as you're still breathing, there's no such thing as too far gone.

Typically by not reacting right away, we are better able to gather our thoughts, see the situation more clearly and from other perspectives, and respond more calmly. When faced with a stressful situation, you can give yourself a time out by removing yourself from the stress and spend 5 minutes taking deep breaths (breathe in slowly counting to 4 and breathe out even slower counting to 6), while focusing and thinking only about your breathing. How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

It's kind of like an audition.  You need to find someone who you feel comfortable with and respect.  Many therapists provide short, free, consultations.  That is a good way to see if they seem to understand and empathize with you in a way that puts you at ease.  If you have specific issues that you need to work on. look for someone who specializes in what is troubling you.  The therapist should be able to provide evidence-based treatment and should discuss with you why they think this is the best way to proceed.  Every counseling client should feel free to have input on their goals and desired outcomes.
How does a person start the counseling process?

First, identify the areas that you need help with. What are the issues that are most troubling you? Are these situations creating an impact on your daily routine?Second, do some research as to the type of counselling service you are looking and that would best suit your needs. Are you looking for individual sesssions, couples/family sessions, etc. And research potential therapists in your area that focus their counselling approach on your therapeutic needs. Third, contact the therapist (most don't answer the phones, so leave a message or send an email). Don't be affraid to ask questions. You want to make sure that this professional is a good "match" for you and will work with you at working toward your therapeutic goals (the things you want to address/work on during the sessions).Fourth, have the expectation that, depending on the issues, you will need multiple sessions/appointments with the therapist to really address the issues and work toward your therapeutic goals.It takes strength and courage to reach out for help, but I know you can reach your goals. It takes time, patience, and practice do really address your needs. Good luck!

You are right that his insecurities are at the root of the issue.  You cannot change that for him.  He will have to do the work to handle those emotions on his own.  What you can do is reassure him in whatever ways possible, but always recognizing that you can't "fix" this for him.  When I work with people who struggle with their partner's past experiences, I always frame it like this:  Everything that you've experienced has resulted in you being the person you are today.  The person they claim to love.  If you had not gone through some of those experiences, you would not be in the position you're in now, ready to commit to him and know that you're satisfied with that.  Just as when bad things happen to us, we have to find a way to appreciate the lessons learned your fiance has to accept that you're the person you are today because of what you have gone through.  Celebrate that you have moved through that and have landed in this perfect position with him!Hope that helps, Allison

At times, stress takes such control over me that I experience elevated levels of frustration and anger towards myself and others. It feels like a cycle that I can't break free from.

Managing stress can be challenging, but there are strategies you can try to help break free from the cycle of frustration and anger. Here are some suggestions that might be helpful:

1. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to take care of your physical and emotional wellbeing. Engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as exercise, meditation, or spending time with loved ones.

2. Identify triggers: Pay attention to situations or people that tend to exacerbate your stress levels, frustration, and anger. By recognizing these triggers, you can be better prepared to manage them when they arise.

3. Practice deep breathing exercises: When you notice yourself becoming overwhelmed by stress, take a few moments to focus on your breathing. Slowly inhale through your nose, hold for a few seconds, and exhale through your mouth. This simple technique can help calm your nervous system and reduce feelings of anger and frustration.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Stress often leads to negative thinking patterns. Take a moment to identify any negative thoughts or beliefs that may be contributing to your frustration and anger. Ask yourself if there is evidence to support these thoughts and consider alternative perspectives or more balanced interpretations.

5. Set realistic expectations: Sometimes, we put excessive pressure on ourselves and others to meet unrealistic expectations. Assess what is truly within your control, and aim for achievable goals. Remember to practice self-compassion and acknowledge that it's okay to make mistakes or encounter setbacks along the way.

6. Seek social support: Sharing your feelings and experiences with trusted friends or family members can provide comfort and perspective. They can also offer support and practical advice. Additionally, consider connecting with local support groups or seeking online communities where you can engage with others who may have similar struggles.

There's been ongoing conflict between me and my siblings ever since we were young. We struggle to communicate effectively and often misunderstand each other's intentions. I desire a closer and more understanding relationship with them, so I'm seeking counseling to facilitate positive change in our family dynamics.

Building healthier and more understanding relationships with your siblings is definitely a worthwhile goal, and seeking counseling can be a great step toward achieving that. Here are some suggestions to consider as you work towards positive change in your family dynamics:

1. Open Communication: One important aspect of fostering better relationships is through open and honest communication. Take the initiative to express your thoughts and feelings calmly and respectfully, and encourage your siblings to do the same. Active listening can also play a role here - making a genuine effort to understand their perspective can go a long way.

2. Empathy and Understanding: Remember that each person has their own unique experiences and emotions. It's essential to approach conversations with empathy and try to see things from their point of view. By acknowledging their thoughts and feelings, you can demonstrate your commitment to building a closer relationship.

3. Reflect on Past Interactions: Take some time to reflect on past conflicts or misunderstandings and evaluate what contributed to those situations. Consider what patterns might exist and how they could be addressed moving forward. This self-reflection can help you identify areas where adjustments can be made and offer insights into finding common ground with your siblings.

4. Conflict Resolution Skills: Building effective conflict resolution skills can greatly improve family dynamics. Seek opportunities to learn about healthy ways to resolve disagreements, such as active listening, compromising, and finding win-win solutions. By acquiring these skills, you'll be better equipped to navigate future conflicts constructively.

5. Quality Time Together: Spending quality time together outside of moments of conflict can help strengthen your bond. Engaging in shared activities or even having regular family meetings can foster a sense of unity and connection. Showing your siblings that you value their presence by investing time and effort into the relationship can have a positive impact.

6. Professional Guidance: As mentioned earlier, pursuing counseling can be highly beneficial for improving your family dynamics. A trained therapist can provide you with additional tools and strategies tailored to your specific circumstances. They can help facilitate communication and guide you towards a more understanding and harmonious relationship with your siblings.

Remember, change takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself and your siblings as you work together on building healthier relationships.

For instance, last month, I had to make a significant career choice, and the thought of making the wrong decision consumed my mind entirely. I couldn't sleep, experienced restlessness, and found it hard to concentrate due to racing thoughts.

The frequency of my anxious thoughts has become almost daily, lasting anywhere from several hours to the entire day. The intensity varies depending on the situation, but it often leaves me feeling physically and mentally drained.

In terms of my upbringing, I grew up in a family where high achievements were praised and failure was not an option. This constant pressure to perform well may have contributed to my tendency to overanalyze and worry excessively about potential negative outcomes.

To manage my anxiety, I've tried journaling and practicing positive affirmations. While they provide temporary relief, I'm looking for additional tools or techniques that can help me better control my anxious thoughts.

Is cognitive-behavioral therapy an effective approach for managing generalized anxiety? How long does the treatment typically last?

A helpful approach for managing generalized anxiety is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and changing negative thinking patterns that contribute to anxiety. Through this therapy, you can learn strategies to challenge your anxious thoughts and develop healthier coping mechanisms.

The length of treatment for CBT can vary depending on individual circumstances, but it typically ranges from 12 to 20 weekly sessions. During these sessions, you would work collaboratively with a therapist who will help you understand the root causes of your anxiety and provide you with techniques and skills to manage it effectively.

In addition to CBT, there are other techniques that can complement your therapy and support your journey in controlling anxious thoughts. One effective tool is mindfulness meditation. Mindfulness involves focusing your attention on the present moment and accepting it without judgment. This practice can help reduce rumination and bring about a sense of calmness.

Another technique worth considering is progressive muscle relaxation. It involves tensing and then relaxing different muscle groups progressively to release tension and promote physical relaxation. Engaging in regular exercise, such as yoga or walking, can also be beneficial in reducing anxiety symptoms.

Additionally, establishing healthy lifestyle habits such as getting sufficient sleep, practicing deep breathing exercises, and maintaining a balanced diet can have a positive impact on your overall well-being and anxiety management.

Remember, everyone's situation is unique, and what works for one person might not work for another. It may take some trial and error to find the right combination of strategies that best suit you. Regular communication and collaboration with a mental health professional will allow for personalized guidance and adjustments based on your progress and needs.

It's important to remind yourself that managing anxiety is a process, and it's normal to have setbacks along the way. Be patient and kind to yourself as you explore various techniques and continue your journey towards finding effective ways to cope with your generalized anxiety.

I'm obsessing about a terrible breakup. Everything is a constant reminder. How do I move on?

Initially, everything is a reminder because there is a trace of that other person present in everything in your life. When we lose someone, we're saying goodbye to what we thought our future was going to be.  Accepting that's changed and allowing ourselves to envision a new future is necessary to "move on". Start learning something new or try a new activity that you've always wanted to do.  Find whatever is "good" about being out of the relationship and focus on those things.  This can be an exciting time of transformation for you.   As time goes by, you'll add new things in your life that aren't entwined with this relationship and those things will begin to crowd out those things associated with the relationship.  Give yourself a little empathy, no one goes through a breakup without being sad.  It's ok to be sad.  It's even ok to feel devastated.  Loss of a relationship touches a primal need we have to belong.  It makes us feel insecure, unanchored.  In truth, we are ok, safe even.  This experience will open different perspectives for you.  There are lessons you'll take from it that will add another facet to you as a person.  Maybe in time, you'll even appreciate this experience.  I'm sorry you're hurting right now.  Best wishes to you, Allison

I have been experiencing intense anxiety on a regular basis and it's affecting multiple aspects of my life. My goal for counseling is to gain a better understanding of my anxiety and develop effective coping mechanisms to manage it. The anxiety seems to be triggered by situations with high levels of uncertainty or when I feel like I'm not in control. One recurring example is public speaking engagements for work, which cause me significant distress leading up to the event. Symptoms occur multiple times per week and can last for hours, making it difficult for me to focus or sleep. I have attempted deep breathing exercises and mindfulness techniques during anxious moments, but they only provide temporary relief. Is there a more comprehensive approach we could explore to reduce my anxiety symptoms?

Thank you for sharing your experience with intense anxiety. It's understandable that this has been affecting various aspects of your life, and it's great that you've recognized the importance of gaining a better understanding of your anxiety to develop effective coping mechanisms.

The fact that uncertainty and lack of control trigger your anxiety is common among many individuals. One situation you mentioned, public speaking engagements, is particularly challenging for you. The distress leading up to these events can be overwhelming, impacting your ability to focus and sleep. 

While deep breathing exercises and mindfulness techniques provide temporary relief, it's worth exploring additional strategies to reduce your symptoms and manage your anxiety more comprehensively. Here are some suggestions:

1. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): CBT focuses on identifying and modifying negative thought patterns and beliefs that contribute to anxiety. By working with a therapist trained in CBT, you can learn techniques to challenge and reframe anxious thoughts, helping you build a healthier perspective.

2. Gradual Exposure: Since public speaking is a significant trigger for you, gradually exposing yourself to similar situations can help desensitize your anxiety response. Start by practicing in smaller, more comfortable settings and gradually work your way up to larger audiences. This gradual exposure approach can help build confidence over time.

3. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR): While you've mentioned trying mindfulness techniques, MBSR is a structured program designed specifically to reduce stress and cultivate greater awareness. Consider finding resources or courses focused on MBSR, as they typically include guided meditations, gentle movement practices, and teachings about managing thoughts and emotions.

4. Physical Activity: Engaging in regular physical exercise can significantly reduce anxiety symptoms. Find activities you enjoy, such as walking, yoga, dancing, or any form of exercise that gets your body moving. Exercise releases endorphins, which improve mood and promote overall well-being.

5. Self-Care Practices: Incorporate self-care activities into your routine to help manage anxiety. This may include doing things you find enjoyable, like reading, taking baths, listening to calming music, connecting with loved ones, or pursuing hobbies that bring you joy and relaxation.

6. Support System: Establishing a strong support system can be immensely helpful when dealing with anxiety. Consider confiding in trusted friends or family members who can provide emotional support. Sharing your experiences and feelings with others who understand can alleviate some of the burdens associated with anxiety.

It's important to remember that everyone's journey is unique, so finding the right combination of strategies may take time. Consult with a mental health professional who can guide you through these techniques tailored to your specific needs and circumstances. Remember to be patient and kind to yourself as you explore different approaches to reduce anxiety symptoms and improve your overall well-being.

Hi Troy, I totally get this. It's a dilemma; you want your dad to know how he's hurting you but you don't feel safe enough to say anything to him. Your reaction is understandable; it's his responsibility as a parent to work harder than you to create that safe place for you to be open. But that's not who your dad is. Your dad is your dad, and waiting for him to change won't really help. Nothing you do can change your dad, but...there are things you can do for yourself and your relationship with him. While your response of avoiding him is understandable, I wonder what effect it has on your dad. It's possible that he's feeling frustrated, rejected and punished by your withdrawal. You may think he knows that you're feeling hurt, but he probably doesn't. So this is the squirrel chasing its tail: your dad is rude, so your habit is to be silent, then he maybe feels abandoned and frustrated. His frustration comes out as more rudeness, which makes you want to withdraw more, and the cycle starts all over again. You can't change his part of the cycle but you can change yours.Are you willing to take a risk? Can you be honest about how you're feeling? What's the worst thing that could happen if you said to your dad "You know why I avoid you? I stay silent because when I talk to you say rude things. So if you want me to talk, I need to know you can listen." I imagine it would come out differently because you're a few generations younger than me, but put that into your own words.I don't know the level of your dad's 'rudeness'. If he is abusive, then a better plan is to see a therapist alone or talk to someone about this. I don't want to put you at any risk. But if you don't worry your dad will hurt you, maybe give honesty a try.My point is that, as rude as your dad may be, checking out of a relationship by being silent is also rude. It's powerful...your silence. Your dad can't read your mind, and if you want things to be better you will need to get in that ring with him.And, if you're both open to it, seeing a therapist together can be really helpful. :)

Staying present is an attitude most of us aspire
to, and most of us have to work at it—certainly at first. I’m here to tell you
that living in the now or being mindful is a skill anyone can learn. Unfortunately,
the only way to do it is to do it. What a paradox! But there are plenty of
other skills that we are not born with: walking on stilts, riding a bike,
swimming, and driving a car are good examples. You can’t learn them by reading about
them.Having said that, I can recommend two books on
the subject: Eckhart Tolle’s The Power of
Now and David Richo’s When the Past
is Present. Richo asks that we don’t beat ourselves up about dwelling on
past events. This is nature’s way of reminding us that we have unfinished
business. But while we are attended to the wounds and confusion that litter our earlier lives, we can prepare to inhabit the expanded present that awaits us.He offers three helpful steps to making any important life
change:Step One: Hold in awareness the behavior,
belief, attitude, or characteristic you want to change in yourself and how you
want to be different. Awareness is the opposite of distraction and stuffing.Step Two: Live as if you have
already made the change. (This is hard and takes courage, but you can do it.
Ride that bike—even if for a foot or two.)Step Three: Be persistent.
(Practice, practice, practice.)Just as two-year-olds are able to walk
confidently after hundreds of hours of practice, you’ll be able to stay in the
here and now as long as you want after trying and failing many, many times.

As a single parent, I often feel overwhelmed and inadequate. There are moments when I lose my temper with my children and then feel immense guilt afterwards. It's affecting both their well-being and mine. I want to learn effective parenting techniques and ways to manage my frustrations better.

Parenting can be challenging, especially as a single parent. It's understandable that you sometimes feel overwhelmed and inadequate. Remember that many parents experience similar emotions, so know that you are not alone. 

To start managing your frustrations better, it might help to try some coping strategies. Taking deep breaths when you're feeling stressed or overwhelmed can provide some immediate relief. Additionally, finding healthy outlets for your emotions such as journaling, exercising or engaging in a hobby can also be beneficial.

When it comes to effective parenting techniques, communication is key. Make sure to have open and honest conversations with your children about their behaviors and feelings. By doing this, you create an environment where they feel comfortable expressing themselves. Active listening is important too - show empathy, validate their emotions, and try to understand their perspective.

Setting clear boundaries and consistent expectations can also contribute to a more harmonious household. Establish rules together with your children and explain the reasons behind them. Consistency is crucial, so try to enforce these rules fairly and consistently.

Another technique you can use is positive reinforcement. Acknowledge and praise your children when they demonstrate good behavior or meet certain goals. This helps build their self-esteem and encourages them to continue making positive choices.

Remember, no parent is perfect, and it's okay to make mistakes. When you do lose your temper, take a moment to reflect on what triggered your reaction and consider healthier ways to cope next time. Apologize to your children and discuss different ways you could handle those situations together in the future.

Lastly, don't forget to prioritize self-care. As a caregiver, it's easy to neglect your own well-being. Take time for yourself, whether it's through relaxation techniques, exercise, spending time with friends, or seeking support from loved ones.

By implementing these suggestions, you'll be taking steps towards creating a healthier and happier home environment for both you and your children.

Does counseling really do anything that can help people?

I believe that counseling (and finding a GOOD therapist)
will be of significant help when the individual seeking therapy desires change,
improvement, and overall growth. Most counseling involves homework and a level
of commitment outside of session that also contributes to resolution of
problems and an ability to cope with stresses in a productive way. Here are
some of the key ways that therapy can help. 
1. Helps to define the problem and gain a clearer
understanding of where it originates. Many people seek counseling because of symptoms they are
experiencing. These can include feeling sad, increased sleeping, substance use,
panic attacks, self-harm, isolating one’s self, academic decline, etc. Often
times, people are not aware of what is causing these symptoms. Having a
therapist to help guide and explore why the symptoms are occurring and where
they come from will give individuals increased insight and awareness into their
problems. 
2. Allows for a safe outlet to vent.
Not everyone likes to share their problems with close
friends or family members. Maybe they don’t want others to know of their flaws.
Maybe they don’t want to burden others with their problems. Or maybe they just
are not comfortable talking about themselves. And in some situations people do
not have the option of talking with someone they know because they have no
friends or family. While talking with those we know can help bring some relief
it is also nice to talk with someone like a therapist who is objective and
emotionally removed from given situations. Counseling gives a safe outlet in
which one can express their personal feelings and thoughts without feeling
judged.
3. Counselors can offer various problem solving solutions.

A good therapist usually will not directly point their
client in the direction they need to go. Counseling is about growth and
teaching the client to identify triggers and use effective coping strategies
that will bring about emotional and psychological relief. Counselors will help
clients to explore the various options available in given situation, based on
the client’s needs, wants, and values and will help them to choose the option
that best fits with their desired outcome. 
4. Gives one the tools needed to cope with current and future
problems.
Many individuals that seek therapy have never learned
good coping strategies. Perhaps they did not have parents or caretakers to
model productive ways to cope or maybe the symptoms they are suffering from are
overbearing and take away the energy needed to cope. Different diagnoses
require different tools; however some are beneficial for any problem and any
individual. These include but are not limited to relaxation techniques,
breathing exercises, development of healthy routines, using mindfulness,
improving communication skills, and recognizing and changing maladaptive
thought patterns. A good counselor will teach clients how to use these tools,
will often practice them during session, and will assign homework for further
practice and mastery of the skills.

Managing stress levels can be challenging, especially when it feels like everything is piling up. It's great that you're reaching out for help and recognizing the physical symptoms you're experiencing. Here are some suggestions to help you navigate this difficult time:

1. Take breaks: Allow yourself regular moments throughout the day to rest and recharge. This could include short walks outside, deep breathing exercises, or engaging in activities you enjoy.

2. Practice relaxation techniques: Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided imagery can help reduce muscle tension and promote a sense of calm. You can find numerous resources online that provide step-by-step guidance on these techniques.

3. Prioritize self-care: Set aside dedicated time each day for activities that nourish your mind and body. This might include hobbies, exercise, journaling, connecting with loved ones, or enjoying a hot bath. Remember, taking care of yourself is not selfish but necessary for overall well-being.

4. Break tasks into smaller steps: When work demands become overwhelming, break them down into smaller, manageable tasks. This can make them feel less daunting and helps maintain focus and productivity.

5. Delegate and ask for support: If possible, delegate some tasks at work or seek support from coworkers or loved ones. Sharing responsibilities can lighten the load and prevent burnout.

6. Establish boundaries: Learn to say no when you feel overwhelmed with additional obligations. Setting clear boundaries allows you to prioritize what truly matters and reduces unnecessary stress.

7. Financial worries: Develop a budget to gain control over your finances. Seek advice from financial experts if needed. Identifying areas where you can cut back expenses or create a saving plan may alleviate some of the concerns related to money.

8. Mindfulness and meditation: Practicing mindfulness and meditation can help you stay present and focused, reducing anxiety about the future. Engaging in simple mindful activities like deep breathing or paying attention to the sensations around you can bring a sense of calm.

9. Seek support from loved ones: Share your feelings with trusted friends or family members who can provide emotional support and lend a listening ear. Sometimes, simply verbalizing our concerns can alleviate some stress.

Remember, these are just suggestions, and it's important to find what works best for you. If your stress levels persist or worsen, consider reaching out to mental health professionals who can provide additional guidance tailored to your specific needs.

Whenever I'm confronted with uncertainty or face unexpected changes, I become overwhelmed with anxiety. This fear of the unknown prevents me from taking risks and pursuing new opportunities. I want to overcome this barrier and build resilience so that I can embrace change and thrive in different circumstances.

It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of anxiety when it comes to uncertainty and unexpected changes. It's completely understandable that this fear of the unknown is preventing you from taking risks and pursuing new opportunities. Building resilience in these situations can be challenging, but it is definitely possible. Here are some suggestions that may help you:

1. Recognize and accept your feelings: It's important to acknowledge and accept your anxiety as a natural response to uncertain situations. Instead of trying to push away or ignore your emotions, allow yourself to feel them and understand that it's okay to be anxious.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: When facing uncertainty, our minds often go to worst-case scenarios. Try to identify any irrational or negative thoughts that might be contributing to your anxiety. Ask yourself if there is evidence supporting those thoughts, and try to come up with more realistic and balanced alternatives.

3. Focus on what you can control: While you cannot control everything in life, there are aspects within your control. Shift your focus to what you have influence over and take action accordingly. By doing so, you will regain a sense of empowerment and reduce your anxiety.

4. Break things down into smaller steps: Overcoming barriers and embracing change can seem overwhelming when viewed as one big task. Break down your goals into smaller, manageable steps. This approach allows you to make progress at your own pace and reduces the pressure you may feel.

5. Seek support: Opening up to someone you trust about your fears and concerns can provide relief and support. Consider sharing your struggles with a friend, family member, or even an online community where others can relate to what you're going through. Connecting with others who have faced similar challenges can also offer valuable insights and coping strategies.

6. Practice self-care: Taking care of your overall well-being is crucial during times of stress and uncertainty. Make sure you prioritize activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Engage in regular exercise, practice deep breathing or meditation, maintain a balanced diet, and ensure you are getting enough restorative sleep.

7. Challenge yourself gradually: Overcoming the fear of the unknown takes time and patience. Start by taking small steps outside of your comfort zone each day. Gradually expose yourself to situations that make you feel uncertain, and remember to celebrate even the smallest victories along the way.

Remember, building resilience is a process, and it won't happen overnight. Be kind to yourself as you navigate these challenges, and don't be afraid to seek professional help if needed. You have the strength within you to overcome this barrier and embrace change in order to thrive in different circumstances.

We're in an eight year relationship. My boyfriend drinks a lot. He experienced childhood trauma. I don't know how to deal with violent outbursts.

First, let me extend my compassion to both of you -- it sounds like you have a lot on your plates. Childhood trauma carries its negative effects into our adulthood and affects everyone who loves us. Your question is brief, so I'll just try to give general answers as best I can. From my experiences treating many people with your boyfriend's experiences, the short, healthy answer is that you can't fix the situation and maybe not even be able to help. He needs a professional. Period. What you can do, is take care of yourself. With his background, it is not likely that he will be able to help you or take care of you in a healthy way. Your task needs to prioritize your own safety and well-being. Trauma and substance abuse are the definition of being out of control, unable to set and manage appropriate boundaries, manage his own emotions and behaviors. So your boyfriend is unlikely to be able to change in the near-term, certainly not without professional help. You might also benefit from help and support, to understand your own role in your relationship and how you can make changes in your life. I am NOT blaming you for any aspect of your boyfriend's behavior, only acknowledging that there are two people in every relationship. If you have accepted your boyfriend's drinking and violent outbursts in the past (by staying in the relationship), that is likely to perpetuate his behavior. And there isn't any way to "handle violent outbursts." They shouldn't be handled at all, and if you have to be away from your boyfriend during his outbursts in order to be emotionally and physically safe, then that may be what you will have to do. We can never really change anyone else. The only person we can change is ourselves. Sometimes our behavior changes the odds of another person's behaviors, but it doesn't control it. I would recommend that you work with a professional to first, ensure your own safety above all. Then make decisions about what behavior you are willing to accept or be connected to, and which you want to separate from. Whatever your boyfriend does in his life, you will be happier if you manage your own feelings, set boundaries, etc. Let me say again that you also would benefit from some good insight and support as you continue your journey. Wishing you and your boyfriend healing and recovery.

A great place to start is at www.psychologytoday.com.  You can search by location and identify therapists who have expertise in your area of concern.  Once you find a few people that fit your criteria, read about them on Psychology today as well as check out their website if they have one.  Next, either call or email them to set up a time to talk for a few minutes.  When you speak with them, you want to know a few things: do they have a decent amount of experience in your area of concern?  Are their fees, insurance coverage and scheduling availability a good fit for you?  Most importantly, see if you feel comfortable when you speak to them on the phone!  If this person is a good match in these areas, schedule an initial consultation so that you can see if you are also a good match in person.

This is a difficult situation to be in, as it sounds like you are feeling very isolated from both your family and your friends.   I don't know your age or gender so please excuse any incorrect assumptions about you being under 18 and use what is useful from the ideas if you are older.  One idea is to research online to find a therapist or a local clinic that has a therapist who is a "Gender Therapist" or a "Gender Specialist."  Most therapists who are transgender affirmative also have other specialties and do general therapy.  Though I don't think lying to your parents is a good idea, if you feel you truly can't talk to them about your gender, then perhaps you can find a therapist with a specialization in gender identity who can help you cope with your gender dysphoria.  You can let your parents know that you would like to see that particular therapist for other reasons, such as anxiety/worry, and that you researched them and liked their website.  Work to find a therapist who takes your parents insurance if you can.  You can also talk to the therapist on the phone first, before you talk to your parents about scheduling the first therapy visit. Therapists can help you learn some ways to manage feelings of worry, shame, and fear related to gender dysphoria. Depending on your family situation, many therapists will work to help you learn skills to safely communicate with your parents about what is troubling you.  Your parents may actually surprise you and be more accepting than you think.  Usually when parents learn that you are suffering, they want to be open to learning how they can help you, even if awkwardly at first.Reframing is a tool that helps you think about your situation from other perspectives.  It's kind of how you can look at the same picture with a different picture frame and it makes the same picture look a little different.   Keep in mind your situation is probably temporary and think about in the context of your whole long life (can you tolerate another 2 to 4 years living like you are if you have another X number of years to live?).  If you are living at home, you will eventually be more independent and be able to make more of your decisions about your gender expression. Keep the idea in mind the concept that is popular in mindfulness classes I teach, that "This too shall pass" or "This is only for now" when you start to feel hopeless. If you start to over focus on your gender or body issues, try to distract yourself with things that make you feel happy (your pet, music, art, sports etc) or stay busy.  If you can, find any GSA or LGBTIQQ youth group that you can attend confidentially, further away from home, to get some support.  Work to find an ally, one person, that you can talk to about what you are feeling. Making new friends online through social media can sometimes be a start in breaking down the isolation you feel. Another idea, if you are under 24 years old, there is a phone line (866-488-7386)  to call in case you are ever feeling you are in crisis.  You can also text chat! Trevor Project: http://www.thetrevorproject.org/There is also a trans teen online chat group if you are 12-19 http://www.glbthotline.org/transteens.htmlIf you are an adult you can get numbers to call in your state if you start to feel suicidal:http://www.suicidepreventionlifeline.org/Day to day, can you creatively work on your gender dysphoria?  Yes!  Are there ways you can focus on parts of your body you love?  Can you focus on that when you look in the mirror?  Are you a writer?  Can you write stories or poetry about the life you imagine for yourself in the future?  Can you do small things that help you get more in touch with your gender day to day like making small choices about your clothing, like wearing clothes that are more unisex,  that only you know are gender related but others won't notice?  You cannot force others to accept you but you can work on your self-acceptance and self-compassion. That work is something that is best done in the company of others like you as well as with at least another person who gets you and whom you can trust.  Good luck to you!

How many people live in California?

California is a state in the Western United States, located along the Pacific Coast. With nearly 39.2 million residents across a total area of approximately 163,696 square miles (423,970 km2), it is the most populous U.S. state and the third-largest by area. It is also the most populated subnational entity in North America and the 34th most populous in the world. The Greater Los Angeles and San Francisco Bay areas are the nation's second and fifth most populous urban regions respectively, with the former having more than 18.7 million residents and the latter having over 9.6 million. San Francisco is the second most densely populated major city in the country. Los Angeles County is the country's most populous, while San Bernardino County is the largest county by area in the country. California borders Oregon to the north, Nevada and Arizona to the east, the Mexican state of Baja California to the south; and it has a coastline along the Pacific Ocean to the west.

California's economy is the largest of any state within the United States, with a $3.37 trillion gross state product (GSP) as of 2022. It is the largest sub-national economy in the world. If California were a sovereign nation, it would rank as the world's fifth-largest economy as of 2022, behind India and ahead of the United Kingdom, as well as the 37th most populous. The San Francisco Bay Area Combined Statistical Area had the nation's highest gross domestic product per capita ($106,757) among large primary statistical areas in 2018, and is home to five of the world's ten largest companies by market capitalization and four of the world's ten richest people. Stay Calm and Focused: Getting lost in a maze can be frustrating, but it's important to stay calm and focused. Take deep breaths, relax, and clear your mind. This will help you to think more clearly and make better decisions.

Plan Your Route: Take a few minutes to look at the maze from above, if possible, and try to identify the route to the exit. Identify landmarks or walls that you can use as reference points. Look for any dead ends, and try to avoid them.

Follow One Wall: If you can't identify the exit route, try to follow one wall of the maze. Keep your hand on the wall and follow it all the way around the maze. This will help you to stay on track and avoid getting lost in circles.

Mark Your Path: If you have something to mark your path, such as chalk, breadcrumbs, or a pen, use it to mark your route as you go. This way, you can avoid taking the same path multiple times and can backtrack if necessary.

Look for Clues: Keep an eye out for clues that may help you find your way out, such as arrows or signs. Many mazes also have hidden clues or puzzles that can help you find the exit, so keep your eyes open.

Ask for Help: If you're still struggling to find your way out, don't be afraid to ask for help. Many mazes have staff members who can guide you out or provide you with clues.

With these tips in mind, you should be able to find your way out of a maze. Remember to stay calm, plan your route, and look for clues, and you'll be out in no time!

"In my current relationship, there are trust issues and constant arguments. I want to address these problems and improve the overall quality of our relationship. I look forward to exploring communication tools and learning how to rebuild trust."

Improving the quality of your relationship and addressing trust issues can take time and effort, but it's definitely possible. Here are some suggestions to help you work towards that goal:

1. Start by having an open and honest conversation with your partner about your concerns. Express your desire for a healthier relationship and explain why trust and communication are important to you.

2. Explore different communication tools together. Effective communication is crucial in any relationship. Consider using "I" statements instead of blaming or criticizing each other. This approach encourages understanding and empathy. Practice active listening by giving each other undivided attention and validating each other's feelings.

3. Rebuilding trust requires consistency and transparency. Be reliable and follow through on your commitments. Avoid keeping secrets or withholding information from your partner. It's vital to rebuild trust through actions rather than just words.

4. If there are specific incidents that have caused trust issues, talk about them openly. Listen to your partner's perspective without judgment and share how those incidents made you feel. Discuss ways to prevent similar situations from occurring in the future.

5. Consider seeking professional support if necessary. Couples therapy can provide a safe space to navigate these challenges with the guidance of a trained therapist. They can offer helpful insights and techniques tailored to your situation.

6. Remember to prioritize self-care. Take care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally. Engage in activities that bring you joy, reduce stress, and promote overall well-being. When you are in a good place personally, it positively impacts your relationships.

7. Finally, be patient and kind to yourself and your partner as you work through these issues. Relationships require continuous effort and growth. Celebrate small victories along the way and recognize that progress takes time.

Remember, improving a relationship is a joint effort that requires commitment and willingness from both partners. By actively working on communication and rebuilding trust, you're taking positive steps forward.

Hello, and thank you for your question. First, I want to say that it is great that you are are willing to admit that you share some responsibility in some of the relationship problems you are having. This isn't always easy to do, but it sure is important if you want to see improvement. It does sound cliche, but communication really is the bedrock of relationships.
