I have a mother who is still running my life even though I'm almost 30 years old. I want to move out and live my own life, but it feels like as long as I do what my mom wants our relationship is okay. It's never okay if I don't do what she wants.    I don't know how to start making my own decisions and not worry about whether it's right in her eyes. Would it help for me to talk to someone about this?

ABSOLUTELY.  Having someone who's outside the situation and, even more so, with knowledge and experience in human behavior and relationship dynamics such as a counselor can do wonders in helping us feel less alone in frustrating situations like the one you're currently stuck in with your mother.  A professional can also assist you in finding some assertiveness techniques, communication strategies, and coping skills to help you find your voice and stand your ground in a way that feels most authentic to you.In a healthy parent-child dynamic, there comes a normal developmental shift when, as the child reaches each new stage of maturity and responsibility, the parent backs off to provide a more supportive role instead of directive role.  We call this "redefining relationships." (We also do it with our friendships and colleagues here and there over time as needed). It's absolutely vital. Sounds like your mom may have missed that memo. Like many parents, she may feel your behavior and choices is a direct reflection of her. Or that her role as your mother allows her greater latitude than it should.  Or like many other people in general, that her way is the ONLY way. Regardless, this is YOUR life.  And as far as we know, it's not a dress rehearsal. You certainly don't want to wake up some 50 years from now regretful or resentful. That being said, there are certainly ways to show her love and respect while doing what makes you happy. I would encourage you to Google therapists near you whose bios resonate with you and what you're looking for and start on a the journey towards a new chapter of freedom and hopefully a deeper, more satisfying mother-daughter relationship for both of you.Warmest regards,Tamara Powell, LMHC

Hello, and thank you for your question. When faced with these kinds of difficult challenges, I usually encourage people to look to their values for help in determining what their behavior should be. Indeed, it is usually when our behaviors conflict with our values that we don't feel very content with our lives. Perhaps you can take some time to think through a couple of these questions: What kind of person do I want to be deep in my heart? What kind of character do I want to have when in public and in my private world when nobody is watching? How would I want others to describe me? Let's say that you want others to see you as being authentic, and YOU also value authenticity as something you want to live by. You may feel like this value is currently at odds with the behaviors you are engaging in right now. That you are not being the person that you really are deep in your heart. This is not an unusual struggle when it comes to sexual behavior and sexual orientation. So please, try not to feel alone. We all know quite well how unacceptable it may be to be seen as gay, lesbian, bisexual, etc. And I am not just talking about being unaccepted by others, but a person may have a VERY hard time accepting themselves. Thinking about your values and living a life based on them can bring a lot of freedom, but I won't lie, it can also bring a lot of pain at the same time. For example, someone with the value of living authentically may decide they have to tell others who they are and what they stand for, even if that means people may disapprove. That may cause a lot of pain, but it may also come with a sense of freedom to live a life based on honesty and authenticity. It may be helpful to find a counselor who is trained in affirmative therapy, which is recommended for people who are navigating their sexual behaviors and figuring out what is right for them. I would also sit down and think through some of the questions above and consider what your values are... both as an individual and as someone's fiancé.Above all, I wish you well in this journey. Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

After first meeting the client, what is the process that a counselor facilitates?

Each counselor may have a different process, so I'm not the end all authority here.  For myself, I review policies and confidentiality concerns with people first and answer any questions they have. Then I'll let them know I'll be writing a lot in this session and I have an assessment form that I like to get completed, but I want to have a conversation and I'll ask questions as we go.  My first question is usually, "How do you feel I can best help you today?"  Some people are very at ease and tell me many details.  Others are a bit more reserved and I have to demonstrate more curiosity.  Even people who have been very apprehensive are usually feeling very relaxed by the time the session is over.  Usually, when we get close to end of session time, I'll summarize what I think are the biggest concerns from what I've heard and confirm whether or not the person wants to work on those things.  I also try to give an exercise targetting my biggest concern for them to work on in between sessions.  For instance, a relaxation method if they are very anxious.  Counselors are just humans as well, so it does take a bit of time to really get to know another person.  I always tell people that are apprehensive to give the counselor 3 or 4 sessions to determine if they really connect with them.  I hope that helps, Allison

To heal and process past traumatic experiences.
Description: I've experienced traumatic events in the past that still haunt me. It’s important for me to work through these experiences so they don't continue impacting my mental health negatively.

Triggering events: During my adolescence, I was a victim of bullying at school, which left deep emotional scars. Additionally, as an adult, I encountered a life-threatening event that further intensified my trauma response.

Symptoms: Recurring flashbacks and nightmares related to these traumas have significantly affected my quality of life. I'm constantly on edge, hyper-vigilant, and find it challenging to trust others.

Coping strategies: I've tried suppressing the memories, thinking they would eventually fade away with time. However, this approach has proven ineffective, and the unresolved trauma continues to resurface.

Inquiries: How can counseling help individuals like me recover from traumatic experiences? What therapeutic techniques are typically used to process trauma? Are there any support groups or additional resources available for survivors of trauma?

To begin, it's important to acknowledge that healing from past traumatic experiences is a deeply personal and unique journey. Counseling can be a valuable tool in helping individuals like you process trauma and begin the healing process.

In therapy, there are various therapeutic techniques that can be used to address trauma effectively. One commonly used approach is called cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on identifying and challenging unhelpful thoughts and beliefs related to your trauma. CBT can also help you develop healthier coping mechanisms, manage distressing symptoms such as flashbacks or nightmares, and gradually expose yourself to triggers in a safe and controlled manner.

Another technique often utilized in trauma therapy is Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). This method involves focusing on specific memories while engaging in bilateral stimulation, such as following a therapist's finger movements. EMDR aims to reprocess and reduce distress associated with traumatic events.

Support groups can be incredibly helpful for survivors of trauma, as they provide a safe space to connect with others who have had similar experiences. Being part of a support group allows you to share your feelings and stories, gain validation, and learn from one another's coping strategies. You may consider researching local organizations or online communities that offer trauma-specific support groups.

In addition to counseling and support groups, there are many resources available for survivors of trauma. Books, websites, podcasts, and even apps can offer information, guidance, and tools for healing. It may be beneficial for you to explore these resources to complement your therapy sessions.

Remember that everyone's healing journey is different, and it's essential to find an approach that feels right for you. Don't hesitate to discuss these therapeutic techniques and additional resources with a mental health professional. They will be able to guide you further based on their expertise and understanding of your situation.

I have so many issues to address. I have a history of sexual abuse, I’m a breast cancer survivor and I am a lifetime insomniac.    I have a long history of depression and I’m beginning to have anxiety. I have low self esteem but I’ve been happily married for almost 35 years.
   I’ve never had counseling about any of this. Do I have too many issues to address in counseling?

The short answer is: absolutely not! The longer answer is that it might take some time to process all of the issues, and it may feel quite "muddy" in the issues for a lot longer than is tolerable (which is why counseling may have been postponed to begin with for you.) It's important to be realistic when entering counseling of any sort, and that the therapist be realistic with you about what you might be able to expect working with that person (I use the words "might be able to expect" because therapy experiences can vary.) But that not having counseling about trauma that you have experienced much earlier in your life can play a significant role in the process and how long that process could take to unpack all that may have been buried over time.It might also be helpful in counseling to work with the therapist on figuring out where to begin, but to also manage the feelings of being overwhelmed that may make it hard to continue to show up and do the work required, week in and week out. It isn't easy work trying to process past pain that you experienced, and so consistent practice of self-care, including leaning on support systems outside of therapy, is key.

When someone tells me that they wish their child would do better in school, I always ask what that means. Sometimes it means that their grades are D's and F's. For other families, it means that the grades dropped below 95% and in that family, that is unacceptable. A recent situation that triggered my anxiety was starting a new job. Anxiety symptoms are present almost daily for me, particularly when facing uncertainty or worrying about future outcomes. The intensity varies depending on the situation, but it often feels like a weight pressing down on my chest, making it difficult to think clearly or make decisions.

Reflecting on my past, childhood experiences of unstable environments and frequent changes can be connected to my current struggles with anxiety. These early life events have shaped my perception of unpredictability, further contributing to my heightened sensitivity to change.

To cope with anxiety, I have attempted grounding techniques such as focusing on the present moment and practicing self-care activities. While these strategies offer temporary relief, I'm eager to explore additional tools that will help me manage anxiety more effectively.

I completely understand how anxiety can significantly impact your everyday life, especially during times of uncertainty or change.

CBT focuses on identifying negative thinking patterns and replacing them with more positive and realistic thoughts. This approach can be effective in helping you challenge anxious thoughts and reduce their power over you.

Another technique we can incorporate is mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) which involves focusing on the present moment and accepting it without judgment. MBSR teaches us to observe our thoughts and emotions without getting caught up in them, which can help alleviate anxiety symptoms.

Through repeated exposure, you can learn that anxiety does not need to control your actions or outcomes.

Understanding the connection between childhood experiences and your current struggles with anxiety is crucial. Exploring those early life events with empathy and compassion can provide insights into why unpredictability triggers intense anxiety for you. It would be helpful to process these experiences together in order to reframe your perception of unpredictability and reduce its impact on your day-to-day life.

Aside from therapy, there are also some self-care practices you can incorporate into your routine to complement your progress. These may include regular physical exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, practicing relaxation techniques like deep breathing exercises, engaging in hobbies and activities that bring you joy, and establishing healthy sleep habits.

Remember, managing anxiety effectively takes time and practice. In our counseling sessions, we can continuously evaluate your progress and adapt our treatment plan accordingly. By actively participating in therapy and consistently applying the tools and techniques we discuss, you can gradually build resilience and better manage uncertainty.

I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.

Getting your first job is an exciting, terrifying, and challenging experience. It is something you will remember for a long time and it shapes how you begin to think about yourself as a worker. You are literally "learning as you go" in this completely new environment. You are going to make mistakes. You are not going to get it right the first time. It can be even more challenging if you are having a difficult time building relationships that are supportive at work. A couple of things to remember here: 1) You are there to do a job and you are getting paid to do it, 2) There is a reason or reasons for you wanting to be there and do that work, 3) you know best what you need in order to be successful. These three items can be helpful to remember, especially when we feel our emotions are taking over in a place where we do not feel safe to express them fully. If you feel like your supervisor is approachable, meaning someone you could talk to because they express confidence in you, let them know you are nervous about doing a good job. Also let them know how you learn new tasks, information, or expectations so they can deliver the message in a way that you understand. Becoming a successful worker doesn't happen overnight, but each day you can identify what works for you and what doesn't by communicating with your work team, the easier it will be for you. We all had a first job once, and were all worried about doing well. Hang in there, and call a counselor if you need more help.

Hey there, I'm Sarah and I suffer from anxiety. In particular, I struggle with social situations. The mere thought of attending parties or speaking up in meetings triggers a deep sense of unease. Recently, I had an important work presentation and I couldn't sleep for days leading up to it. My mind was flooded with negative thoughts about embarrassing myself in front of my colleagues.

It can be really challenging to experience anxiety, especially when it affects your ability to engage in social situations. It's great that you reached out for support. Here are a few suggestions that may help you manage your anxiety in these situations:

1. Prioritize self-care: Engaging in activities that promote relaxation and well-being can help reduce overall anxiety levels. Consider incorporating activities like exercise, meditation, deep breathing exercises, or engaging in hobbies that bring you joy.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: Negative thoughts often play a significant role in escalating anxiety. Try to identify any irrational thoughts or fears related to social situations and challenge them by asking yourself if there is evidence to support these thoughts. Additionally, try replacing negative thoughts with more positive or realistic ones.

3. Gradual exposure: If social situations trigger intense anxiety, consider exposing yourself gradually to those situations. Start small by attending gatherings or meetings with people you feel comfortable around, and gradually work your way towards larger events. This gradual approach allows you to build confidence and coping skills over time.

4. Practice relaxation techniques: Before upcoming social events, practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation. These techniques can help calm your mind and body, reducing anxiety symptoms.

5. Seek support from trusted individuals: Having supportive friends, family members, or colleagues who understand your struggle can make a significant difference. Talk to them about your anxiety and let them know how they can offer their support during challenging situations.

Remember, managing anxiety takes time and effort. Celebrate each small step you take towards facing your fears and seeking personal growth. If your anxiety persists and significantly interferes with your daily functioning, I would encourage you to consider seeking professional guidance for additional support tailored to your specific needs.

Hello, and thank you for your question. Loving someone who
doesn’t respect or treat you well can be enormously difficult and painful. 
Many people who find themselves in an emotionally hurtful
relationship say that it was wonderful when it first started, but that over
time their partner’s behaviors changed and they became emotionally or
physically abusive. 
I want to say right away that it is not your fault in any
way if someone is abusive to you. It does not mean that you are broken or that there
is something wrong with your character if you have not left the situation.
People stay for many reasons, such as fear, finances, children, pressure from
others, and love. 
Many people have had to leave their abusive partners who
they still love to preserve their own safety and regain the sense of self they
may have lost. It is a very difficult thing to do, even if you know it is the
right thing. 
The person who really needs to take a hard look at
themselves is the person doing the abusing.
It is very common for mental and emotional abuse to wear
away at someone’s self-esteem. This can lead to other problems, like depression
and anxiety. These issues sometimes require professional support to manage,
such as a counselor or perhaps a doctor who may prescribe medication. 
A counselor may be able to help you sort through your fears
and concerns about staying or leaving. To look at things from different angles,
and to help you decide what is best for you. 
You have not said that your husband has been physically abusive
to you, but if that has been the case, then you must consider your physical
safety first. Leaving an abusive relationship is the most dangerous time.
Getting help from professionals would be critical, and I would recommend your
local domestic violence program. 
Whatever you decide to do is the right thing for you. I
would encourage you to ask yourself honestly about your reasons for staying and
the barriers that may keep you from going. You do deserve to be happy and
emotionally safe. If you do not feel like you have that safety, then seeking
someone to help you sort through these things is a good plan. 
I wish you well.
Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Hi California, What you're experiencing is indeed anxiety; it's very common. Through research we know a lot of things about how to reduce anxiety. I'll get you started and it's a great idea to connect with a therapist who can build on these ideas and get to know you well.It's natural to have random thoughts that unsettle us. Our brains are complex, wonderful things. Fearful and anxious thoughts are a part of this picture; their purpose is to prepare us for the future and to help us make sense of the past and learn from it. But what happens sometimes is that our alarm systems get out of whack and get set off too easily. We often spend TOO MUCH time worrying about things that happened or might happen. When these thoughts take away from our enjoyment of life, it becomes a problem. So, while fear and anxiety try to protect us, they also seek power and will take any power they can get.In general, fear and anxiety try to tell us one or both of two things: that something is wrong with us, or that something bad will happen (or that something bad will happen because there's something wrong with us). They will use anything they can as evidence to convince you. For example... "That person looked at you funny. You're strange looking". Well there are dozens of possible explanations for the look on that person's face, and it's unlikely it had anything to do with you. For you personally, your thoughts are about the afterlife...about living forever. What does fear tell you will be uncomfortable about living forever? What would the worst part be? A therapist would help you dig deep to find the core of what you fear. It might be that you have no control over who you are or where you go. It might be that you fear going to hell because you're "bad". Search for that deepest fear.I invite you then to picture that thought as a glass of water on a shelf. It's a heavy glass, and if you held it in your hands for a while and stared at it, it would get in the way; you'd be uncomfortable and unable to focus on your life. That's what's happening now. I suggest that the problem is not so much the thought you're having; we all have random silly thoughts that usually aren't true. The problem is how long you're holding it in your hand. You could have that thought (pick up that glass) a hundred times a day and, as long as you put it right back on the shelf, it's not a problem. The trick is to get it back on that shelf.Right now, you're using distraction to do this. You're trying to focus on other things around you, but I think the glass is still in your hand. It's not enough; you're looking for more tools to get that glass back on the shelf.  And the key is in your thoughts. Once you find out what fear is trying to tell you, then you can "talk back to" fear. So, as an example, if fear is saying to you "you have no control over anything", then you can work to accept the pieces you don't have control over, learn to tolerate that feeling, and claim back the pieces you CAN control. You CAN control the extent to which you let fear take you over. With a therapist you can learn to "refute" fears' ideas. You can learn to look for concrete evidence of fear's lies and gain back control over your thoughts. I wish you the best!

Being aware of your emotions can help you address them more effectively.

2. Establish boundaries: Setting healthy boundaries is crucial in any relationship. Consider what boundaries you would like to set with your parents to protect your emotional well-being. Communicate these boundaries calmly and assertively, making sure to express your needs without blaming or accusing them.

3. Improve communication: Effective communication is key to resolving conflicts and building stronger connections. One technique you can try is active listening - make an effort to truly listen to your parents' perspective without interrupting or judging. When expressing yourself, use "I" statements to share your thoughts and feelings in a non-confrontational way, focusing on how their actions impact you personally.

4. Seek resolution through dialogue: Instead of letting conflicts simmer and build up, consider initiating honest conversations with your parents about the issues that cause distress. Choose a suitable time and place where everyone feels comfortable and safe to express themselves. Approach the conversation with empathy and a willingness to understand each other's perspectives.

5. Find support: It may also be helpful to find support outside of the parent-child relationship. Consider talking to a trusted friend, family member, or even a therapist who can provide guidance and help you process your emotions in a neutral and supportive environment.

6. Focus on self-care: Prioritizing self-care activities can go a long way in managing emotional distress. Engage in activities that bring you joy, relaxation, and fulfillment. Explore new hobbies, practice mindfulness or meditation, exercise regularly, and make sure to get enough restful sleep.

7. Nurture other relationships: Strengthening connections with other loved ones in your life can provide additional support and a sense of belonging. Surround yourself with people who uplift you and understand your experiences, and lean on them for emotional support when needed.

Remember, improving relationships takes time and effort from both sides. It's important to be patient with yourself and your parents as you work towards healthier connections. Taking small steps and focusing on open communication and self-care can contribute positively to your overall well-being.

More information would be needed for me to accurately answer this question, such as your age, whether you live with your dad or not, and what other family members live in the household. Something like this, alcoholism, is a whole family disease. In other words, family members often unknowingly contribute to the alcoholism and enable the alcoholic to continue the destructive behavior.First of all, you can’t make your dad do anything, and constantly nagging him or begging him to stop is just going to make him defensive and make this worse. Nobody can change another person. What you can do is change how you react to him and the things that you and other family members do for him. Research codependency. There’s a great book called Codependent No More. There are a lot of articles on the internet that you can read. In short, you have to stop enabling him. Like I said, you cannot control him, but you can control yourself. This means do not buy his alcohol. Do not make it easy for him to get. Don’t loan him the car keys or pay any household bills for him. Don’t call in sick to work for him or make excuses for him in any way. Do not bail him out of jail when he gets arrested. He needs to be responsible for himself. This may mean losing his job or losing his driver’s license. This may mean that he loses his family if he doesn’t stop. What you and your family can do is set boundaries about what you will put up with. It is his choice to drink, but it is your choice to put up with the behaviors of his drinking. A lot of people go into rehab because their spouse said if they don’t then they are getting a divorce.If you are an adult and you don’t live with your dad, then the best thing you can do for him is STOP doing things for him. If you are a child who lives at home with him, then this could be a case for child protective services. In my state this is called DHS. A report is made to this organization for child abuse or neglect. Substance abuse in the home qualifies. Of course, alcohol is legal and when consumed in moderation, there is no problems. The problem will be the result of his alcohol consumption. Does he drive with children in the car while intoxicated? Is he left to care for minors while in an intoxicated state? Are there any domestic violence issues due to his drinking? This could be a reason for the authorities to step in. You can look for a local meeting for family members of alcoholics. They are similar to the AA meetings that an alcoholic should go to, but are for the family members. They can help you.

In a way, self-harm can present somewhat like an addiction.  According to new research within the field of neuroscience there is a valid explanation for this.  When a person cuts or uses other forms of self harm, the body produces endorphins to help make a person feel better.  If a person was dealing with depression or high anxiety, that might be misinterpreted by the brain as a way to help oneself feel better and a new neural network or map might form (addiction) that would utilize this new behavior.  Another way to look at it would be thru a behavioral lens, a positive reward for a behavior, even though the behavior has other long term negative consequences.  Consider working with someone who can both have you work on and address those items that trigger your behavior and the root causes, in this case sadness or depression, and second find someone who can help give you alternatives that take into account the neurological requirement by replacing the behavior with another behavior (such as snapping a rubber band on the wrist) and working to extinguish the unwanted behavior.   Someone who is trained in Dialectic Behavior Therapy and/or Interpersonal Neurobiology would most likely have the skills and means available to address this with you.

Anxiety has made it difficult for me to trust others. I constantly worry about being betrayed or hurt by the people around me. This fear often leads to strained relationships and feelings of isolation. How can I learn to let my guard down and build meaningful connections?

It can be challenging when anxiety interferes with our ability to trust others and form meaningful connections. Trust is an essential component of healthy relationships, and it's understandable that your fear of being betrayed or hurt has led to strained relationships and feelings of isolation. Here are some suggestions to help you learn to let your guard down and build meaningful connections:

1. Self-reflection: Take some time to reflect on any past experiences that may have contributed to your fear of trusting others. Understanding the root causes of your anxiety can provide valuable insights into why you feel this way.

2. Challenge negative thoughts: Anxiety often leads us to assume the worst about people's intentions. When these thoughts arise, try to challenge them by asking yourself if there is any evidence supporting these beliefs. Remind yourself that not everyone will betray or hurt you.

3. Start small: Building trust takes time, so start by gradually opening up to people you feel comfortable with. Share your thoughts and feelings in a controlled manner, allowing yourself to experience vulnerability at your own pace.

4. Communicate openly: Effective communication is crucial for building trust. Express your concerns and fears to those close to you, helping them understand your struggles. Honest conversations can foster understanding and strengthen relationships.

5. Set boundaries: It's important to establish healthy boundaries in relationships. Clearly communicate your needs and expectations, ensuring that both parties feel respected and understood. Boundaries can help create a sense of safety while still allowing for connection.

6. Seek support: Consider reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or even a therapist who can provide guidance and support as you navigate your journey towards building trust. They can offer a fresh perspective and help you develop strategies specific to your situation.

7. Practice self-care: Prioritize self-care activities that promote relaxation and reduce anxiety. Engage in hobbies, exercise regularly, practice mindfulness or meditation, and ensure you're getting enough restful sleep. Taking care of yourself can improve your overall well-being and make it easier to trust others.

Remember, building trust takes time and patience. Be kind to yourself throughout this process and celebrate small victories along the way. With perseverance and a willingness to take risks, you can learn to let your guard down and cultivate meaningful connections with others.

Tell me about the first commercial winery in California.

The first commercial winery in California was founded in 1857 by Hungarian-American Agoston Haraszthy who is referred to as the "Father of California Wine" (this moniker also is applied to Spanish Jesuit missionary, Father Junípero Serra). 

Haraszthy opened Buena Vista Winery in Sonoma. By 1859, the winery was producing two million gallons of wine a year and one of its most popular products was sparkling wine. 

The winery faced numerous troubles over the years, such as bankruptcy, a devastating infestation of Grape phylloxera, and Prohibition. The winery was acquired at auction and original vines replanted and reopened in the 1940s. In 1984, the winery estate expanded an additional 1,000 acres after it was purchased by a West German company. The winery continued to change hands and is now under the ownership of Jean-Charles Boisset, who operates over two dozen wineries under his wine group, Boisset Collection. 

The winery still sits on its original location and has been added to the US National Register of Historic Places and the list of California Historical Landmarks.

I've hit my head on walls and floors ever since I was young.  I sometimes still do it but I don't exactly know why, 

I have anxiety and I had a rough childhood but now I'll start to hit my head and sometimes not realize it but I don't know how to stop or even why I'm doing it. 

How can I help myself to change my behavior?

Hello. I have to wonder from a behavioral perspective if what you are doing is useful for you. In other words, does it serve a purpose in some way when you find yourself doing it. Yes, this could well be an expression of anxiety, or maybe some type of coping skill you have developed over the years to deal with stressful situations. Yet it sounds like you have developed a sort of knee-jerk behavioral conditioning that causes you to do this behavior during specific (or perhaps even non-specific) circumstances. Do you think it is a self-soothing behavior? Do you feel good after you have done it? The behavior itself is likely causing some form of slow physical damage, so I would recommend you have yourself checked by a doctor, to rule out any injury. If none exists, this obviously doesn't excuse the behavior, it just says that for the moment luck is on your side.When we do any behavior of any kind, it is good to ask if what we are doing has merit or value. Is the behavior helping us to solve our problem, or is it merely creating yet another problem by doing the behavior in the first place. In the same way that a person might drink excessively because they are stressed and need to cope with some unresolved issue, when they are done drinking the original problem will still likely be there, but now they are intoxicated. No closer to solving the issue. When we deal with things like anxiety or depression, we need to do things that work on dealing with the symptoms, but also get to the root issue that created those feelings and find effective solutions. So the things we do to cope with life events need to not be ones that cause us harm, but rather support us as we move forward and work to deal with what life throws at us.Sometimes seeking support from a friend or a counselor is a good idea. Being given the opportunity to express your feelings about what is going on around you and getting feedback and insight from others is much more effective than actions of self-harm, wouldn't you agree? So I would encourage you to find a counselor or a trusted friend who can help you find positive behaviors you can take to deal with your feelings, as you also work to find the answers to the day to day issues of living a life filled with promise and opportunity.Reach out if you need help...there will likely be a hand there waiting for you.

We used to think that children were almost always harmed by divorce, unless there was extreme conflict or violence. More recent data shows that children are not necessarily harmed by divorce if they keep both their parents. In other words, the damaging part is losing half of themselves and losing the value of being connected to everyone who loves them, especially the other parent, in addition to the extra benefit there is from the other parent's perspective, strengths and so on. The best thing for your child is for you to be available and loving and doing everything possible to allow the child to be whole - a person who incorporates BOTH parents. It's a tragedy for everyone to use a child to achieve adult aims, like getting back at a former spouse. In such a circumstance, your child needs you more than ever. Sometimes I can't stop thinking about life after death. I was raised in a religion that teaches that we will live on forever either in hell or in heaven.  When I think of living forever (even if it is in heaven which should be good), I feel overwhelmed. I don't like the thought of living forever and ever and ever. Sometimes I just can't get the thought out of my mind and the thoughts lead to panic and anxiety.  Am I crazy? I don't think these thoughts are normal.

Hi California, What you're experiencing is indeed anxiety; it's very common. Through research we know a lot of things about how to reduce anxiety. I'll get you started and it's a great idea to connect with a therapist who can build on these ideas and get to know you well.It's natural to have random thoughts that unsettle us. Our brains are complex, wonderful things. Fearful and anxious thoughts are a part of this picture; their purpose is to prepare us for the future and to help us make sense of the past and learn from it. But what happens sometimes is that our alarm systems get out of whack and get set off too easily. We often spend TOO MUCH time worrying about things that happened or might happen. When these thoughts take away from our enjoyment of life, it becomes a problem. So, while fear and anxiety try to protect us, they also seek power and will take any power they can get.In general, fear and anxiety try to tell us one or both of two things: that something is wrong with us, or that something bad will happen (or that something bad will happen because there's something wrong with us). They will use anything they can as evidence to convince you. For example... "That person looked at you funny. You're strange looking". Well there are dozens of possible explanations for the look on that person's face, and it's unlikely it had anything to do with you. For you personally, your thoughts are about the afterlife...about living forever. What does fear tell you will be uncomfortable about living forever? What would the worst part be? A therapist would help you dig deep to find the core of what you fear. It might be that you have no control over who you are or where you go. It might be that you fear going to hell because you're "bad". Search for that deepest fear.I invite you then to picture that thought as a glass of water on a shelf. It's a heavy glass, and if you held it in your hands for a while and stared at it, it would get in the way; you'd be uncomfortable and unable to focus on your life. That's what's happening now. I suggest that the problem is not so much the thought you're having; we all have random silly thoughts that usually aren't true. The problem is how long you're holding it in your hand. You could have that thought (pick up that glass) a hundred times a day and, as long as you put it right back on the shelf, it's not a problem. The trick is to get it back on that shelf.Right now, you're using distraction to do this. You're trying to focus on other things around you, but I think the glass is still in your hand. It's not enough; you're looking for more tools to get that glass back on the shelf.  And the key is in your thoughts. Once you find out what fear is trying to tell you, then you can "talk back to" fear. So, as an example, if fear is saying to you "you have no control over anything", then you can work to accept the pieces you don't have control over, learn to tolerate that feeling, and claim back the pieces you CAN control. You CAN control the extent to which you let fear take you over. With a therapist you can learn to "refute" fears' ideas. You can learn to look for concrete evidence of fear's lies and gain back control over your thoughts. I wish you the best!

Finally, therapy can indeed play a significant role in helping you navigate these challenging feelings. Therapy provides a safe space for exploring underlying causes of depression, understanding patterns, and developing strategies for healing and rediscovering happiness. I have been repeating the same thought pattern for seven years and have completely lost control of any situation. I am in my early 30s, and I feel like I am trapped in my body, mind, soul, and house because I feel embarrassed to go anywhere or talk to anyone.

There's SO much help for repetitive thoughts in the counseling world!  The one thing I'd for sure ask if we met in person is what those repetitive thought patterns look like.  Some repetitive thoughts are more like obsessive thoughts.  For example, that may mean that every time you leave a room, your obsessive thought is to switch the light on and off 5 times.  Or every time you touch a door handle, you think about the germs you came into contact with and washing your hands multiple times.  Sometimes it's more about the same thoughts repeating about bad things that may happen, or critical thoughts we have about ourselves.  Your statement about "feeling confident again" gives me the sense that maybe you struggle with the ways in which you think about yourself.Assuming it's obsessive thoughts: exposure and response prevention therapy is an excellent form of treatment.  Typically, obsessive thoughts influence compulsions, which usually show up as very strict, repetitive rituals in order to manage anxiety.  Exposure and response prevention exposes you to the things that increase anxiety, while response prevention helps you to sit through that anxiety response without performing a compulsion.  For example, you touch a door handle.  Your anxiety increases.  You obsess about the germs you came into contact with and have a strong urge to wash your hands multiple times.  Instead, you sit through the anxiety, let the anxiety decrease on its own, and slowly unpair that anxious response with the behavior.  The more you do this, the more it breaks up those thinking/behavior patterns that make you feel chained to them.Assuming it's self-critical thoughts: cognitive-behavioral therapy can work well here.  Everyone's brain has a default track, that when met with struggle, plays over and over like a broken record.  The more you give into that, the more it plays.  The trick here is creating a competing track, or turning the volume up on a track that boosts your confidence instead of shooting it down.  Some ways to do that are really identifying and writing down what those repetitive thoughts are.  You probably already know them pretty well if they repeat often.  Then next to them--write out a line that has an heir of confidence and/or gentleness.  For example, if your repetitive thought is that you are a failure, you may write out a sentence that is something like:  I may be struggling greatly with this situation, yet I am still trying super hard to get better and that's definitely not a failure.  Every separate repetitive thought can have its own competing sentence.  Initially, these new thoughts will feel weird, foreign, and maybe even like they don't do anything.  Give it time.  The repetitive thoughts have had years to grow, so these new thoughts need time, too.  They are, literally, new pathways in the brain and the more they are traveled, the stronger they will get.I'm also sensing that there's a combination of anxiety and depression.  I would assume that you are probably feeling pretty cut off from the world if you don't want to talk to anyone.  That can be so lonely and isolating.  Because connection is basically crucial for healing, it may be very beneficial for you to see a counselor or find a support that feels safe to you.  Counselors are usually trained very well in these types of issues and some offer telehealth if you are having trouble leaving your home.  It might feel scary and strange at first, but you are in a lot of pain and deserve healing.Hope this helps a bit.  Go with your gut and do what you feel is right for you!  I wish you all the best.

Finding alternative coping strategies can greatly assist in managing stress and emotional pain. Engaging in regular physical activity, such as walking, jogging, or yoga, can release endorphins and improve your mood. Exploring creative outlets like painting, writing, or playing an instrument can also serve as effective emotional outlets. Experiment with different activities to discover what brings you joy and relaxation.

Seeking professional help from a mental health therapist or counselor specialized in addiction recovery could be beneficial as well. They can provide guidance, structure, and support tailored to your unique situation. Additionally, therapists often utilize evidence-based techniques such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) to address underlying issues and develop healthier coping mechanisms.

Lastly, celebrate your successes along the way, regardless of how small they may seem. Recovery is a journey filled with ups and downs, so be kind to yourself when faced with setbacks. Remember, each effort towards positive change matters.

By taking these steps to overcome addiction and finding healthier ways to manage your emotions, you're prioritizing your well-being and paving the path toward a more fulfilling future. Stay committed, reach out for support, and believe in your ability to heal.

Stress has been wreaking havoc on me lately, especially with the current circumstances. I find it hard to relax or switch off, constantly worrying about the future. This heightened state of stress brings along an array of physical symptoms like headaches, tense muscles, and difficulty sleeping. In counseling, I want to understand how stress impacts my well-being and discover effective strategies to alleviate its effects on my daily life.

It sounds like you've been dealing with a lot of stress lately, which can definitely take a toll on your overall well-being. It's understandable that the current circumstances are adding to this feeling of being overwhelmed.

Stress is known to affect both our physical and mental health, so it's important to address it in order to improve your daily life. A good starting point would be gaining a better understanding of how stress impacts you personally. Take some time to reflect on what triggers your stress and how it manifests in your body and mind.

Once you have a clearer picture of the impact stress has on you, you can explore different strategies to alleviate its effects. Everyone copes with stress differently, so it's about finding what works best for you. Here are a few suggestions:

1. Mindfulness and relaxation techniques: Engaging in activities such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or yoga can help calm your mind and relax tense muscles. Building a regular practice around these techniques can make a significant difference in managing stress.

2. Establishing boundaries: Setting boundaries with work, social obligations, or even technology can create space for you to recharge and prioritize self-care. Remember, it's okay to say "no" when necessary.

3. Physical activity: Regular exercise not only boosts endorphins but also helps reduce stress levels. Find an activity you enjoy, whether it's walking, dancing, or playing a sport, and incorporate it into your routine.

4. Healthy coping mechanisms: Instead of turning to unhealthy habits like excessive drinking, smoking, or overeating, try replacing those with healthier options. Connect with loved ones, engage in hobbies, or find creative outlets to distract yourself from stressors.

5. Time management: Break down tasks into smaller, manageable parts and create a schedule that allows for breaks and relaxation. Prioritizing your responsibilities can help reduce feelings of overwhelm.

6. Seek social support: Talk to trusted friends or family members about what you're going through. Sometimes, simply verbalizing your concerns and receiving support can help alleviate stress.

Remember, it's important to be patient with yourself throughout this process. Finding effective strategies takes time and experimentation. If stress continues to have a significant impact on your daily life, it may also be helpful to seek professional guidance from a mental health expert who can offer personalized advice and support tailored to your specific needs.

Addiction has consumed my life—it affects both my personal and professional relationships, leading to almost constant feelings of guilt and shame. It all started after a significant loss in my life. Instead of properly grieving, I turned to substances as a way to numb the pain, but it only made everything worse. Even small triggers, such as stress or social gatherings associated with substance use, intensify my cravings and make it incredibly difficult to resist temptation. I exhibit symptoms of addiction daily, ranging from physical withdrawal symptoms to overwhelming psychological dependence. Growing up, I witnessed addiction within my family, and that may have made me more susceptible to substance abuse. To cope, I've tried attending support groups, but they haven't provided the long-term assistance I need. Can you shed some light on your approach to addressing addiction during counseling sessions? I'm eager to explore all possible avenues for recovery.

It sounds like you have been facing a challenging battle with addiction for quite some time, and I commend your courage in seeking guidance and support. Overcoming addiction is a difficult journey, but with the right strategies and support, lasting recovery is possible.

In counseling sessions, my approach to addressing addiction involves understanding the root causes of your addiction and developing personalized strategies for recovery. We will work together to explore the underlying factors that may have led to your substance abuse, including any significant losses or traumas you've experienced. By delving into these root causes, we can begin to unravel the emotional pain that lies beneath your addictive behaviors.

One important aspect of our work will be finding healthier coping mechanisms for dealing with stress, triggers, and cravings. It's understandable that small triggers such as stress or social gatherings associated with substance use intensify your cravings and make it more difficult to resist temptation. Together, we can identify alternative ways to manage stress and navigate social situations without turning to substances. This might involve exploring new hobbies, practicing relaxation techniques, or fostering supportive relationships.

Additionally, we'll focus on building a strong support network around you. Attending support groups is a great step, but if they haven't provided the long-term assistance you need, we can explore other options. This could include connecting you with community resources, reaching out to trusted friends or family members who can provide a listening ear, or even considering individual therapy to complement our counseling sessions. Building a reliable and compassionate support system is crucial for your recovery journey.

Throughout our counseling sessions, we'll also address both the physical and psychological aspects of addiction. If you're experiencing physical withdrawal symptoms, we can discuss techniques and strategies for managing them safely and effectively. Additionally, we'll focus on developing strategies to lessen the psychological dependence on substances, while promoting self-care, self-compassion, and personal growth.

Remember, recovery is a process that takes time, patience, and perseverance. It's important to approach it with compassion for yourself and celebrate each step forward, no matter how small it may seem. Together, we will explore all possible avenues for recovery and work towards a brighter and addiction-free future.

I have a mother who is still running my life even though I'm almost 30 years old. I want to move out and live my own life, but it feels like as long as I do what my mom wants our relationship is okay. It's never okay if I don't do what she wants. 

I don't know how to start making my own decisions and not worry about  whether it's right in her eyes.  Would it help for me to talk to someone about this?

ABSOLUTELY.  Having someone who's outside the situation and, even more so, with knowledge and experience in human behavior and relationship dynamics such as a counselor can do wonders in helping us feel less alone in frustrating situations like the one you're currently stuck in with your mother.  A professional can also assist you in finding some assertiveness techniques, communication strategies, and coping skills to help you find your voice and stand your ground in a way that feels most authentic to you.In a healthy parent-child dynamic, there comes a normal developmental shift when, as the child reaches each new stage of maturity and responsibility, the parent backs off to provide a more supportive role instead of directive role.  We call this "redefining relationships."  (We also do it with our friendships and colleagues here and there over time as needed). It's absolutely vital. Sounds like your mom may have missed that memo. Like many parents, she may feel your behavior and choices is a direct reflection of her.  Or that her role as your mother allows her greater latitude than it should.  Or like many other people in general, that her way is the ONLY way.  Regardless, this is YOUR life.  And as far as we know, it's not a dress rehearsal.  You certainly don't want to wake up some 50 years from now regretful or resentful. That being said, there are certainly ways to show her love and respect while doing what makes you happy. I would encourage you to Google therapists near you whose bios resonate with you and what you're looking for and start on a the journey towards a new chapter of freedom and hopefully a deeper, more satisfying mother-daughter relationship for both of you.Warmest regards,Tamara Powell, LMHC

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

Finding the right therapist can be difficult, especially if you've never tried it before. Things to consider are location, availability and what specifically are you looking for. Some practitioners specifically only work with a certain type of issue (i.e eating disorders, adolescents, anger management, life transitions, anxiety...etc) and others can work with a variety of concerns. As far as training your therapist, you can't. You simply let them know what you are looking to work on or what you think may be an issue for you. Depending on the way they practice(their style of working with clients) is how they will then decide to make a treatment plan that works best for you. You can always ask them their specialty practice population, the problems they generally help others with and what type of mental health provider they are (Psychologist, social worker, licensed mental health counselor).

I understand that your emotions are currently swinging between sadness and emptiness, making it challenging to experience any positive feelings. It's important to address these negative thoughts like feeling burdensome or thinking life is not worth living.

In terms of treatment for depression, therapy sessions are one effective approach. Therapy can provide a safe space for you to explore and work through your emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. There are different types of therapy, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and behaviors. Other approaches include psychodynamic therapy, interpersonal therapy, and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). The specific therapy type may depend on your needs and preferences, and your therapist can guide you in determining the most suitable approach.

Medication can also play a role in managing depressive symptoms alongside therapy. Antidepressant medications can help regulate brain chemicals that impact mood and reduce symptoms of depression. However, it is essential to emphasize that medication should be prescribed by a healthcare professional, such as a psychiatrist, who can assess your specific situation and monitor your progress during treatment.

In addition to therapy and medication, there are other self-help strategies that can complement your treatment. These include engaging in regular physical exercise, establishing a healthy sleep routine, maintaining a balanced diet, and seeking support from loved ones. It may also be helpful to engage in activities that bring you joy, even if you don't currently feel interested in them. Gradually reintroducing enjoyable activities into your life can have a positive impact on your mood over time.

My fiancé and I come from a strong Christian background but both went off the "straight and narrow" once before. He is having a hard time accepting my past, especially  that I'm not a virgin. He has a hard time in general accepting himself and others. 

His insecurities are hurting our relationship. How can I help him let go of my past and decide to live in the present?

Sometimes we have difficulty keeping the past in the past. The best way to build a great relationship and have a great future, believe it or not, is to be firmly placed in the present. That means that when we stay in the moment with our partner and can notice what we are experiencing in the here and now we reap the best benefits of that relationship. We notice the good things that are happening in the moment. We are reacting to what we are experiencing in the moment, not reacting to a worry about the past. We notice, especially, who the person is right now and not who they were in the past.  We can connect with the things we love about them, too.I think it is great that you want to help him and the choice to stay in the present and move forward in the relationship will mostly be up to him. We cannot change another person. It sounds like couples counseling might be a great step for you because you can both learn the skills you need to stay in the present and also learn some helpful "active listening" skills so that you can really listen to one another and understand each other. Communication skills can really be helpful. You can both have the opportunity to hear each other and support each other. We cannot change the past, but we can create the future we want.Best of luck to you both!

As a parent, I sometimes feel overwhelmed and unsure if I'm doing a good job. My child is going through a rebellious phase, and it's challenging to navigate this new territory. I want to establish boundaries and discipline them effectively, but I also want to maintain a loving and supportive relationship. I worry that I might be too strict or too lenient at times, and it leaves me questioning my parenting abilities. I would appreciate some guidance on how to strike a balance and foster a healthy environment for my child's growth.

Parenting can definitely be overwhelming at times, and it's completely normal to question your abilities. It sounds like you're really committed to finding a balance between setting boundaries and maintaining a loving relationship with your child, which is fantastic.

One suggestion I have is to establish clear and consistent rules in your household. Sit down with your child and discuss these rules together, so they feel involved and understand the expectations. This way, they'll know what behavior is acceptable and what isn't. Consistency is key here, as it helps create a sense of stability for your child.

Another idea is to practice positive reinforcement. When your child displays good behavior or follows the established rules, make sure to acknowledge and praise them. This will encourage them to continue behaving well and strengthen your bond with them. Remember, reinforcing positive behavior is often more effective than solely focusing on discipline.

It might also be helpful to set aside quality time each day to connect with your child. This could involve engaging in activities they enjoy or simply having meaningful conversations. By doing this, you'll be able to build a strong foundation of trust and open communication, making it easier to address any challenges that arise during their rebellious phase.

Lastly, don't forget to take care of yourself too. Parenting can be demanding, and it's important to prioritize self-care. Make sure to carve out some time for activities that recharge you, whether it's reading a book, going for a walk, or pursuing a hobby. Taking care of your own well-being will ultimately benefit both you and your child.

Remember, every parent-child relationship is unique, and there's no one-size-fits-all approach. Trust your instincts, be patient with yourself, and remember that mistakes are part of the learning process. You're doing an amazing job by seeking guidance and wanting the best for your child.

Hello, and thank you for your question. The question about
whether or not to cheat is based on personal values that can only be answered
by you. However, here are a few things to consider and questions to ask
yourself to help you find your answer:
1.    
Do you feel like you are violating your own
values or morals? This is important, because we all have different values and
morals surrounding sex, love, and monogamy. If you value monogamous
relationships and find yourself cheating on your partner, then you may feel
like you are living in contradiction to your values, and most people are not
happy when they do that. However, if monogamy is not something you value, then
perhaps it is time to re-evaluate the relationship and determine if it is still
right for you. Not all people want monogamous relationships, and that
is alright. Finally, if you value your husband’s feelings and know that the
affairs would hurt him, then your behaviors may again be in contrast to your
own values. That can only be determined by you. 
2.      Based on how you describe your relationship, it
sounds like you are not very satisfied with the way it is.  From the outside, it looks like the affairs
are a way to “get even” with your husband or to feel better after an argument. This
is something that can happen when mutual respect starts to fade in a
relationship and gets replaced with contempt. We can simply stop caring about
how our actions hurt each other, or potentially hurt each other. Perhaps the
question to ask here is, when you look out toward the future with your husband,
is this the pattern that you want to keep? The pattern of very little sex,
argument, and then satisfying the pain or dissatisfaction with affairs. 
 3.      What are your goals for this relationship? If we
start to become disconnected in a relationship, we can begin to do things on
autopilot. Get up, get the kids up, go to work, come home, and go to bed. None
of which requires any intimacy at all. Are you still able to see the hopes and
dreams you once had for this relationship?
 4.     
Have you considered seeking marital counseling? Not
having affairs won’t actually fix the part of the relationship that is leading
you to have them. If there is something broken, it sometimes requires some help
to get it fixed. 
 Hopefully these questions and thoughts will help you come to
some kind of conclusion about what is right for you and your relationship. I certainly
wish you well. 
 Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Lately, I have been struggling with excessive worry and unease that is interfering with my daily life. My goal for this counseling session is to find ways to manage and alleviate my anxiety so that I can regain control over my thoughts and actions. The anxiety seems to have originated from a past traumatic experience where I was held at gunpoint during a robbery. Since then, I've become hyper-aware of my surroundings and constantly anticipate danger in everyday situations. For instance, going to crowded places like shopping malls triggers intense panic attacks, with heart palpitations and a strong urge to escape. These anxiety episodes are becoming more frequent and more severe, often lasting for several hours each time they occur.

It's understandable that you're feeling worried and uneasy due to the impact anxiety is having on your daily life. Managing and alleviating anxiety is a common goal in counseling sessions, and I'm here to help you with some suggestions.

Given that you mentioned a past traumatic experience of being held at gunpoint during a robbery, it seems like this incident has significantly affected your overall well-being. It's important to acknowledge that such experiences can have long-lasting effects on our mental health. 

To start regaining control over your thoughts and actions, it may be helpful to explore different coping mechanisms and relaxation techniques. Breathing exercises, for example, can assist in reducing symptoms of panic attacks by focusing on slow, deep breaths. This technique can help calm your body and clear your mind when facing triggers or intense episodes of anxiety.

Additionally, implementing mindfulness practices into your daily routine might be beneficial. Mindfulness involves being fully present in the moment and observing your thoughts and sensations without judgment. By cultivating this skill, you can learn to tune into your surroundings in a more balanced manner, distinguishing between actual threats and perceived dangers.

When facing situations that provoke anxiety, gradually exposing yourself to these situations can be an effective strategy. Start small and work your way up, challenging yourself to face progressively more crowded places over time. Breaking down these experiences into smaller steps will allow you to build resilience and confidence in managing your anxiety.

Engaging in regular physical exercise can also contribute to reducing anxiety symptoms by releasing endorphins, which are natural mood enhancers. Finding an activity that you enjoy, such as walking, jogging, or even yoga, can serve as a healthy outlet to channel your anxious energy and promote a sense of well-being.

Lastly, seeking support from friends, family, or even joining support groups could provide you with additional resources and perspectives. "I've heard about different therapy approaches like cognitive-behavioral therapy and psychodynamic therapy. Which one would be more suitable for my situation? Can you explain the differences between these approaches and their potential benefits?"

Both cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and psychodynamic therapy are valid approaches, but they differ in their focus and methodologies. 

Cognitive-behavioral therapy aims to help individuals identify and challenge unhelpful thoughts and behaviors that contribute to their difficulties. It focuses on the present moment and emphasizes practical strategies for changing negative patterns. CBT can be effective in addressing specific issues like anxiety, depression, or phobias as it provides tools and techniques to manage symptoms and develop healthier coping mechanisms. Its benefits include learning new skills, gaining insight into thought processes, and fostering positive behavioral changes.

On the other hand, psychodynamic therapy explores how past experiences and unconscious conflicts impact your current emotions and behavior. This approach delves into unresolved issues from childhood or past relationships, seeking to create a deeper understanding of yourself. Psychodynamic therapy is often used when there's a need for self-reflection and exploration of complex emotions, relationship patterns, or unresolved trauma. The potential benefits of this approach include increased insight, improved self-esteem, better interpersonal relationships, and emotional healing.

Determining which approach is more suitable for you depends on your specific needs and preferences. If you're looking for short-term, goal-focused strategies to address a specific issue, CBT might be a good fit. However, if you're open to exploring the underlying causes of your distress and desire to gain a deeper understanding of yourself, psychodynamic therapy can be beneficial. 

It's important to remember that therapy is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Finding the right therapeutic approach involves considering factors such as your personal history, goals, and therapeutic relationship. I recommend discussing these options with a mental health professional who can provide you with tailored guidance based on your unique circumstances.

Stress has been an ongoing struggle for me, and I want to find ways to better manage it. Lately, my stress levels have been particularly high due to a combination of work pressures, marital difficulties, and financial concerns. 

One specific situation that triggered my stress recently was when I received unexpected medical bills. The amount was significantly higher than what I had anticipated, causing me worry about our ability to pay the bills on time and take care of other essential expenses.

The symptoms of stress are manifested by frequent irritability, difficulty sleeping, and persistent muscle tension in my neck and shoulders. These symptoms last for hours at a time and occur multiple times throughout the week.

It sounds like you're dealing with a lot of stress recently, and I can imagine how overwhelming that must be. It's great that you're reaching out for help and looking for ways to better manage your stress. Here are some suggestions that may assist you:

1. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of yourself should be a priority during stressful times. Engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as practicing mindfulness or deep breathing exercises, going for walks, listening to music, or engaging in hobbies or interests.

2. Establish a daily routine: Having a structured daily routine can provide a sense of stability and control amidst chaos. Set aside specific time slots for work, leisure, exercise, rest, and spending quality time with loved ones. Stick to this routine as much as possible to create a sense of predictability in your day-to-day life.

3. Communication is key: When facing marital difficulties, open and honest communication is vital. Find a suitable time and place to have an open conversation with your partner about the issues that are causing strain in your relationship. Active listening and expressing empathy towards each other's concerns can help you find common ground and work through the challenges together.

4. Seek financial support: If you're feeling overwhelmed by financial concerns, consider reaching out to professionals who specialize in financial planning or counseling. They can offer guidance on budgeting, debt management, and potential resources that might be available to you. Exploring options such as payment plans or negotiating with medical providers could also alleviate some of the stress surrounding unexpected bills.

5. Exercise regularly: Engaging in physical activity has been proven to reduce stress levels. Consider incorporating regular exercise into your routine, whether it's going for walks or runs, doing yoga, dancing, or any other form of movement you enjoy. Not only will exercise release endorphins, but it can also serve as a healthy outlet for built-up tension.

6. Take breaks: It's important to create moments of rest and relaxation throughout your day. Allocate short breaks during work hours or at stressful times to engage in activities that help you recharge, such as taking a few deep breaths, stretching, listening to calming music, or simply stepping away from your current environment.

7. Connect with support systems: Reach out to friends, family members, or support groups who can offer a listening ear, guidance, or simply provide emotional support. Sometimes sharing your feelings with someone who understands can bring relief and new perspectives.

Remember that everyone's experience with stress is unique, and what works for one person may not work for another. These suggestions are meant to be general guidance, but it's essential to find the strategies that resonate with you personally. If you feel overwhelmed or if your symptoms persist, consider seeking professional help from a mental health expert who can provide further assistance tailored to your specific situation.

Anxiety has become debilitating for me, and I'm searching for effective strategies to regain control over my life. Alongside constant worry and fear, I experience physical symptoms such as racing heartbeat, trembling, and dizziness. Social interactions are particularly challenging due to a fear of judgment and embarrassment. Throughout our sessions, I hope to gain insights into how I can manage these anxieties and build up my self-confidence.

It's great that you're seeking strategies to regain control over your life and manage your anxiety. Anxiety can indeed be debilitating, but there are effective ways to cope with it. Here are some suggestions for managing your anxieties and building up your self-confidence:

1. Deep breathing exercises: When you notice yourself becoming anxious, try taking slow, deep breaths. Inhale through your nose for a count of four, hold for a count of four, and exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of four. This technique can help calm your racing heartbeat and reduce feelings of dizziness.

2. Grounding techniques: When you feel overwhelmed by worry or fear, focus on grounding yourself in the present moment. You can do this by using your senses. Notice five things you see, four things you can touch, three things you hear, two things you smell, and one thing you taste. Engaging your senses can help bring your attention back to the present and decrease anxiety.

3. Challenging negative thoughts: Anxiety often stems from negative thoughts or beliefs about ourselves and others. Take a moment to identify any recurring negative thoughts or assumptions you might have during social interactions. Then, actively challenge those thoughts by asking yourself if they are realistic or based on evidence. Remind yourself of your positive qualities and past successes to counteract any self-doubt.

4. Gradual exposure: It's common to feel apprehensive in social situations due to a fear of judgment and embarrassment. Consider starting with small steps towards gradually exposing yourself to these situations. Begin by engaging in low-pressure social activities, such as joining a club or attending a casual gathering with supportive friends. As your comfort level increases, you can gradually challenge yourself with more intimidating situations.

5. Self-care routines: Establishing regular self-care practices can significantly contribute to reducing anxiety symptoms and improving self-confidence. Ensure you prioritize activities that promote relaxation, such as engaging in hobbies, practicing mindfulness or meditation, getting regular exercise, maintaining a healthy diet, and ensuring sufficient sleep. Taking care of your physical and emotional well-being is crucial in managing anxiety.

Remember, these suggestions are general and might not address all aspects of your specific situation. It can be helpful to explore these strategies further with a mental health expert who can provide personalized guidance and support on your journey towards regaining control over your life.

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

This is a great question!  I imagine people wonder this all of the time, as it's a conversation I have had with many of my clients.  One thing to think about is advice that I give regarding many different types of relationships: what brings you together has to be more than what draws you apart.  In this case, therapy will likely make you uncomfortable at times and feel difficult.  But the right therapist will always help you to feel safe and supported through that.  As far as "training" your therapist, I encourage you to think about it from the perspective of how you can best be assertive about what you're looking for- and what you're NOT looking for! Most therapists will be happy to talk about their approaches or beliefs to help you better understand their work and what you might be doing with them in your time together.  If these conversations don't feel satisfying, feel free to move on.  Not everyone is the perfect fit, and that is okay.

It sounds like you've been going through a difficult time dealing with your depression, John. I want to reassure you that seeking guidance and support is an important step towards healing and finding tools to overcome what you're experiencing.

Losing a close friend can be extremely challenging, and it's understandable that their absence would trigger waves of sadness and despair for you. Grieving takes time, and it can be helpful to give yourself permission to mourn the loss while acknowledging your feelings. 

Feeling disconnected during social gatherings is common for someone experiencing depression. It can amplify the sense of isolation and make it more challenging to find happiness within oneself. Remember that everyone's journey is unique, and comparing yourself to others may not accurately reflect your own progress or experiences. 

The symptoms you've described, such as deep sadness, sleep disturbances, loss of appetite, and losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, are all indicators of depression. It's essential to remember that these symptoms are treatable, and there are various strategies available to help manage them effectively.

You mentioned practicing mindfulness meditation and journaling as coping mechanisms, which are great methods for self-reflection and stress reduction. However, different techniques work differently for each individual, so it's possible that they might not provide immediate relief for you. Exploring alternative practices or adjusting your current approach could potentially yield better results. Consider speaking with professionals who specialize in mindfulness or exploring other relaxation techniques that align with your preferences and needs.

You expressed an interest in learning about therapy approaches like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and medication. Both CBT and medication have helped many individuals with similar struggles by providing valuable tools and support.

Medication, on the other hand, can be prescribed by a healthcare professional to address the chemical imbalances that contribute to depression. It's important to keep in mind that medication is not a cure, but it can help alleviate symptoms and make it easier to engage in therapy.
