What makes a healthy marriage last?

This is a fantastic question. In one sentence, I would say the following:Recognize that while you and your partner probably have common interests and areas of commonality, you are separate people, each with different wants, wishes, and desires – if you consider a diagram of two overlapping circles, they may share perhaps a third of the circle with overlap to indicate commonality (could be more or less) and then there are parts of the circles that are not overlapping, indicating separate interestsAs for ways that may strengthen any relationship, even the great ones, this is what came to mind. There are certainly more specific unique answers or elements for different people as far as the details, but here are some general ideas:Try to have at least 15 minutes a week where you are spending time together and not problem-solvingRealize that listening to your partner does not mean that you are agreeing with them, it just means that you are saying that you hear where they are coming fromLearn to hold on to your own wants, wishes, and desires while also recognizing those of your partnerSet boundaries for what is and isn't acceptable behavior during an argument or difficult discussionDiscuss how having important discussions can be anxiety-producing and consider having an understanding that if one of you (or both of you) feels overwhelmed, you can take a timeout for a certain amount of time. For example, you may say "okay, I'm feeling really stressed about this right now. Let's discuss it in an hour." And at that time, go back to the discussionConsider what your partner's top three or four complaints about you may be. Check in with them and see how accurate you are. If you see validity in their responses, consider whether or not you may want to make changesDiscover what makes your partner feel loved, valued, appreciated, or specialRelationships are always in progress and constantly changing. Some anxiety around change is typical. Being able to effectively discuss the anxiety and actually listen to one another without being defensive, name calling, finger-pointing, or asking each other to change is a true gift.You may enjoy this quote: "Connection is the energy that is created between people when they feel seen, heard, and valued; when they can give and receive without judgment." ~Brene Brown

Taking the first step in acknowledging your feelings of depression is a significant achievement. It's important to recognize that isolating yourself from friends and family can be both a symptom of depression and a contributing factor, as social connections are vital for our well-being. While it may feel challenging, here are some suggestions that might help you gradually get back into social interactions:

1. Start small: Begin by reaching out to one or two people whom you feel comfortable with. You don't have to dive into large gatherings right away.
2. Choose familiar settings: Consider meeting up in a place where you already feel at ease, such as a favorite coffee shop or park. Familiar surroundings can provide a sense of security during social encounters.
3. Seek support groups: Look for local support groups or online communities centered around shared interests or experiences. Connecting with others who understand what you're going through can make it easier to engage socially.
4. Join an activity or class: Engaging in activities or classes that align with your interests can expose you to like-minded individuals. This provides an opportunity for gradual social interaction while doing something you enjoy.
5. Communicate your needs: If certain aspects of socializing seem overwhelming, let your close friends and family know about it. Honest communication can help them understand your situation better and potentially adapt to accommodate your comfort levels.
6. Practice self-care: Prioritize self-care activities that boost your mood, such as exercise, meditation, or engaging in hobbies. Taking care of yourself can improve motivation and overall well-being, making it easier to regain the desire to leave the house.
7. Reach out for professional help: Consider seeking guidance from a mental health professional who can provide personalized strategies and support tailored to your specific circumstances.

Remember, progress takes time and effort, so be patient with yourself throughout this process. Celebrate every small step forward, and don't hesitate to ask for help when needed.

I'm always listening to my husband, but it feels like he never listens to me.    How do I get my husband to listen to me instead of me listening to him all the time?

Thanks for writing. There are many different house of things that may be helpful here. I can give you some general ideas, but if some of these things don't get you to where you would like to go, consider seeing a therapist who specializes in couples:Remember that you can only guarantee change in yourself. You can ask him to make changes, but you can't control whether he does or not. You can control your reactions and what you do about your own thoughts, feelings, and actions in the relationship.If you're going to talk about something important or you really want him to listen, first ask whether this is a good time.Try to talk to him without blaming, finger-pointing, or asking him to change (this can be difficult, but it also opens a lot of doors for effective discussions).Be mindful of your packaging. By that, I mean that you may have a very important message that you're trying to get across. If you able to say it in a way that is clear and wrapped in such a way that he can hear what you're actually saying, that is helpful. If you are talking in ways that are angry, or as I sometimes say, wrapped in spikes, that can be difficult to hear and receive. Rather than hearing what you're actually trying to get across, he may just hear the fact that you are angry.If your husband is able to listen to you and/or restate what you are saying and get it right or close to right, let him know what that feels like to you and how important it is.If you're asking questions, try to avoid "why" question and use "what makes, how, when, where, who" instead. Questions starting with "why" can not only be difficult to answer, but can also trigger a lot of emotions that some people are not ready to deal with right away.Also, keep in mind that listening and being able to reflect what you are saying does not imply agreement. This may be something that would be good to discuss with your husband – just because he is hearing what you're saying doesn't mean that he's agreeing with you.Lastly, but importantly, some people really don't know how to listen effectively. There are people who just are not taught to do that until much later in their lives. Sometimes listening to someone can actually be very vulnerability-producing. It may be helpful to ask your husband if he knows what makes him struggle with being able to listen if you notice that he's really struggling.

I've been dealing with persistent anxiety that significantly impacts my overall well-being. My primary objective in this counseling session is to gain valuable insights into addressing my anxiety and implementing effective coping mechanisms.

My anxiety seems to manifest most prominently in social situations. Even the thought of attending gatherings or speaking up in meetings triggers intense fear and unease. These feelings overshadow many aspects of my life and make it challenging to actively engage in social activities.

An incident that exemplifies my struggle took place during a friend's wedding reception. As the day approached, the magnitude of anxiety increased dramatically. On the actual day, my heart raced, palms became slick with sweat, and negative thoughts flooded my mind. Consequently, I found it extremely difficult to join conversations, let alone enjoy the celebration.

Symptoms of anxiety regularly plague me, ranging from physical discomforts like shortness of breath and trembling hands to psychological symptoms such as catastrophic thinking patterns and anticipating worst-case scenarios. These symptoms often intensify as the event or situation draws near.

I have experimented with various coping strategies in an effort to manage my anxiety better. For instance, I have attempted deep-breathing exercises, positive self-talk, and even exposure therapy to gradually face anxiety-inducing situations. While they occasionally offer temporary relief, the anxiety persists and interferes with my day-to-day life.

Do you have any recommendations for evidence-based interventions that can help alleviate social anxiety? Are there specific techniques that could enable me to challenge and redirect my anxious thoughts effectively?

Based on what you shared, it's clear that your persistent anxiety is having a significant impact on your well-being and specifically manifests in social situations. I understand how challenging it must be to navigate gatherings and meetings with these intense feelings of fear and unease.

One suggestion for addressing social anxiety is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which has been found to be effective in treating this condition. CBT focuses on identifying and changing unhelpful thoughts and behaviors that contribute to anxiety. One technique commonly used in CBT is called cognitive restructuring. This involves examining and challenging negative thoughts or assumptions that may contribute to your anxiety, and replacing them with more realistic and positive ones.

Another evidence-based intervention is exposure therapy, which you mentioned you have already tried to some extent. Exposure therapy gradually exposes individuals to anxiety-inducing situations in a controlled environment, allowing them to practice coping skills and experience reduced anxiety over time. It's essential to work with a trained professional to guide you through this process and tailor it to your specific needs.

In addition to these interventions, mindfulness techniques can also be helpful in managing anxiety. Mindfulness involves focusing your attention on the present moment without judgment. Regular practice of mindfulness exercises such as deep breathing, body scans, or meditation can help cultivate a sense of calm and reduce anxiety symptoms.

Building a strong support system can also be beneficial. Consider reaching out to trusted friends, family members, or support groups who can offer understanding and encouragement as you navigate your anxiety. Sometimes just sharing your experiences and struggles with others who have gone through similar challenges can provide validation and perspective.

Lastly, don't hesitate to seek professional help from a mental health therapist who specializes in anxiety disorders. They can provide personalized guidance and support tailored to your unique situation.

Remember, overcoming social anxiety takes time and effort, but with persistence and the right strategies, it is possible to improve your well-being and engage more actively in social activities.

When I am stressed, I notice physical symptoms such as tense muscles, headaches, and difficulty concentrating. The duration and intensity of these symptoms vary depending on the specific workload and external pressures. Typically, it takes me several days or even weeks to fully recover from highly stressful periods.

For coping, I have tried prioritizing tasks and practicing time management techniques. While they provide some relief, I still struggle with finding a healthy work-life balance. I'm interested to learn about additional strategies or therapies that can help me effectively manage stress without sacrificing my well-being. How has biofeedback therapy helped others reduce their stress levels?

One approach you can consider to help manage your stress is biofeedback therapy. Biofeedback therapy involves using electronic sensors to monitor and provide feedback about certain bodily functions, such as heart rate, muscle tension, and skin temperature. By gaining awareness of these physical responses to stress, individuals can learn how to effectively regulate their body's reactions.

Biofeedback therapy has been found helpful for many people in reducing stress levels. It can teach you how to recognize the early signs of stress and respond appropriately, preventing it from escalating further. The feedback received during sessions helps you become more aware of your body's stress signals, allowing you to develop techniques to relax and reduce tension.

In addition to exploring biofeedback therapy, there are other strategies you can try to better manage your stress and maintain a healthy work-life balance:

1. Set realistic goals: Break down tasks into manageable steps and set realistic timelines. This will alleviate the pressure of trying to accomplish everything at once.

2. Practice self-care: Make sure to prioritize self-care activities that promote relaxation and rejuvenation, such as getting enough sleep, engaging in exercise or physical activity, and practicing mindfulness or meditation techniques.

3. Establish boundaries: Learn to set clear boundaries between work and personal life. Allocate specific time slots for work-related tasks and make intentional efforts to disconnect and engage in activities you enjoy outside of work.

4. Delegate when possible: Identify tasks that can be delegated to others, whether at work or in your personal life. Asking for help can relieve some of the burden and allow you to focus on what truly requires your attention.

5. Seek social support: Reach out to trusted friends, family members, or colleagues who can offer understanding and encouragement. Sharing your experiences and concerns with others can provide emotional support and perspective.

Remember, everyone's journey in managing stress is unique, and not all strategies may work equally well for everyone. It may be worth experimenting with different approaches and seeking professional guidance to find what works best for you.

Lately, anxiety has been overtaking my life, and I'm seeking counseling to find ways to cope with it effectively. My goal is to gain control over my anxious thoughts and stop them from hindering my day-to-day activities.

My mind feels constantly occupied by worst-case scenarios and constant worry. One particular event that triggered intense anxiety was having to speak in public during a work meeting. The fear of being judged and ridiculed overwhelmed me to the point where I experienced trembling, sweating profusely, and even had difficulty speaking coherently.

These symptoms of anxiety occur frequently, often multiple times throughout the week. I also experience physical manifestations such as stomachaches and muscle tension. The anticipation of potential future stressful events exacerbates these symptoms further.

Looking back at my childhood, I recall experiencing high levels of pressure to excel academically and meet unrealistic expectations set by my parents. This upbringing created a deep-rooted fear of failure, which continues to contribute to my anxiety today.

To manage anxiety, I've tried various relaxation techniques, including progressive muscle relaxation and guided imagery. These strategies provide temporary relief but do not address the underlying issue of controlling my anxious thoughts and preventing them from dominating my daily life.

I am curious about whether therapy can assist me in finding sustainable methods for overcoming anxiety. Additionally, understanding your therapeutic approach to treating anxiety would greatly aid me in deciding how best to move forward in this journey.

It's great that you're seeking counseling to cope with your anxiety and regain control over your thoughts and daily activities. Anxiety can be overwhelming, but there are ways to manage it effectively.

Based on what you've shared, it seems like your anxiety is triggered by situations where you have to speak in public or when you anticipate future stressful events. These anxious thoughts occupy your mind and lead to physical symptoms such as trembling, sweating, difficulty speaking, stomachaches, and muscle tension.

Exploring your childhood experiences, you mentioned the pressure to excel academically and meet unrealistic expectations set by your parents. This upbringing has contributed to a deep-rooted fear of failure, which continues to fuel your anxiety today.

Therapy can definitely assist you in finding sustainable methods for overcoming anxiety. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) could be a beneficial approach for you. CBT helps individuals identify and change unhelpful thought patterns, develop coping strategies, and gradually face feared situations through exposure exercises. By challenging negative thoughts and beliefs related to judgment and failure, you can learn to replace them with more realistic and positive ones.

In addition to CBT, other therapeutic approaches such as mindfulness-based therapies, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and psychodynamic therapy may also be useful, depending on your preferences and needs. It's important to find a therapist who specializes in anxiety and discusses their therapeutic approach with you.

Remember that therapy is a collaborative journey, and it will require effort and commitment from you. Alongside therapy, practicing self-care, engaging in regular exercise, maintaining healthy sleep habits, and reaching out to supportive friends and family members can also contribute positively to managing anxiety.

By working with a therapist, addressing underlying issues, and learning effective coping mechanisms, you can gain sustainable strategies for overcoming anxiety and regaining control over your life.

"I often experience panic attacks that feel like a sudden wave of terror crashing over me. The symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and an overwhelming sense of impending doom. These episodes are triggered by situations where I feel trapped or out of control. Panic attacks have disrupted my ability to live a normal life, and I desperately want counseling to provide me with strategies to manage and prevent these intense moments of fear."

It may be helpful for you to practice some coping techniques that can assist in managing and preventing panic attacks. One technique is deep breathing exercises, which involve taking slow, deep breaths to help calm your nervous system. You can try inhaling deeply through your nose for a count of four, holding your breath for a count of four, and then exhaling slowly through your mouth for a count of six or eight.

Another strategy you could use is grounding yourself. This involves focusing on the present moment and using your senses to anchor yourself. For example, you could try identifying five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Engaging your senses like this can redirect your attention away from the panic attack and back into the present.

Finding healthy ways to manage stress in general can also be beneficial in reducing the frequency and intensity of panic attacks. Regular exercise, such as going for walks or engaging in activities you enjoy, can help relieve stress and release endorphins. Additionally, practicing relaxation techniques like meditation or progressive muscle relaxation can provide further relief.

It might be worth exploring any underlying triggers or patterns that contribute to your panic attacks. Consider making note of the situations or thoughts preceding the attacks. By recognizing these potential triggers, you can work on finding constructive ways to address them and reduce their impact over time.

Connecting with supportive individuals in your life can also prove valuable. Friends, family members, or support groups can offer understanding and encouragement during challenging moments. Reaching out to someone you trust and discussing what you're experiencing may help alleviate some of the emotional burden associated with panic attacks.

Lastly, self-care should not be overlooked. Ensure you are getting enough quality sleep, maintaining a balanced diet, and engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Prioritizing your mental and physical well-being is essential in managing anxiety and panic attacks.

Remember, these suggestions are techniques that may help you manage and lessen the impact of panic attacks. If your symptoms persist or worsen, it's important to seek professional support from mental health experts who can tailor their guidance specifically to your needs.

It sounds like you've been experiencing a lot of distress lately, especially when it comes to socializing or facing new situations. It can be really challenging to feel overwhelmed with constant worry and fear.

Additionally, it might be helpful to challenge the catastrophic thoughts that are filling your mind. Ask yourself if there is any evidence to support these thoughts, or if they are just automatic negative assumptions. Try to replace them with more realistic and balanced thoughts. Remember that catastrophizing tends to magnify the worst-case scenarios, while often neglecting the more likely positive outcomes.

Another approach to consider is gradually exposing yourself to the situations that trigger your symptoms. Start with small steps and build up at your own pace. For example, if socializing is difficult for you, perhaps begin by attending smaller gatherings or engaging in activities where you feel more comfortable. Over time, as you gain confidence, you can slowly increase the level of exposure.

In addition to these strategies, self-care plays a crucial role in managing anxiety. Make sure you're prioritizing activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Engage in hobbies, spend time with loved ones, prioritize sleep, exercise regularly, and maintain a healthy diet. These actions can positively impact your overall well-being and possibly alleviate some of the symptoms you're experiencing.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, so finding what works best for you may take some time. If these suggestions don't seem to improve your symptoms significantly, it could be beneficial to seek support from a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and techniques specific to your situation.

I'm here to provide guidance on understanding the root causes of your depression and exploring effective treatment options.

The range of emotions you described - sadness, emptiness, and numbness - are common experiences for those struggling with depression. Losing interest in activities that once brought joy or fulfillment is also a common symptom. It's understandable that your recent breakup has triggered these feelings of rejection and unworthiness of love.

It's concerning to hear that your lack of motivation is preventing you from taking care of your basic needs. Neglecting self-care, such as proper eating and personal hygiene, can further contribute to the sense of hopelessness. For example, setting achievable goals like preparing simple meals or engaging in a brief grooming routine can gradually help improve your overall well-being.

The episodes of deep despair that persist for weeks can understandably feel unbearable. The weight of suppressed emotions from your upbringing adds another layer to the challenges you're facing. In therapy, various techniques can be utilized to address self-worth issues related to rejection and relationship difficulties. One approach is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on examining and changing negative thought patterns that contribute to feelings of low self-worth. Additionally, psychodynamic therapy aims to explore the underlying dynamics and past experiences that influence your current struggles. This type of therapy can offer insights into unresolved issues surrounding rejection and relationships, helping you understand any repetitive patterns in your life that might perpetuate these feelings.

While there isn't a specific treatment solely tailored to post-breakup depression, therapy can provide a supportive space for processing your emotions surrounding the breakup and working towards healing. I’ve been on 0.5 mg of Xanax twice a day for the past month. It hasn't been helping me at all, but when I take 1 mg during a big anxiety attack, it calms me down. In general, Xanax is very short-acting. You mentioned that you are afraid that your medical provider will take you off of the Xanax and put you on something else. If the Xanax is not working well for you, I wonder if something else may work better. What is your reasoning there? Also, sometimes there are medications that you can take in addition to Xanax.In addition to talking with your medical provider about changing the medication, try to track your levels of anxiety on a scale of 1 to 10 throughout the day so you can get a pattern of what is happening. Also consider writing down what is happening before you have anxiety attacks. This may help your medical provider know what medication may be helpful to you or what changes could be made.As far as how to discuss this with your medical provider, I would suggest mentioning the symptom changes you are having (anxiety attacks that are not helped with 0.5mg of Xanax) and ask what they would suggest that might help. If your medical provider suggests taking you off of the Xanax, I would recommend talking about the reasons why you would prefer to stay on the Xanax and what your concerns are about coming off of it. You could also ask whether anything could be combined with Xanax.There are also many other anxiety medications. I have seen lots of people that take more than one medication to lessen anxiety that they are having.I would also consider talking with a therapist (unless the person who is prescribing a medication is also doing therapy with you). Getting more information about your anxiety and how it is affecting you may be greatly helpful to you.

You're in a difficult situation and on behalf of you and your child, I commend you for trying to find the right thing to do.Short version: your child needs you as much as possible. period. Always. We used to think that children were almost always harmed by divorce, unless there was extreme conflict or violence. More recent data shows that children are not necessarily harmed by divorce if they keep both their parents. In other words, the damaging part is losing half of themselves and losing the value of being connected to everyone who loves them, especially the other parent, in addition to the extra benefit there is from the other parent's perspective, strengths and so on. The best thing for your child is for you to be available and loving and doing everything possible to allow the child to be whole - a person who incorporates BOTH parents. It's a tragedy for everyone to use a child to achieve adult aims, like getting back at a former spouse. In such a circumstance, your child needs you more than ever. If you and your wife have different rules and so on, your child will learn to adjust and adapt, just as they would if you remained in the household. A child quickly learns that they talk to mom about x,y,z or get away with whatever, but has different rules with dad. He/she will not be too confused in the long run. Please stay the course in dealing with a difficult ex-wife for you and your child's wellbeing. Best of luck to all.

The easiest way to start the counseling process is to do a little research online. A quick search for the type of counseling you are looking for can be helpful. If you have any questions about that process or just want some help in getting your benefits from the insurance company once you've started counseling, Better is a good option. Once you've found a Counselor you think is a good fit for you, normally the best step to take here is to call and schedule your very first appointment. With many Counselors you can now send an email, but a phone call can normally tell you quite a bit about someone and their clinic. Another trigger for my anxiety is social situations. Even in casual gatherings or parties, I feel an overwhelming sense of self-consciousness and fear of being judged by others.

It can be challenging to navigate social situations when anxiety is present. The fear of being judged by others and feeling self-consciousness can certainly contribute to this overwhelming sense you're experiencing. Here are a few suggestions that may help you manage your anxiety in social settings:

1. Prepare yourself: Before attending any social gathering, take some time to mentally prepare yourself. Remind yourself that everyone has their own insecurities and that people are generally more focused on themselves than on judging others. Visualize positive outcomes and try to maintain a realistic perspective.

2. Start small: If large gatherings trigger your anxiety, consider starting with smaller, more intimate social interactions. Meet up with a close friend or family member for coffee or lunch. Gradually expose yourself to larger groups as you become more comfortable.

3. Focus on the present moment: Anxiety often stems from worrying about what might happen in the future or dwelling on past experiences. Practice mindfulness techniques to bring your attention back to the present moment. Engage your senses by noticing the sights, sounds, and smells around you. This can help ground you and reduce anxious thoughts.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: When you start feeling self-conscious or fearing judgment, challenge those thoughts with evidence-based reasoning. Ask yourself if there's any concrete proof that supports these fears. Often, our anxieties are based on assumptions rather than reality. Remind yourself of your strengths and accomplishments.

5. Seek support: Consider confiding in a trusted friend or family member about your anxiety. Having someone who understands and supports you can make social situations feel less daunting. Additionally, they may offer helpful advice or accompany you to events until you feel more at ease.

Remember, managing anxiety takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself and celebrate even small victories along the way. If your anxiety continues to significantly impact your daily life, it may be beneficial to seek professional guidance from a mental health expert.

Remembering that it's okay to ask for help or set realistic expectations for yourself might help relieve some of the overwhelming feelings.

To manage stress more effectively, there are several strategies you can try:

1. Prioritize and delegate: Take a step back and identify your top priorities. Focus your energy on those areas while delegating some tasks to others if possible. Is there anyone who can lend a hand with caring for your elderly parents or lightening your workload at the job?

2. Time management: Organizing your daily schedule can be helpful. Consider creating a to-do list or using a planner to map out your tasks, allowing yourself enough time for breaks and self-care activities. Prioritizing rest and relaxation is crucially important for managing stress.

3. Self-care: Make sure to carve out time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Engaging in hobbies, exercising regularly, practicing deep breathing exercises, or even just spending quality time with loved ones or alone can help alleviate stress levels.

4. Boundaries: Setting clear boundaries is vital for preventing burnout. Learn to say "no" when necessary and establish limitations for how much you take on. Communicate your needs to others so they understand what you are capable of handling that particular moment.

5. Seeking support: It may also be helpful to reach out to friends, family members, or support groups who may relate to your experiences. Having a supportive network can provide emotional validation and offer practical advice based on their own experiences.

What is the appeal of Flathead Lake as a Summer vacation destination?

Flathead Lake is the largest natural freshwater lake West of the Mississippi in lower 48 contiguous states, with over 200 square miles of water and 185 miles of coastline.   It is a beautiful lake, surrounded by the tall and impressive Mission Mountains on the east and the smaller Salish Mountains to the west.  It borders several Indian reservations on the Southern end of the lake.

The lake offers an abundance of Summer activities including: sailing, boating, swimming, and camping.  The lake offers excellent fishing and the fish species in the lake consist primarily of lake trout, pike, yellow perch and whitefish, with some rainbow trout, bass, and salmon. The lake trout can reach monstrous sizes, frequently exceeding twenty-pounds.

Overall, Flathead Lake is one of the premiere recreational and fishing lakes in Montana. It is popular for both fishing and pleasure boating and  the sheer beauty of the lake makes it a memorable one regardless of which activity is pursued.

I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it.    How should I deal with this?

Long distance relationships are very difficult to maintain, not just for the lack of communication, but also because of the lack of intimacy that comes along with it. Even if you have spectacular communication while in a long-distance relationship, it is difficult to maintain intimacy because you are lacking in the physical contact aspect of intimacy. Here, we are not talking about sex, but about the emotional connection that happens along with physical contact. It is also hard to have shared experiences when the two of you are in separate places. These are the challenges that you face, but there are some ways to improve your odds. The first thing to remember here is that dating is all about finding a person that you want to eventually dedicate your time, resources, and self to. If either of you finds that the relationship is one that you are not necessarily committed to, it is better to find out and have the opportunity to date others before a commitment is made. The second thing to remember is that open communication is a good sign in a relationship. That being said, I do not believe that sharing details about your "crushes" is the best thing for a relationship. Instead, I would recommend working on improving the relationship as best you can. It is a wonderful thing when we can feel that we have given our best efforts on something, especially something as important as the act of loving. Here are a couple things that you can do to improve even a long-distance relationship. Start by downloading the Gottman Card Decks App here https://www.gottman.com/couples/apps/. While on the phone or video chat, try asking each other some of these questions so that you can build a deeper knowledge of one another. Some may seem silly, but they help you know the other person more intimately. It is also helpful to make sure that you are having regular communication with each other. Some situations make it very difficult to communicate, but if at all possible, daily communication via phone or video chat would be best. Even if it is just for 30 minutes a day, really dedicate your time and attention to each other during those calls. Next, it can be helpful to know each other's love languages so you can show each other how much you really care. Take the assessment for the 5 Love Languages and talk about the results together. You can find the assessment here: http://www.5lovelanguages.com/profile/Attraction to other people is completely normal and involves biological processes. Intimacy, on the other hand, creates real connection and dedication to each other. Learn about each other, spend time together, and you will create intimacy.

When does daylight savings start and end in Sydney?

Sydney is in New South Wales (NSW), Australia, and NSW participates in daylight savings. Daylight savings starts at 2am on the first Sunday of October; and ends at 3am on the first Sunday in April

In 2023:
- Daylight savings ends at 3am on Sun 2 April
- Daylight savings starts at 2am on Sun 1 October

Next year, in 2024:
- Daylight savings ends at 3am on Sun 7 April
- Daylight savings starts at 2am on Sun 6 October

It can be challenging when stress feels like a constant companion, impacting various aspects of your life. The racing heart and thoughts you experience are common symptoms of stress, but there are steps you can take to manage it more effectively.

Firstly, identifying your stress triggers is an important starting point. Take some time to reflect on situations or circumstances that consistently cause you stress. It could be deadlines at work, conflicts in relationships, or feeling overwhelmed by personal responsibilities. By pinpointing these triggers, you can begin to develop strategies specifically tailored to address them.

Once you have identified your stress triggers, focus on developing coping mechanisms that work for you. Different techniques may resonate with different individuals, so it's essential to find what suits you best. Some people find relaxation exercises helpful, such as deep breathing, meditation, or progressive muscle relaxation. These techniques can help calm both the body and mind, promoting a sense of relaxation.

Engaging in regular physical activity can also be beneficial for managing stress. Exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters, and helps reduce tension in the body. Find activities that you enjoy, whether it's going for a walk, practicing yoga, or participating in a sport. Incorporating exercise into your routine can provide a healthy outlet for stress and contribute to overall well-being.

In addition to these self-help strategies, consider seeking support from trusted friends, family members, or even joining a support group. Talking about your experiences and sharing your feelings can provide emotional relief and a fresh perspective. Sometimes, simply knowing that others understand and empathize with your situation can make a significant difference.

Remember, managing stress is an ongoing process, and it takes time to find what works best for you. Be patient with yourself and celebrate small victories along the way. If you continue to struggle with overwhelming stress despite trying these suggestions, it may be beneficial to seek professional guidance from a mental health expert who can offer personalized support and additional coping strategies.

Take care of yourself, and remember that you have the strength to navigate through this challenging period.

Finding a way to overcome depression is a valid and important goal, and I'm here to support you in that journey. It sounds like your depression has been impacting multiple areas of your life, from work to relationships, which can be incredibly challenging to navigate on your own. The fact that you've recognized these symptoms and reached out for help is commendable.

The feelings of sadness and loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed are common experiences with depression. Waking up with a sense of emptiness and hopeless thoughts can make each day feel like an uphill battle. It's understandable that failures or rejections would trigger negative emotions, as they can often have a significant impact on our self-worth.

In terms of specific treatment options for managing depression, therapy is generally considered one of the most effective approaches. Working with a therapist who specializes in depression can provide you with valuable tools and strategies to cope with your symptoms more effectively. They can also help you explore the underlying causes of your depression and develop personalized coping techniques.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is a well-known therapeutic approach used for treating depression. CBT focuses on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns and replacing them with more positive and realistic ones. By changing our thoughts, we can often change how we feel and behave.

Another commonly used treatment option is medication. Antidepressant medications can help alleviate the symptoms of depression by balancing brain chemicals that affect mood. It's important to note, though, that medication isn't always necessary or the right choice for everyone. Ultimately, the decision to explore medication should be made together with a mental health professional after discussing your specific situation.

Lifestyle changes such as regular exercise, healthy eating habits, and maintaining a consistent sleep schedule can also have a positive impact on your overall well-being and help manage depressive symptoms. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and setting achievable goals can contribute to a sense of purpose and fulfillment.

Remember, overcoming depression takes time and effort. It's important to be patient with yourself and practice self-compassion along the way. This depressive state has made it incredibly challenging for me to find any motivation or meaning in life. Can counseling help me navigate through this grief and rebuild a sense of self-worth?

It can be incredibly difficult to navigate through depression and the emotions that come with it. The feelings of defeat and worthlessness can be overwhelming, especially when triggered by a significant loss like the relationship you mentioned. It's important to remember that you're not alone in this struggle.

Counseling can definitely provide support and guidance as you work through your grief and rebuild your sense of self-worth. A therapist can help create a safe space where you can openly express your emotions and concerns without judgment. They can assist you in exploring the root causes of your depression and how it relates to the recent loss. By understanding these connections, you may gain insight into your thought patterns and start challenging negative beliefs about yourself.

In counseling, you can also learn coping strategies for managing depressive symptoms. These techniques may include identifying triggers and finding healthier ways to cope with them, developing positive daily routines, engaging in activities that bring you joy or purpose, and practicing self-care.

Additionally, therapy may focus on rebuilding your self-worth by cultivating self-compassion and setting realistic goals. Your therapist can help you recognize your strengths and past achievements, fostering a more positive self-image. Together, you can explore your values and interests to gradually find meaning and motivation in life again.

Remember, recovery takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself throughout this process. Celebrate small victories and acknowledge that setbacks are normal. You deserve support and healing, and counseling can be an invaluable resource in helping you navigate through this journey of rebuilding and rediscovering your sense of self-worth.

How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

Ideally, termination should be a mutual process. It's not that the therapist kicks the client out at some point and says, "Okay, you're done." Rather, over time the client will decrease the frequency with which he/she comes to session so that it may start off as weekly, then decrease to biweekly, then perhaps once every three weeks, then once/month and so on. Throughout this process, the therapist and client should have had regular check ins about progress toward goals. If the client feels good about where he/she is in life, he/she might decide to suspend therapy for now. That being said, the therapist should make it very clear that if the client ever decided to return for "maintenance" therapy or a check in, he/she would always be welcome. There is no hard and fast rule to ending or a particular time period in which it must end. What matters most is that the client feels good about it and knows that the therapist will always be there should he/she wish to return.

To begin managing your stress more effectively, consider implementing some healthy coping mechanisms. One technique is deep breathing exercises, which help activate your body's relaxation response. Simply inhale deeply through your nose for a count of four, hold your breath for a count of seven, and exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of eight. Repeat this cycle several times whenever you feel stressed.

Another tool to explore is progressive muscle relaxation. This involves tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body, starting from your toes up to your head. By deliberately relaxing each muscle, you'll promote physical and mental relaxation.

In addition to these techniques, incorporating regular exercise into your routine can have significant benefits for stress management. Whether it's going for walks, practicing yoga, or engaging in any other form of physical activity you enjoy, exercise helps release endorphins that improve your mood and reduce stress.

Finding time for self-care activities is also crucial. Allocate moments during your day to do something you find enjoyable and fulfilling. It could be reading a book, taking a long bath, listening to music, or engaging in a hobby that brings you joy. Prioritizing these activities will help restore balance to your life.

Lastly, if your stress continues to affect your daily functioning, it may be beneficial to seek support from loved ones or friends. Having someone to talk to and share your feelings with can provide emotional comfort and perspective.

Remember, everyone copes with stress differently, so experiment with various techniques to discover what works best for you. If you find that your stress becomes unmanageable despite your efforts, please consider reaching out to a healthcare professional who can offer additional guidance tailored to your specific needs.

Good day, therapist. Lately, life has felt incredibly overwhelming. Excessive work demands, personal conflicts, and financial pressures are creating an immense amount of stress. This chronic stress is affecting my physical and emotional well-being, leading to constant fatigue, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. How can I find healthy ways to cope with this ongoing stress?

Finding healthy ways to cope with chronic stress is an important step towards maintaining your physical and emotional well-being. Here are some suggestions for managing the overwhelming challenges you're facing:

1. Prioritize self-care: Carve out time in your schedule for activities that promote relaxation and rejuvenation. Engage in hobbies or interests that bring you joy, such as reading, exercising, listening to music, or spending time in nature.

2. Establish boundaries: Setting clear boundaries at work and in personal relationships can help alleviate some of the pressure you're experiencing. Learn to say "no" when necessary and communicate your limits assertively but respectfully. This can create a healthier balance between your responsibilities and your own needs.

3. Practice stress management techniques: Explore various stress-reducing techniques like deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation. These practices can calm your mind and body, allowing you to better manage stressors as they arise.

4. Seek social support: Sharing your feelings and concerns with trusted friends, family members, or support groups can provide a sense of understanding, validation, and encouragement. Connecting with others who may have experienced similar challenges can offer fresh perspectives and coping strategies.

5. Maintain a balanced lifestyle: Pay attention to your physical health by eating nutritious meals, getting regular exercise, and ensuring adequate sleep. When stress becomes overwhelming, it's crucial to take care of your basic needs to support overall well-being.

6. Consider professional help: If these coping strategies don't seem to alleviate your distress, seeking support from a mental health professional may be beneficial. They can help you explore underlying factors contributing to your stress and develop personalized coping skills.

"Relationships have always been difficult for me, particularly romantic ones. I find myself constantly questioning whether I deserve love and whether others truly care about me. These insecurities have caused strained relationships in the past and it's something I'd like to work on."

Navigating relationships can be challenging, especially when it comes to romantic ones. It's common for people to question their worthiness of love and whether others genuinely care about them. These insecurities can certainly put a strain on relationships. Here are some suggestions on how you can work on this:

1. Self-reflection: Take some time to explore your thoughts and feelings about yourself. Reflect on any experiences or past events that may have contributed to your insecurities. Developing self-awareness can help you understand the root causes behind these doubts.

2. Challenge negative beliefs: Try to challenge the negative thoughts and beliefs that arise regarding your worthiness of love and care. Instead of automatically assuming the worst, question the evidence behind those beliefs. Remind yourself of positive qualities and experiences that counteract any self-doubt.

3. Practice self-compassion: Treat yourself with kindness and understanding. Offer yourself the same compassion you would extend to a close friend facing similar struggles. Recognize that everyone has flaws and moments of doubt, but it doesn't diminish our value as individuals.

4. Seek support from loved ones: Share your concerns with trusted friends or family members who can provide reassurance and perspective. Opening up to someone you feel safe with allows them to give you feedback and remind you of the love and care they have for you.

5. Set realistic expectations: Remember that no relationship is perfect and there will be ups and downs. Avoid seeking constant validation or relying solely on others' opinions to measure your self-worth. Focus on building a healthy, balanced relationship based on mutual respect, trust, and open communication.

6. Therapy resources: Consider exploring therapy options if these insecurities persist and significantly affect your daily life. A therapist can guide you through deeper introspection, provide coping strategies, and support you in developing healthier patterns of thinking and relating to others.

Remember, progress takes time, and overcoming insecurities requires patience and self-compassion. With dedication and effort, you can work towards building healthier relationships where you feel deserving of love and care.

I'm transgender, I know I am, but I've only told a few friends. I know I can't tell my family because of previous conversations we've had. They just wouldn't accept it.
 My gender dysphoria is getting really difficult to deal with on my own. I need some strategies for dealing with it. What should I do?

Hello, and thank you for your question. I am so glad that you reached out for help. I know that the dysphoria can feel nearly impossible to handle, especially since you have limited support from people who accept who you are. You may already know some of these resources, but I am going to share a few. 1. The website www.letsqueerthingsup.com is a blog from a very good writer that I know. His name is Sam Dylan Finch, and he is transgender. He writes about mental health, transgender issues, and many other topics. I know he has frequently written about gender dysphoria and ways to manage it. You may want to check out his site and do a search on there. 2. The website www.everydayfeminism.com employs many transgender writers and several have written about gender dysphoria and have given ideas for managing it. If you search for gender dysphoria on their site, many articles pop up. It may be a good resource for you, especially if you ever feel lonely and start to forget that there are others out there who are like you and have your back. 3. I am not sure where you live, but there are counselors who specialize in affirmative therapy, which is what is recommended for folks who are part of the LGBTQ community. So, if you decide to see a counselor about the dysphoria, try to find one that specifically says they have been trained in the affirmative approach. In addition, feel free to ask questions of the counselor before agreeing to see them for counseling. An ethical counselor would have no problem answering them before having you come in. 4. If there are some LGBTQ resource centers in your area, try to reach out to them and see if there are support groups. Gaining more support from others would be helpful. Sometimes LGBTQ-friendly counselors leave their contact information for people in resource centers. 5. Finally, I know you have not mentioned being depressed or suicidal, but I also know that it is very common for people to consider suicide when they are struggling with dysphoria, dealing with transphobia, etc. If this ever happens to you, please call 911 or the Trans Lifeline. It's free at 877-565-8860. Visit their site at www.translifeline.org. I hope some of these ideas help. Feel free to send another message if you have a follow-up question.Be well....be YOU.Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC
I start counseling/therapy in a few days (I'm freaking out) but my main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself, is it something to worry about?

People do cry in therapy sometimes, but it's not at all necessary to cry in order for most kinds of therapy to be helpful. When you start counseling you don't yet know your counselor very well, so it's normal to keep your feelings in check until you feel comfortable and a bit more relaxed with your counselor and with the situation. Sometimes, though, there are emotions that have been waiting and waiting to finally find someone who will listen with a kind ear. If you feel safe right away in the situation with your counselor, you might just cry in spite of your fears about it. Your therapist is used to people expressing how they feel and will keep strict confidentiality, so even though it's embarrassing, finally experiencing someone truly listening with empathy and kindness may just be worth it. It's okay too to let your counselor know right at the beginning that you're kind of freaked out about getting too emotional in front of another person.

I've noticed that I have a tendency to constantly seek validation from others in my social relationships. I rely heavily on external approval and it's starting to take a toll on my self-worth. I want to break free from this pattern and learn how to validate myself instead of depending on others for validation. Can you provide any guidance or exercises that can help me build a stronger sense of self-esteem and reduce my need for external validation?

It's great that you're recognizing this pattern and wanting to make a positive change in your life! Building self-esteem and reducing the need for external validation is definitely possible. Here are some suggestions and exercises that may help:

1. Start by practicing self-reflection: Take some time each day to reflect on your own thoughts, feelings, and accomplishments. Write down things you appreciate about yourself or moments when you felt proud. This can help shift your focus from seeking approval externally to recognizing your own worth.

2. Set realistic goals: Break down larger goals into smaller, achievable steps. When you accomplish these smaller goals, it will boost your confidence and reinforce your belief in your abilities. Celebrate each achievement, no matter how small they may seem.

3. Challenge negative self-talk: Pay attention to any negative thoughts or beliefs you have about yourself. Replace them with more positive and realistic statements. For example, if you catch yourself thinking "I'm not good enough," challenge that thought by reminding yourself of times when you succeeded or received positive feedback.

4. Practice self-care: Engage in activities that bring you joy and make you feel good about yourself. It could be anything from hobbies, exercise, spending time in nature, or pampering yourself. Taking care of your physical and emotional well-being can greatly contribute to building self-esteem.

5. Surround yourself with supportive people: Seek out relationships with individuals who uplift and encourage you. Having a strong support system can provide the validation and reassurance you seek while also helping you build your self-worth.

6. Focus on personal growth: Invest time and energy into learning new skills or pursuing interests that align with your values. As you develop competence in different areas, you'll naturally gain confidence and rely less on external validation.

Remember, building self-esteem takes time and effort. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. If you find it challenging to break free from this pattern on your own, consider reaching out to a trusted friend or family member who can provide additional support.

Is it normal for people to cry during therapy, or is it just me?

Crying in
therapy is definitely normal. A lot of people, if not most, cry in therapy. Why
does it happen? During therapy you'll explore your thoughts and emotions. Some
of them will be pleasant: joy, hope, excitement, etc., so you will smile and
laugh. Others may be more unpleasant, such as grief, sadness or anger, so you
may feel like shouting or crying. It's healthy to accept and feel all your
emotions and to express them in appropriate ways. Crying is a good way of
expressing sadness, disappointment and helplessness. If you try to cut off some
of the "negative" feelings, you are likely to also cut off your
positive ones and feel numb as a result. Crying in therapy speaks to your

One approach to managing severe anxiety is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns, as well as developing coping strategies. This type of therapy could help you recognize the relationship between your thoughts, physical symptoms, and behaviors, ultimately reducing your anxiety.

Another potential treatment option is exposure therapy. This technique involves gradually exposing yourself to situations or triggers that cause anxiety in a controlled and supportive environment. With repeated exposure, you can learn to decrease fear and eventually feel more comfortable facing those situations outside.

Mindfulness practices, such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, and progressive muscle relaxation, may also be beneficial for managing anxiety. These techniques can help you become present in the moment and reduce stress levels.

In some cases, medication may be prescribed by a medical professional to help manage severe anxiety. Medications like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or benzodiazepines may be considered.

Lifestyle changes can also play an important role in managing anxiety. Regular exercise has been shown to have positive effects on mental health, so incorporating physical activity into your routine might be helpful. Additionally, ensuring you're getting enough sleep, maintaining a healthy diet, and limiting caffeine and alcohol intake can contribute to overall well-being.

It's essential to remember that everyone's experience and needs are unique. Finding the right treatment approach may require some trial and error, and it's normal to explore different options until you find what works best for you. Questions for the mental health professional: What ethical guidelines do therapists follow to maintain professionalism? How can I ensure that my privacy and confidentiality will be respected? Are there specific red flags or warning signs that indicate a breach in professional ethics or inappropriate behavior?

Understanding professional ethics in therapy is an important aspect of ensuring a safe and trusting environment. Therapists are guided by ethical guidelines that help them maintain professionalism and provide effective treatment. Here are some key points to consider:

1. Confidentiality: Therapists have a duty to protect your privacy and keep the information you share with them confidential. They should only disclose information when required by law or if there's a concern for your safety or the safety of others. If you want assurance about confidentiality, it's appropriate to discuss this topic with your therapist during the initial session.

2. Boundaries: Ethical therapists maintain clear boundaries with their clients. This means they establish and respect appropriate limits on personal involvement, physical contact, and other potential areas of ambiguity. Ensuring healthy boundaries fosters trust and creates a therapeutic space where you can focus on your well-being.

3. Informed Consent: Before starting therapy, therapists must explain the nature of the therapeutic process, their credentials, and how they handle certain situations such as emergencies or missed appointments. You have the right to ask questions and give informed consent before participating in any treatment modality or intervention.

4. Dual Relationships: It's generally considered inappropriate for therapists to engage in dual relationships with their clients. A dual relationship occurs when the therapist has another role in your life outside of therapy (e.g., friend, employer). Maintaining professional boundaries and avoiding conflicts of interest are crucial to providing objective and unbiased support.

5. Professional Competence: Ethical therapists continuously strive to enhance their competence through ongoing education, supervision, and staying updated on research and best practices. They should engage in therapies or techniques recognized within their field and ensure they have the necessary skills to address your needs effectively.

6. Reporting Potential Harm: Therapists have an obligation to protect their clients from harm. If there are concerns of child abuse, elder abuse, or threats of violence, therapists may need to report the situation to appropriate authorities. This is done in your best interest and safety.

To ensure your privacy and confidentiality, it's essential to have an open conversation about these topics with your therapist. Ask them about their approach to maintaining professional ethics, inquire about their training and qualifications, and discuss any concerns or boundaries you may have. If you notice warning signs of potential breaches in professionalism, such as inappropriate behavior, lack of respect for boundaries, or breach of confidentiality, trust your instincts and consider seeking support from another mental health professional.

Remember that ethical guidelines are designed to protect you as a client and create a safe therapeutic space. It's important to be informed and empowered when participating in therapy, ensuring that your well-being remains a top priority.

Explain away goal rule in soccer.

Away goal rule was first introduced in 1965/66 season of the UEFA European Cups Winners’ Cup and abolished at the end of 2020/21 season. All of the UEFA club competitions’ knock-out stages (except the final) are played as a two-leg fixtures (team plays one game at home and one game away against the same team). The away goal rule was a tie breaker in case the winner of the fixture in the knock-out stage could not be determined after adding up scores from both games. In case there is a  tie when you add up the scores of both games, the team that scored more away goals would advance to the next round of the competition. For example, if Team A lost the first game 2:1 playing away and won the second game with the score of 1:0 at home, the aggregate score of those two games is 2:2 (a tie), but since Team A scored 1 goal playing away and Team B scored 0 away goals, Team A would advance the next round.

Managing anxiety and developing healthy coping mechanisms are key goals in counseling, so I'm glad you've reached out for support. The pressures of college and the high expectations placed on you by your family can definitely contribute to feelings of anxiety. Firstly, recognizing your triggers and understanding how they impact you is an important step. You mentioned experiencing shortness of breath, dizziness, and fear of failure before exams. Identifying these physical symptoms and thoughts will assist us in developing targeted techniques to manage them more effectively.

One approach we could explore together is grounding exercises. These can help bring you back to the present moment when anxiety starts to feel overwhelming. One technique involves focusing on your senses - noticing five things you can see, four things you can touch, three sounds you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This exercise helps to shift your focus away from anxious thoughts and into your immediate surroundings.

Another strategy we can look into is deep breathing exercises. When you notice the signs of anxiety creeping in, take a pause and consciously slow down your breathing. Breathe in deeply for a count of four, hold it for a second, then slowly exhale for a count of four. Repeat this process several times, allowing yourself to relax as you go through each breath.

Additionally, regular practice of stress-management techniques like meditation or mindfulness exercises can be beneficial. These practices promote relaxation and help train your mind to stay present and focused instead of getting carried away by anxious thoughts.

This sounds like a possible boundary issue. Boundaries are important in relationships. They are invisible lines that we will or will not cross. It is up to us to create and hold them. We have the ability to rethink them and change them as needed. It sounds like you have thought it through and would like to makes changes in the relationship between your mother and you. In the main question, you want to avoid the family member, however in the following comment, it sounds like you may just want the avoid that conversation, not so much your mother. Once we review the issue and decide what we need (create the boundary), I suggest opening talking with the person when everyone is calm (not in the middle of a stressful moment when we often are unable to focus and hear the other person). Always understanding that we had time to think about this issue and the other person has not (catching them off guard). State clearly your need. Such as "I am not comfortable with hearing about my sister. It stresses me out. I would appreciate it if you would not bring it up anymore. If you do, I will not respond and I will change the subject " It is important to use "I" statements. I feel" this way". I will "do this". We only have power over our actions. Also when we use "you " comments, the other person can become defensive and unable to hear what we are saying. Once we let ourselves know what we need, then let the other people know our new boundary, then it is up to us to follow through. We will make mistakes. Not follow through every time with our boundary. That is okay. Start again. It gets easier with practice. It is also appropriate to reconsider and change your boundary as needed. Just let the others know when you need to change it. "Anxiety frequently overwhelms me, particularly when driving. Even the thought of getting behind the wheel sends panic through my body. I often experience shortness of breath, trembling hands, and an intense fear of losing control. I want to overcome this fear so that I can regain my independence and drive confidently again."

When it comes to dealing with anxiety while driving, there are a few strategies that can help you regain your confidence on the road:

1. Gradual exposure: Start by taking small steps towards facing your fear. Begin by sitting in a parked car without actually driving. Spend some time in the driver's seat and get comfortable with the environment.

2. Relaxation techniques: Practice deep breathing exercises or progressive muscle relaxation to help calm your mind and body when anxiety arises. These techniques can be helpful in reducing panic symptoms like shortness of breath and trembling hands.

3. Cognitive restructuring: Pay attention to any negative thoughts or beliefs that may be contributing to your anxiety. Challenge these thoughts by asking yourself if they are based on evidence or if they are just assumptions. Reframe them into more rational and positive perspectives. For example, instead of thinking "I will lose control," replace it with "I have successfully driven many times before without incident."

4. Create a supportive environment: If possible, bring along a supportive friend or family member who can accompany you during your initial drives. Having someone there for reassurance and guidance can alleviate some of the anxiety.

5. Exposure therapy: Once you feel ready, gradually increase the difficulty level of your exposure. Start by driving in low-stress situations such as quiet residential areas before progressing to busier roads or highways. The key is to take small steps and build up your tolerance over time.

6. Seek professional support: Consider reaching out to a mental health professional who specializes in anxiety disorders. They can guide you through specific techniques and provide additional support tailored to your needs.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and patience. Celebrate each small victory along the way and don't be too hard on yourself if setbacks occur. With persistence and a gradual approach, it's possible to regain your independence and drive confidently again.

When stress builds up in our lives, it can have a significant impact on both our physical and emotional well-being. It's great that you've reached out for guidance, as counseling can indeed provide relief and support during challenging times.

The chest tightening and difficulty with deep breaths that you experience during stressful situations are common physical symptoms of anxiety. When these sensations occur alongside negative thoughts and feeling overwhelmed, it can be helpful to employ some stress management techniques to alleviate the symptoms.

One effective strategy is deep breathing exercises. These exercises focus on taking slow, deep breaths, which can help reduce tension in your chest and promote relaxation. You can try diaphragmatic breathing by sitting or lying down comfortably, placing one hand on your abdomen and the other on your chest. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, allowing your breath to fill your belly (you should feel your hand rise), hold for a few seconds, and exhale through your mouth slowly. Repeating this for several minutes whenever you feel stressed can help calm your body and mind.

In addition to deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation is another technique worth exploring. This involves tensing and then releasing each major muscle group in your body, helping to release physical tension associated with stress. Start from your toes and work your way up to your head, tensing each muscle group for a few seconds before letting go. Pay attention to any differences you feel between the tense and relaxed states of your muscles.

Other stress reduction recommendations include engaging in regular physical activities like walking, jogging, or yoga, as exercise releases endorphins that elevate mood and reduce stress levels. Taking breaks throughout the day to engage in self-care activities, such as listening to music, reading, practicing mindfulness or meditation, can also contribute to stress relief. Additionally, maintaining a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and connecting with supportive friends or family members can play vital roles in managing stress-related symptoms.

Remember, everyone's experience with stress is unique, so it may be helpful to experiment with different strategies and techniques to find what works best for you.

I always feel the need to impress people, whether it's my family, the people at school, or just random people. I know that no matter what I do or how I change, there will always be some people who hate me. Why do I feel this way?

It is normal to seek other’s attention and noticing that some people would not be interested.  After all, we belong to a social environment where we constantly receive other’s feedback, which at times validates us, makes feel important and useful, like we belong; but also at times makes us feel isolated, different and neglected, which we could interpret as hate.The key is to be aware of what you think about what people think of you.   Got it?  This part can be tricky at times, because, what others think about us does not really affect us, what really affects us is what we decide to believe, internalize, and make our reality.  For example, I could choose to ignore a person’s comment about me, or I could decide to focus on it all day, analyze why they said that and what have I done to them to get to that conclusion.  Eventually, since we became so focused on that thought, we may end up believing that what the other person said about us was true, even if we did not agree to begin with.So how can we fix this?  Awareness is the key!  It is important that you understand the way you internalize external inputs, like comments, and to go through a process of discarding negative ones.  It is also helpful to talk to your counselor about how you process feedback and validation so you learn to balance your positive traits from negatives and how that affects your relationships and self-esteem.¿Cómo me puede importar menos lo que la gente piensa?Siempre siento la necesidad de impresionar a otros, ya sea mi familia, la gente de la escuela o extraños.  Y sé que no importa lo que haga o cuanto haga, siempre habrá personas que me odian.  ¿Por qué me siento así?Es común que busquemos la atención de otros y notemos que algunas personas no están interesadas.  Después de todo pertenecemos a un ambiente social donde constantemente recibimos comentarios, que a veces nos validan, alagan y nos hacen sentir como parte importante y funcional de la sociedad; pero en otros momentos nos hacen sentir aislados, ignorados y diferentes, lo cual lo pudiéramos interpretar como odio.La clave es estar conscientes de lo que pensamos que los otros piensan de nosotros. ¿Me sigues?  Esta parte puede ser algo confusa, porque lo que piensan otras personas de nosotros, no nos afecta directamente, lo que si nos afecta es lo que decidimos creer que otras personas piensan de nosotros; y luego lo internalizamos y hacemos parte de nuestra vida.  Por ejemplo,  podemos decidir ignorar lo que una persona dice de nosotros, o podemos decidir enfocarnos en ello todo el día, analizando en detalle porque lo dijeron y que hemos hecho para hacer que ellos piensen así. Eventualmente nos enfocamos tanto en ese pensamiento, que terminamos creyendo que es verdad, aun cuando originalmente no lo creíamos así.¿Entonces como lo arreglamos? La clave es concientización.  Es importante entender la manera en que internalizamos las opiniones de otros, y que pasemos por un proceso de discriminación, donde descartemos los comentarios negativos, hasta que aprendamos a ignorarlos. También ayudaría hablar con un Consejero sobre como internamente validas y descartas los comentarios y opiniones externas, y como eso puede estar afectando tus relaciones y tu autoestima.

I have a problem with binge eating, especially during times of stress. I binge eat and feel so overwhelmed with shame and disappointment that I end up going to the gym and trying to exercise the calories off. I am in my late 20s, and I have been dealing with this since I was a teenager. Are there any coping mechanisms I can use to break this cycle?

Hello,This question describes a very typical setup of what is called the  Binge, Repent, Repeat cycle. This means that typically after you binge, you experience emotions as you described "shame and disappointment" and then because of these emotions you "repent" (i.e. vow to never binge again, promise to "do better," go to the gym, etc.) and then ultimately end up bingeing again. There are many coping mechanisms for binge eating and one of the best is actually attempting to NORMALIZE eating. Meaning you need to attempt to eat normally, eating appropriately portioned meals 3 times a day, with snacks in between. IF you binge, then it may be helpful to remind yourself that when you attempt to compensate for your bingeing behaviors, and you end up feeling restricted from over exercising or undereating, then this actually leads to a binge again. Thus, reverting you back to the cycle. If you binge, it will be helpful to try and get back on a normal schedule of eating instead of trying to compensate for the binge. Although it may feel counterproductive, getting back on a normal eating schedule will prevent you from entering into the restrictive cycle. It can also be helpful to remind yourself that the binge has already occurred, it is in the past and the goal is to move forward without focusing on the past. Focus on what you can do differently next time. What emotions or situations led up to the binge? What can you to do prevent or change the circumstances that led to the binge, or the way that you handled the situation? Lastly, if you're struggling with "normalizing" eating, it can be helpful to work with a professional that can provide counseling and coaching to help you learn how to eating normally, mindfully and without feeling the guilt and other harmful emotions sometimes associated with disordered eating. I would be more than happy to assist you if you ever have any questions or want to reach out to somebody. You can contact me via my website: http://www.maddenwellnessky.com/

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

Hi, A good fit should have expertise in your issues. Generally, if you read their profile it should resonate with you...like they are talking directly to you. When you get into the therapy sessions, a good therapist will adapt their style to match your needs, they have done years of training to make sure they can help, so you should not have to "train your therapist" :) If you do, they are NOT a good fit. The idea of coming to therapy, is that you are there to get a different perspective and change what is not working for you, by that definition, you may not know what you need from therapy and that is where your therapist should be guiding you. That being said, in order for your therapist to give you the best service possible, they do need for you to be honest and let them know if you are willing or unwilling to incorporate the strategies they are offering. They need you to be willing to try things that are uncomfortable. A good therapist will also challenge your beliefs, make you question what you have done before...occasionally you should leave lighter, sometimes heavier, sometimes happy, sometimes lost in thought. If they are a good fit, you should feel like you can be your authentic self and feel safe, even if it is not easy. If you leave their office feeling like they are just a friend and you are not growing, they probably are not a right fit. If you leave their office feeling constantly frustrated, they are probably not a good fit. If they are not, let them know. A lot of times they can change their style or refer you to someone who is a better fit. It is okay to let your therapist know it does not seem to be working for you.
