I've been having a difficult time with my relationships lately, and it's really affecting me. I find myself constantly questioning whether people truly care about me or if they're just pretending. This lack of trust is making it hard for me to form deep connections with others. My goal through this counseling session is to understand why I struggle so much in relationships and learn how to build healthier connections.

Building healthier connections and understanding why you struggle in relationships can be a transformative process. It's great that you're seeking support through counseling.

To start, it might be helpful to explore any past experiences or patterns that may have contributed to your difficulty in forming deep connections. Sometimes, our previous interactions or even childhood experiences can shape the way we approach relationships as adults. Reflecting on these experiences with your counselor could uncover insights into any underlying beliefs or fears that are impacting your ability to trust others.

Additionally, it can be valuable to examine your own self-perception and feelings of worthiness within relationships. A lack of trust often stems from insecurities about ourselves. Consider practicing self-compassion and nurturing a positive self-image. Acknowledge and appreciate your own qualities, reminding yourself of the value you bring to any relationship. By developing a stronger sense of self-worth, you may find it easier to open up to others and believe in their genuine care for you.

Communication is another crucial aspect to work on. Expressing your concerns and doubts to those close to you can foster deeper connections. When feeling uncertain about someone's intentions, try engaging in open and honest conversations. Share your thoughts and ask them directly about their feelings towards you. This vulnerability can help build trust and clarify any misconceptions you may have.

Alongside building healthy connections, it's important to set boundaries and assess whether your expectations align with reality. Unrealistic expectations can lead to disappointment and strain relationships. Identify what you genuinely need from others and establish clear boundaries around those needs. Keep in mind that healthy relationships involve mutual respect, reciprocity, and open communication.

Lastly, while exploring the reasons behind your struggles in relationships, remember to be patient with yourself. Building new habits and dismantling deeply rooted beliefs takes time and effort. Celebrate small victories along the way and don't be too hard on yourself when facing setbacks. With dedication and support, you'll be able to develop healthier connections and cultivate fulfilling relationships.

Often times I find myself thinking scary thoughts and sometimes  I even scare myself into thinking that something bad is going to happen to me. Once it starts, the thought continues going through my head and I can't get it out.  How can I stop these thoughts?

Scary thoughts can feel overwhelming at times as well as feeling quite real. I want to acknowledge how scary they can feel, but there is hope and new skills you can learn to work with these types of thoughts. The first step in working with scary or negative thoughts is to acknowledge that they are just thoughts and we can choose to follow the scary thought streams or work with cutting them off or ignoring them. I also realize that might seem really hard to do, but here's a good way to think about the brain and how thought patterns work. Thoughts arise in the mind all the time, our brain is a thought machine. Many thoughts drift by like clouds and we don't pay any attention while other thoughts arise and they trigger us in a particulate way, i.e., scary, angry, happy, sad, and when those thoughts arise we can chose to pay more attention to the thought which can lead us down that particulate thought stream that will lead to fear and anxiety. So, how do we work or stop those scary thought streams? One new skill to implement comes from the work of Rick Hansen, he wrote the book Buddha's Brain," he teaches that we need to give more energy and attention to the positive thoughts or positive memories we hold in our mind and pay less attention to the negative thoughts. Hansen asks us to imagine the brain this way, the brain is like Velcro with negative thoughts and like teflon when it comes to positive thoughts. There are reasons that our brain works this way, but I don't have time to go into all of that in this response. So, it's just important to remember we have to work at positive thinking, actually pausing throughout the day to focus on positive feelings and memories,  this will help the mind reinforce positive thought streams and help reduce negative thought streams over time. If a scary thought arises try to replace it with a happy experience for at least a couple of moments, and see if that helps reduce the negative charge connected with that scary thought.

Hello, and thank you for your question. This is a very serious time. I don't mean to frighten you, but you are right to be concerned. The time right after people leave the hospital after receiving psychiatric services is a time of high risk for suicide. It is very important, after hospitalization, to get follow-up care with a professional as soon as possible. If your husband has an established therapist, this is the time to call. It is also a good time to alert your support system of friends, family, clergy or others to let them know he is still struggling. This is good support for him AND you.It is important to think about means and opportunity to make another attempt. Means really do matter.  So, if you have a firearm in the home, it is really important to remove it. You can't remove all things that a person may hurt themselves with, but some things are more lethal than others. Firearms are very lethal. I am not sure what means he used last time, but try to reduce the opportunity for him to access it again. This is where your support system can help out. People can take turns hanging out with him until you are sure the crisis is over.If you believe that an attempt is going to occur, talk to your husband about going back to the hospital. If he refuses, you will want to find out what your options are to have him go even if he doesn't want to. I know the thought of that really hurts, but it can save his life. Calling 9-1-1 is always a good option if you are not sure. Usually a suicide crisis, meaning they want to harm themselves right now, lasts a few minutes, hours or days. Sometimes when you get them through the crisis stage, they no longer want to commit suicide. But, as you are indicating, that feeling of wanting to commit suicide can come back again. So, it is always good to have a plan. If you want more information, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline. They will always answer: 1-800-273-8255. Avoid using extreme, black and white language (i.e. always and never). For example, you may say something such as, "I feel confused that we are rarely intimate and I'm wondering if you've also noticed this change" versus "You are never intimate with me anymore." Don't be afraid to ask him questions. Due to recent changes in my life, I'm dealing with heightened levels of stress. It feels like everything is changing at once, and I struggle to keep up. Sleep has become elusive, as my mind is constantly racing with worries and uncertainties about the future. Even when I do manage to sleep, I wake up feeling exhausted. My main goal for this counseling session is to develop healthy coping mechanisms to deal with this overwhelming stress so that I can regain a sense of stability and peace within myself.

To cope with the heightened levels of stress you are experiencing, it can be helpful to prioritize self-care. Taking care of your physical and mental well-being can greatly contribute to managing stress. Here are some suggestions:

1. Establish a consistent sleep routine: Create a relaxing bedtime routine that allows you to unwind before going to bed. Set a regular sleep schedule by going to bed and waking up at the same time each day, even on weekends.

2. Practice relaxation techniques: Engage in activities that promote relaxation such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or yoga. These practices can help calm racing thoughts and ease anxiety.

3. Incorporate regular exercise into your routine: Physical activity releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters. Find activities you enjoy and try to engage in them regularly, whether it's walking, dancing, or playing a sport.

4. Prioritize healthy eating habits: Nourishing your body with balanced meals can have a positive impact on your mood and energy levels. Aim for a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins while minimizing processed foods and excessive caffeine or alcohol intake.

5. Engage in enjoyable hobbies and activities: Carve out time for activities you find pleasurable and make you feel good, whether it's reading, writing, painting, listening to music, or spending time in nature. These activities can provide an outlet for stress and promote relaxation.

6. Seek social support: Reach out to trusted friends or family members who can offer support and understanding. Talking about your challenges and concerns can help alleviate stress and provide different perspectives.

7. Take breaks and set boundaries: Recognize when you need to take breaks and step away from stressful situations. Setting clear boundaries with work, relationships, or any other responsibilities can prevent burnout and create space for self-care.

8. Consider journaling: Write down your thoughts, worries, and concerns in a journal. This can help you process your emotions, gain clarity, and reduce the racing thoughts experienced during sleep.

9. Explore stress management techniques: Research and experiment with different stress management techniques that resonate with you. Some examples include progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery, or cognitive-behavioral therapy exercises for challenging negative thoughts.

Remember, developing healthy coping mechanisms takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself as you navigate this process. It might also be beneficial to consider seeking support from a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and further assist you in managing your stress.

Stress has reached unbearable levels. It feels like every aspect of my life is crashing down simultaneously. My heart races, my thoughts race, and it's difficult to concentrate on anything. Every little issue becomes a mountain, and even minor setbacks send me into a panic. One specific event that triggered these feelings was when my car broke down unexpectedly, leading to financial strain and transportation difficulties. The stress from this incident compounded all the other existing pressures in my life. I would like guidance on how to navigate through stressful situations without feeling overwhelmed and anxious.

When stressful situations reach unbearable levels, it can feel like everything is crashing down simultaneously. The racing heart and racing thoughts you're experiencing are common symptoms of anxiety. Difficulty concentrating and feeling overwhelmed by even minor setbacks are also signs that your stress levels may be overwhelming.

It's understandable that the unexpected car breakdown triggered these feelings, especially considering the financial strain and transportation difficulties that followed. When an event like this compounds existing pressures in life, it's essential to find ways to navigate through it without becoming overwhelmed and anxious.

One helpful strategy is to practice self-care regularly. This involves prioritizing activities that help you relax and recharge. Identify what brings you joy or tranquility, and try to incorporate those into your daily routine. It could be anything from taking a walk in nature, engaging in creative hobbies, practicing deep breathing exercises, or simply spending time with loved ones.

Additionally, finding healthy coping mechanisms for stress is crucial. Consider exploring different techniques such as mindfulness meditation, journaling, or engaging in physical activity like yoga or running. These practices can help calm the mind, promote relaxation, and reduce anxiety.

Effective time management can also play a significant role in reducing overwhelm. Break tasks down into smaller, manageable steps, and set realistic goals for yourself. Prioritize your responsibilities and tackle them one at a time, giving yourself credit for each small accomplishment along the way.

Developing a support system could provide immense help during stressful periods. Reach out to trusted friends or family members who can lend an ear, offer advice, or simply provide emotional support. Sharing your concerns and experiences with someone who cares can alleviate some of the burden you feel.

Lastly, remember to be patient and kind to yourself throughout this process. It takes time to learn how to navigate through stressful situations without feeling overwhelmed and anxious. Celebrate your progress, no matter how small, and acknowledge that setbacks and challenges are a normal part of life. By incorporating self-care practices, healthy coping mechanisms, effective time management, and a support system into your life, you can gradually build resilience and find healthier ways to manage stress.

My mother has been living with advanced cancer for the past year, and her pain has been increasingly difficult to manage. She's been resistant to taking her medication regularly due to its side effects, which include drowsiness and confusion. Recently, however, she's started taking it more consistently, and I've noticed a significant improvement in her alertness and overall demeanor. While I'm grateful for this change, I can't help but worry about the potential long-term side effects and the possibility of addiction.

Your concerns are valid, and it's important to approach this situation with sensitivity and a clear understanding of the complexities involved. First, let's acknowledge that pain management is a critical component of hospice care, and it's essential that your mother receives adequate relief. It's also important to remember that the goal is to improve her quality of life, not just to eliminate pain.

Regarding your concerns about addiction, it's essential to understand that addiction is a complex issue, and it's not solely determined by the presence of a medication. Factors such as the individual's mental and emotional state, their support system, and their personal history all play a role. In your mother's case, her advanced stage of cancer and the associated pain may increase her vulnerability to addiction, but it's not a given.

To address your concerns, I would suggest the following steps:

1. Open communication with your mother's healthcare team: Share your observations and concerns with them, and ask for their professional opinion on the situation. They may be able to provide reassurance or offer alternative solutions if necessary.

2. Educate yourself about the medication and its potential side effects: Understanding the medication's intended use, potential side effects, and the risks and benefits can help alleviate your fears and provide you with a clearer perspective.

3. Encourage your mother to maintain open communication with her healthcare team: Encourage her to ask questions about her medication and to report any changes in her condition or side effects.

4. Explore alternative methods for pain management: Consider exploring complementary therapies, such as acupuncture, massage, or meditation, which may help alleviate pain and improve your mother's overall well-being.

5. Seek support for yourself: Caring for a loved one with a serious illness can be emotionally and physically taxing. It's essential to ensure that you have the necessary support to help you cope with the challenges that come with this role. Consider joining a support group, seeking counseling, or reaching out to friends and family for assistance.

By taking a proactive and informed approach to your mother's care, you can help ensure that she receives the best possible care while also addressing your concerns about addiction and side effects. Remember, open communication, education, and self-care are essential components of effective caregiving.

"I feel like there's a lack of intimacy in my romantic relationship. Physical affection and emotional connection have decreased significantly, and it feels as if we're drifting apart. This is causing distress and insecurity. My goal for therapy is to rediscover intimacy and strengthen the emotional bond between my partner and me."

It can be challenging when you feel a lack of intimacy in your romantic relationship. It's important to address these concerns and work towards rediscovering that emotional connection with your partner. Here are some suggestions:

1. Communication: Open and honest communication is essential for addressing any issues in a relationship. Express your feelings and concerns to your partner in a calm and non-confrontational manner. Share your desire to strengthen the emotional bond between both of you.

2. Quality time: Make an effort to spend quality time together, engaging in activities that you both enjoy. This could be anything from going on dates, taking walks, cooking together, or even having deep conversations. By investing time in each other, you can rebuild the emotional connection that may have been lost.

3. Emotional support: Show empathy and understanding towards your partner's thoughts and emotions. Encourage them to open up about their own feelings as well. By providing a safe space for vulnerability, you can foster a sense of emotional closeness.

4. Intimacy-building exercises: Explore exercises such as shared journaling, where you both write down your thoughts, dreams, and desires and then exchange and discuss them. You can also try practicing active listening, where one person speaks without interruption while the other listens attentively. These exercises can help create deeper emotional bonds.

5. Seek professional support together: If you find that your efforts alone aren't yielding results, consider seeking the guidance of a couples therapist or counselor. They can provide valuable insights and strategies specifically tailored to your situation, helping you navigate through challenges and rediscover intimacy.

Remember, building intimacy takes time and effort from both partners. Be patient and kind with yourselves as you work towards strengthening your emotional bond.

Hello,While one can be sad from time to time, feeling sad "all the time" could be a sign of depression. If you feel sad on most days, it is worthwhile speaking to a psychologist to determine whether you suffer clinical depression. Feeling sadness is a normal response to loss, whether you lose a family, friend, job, or something you deem important in your life. However, feeling sadness all the time is a signal that you are not happy about something in your life. If it is related to your family and often relationship with family members could affect our self-esteem and self-worth, then perhaps it is worthwhile exploring what you find unhappy about your relationship with your family. Is it that you do not feel heard, supported or loved? Is it that you feel disrespected, disregarded or feel unimportant? These are just a few examples of common issues that people report that contribute to their depression. How should I select a tennis racket if I'm completely new to the sport?

If you're a beginner tennis player, you should pick a racket that will help you learn the game quickly. There are a few key factors to consider. The first factor is grip size. There are several ways to measure grip size, but the simplest is to hold the grip and ensure there is about a finger's width remaining between your ring finger and base of your thumb when you hold the racket. Too small a grip may lead to squeezing the racket too hard, and too large a grip will make the racket unwieldy. The second factor is the weight of the racket. A racket in the range of 250 to 310 grams (unstrung) will be suitable for most players. A beginner male player might shoot for something in the 280-305 gram range, and a beginner female might use a racket in the 275-300 gram range. Junior players (age 10+), depending on age and size, should consider rackets in the 250 to 300 gram range. The third factor is the racket head size. You should look for a 100-105 square inch head size. These days even professionals use 100 sq inch commonly, and 95 is considered small (for advanced players). The racket composition is not a key differentiator, as most rackets are made of some sort of graphite composite material. Price is also not an indication of quality. Pricier rackets might be less suited to beginners, in fact. As to brand, it's a very personal choice. I would say choose a brand that you associate with wanting to play (perhaps you're a fan of a player who is sponsored by that brand). You can certainly find rackets at many big box retailers that would check all these boxes. And if you're not sure -- many online as well as local racket retailers run "demo" programs allowing you to try different rackets. Choose one that helps you consistently make contact with the ball and get it over the net. The most important thing is to get out on the court and play!

The demands of everyday life are overwhelming, leaving me feeling stretched thin. Meeting work deadlines while maintaining a healthy home environment feels impossible. It seems like every aspect of life requires undivided attention, causing stress levels to rise excessively. How can I find balance and reduce the burden of stress in my life?

Finding balance and reducing stress in your life can be challenging, but with some small changes and intentional actions, you can make a positive difference. Here are some guidance and suggestions to help:

1. Prioritize Self-Care: It's essential to prioritize taking care of yourself amidst the demands of everyday life. Make sure to carve out time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation. Whether it's reading a book, going for a walk, practicing mindfulness or engaging in hobbies, self-care is crucial for maintaining mental well-being.

2. Set Boundaries: Establishing clear boundaries between work and personal life can help create a healthier balance. Determine specific times for work-related tasks and designate uninterrupted personal time without any work-related distractions. Communicate these boundaries to colleagues and loved ones, so they understand and respect them.

3. Delegate and Seek Support: You don't have to do everything alone. Consider delegating tasks at home or work to lighten your load. Reach out to friends, family, or coworkers for support and assistance when needed. Remember, seeking help is not a sign of weakness, but an acknowledgment of your own limits and a way to ensure better overall well-being.

4. Practice Time Management: Efficiently managing your time can significantly alleviate stress. Start by organizing your day with a schedule or to-do list, prioritizing tasks based on importance and deadlines. Break bigger tasks into smaller, manageable chunks to prevent feeling overwhelmed. Remember to include breaks to recharge and refresh throughout the day.

5. Healthy Coping Strategies: Instead of resorting to unhealthy coping mechanisms like excessive caffeine consumption or procrastination, try incorporating healthy alternatives. Engage in physical exercise regularly, as it can release tension and boost mood. Additionally, explore relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or yoga to manage stress effectively.

6. Maintain Social Connections: Nurturing relationships with friends and loved ones is critical for emotional well-being. Make time to connect with them, whether it's meeting for a coffee date, having a phone or video call, or engaging in shared activities. Social support can provide comfort, perspective, and even practical assistance during challenging times.

7. Seek Joy in Simple Moments: While juggling multiple responsibilities, it can be easy to overlook the small joys in life. Take moments throughout your day to appreciate simple pleasures like enjoying a cup of tea, savoring a delicious meal, or spending quality time with loved ones. Cultivating gratitude and finding joy in everyday moments can help shift focus away from stress and bring more balance into your life.

Remember, finding balance takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself as you make changes and experiment with different strategies. If you continue to struggle, consider seeking guidance from a mental health professional who can provide personalized support tailored to your specific situation.

I recently went through another devastating breakup, and this time it was a marriage dissolution. I am struggling to cope with the loss and envision a future where I can be happy again. My goal is to heal from this traumatic event and rebuild my life.

It's understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed and struggling to envision a happy future after your recent marriage dissolution. Coping with such a significant loss is challenging, but it's important to remember that healing is possible. Here are some suggestions to help you on this journey:

1. Allow yourself to grieve: It's natural to feel a wide range of emotions following a breakup or divorce. Give yourself permission to experience these feelings fully. Cry if you need to, vent your frustrations, and allow yourself time to process the pain.

2. Seek support: Consider reaching out to trusted friends or family members who can provide a listening ear and emotional support. Talking about your feelings with someone who cares about you can be immensely helpful during this difficult time.

3. Focus on self-care: Take care of your physical and mental well-being by engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation. This could include exercise, spending time outdoors, reading, practicing mindfulness, or pursuing hobbies that make you feel alive again.

4. Set small goals: As you work towards rebuilding your life, setting small achievable goals can be empowering. Start by identifying one or two areas where you'd like to see progress, whether it's personal growth, career development, or creating new connections. Break these larger aspirations into smaller steps, celebrating each milestone along the way.

5. Challenge negative thoughts: During times of distress, our minds tend to be flooded with negative thoughts and self-doubt. Practice recognizing these unhelpful patterns and consciously challenge them with more realistic and positive perspectives. Remind yourself that you have the strength and resilience to overcome this setback.

6. Consider professional help when necessary: While support from loved ones can be invaluable, sometimes speaking with a trained mental health professional can offer unique insights and guidance tailored to your specific needs. They can assist you in developing coping strategies and working through any deep-rooted issues related to the breakup.

7. Embrace change and new possibilities: Although it may not feel like it now, your breakup can also be an opportunity for personal growth. Take this time to rediscover yourself, explore new interests, and redefine what happiness means to you. Keep an open mind towards the possibilities that lie ahead.

Remember, healing takes time, and each person's journey is unique. Be patient with yourself and trust in your ability to rebuild your life after this traumatic event.

"Whenever conflicts arise in my relationships, I tend to shut down and withdraw emotionally. This pattern is affecting both my personal and professional life. I need guidance on how to communicate effectively and resolve conflicts."

Conflicts in relationships can be tough to navigate, but it's admirable that you're seeking ways to improve your communication and conflict resolution skills. Here are some suggestions that might help:

1. Take a step back: When conflicts arise, it's important to pause and take a moment to reflect before responding emotionally. This will allow you to gather your thoughts and approach the situation with more clarity.

2. Practice active listening: Effective communication involves not only expressing yourself but also truly hearing and understanding the other person's perspective. Show genuine interest by maintaining eye contact, nodding, and summarizing their points to ensure you grasp their viewpoint accurately.

3. Express your feelings calmly: Instead of shutting down or withdrawing, try to express how you feel using "I" statements. For example, say "I feel hurt when..." rather than accusing or blaming the other person. This helps avoid defensiveness and encourages a healthier conversation.

4. Seek compromise: Conflict resolution often requires finding common ground. Explore possible solutions together and be open to compromising if necessary. Remember, it's about finding a mutually beneficial outcome rather than winning an argument.

5. Consider therapy resources: If you find it challenging to implement these strategies on your own, consider seeking support from a mental health professional. They can provide personalized guidance and offer tools tailored to your specific needs.

6. Reflect on patterns: It may also be helpful to reflect on any recurring patterns or triggers surrounding the conflicts. Identifying these patterns can give you insights into why certain situations provoke such strong emotional reactions, helping you develop coping mechanisms for future conflicts.

7. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of your own well-being is crucial during times of conflict. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help reduce stress. This can include exercise, hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or practicing relaxation techniques like meditation or deep breathing exercises.

Remember, improving communication and conflict resolution skills takes time and practice. Don't be too hard on yourself if it doesn't happen overnight. By being open to learning, practicing empathy, and staying committed to personal growth, you can make progress in your relationships both personally and professionally.

It can be incredibly challenging to manage multiple responsibilities at work and home, especially when the stress becomes overwhelming. The impact on your sleep, concentration, and overall well-being is understandable given the circumstances. It's great that you're eager to learn techniques to better cope with chronic stress. Here are some suggestions:

1. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to prioritize time for yourself each day, even if it's just a few minutes. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help you relax, such as reading, taking a walk, or practicing mindfulness exercises.

2. Establish boundaries: Set clear boundaries between work and personal life. Create designated times for work-related tasks and make an effort to disconnect from work during non-work hours. This will allow you to have dedicated time for yourself and your loved ones.

3. Delegate and ask for support: Recognize that you don't have to do everything alone. Delegate tasks at work and involve family members or friends in household responsibilities. Asking for support can alleviate some of the pressure and create more balance in your life.

4. Time management techniques: Explore different time management strategies to help you stay organized and efficient. Break down tasks into smaller, manageable steps, prioritize them based on importance and deadlines, and consider using tools like calendars or to-do lists to keep track of your responsibilities.

5. Stress-reducing activities: Incorporate stress-reducing activities into your routine. Regular exercise, deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or engaging in hobbies can all help reduce stress levels and promote overall well-being.

6. Seek social support: Connect with others who may be experiencing similar challenges. Sharing your feelings and experiences with trusted friends, family, or support groups can provide emotional support and valuable insights.

Remember, these suggestions are not meant to replace professional help but rather offer guidance and support. If you find that your stress continues to significantly impact your daily functioning, it may be beneficial to reach out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized strategies and support.

I have anxieties about everyday stressors, i.e. finances, work, relationships, kids, and maintaining a household.

Something to remember about anxiety is that it's a useful and necessary response to stressors, and we all have a level of anxiety that falls somewhere on the spectrum from very slight to very overwhelming. Anxiety is our brain's way of prompting us to deal with the stress in our lives by getting us geared up for action. Some helpful ways of managing anxiety are actually very simple. The first I'd recommend is a calm breathing technique - breathe in for 4-5 seconds, and then out for 7-8 seconds. Try to repeat this for 3-5 minutes. Another suggestion is to pay closer attention in the moments you feel the physical symptoms of anxiety and see if you can describe - without judging - the sensations to yourself. Try to be very specific, such as "my palms are feeling very sweaty, and I can feel the slight tightness and fluttering in my belly of the butterflies." Then try to sit with these sensations without deciding if they are good or bad - just experiencing them as intentionally as possible.  Combining the calm breathing with this technique can also be very helpful. If you feel that these techniques don't help and your anxiety about everyday stressors are inhibiting you from being able to engage in life the way you want to, then I'd highly recommend going for an assessment or even just consultation with a professional. This professional can help you determine if therapy/counseling would be helpful for you to develop additional skills for managing those interfering anxiety symptoms.

My spouse and I have been married for several years now, and while we still love each other, our relationship lacks intimacy. It feels like we're more roommates than romantic partners. We rarely have physical or emotional connection anymore, and it's taking a toll on both of us. I want to reignite the spark we once had and find ways to reconnect on a deeper level. It's important to me that we prioritize our marriage and work towards rebuilding the passion we've lost.

It's wonderful that you recognize the importance of prioritizing your marriage and working towards rebuilding the passion you've lost. Intimacy is a vital aspect of any relationship, and it's completely normal for couples to experience changes in their level of connection over time.

To reignite the spark and reconnect on a deeper level with your spouse, here are some suggestions:

1. Open Communication: Start by having an open and honest conversation with your spouse about how you both feel. Express your desire to strengthen your emotional and physical bond. Encourage them to share their thoughts and feelings as well. This will create a safe space for understanding each other better.

2. Quality Time: Set aside dedicated quality time for just the two of you. Plan activities or date nights that you used to enjoy together or explore new hobbies together. It could be something as simple as going for walks, cooking together, or even watching a movie and discussing it afterward. The key is to spend uninterrupted time focusing on each other.

3. Physical Affection: Small gestures of physical affection can go a long way in rebuilding intimacy. Hold hands, hug, cuddle, or give each other massages. These acts of touch can help rekindle the closeness between you.

4. Emotional Connection: Work on strengthening your emotional bond by actively listening to each other and showing empathy. Share your dreams, fears, and aspirations. Engage in deep conversations where you discuss your hopes and goals for the future. By being vulnerable and supportive, you can foster a stronger emotional connection.

5. Surprise and Spontaneity: Surprise your spouse with little gestures or acts of kindness. It could be leaving a sweet note, planning a surprise outing, or doing something special for them without any particular reason. Injecting spontaneity into your relationship can bring back excitement and joy.

6. Seek New Experiences Together: Trying new things together can reignite the sense of adventure and create shared memories. Explore activities you both have an interest in, such as taking a dance class, going on a weekend getaway, or even trying out a new hobby together.

Remember, rebuilding intimacy takes time and effort from both partners. Be patient with each other and celebrate small victories along the way. By prioritizing your marriage and actively working towards reconnecting, you can reignite the spark and deepen your bond once again.

My ex-boyfriend boyfriend and I lived together. He had a two year affair with a girl and had three pregnancies with her. One was an abortion, another was a miscarriage, and then she had the third baby. They are not together, but he continues to contact me and wants me back. He has nothing to offer me.

Hi Attica,This is a question I think a lot of people deal with...they feel confusion about why they can't forget about or get over (or stop connecting with) someone who they absolutely know isn't good for them. In your case, part of the problem is that he keeps trying to get back in touch with you. For some people, honestly, it's a game... to see how much power they have over you or it's their need to control you. If you don't want contact from this person, it's really important to give him clear messages about boundaries ("Don't contact me again"), and then ignore all of their communications. Any interactions or responses from you at all will feed their behaviour. Remind yourself why you don't want to be with them. I hear you doing that already when you say "he has nothing to offer me". That's great self-talk.But let's get back to the question of why we have a hard time letting go of people like this. Sometimes it's because we still hope they will change. Maybe we remember who they used to be or how they used to treat us, and we think it can go back to the way it felt in those "good old days". The problem there is that, over the first few years, as intimacy grows, people tend to show more of who they are, not less. So what they're eventually showing you is who they are and what they're capable of. People do change and grow, but it won't happen at your pace. Accept that person for who they are and stop expecting them to change. Another reason we can't let go is because we picture our ex with someone new in the future and we wonder if they will be a better person for the next partner in their life. This is a normal... but not a healthy... thought. It's as though we want them to stay, maybe apologize, and heal our hurts; maybe make up for past mistakes. You deserve that healing, you deserve better than you got, you deserve apologies, but to expect that from the person who hurt you and hasn't demonstrated that compassion as yet is probably foolhardy. It is my belief that underlying some of the above scenarios is the deep belief that we must somehow be responsible for the hurts our exes have caused. If you blame yourself in any way for someone's poor treatment of you, you will be dancing around trying to do things differently so that they can treat you better. It will be impossible to let go, because you blame yourself for their behaviours.Draw a line. Their behaviours are about them, not you, and the only solution is to challenge and reduce thoughts of them, and create physical and emotional distance. These things plus time will help the events of the past fade from importance.
I start counseling/therapy in a few days (I'm freaking out) but my main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself, is it something to worry about?

Hi there !  As someone who has practiced as a clinical psychologist for 25 years , I would say that crying is NOTHING TO WORRY ABOUT AT ALL ! Almost every single person I have worked with has cried at one point or another.  Starting therapy takes a lot of courage; when you work with a therapist ,once you feel safe ,  you talk about a lot of very private and potentially emotional things that you may have never discussed with anyone before.  I have seen  people cry with sadness , cry with relief at releasing painful things they have held onto for a long time, cry because they feel so relieved that they finally feel heard.   I myself have sometimes cried with clients because some things they talk about are so profoundly moving.   I can assure you that most , if not all , therapists expect clients to cry  and there is nothing to be embarrassed about.   Crying can be very cathartic and can allow us to release a lot of painful feelings we have been stuffing down.   Crying is  often a sign that you are really working things through and getting in touch with feelings that you need to get in touch with in order to heal .So , to summarize , don't worry at all about crying! It will probably feel uncomfortable  at first , but I promise you , you will not be judged for crying in therapy.   And it will be less embarrassing once it happens a time or two and you are assured that your therapist will be there for you and won't judge you !Good luck !!

Anxiety has woven its way into every facet of my existence. My mind feels like a jumble of worries and worst-case scenarios. It's difficult for me to concentrate or engage fully in activities without being distracted by excessive thoughts of potential danger or harm.

One specific situation that triggered immense anxiety recently was attending a social gathering. The mere thought of interacting with strangers and engaging in small talk sent waves of panic through me. Once I arrived at the event, I experienced shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat, and intrusive thoughts about being judged or rejected. Consequently, I left the gathering prematurely.

My anxiety symptoms occur almost daily, leaving me feeling constantly on edge and overwhelmed. They tend to peak during situations requiring social interaction or when faced with uncertainties. The duration of these symptoms varies but often persists for several hours, significantly impacting my ability to fulfill personal and professional obligations.

Reflecting upon my background, growing up, my family emphasized conformity and adhering to societal expectations. This contributed to my fear of judgment and rejection, ultimately fueling my anxiety.

To manage my anxiety, I have explored relaxation techniques such as deep breathing exercises and listening to calming music. While these strategies provide temporary relief, they don't address the underlying causes of my anxiety or equip me with sustainable tools for managing it effectively.

I'm curious about therapeutic interventions that specifically target anxiety disorders. Are there evidence-based treatments you recommend? Additionally, how do therapists assist clients in integrating newly developed coping mechanisms into their daily lives?

It's great that you've reached out for counseling to gain clarity on the triggers behind your anxiety and find effective strategies to regain control over your life. Anxiety can indeed feel overwhelming, making even small tasks seem insurmountable. Let's explore some guidance and suggestions that may help you manage your anxiety symptoms.

Firstly, it's important to acknowledge that excessive worry and worst-case scenarios are common experiences with anxiety. One strategy to address this is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT helps individuals identify and challenge negative thought patterns, enabling them to develop more balanced and realistic thinking. This can lead to a reduction in anxiety levels and an increased ability to concentrate and engage fully in activities without being overly distracted by excessive thoughts.

Additionally, exposure therapy might be helpful in managing anxiety related to social gatherings. Exposure therapy involves gradually and safely facing feared situations to reduce their anxiety-provoking impact. By working with a therapist trained in exposure therapy techniques, you could develop a step-by-step plan to confront and overcome your fears of interacting with strangers and engaging in small talk at social events.

In terms of integrating newly developed coping mechanisms into your daily life, therapists often collaborate with clients to create personalized plans. Together, you and your therapist can develop strategies tailored specifically to your needs. This might include setting achievable goals, practicing new coping techniques during therapy sessions, and gradually incorporating them into your day-to-day routines outside of therapy. The goal is to make these coping mechanisms become second nature as you work toward managing your anxiety effectively.

Besides therapeutic interventions, self-care practices can also contribute to anxiety management. Engaging in regular physical exercise, maintaining a healthy diet, ensuring adequate sleep, and cultivating hobbies or activities that bring you joy can all positively influence your overall mental well-being.

Remember, finding sustainable tools for managing your anxiety takes time and effort. Be patient and kind with yourself throughout this process. It can be beneficial to work with a therapist who specializes in anxiety disorders and offers evidence-based treatments like CBT and exposure therapy. They can guide you on your journey to regain control over your life and provide ongoing support as you integrate coping mechanisms into your daily routines.

In conclusion, by exploring therapeutic interventions such as CBT and exposure therapy, while also implementing self-care practices, you can develop effective strategies for managing your anxiety symptoms. Collaborating with a trained therapist will assist you in creating sustainable tools and integrating them into your daily life. Keep in mind that it's okay to take things one step at a time, and remember to prioritize self-compassion along your healing journey.

Every time I have to face a social situation or speak in public, my heart starts pounding, my palms sweat, and I can hardly catch my breath. The fear of embarrassing myself or being judged by others becomes overwhelming. This anxiety affects my personal and professional life, making it hard to form connections and advance. My goal in counseling is to overcome this social anxiety and live a more confident life.

In situations where you have to face social interactions or speak in public, it seems that your anxiety takes over and manifests through physical symptoms like a pounding heart, sweaty palms, and difficulty catching your breath. The fear of embarrassing yourself or being judged by others becomes overwhelming for you. This anxiety has been negatively impacting both your personal and professional life, making it challenging to form connections and progress.

One approach to overcoming social anxiety is gradually exposing yourself to the situations that cause anxiety while practicing strategies to manage your symptoms. It can be helpful to start with smaller, less intimidating social situations and gradually work your way up to more challenging ones. Within these settings, focusing on deep breathing exercises and relaxation techniques may assist in reducing the intensity of your physical symptoms.

Engaging in cognitive-behavioral techniques can also be beneficial. By identifying and challenging negative thoughts related to social situations, you can reframe them into more positive and realistic perspectives. For instance, instead of automatically assuming others will judge you harshly, consider alternative possibilities such as neutral or even positive reactions from people around you.

Building self-confidence is another important aspect of addressing social anxiety. Remind yourself of past achievements or successes in similar circumstances. Recognize your strengths and skills, and use this knowledge to boost your self-esteem and belief in your ability to handle social interactions effectively. Additionally, setting realistic expectations for yourself can alleviate some of the pressure you put on yourself during these situations.

Seeking support from trusted friends or family members who can provide encouragement and understanding may also prove valuable. Sharing your experiences and challenges with someone close to you can lighten the emotional burden and potentially offer new perspectives.

While overcoming social anxiety can be a gradual process, remember that progress takes time. Be patient and kind to yourself throughout your journey.

Self love and self acceptance is something that many of my clients struggle with, so I can assure you that you are not alone. We are bombarded by media and advertisements everyday that try to sell us things to make us somehow better, thus leading us to believe that we are not enough. For example, did a parent or another loved one criticize you or put you down often? Were you bulled in school? Has a romantic partner emotionally abused you? Usually, there are factors such as these which insidiously lead to low self esteem and self loathing. Once you can identify some of the factors that lead to your self hatred, you can make a decision to not let these things from your past have such power over you any more. You learn to take control of how you feel about yourself, rather than letting others dictate that for you. I do think it is possible to heal from self hatred. It doesn't happen over night, and it takes time and effort. It is about re-training your brain to focus on your strengths rather than on your weaknesses. None of us are ever going to be perfect, and if we look for a flaw we are bound to find one (or two, or three...). Try keeping a self esteem journal. Every night, write down three things that you were proud of that day about yourself. Try reciting positive affirmations every day (such as "I am lovable and beautiful just the way that I am today"), to re-program your mind into thinking highly of yourself, rather than poorly.

Hi New York, I'm happy to hear that your daughter doesn't know about her dad's addictions. Although you don't say how old she is, and I imagine that at some point in her life she will be ready to know the truth, I trust your instinct that now is not the time. Your ability to have clear boundaries about what is adult conversation and what is suitable for a child to know are really important here, and I can tell you're being appropriately protective and a thoughtful parent. As much as this helps your daughter, I sense that you also know you can't take away the emotional pain that comes from having an absent parent. Children tend to blame themselves for a parent's absence. These children need extra love and support wherever they can get it.You say that you feel like there is a wedge between you and your daughter. I understand that having your ex partner's relatives in the same home would make it uncomfortable at times. It is very important to establish boundaries; only you should parent your daughter, but it's also natural for people to want to assist you. Let's trust that their intentions are good, if there is no evidence to the contrary. As much as they support you, they also  have emotional ties to your daughter's father. While there is potential for discomfort in this complex situation, there are also many positive factors here that I invite you to see.I don't know what your culture is, but for your daughter to have the opportunity to preserve her father's heritage language and a relationship with his family are potentially wonderful additions to her life. My hope for you is that you can feel so secure in your own position as loving mother that you will not feel intimidated by other positive connections your daughter has. They are potentially wonderful connections, and she deserves your support in maintaining those relationships if they don't harm her.I suggest that the most important alliances to work on here are between you and your ex's family. Often times I find myself thinking scary thoughts and sometimes I even scare myself into thinking that something bad is going to happen to me. Once it starts, the thought continues going through my head and I can't get it out. How can I stop these thoughts?

When my clients say they are having a similar experience I teach them two main coping skills. The first is to simply say, out loud, STOP! The reasoning behind this is that we cannot talk and have an audible thought at the same time. This will only work in the short term and the rebound thoughts from this can be just as bad or overwhelming so I also teach to couple this with the STOPP Technique. The STOPP technique is:Stop what you’re doing Take a step back to calm and gather yourself. This can be done with Box Breathing where you inhale for a count of 4, hold the breath for a count of 4, exhale for a count of 4, and hold for a count of 4. Repeat this for at least 5 sets.  ObserveTHOUGHTS: What thoughts am I having? What’s going through my mind? What am I saying to myself?BODY SENSATIONS: What physical sensations am I experiencing? Where in my body am I experiencing them?FEELINGS: What feelings or emotions am I experiencing?BEHAVIOUR: What am I doing? How am I acting? What do I want to doPlan: What’s the best/most important thing for me to do right now? Proceed to act mindfully, taking whatever action you’ve planned.Then to see if there are any underlying issues causing the thoughts, I would make an appointment to see a therapist in your area.

Hello, and thank you for reaching out to ask for help. Surely this is a very confusing time for you! If you have never had these
feelings and desires it could certainty shake everything you thought you knew
about yourself. 
My guess is that you becoming sick around the time that this
started is likely a coincidence, but I understand how you would make the
connection. 
I have a feeling that a few things may be going on here. It
is really hard to say since I don’t know you, how old you are, etc. But, I will
share you with you some thoughts. 
Some people, when they have undesirable thoughts that really
surprise them, have a really tough time getting rid of them. Our reaction to
the thought can be very strong and our tendency to try to block it out, stuff
it, avoid it, etc. is not always successful. In fact, it’s usually not. 
It’s like telling you not to think of pink elephants. I
would be willing to bet that you thought of a pink elephant just now. 
So, rather than fighting thoughts that you find confusing,
sometimes it is helpful to allow yourself to explore the thought with curiosity
and without judgement. Where is this thought coming from? What are my feelings
about it? Asking yourself these questions may help you come to a resolution
about what is going on. 
One possibility is that you have developed an anxiety about
your thoughts and now you are in the process of obsessing about them, but
another possibility is that you are legitimately exploring your sexuality and
gender. I get the feeling from your question that you do not want to believe
that it is second possibility. And that is okay. 
You can try some of my suggestions, but you can also see a
counselor who may be able to help you work through your confusion. I would
suggest someone who has experience working with sexuality issues. You can
usually find out what a counselor works with on their website. What is
important is that you find someone who is non-judgmental about what you are
experiencing. 
 
I wish you well.
Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Often times I find myself thinking scary thoughts and sometimes  I even scare myself into thinking that something bad is going to happen to me. Once it starts, the thought continues going through my head and I can't get it out.  How can I stop these thoughts?

Hi there,I first want to let you know that having these thoughts is completely normal. Studies have been done that show that 80% of human thoughts are "negative" so you are not alone. I like to think of thoughts as a tornado... if you are in a tornado, you are completely consumed by it and it is nearly impossible to do anything beneficial. However, when you are, let's say, a mile away from a tornado, it is still scary but you have the option to do something that is important to you such as get shelter or make sure your family and friends are safe. When unhelpful or scary thoughts arise, we tend to start a "war" with them, which is the equivalent of jumping into the tornado. This makes the thoughts and emotions bigger and intensifies the feelings that go with them. So the question I imagine you have is "how do I get out of the tornado?" There are 3 steps to doing this:Get distance from your thoughts by adding "I am noticing I'm having the thought that...." to the front of them. For example, "I am noticing I am having the thought that something bad is going to happen to me."   The purpose of this is not to decrease your fear or get rid of the thought. These thoughts might always be there and that is okay because that is how the mind naturally works so struggling with that is a waste of time and energy. The purpose is to gain some distance from the thoughts so you don't get swept away by them. You can imagine them floating along like leaves in a stream or clouds in the sky (and often the same thought will come back again and again but that's okay... just continue to notice it with curiosity). I imagine the thoughts get in your way of doing what really matters to you so if you can get a little bit of distance, you can do things that are fulfilling and meaningful to you. Tune into your body and notice what sensations come up and where you feel them most intensely. Then breathe into them and make room for them. Our 5 main emotions are: joy, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame, and anger. ALL of these emotions are part of being human and there is no escaping them. So again, struggling with them ends up intensifying them. Instead, let them be and make a little bit of room for them. Often a side effect of this is the intensity will decrease but it might not. The purpose is to keep them from becoming more intense. Contact the present moment. Notice what is happening here and now. One way of doing this is tuning into the five senses. What are some things you hear, see, taste, smell, and feel? Another way is to notice what is happening in your body (without trying to change it). How deep are your breaths, what is happening with your heart rate, are you cold/warm, etc?Implementing these three steps can help you to refrain from getting caught up in your unhelpful thoughts. Unfortunately there is no way to get rid of thoughts or feelings completely. So the only option that works in the long run is to accept them while continuing to do what matters to you and what is fulfilling to you.I hope this helps!

It sounds like you're going through a challenging time with work-related stress and it's impacting your overall well-being. It's great that you're recognizing the importance of managing your stress and creating a healthier work-life balance. Here are some strategies you can explore:

1. Set clear boundaries: Establishing boundaries between work and personal life is crucial. Define specific times when you will focus solely on work, and then allow yourself dedicated break and relaxation times.

2. Prioritize tasks: Start each day by identifying the most important tasks that need to be accomplished. Break them down into smaller, manageable steps to make them less overwhelming. As you complete each task, celebrate your achievements and acknowledge your progress.

3. Practice self-care: Take care of your physical, mental, and emotional well-being. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help you relax. This could include exercise, meditation, journaling, reading, or spending time with loved ones.

4. Communicate your needs: If you're feeling overwhelmed, don't hesitate to reach out to your supervisor or colleagues. Express your concerns, discuss potential solutions, and see if any adjustments can be made to alleviate your workload or provide support.

5. Time management techniques: Consider exploring techniques such as the Pomodoro Technique or time blocking to improve productivity and maintain focus throughout the day.

6. Delegate and seek support: Identify tasks that can be delegated to others or shared with your team. Don't be afraid to ask for help when needed. Sharing the workload can reduce stress and create a more collaborative work environment.

7. Create a calming workspace: Organize your workspace in a way that promotes calmness and reduces distractions. Personalize it with items that inspire and motivate you. Ensure you have proper lighting, comfortable seating, and ergonomic setup to minimize physical discomfort.

8. Take breaks: Regularly take short breaks during the day to rest and recharge. Use these breaks to step away from work, engage in relaxation exercises, or simply take a walk outside.

9. Seek social support: Connect with friends, family, or colleagues who can offer support and understanding. Talking about your experiences and sharing your feelings can provide comfort and help you gain perspective.

10. Reflect on what brings you joy: Take time to reflect on the aspects of your work that bring you joy and fulfillment. Incorporate more of these elements into your daily routine to enhance job satisfaction and reduce stress.

Remember, it's important to be patient with yourself during this process of managing stress and creating balance. Each person is unique, so feel free to adapt these strategies to fit your specific needs. If you find that your stress continues to escalate or becomes unmanageable, consider seeking professional support from a therapist or counselor. They can provide additional guidance tailored to your situation.

Restoring the spark in a marriage can indeed be achieved through counseling. Here are some suggestions and techniques that may help reignite the passion and connection between you and your partner:

1. Communication is key: Continue having open and vulnerable conversations with each other, expressing your desires for reconnection. Take turns actively listening to one another without interruption or judgment. Practice empathy and validate each other's feelings.

The stress of my demanding job has been taking a toll on my mental health. The constant pressure to meet deadlines and perform at a high level has left me feeling overwhelmed and burnt out. I often find myself working late into the night, sacrificing my personal life and self-care in the process.

It's understandable that the stress from your demanding job is impacting your mental health. The pressure to meet deadlines and perform at a high level can be overwhelming, leading to feelings of burnout. It seems like you've been sacrificing your personal life and self-care in order to keep up with work demands.

Here are some suggestions to help manage the situation:

1. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to set aside time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation. This could include hobbies, exercise, spending time with loved ones, or simply taking breaks throughout the day to recharge.

2. Set boundaries: Establish clear boundaries between work and personal life. Avoid working late into the night whenever possible and try to create a routine that allows for dedicated time away from work-related tasks.

3. Delegate and ask for support: If feasible, consider delegating tasks or seeking assistance from colleagues when feeling overwhelmed. Communicate your needs and limitations to your supervisor or team members so they can better understand your workload.

4. Break tasks into smaller steps: When faced with multiple deadlines, breaking down larger projects into smaller, manageable tasks can make them feel less daunting. Prioritize tasks based on urgency and importance, and tackle them one step at a time.

5. Practice stress management techniques: Explore different stress management techniques such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, or mindfulness practices. These can help reduce anxiety and promote overall well-being.

6. Seek social support: Connect with friends, family, or support groups who can provide emotional support and understanding during challenging times. Sharing your experiences and concerns with others can offer perspective and validation.

Remember, it's important to take care of your mental health and find a balance between work and personal life. Implementing these strategies may help alleviate some of the stress and prevent further burnout.

Hello, I need help with my anxiety as it's impacting every aspect of my life. Lately, even mundane tasks like grocery shopping or taking public transportation trigger intense feelings of fear and discomfort. For instance, yesterday while waiting for a bus, I suddenly felt overwhelmed by a sense of impending doom. My heart started pounding, I began sweating profusely, and my legs felt weak. This incident keeps replaying in my mind, fueling my worries and making it difficult to engage in normal activities without experiencing panic-like symptoms. Through counseling, I hope to understand why these physical sensations are occurring and learn practical techniques to cope with them. Is there a way to gradually desensitize myself and regain control over my anxiety?

Managing anxiety can be challenging, but there are strategies that may help you regain control over your symptoms. It's understandable that experiencing intense fear and discomfort during daily activities can be distressing.

Based on what you shared, it seems like you may be dealing with panic attacks, which can manifest in physical symptoms such as a pounding heart, sweating, and weakness. Let's explore some techniques that may assist you in coping with these sensations:

1. Deep Breathing: When you feel overwhelmed, focusing on slow, deep breaths can help regulate your body's reaction to stress. Take a deep breath in through your nose for a count of four, hold for a count of four, and exhale slowly for a count of four. Repeat this process until you begin to feel more grounded.

2. Grounding Techniques: Engaging your senses through grounding exercises can redirect your attention away from anxious thoughts. This involves identifying five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. This practice encourages mindfulness and brings you back to the present moment.

3. Gradual Exposure: Desensitization can indeed be an effective method to overcome anxieties related to specific situations. Start by creating a hierarchy of feared scenarios, ranging from mild to severe anxiety triggers. Begin exposing yourself to the least anxiety-provoking situation and gradually work your way up the ladder at your own pace. Each time you successfully face a feared situation, celebrate the accomplishment and move forward.

4. Self-Care: Prioritize self-care activities that promote relaxation and well-being. Explore hobbies or engage in regular exercise, practice mindfulness meditation, maintain a balanced diet, ensure adequate sleep, and establish a consistent routine. These practices can contribute to overall mental health and support your resilience in managing anxiety.

5. Seeking Support: Consider reaching out to trusted friends, family, or support groups who can provide understanding and encouragement. Sharing your experiences with others who have faced similar challenges may offer additional perspectives and coping strategies.

Remember, everyone's journey with anxiety is unique, so finding what works best for you may involve some trial and error. If these techniques do not provide sufficient relief or if your symptoms worsen, it might be helpful to consult a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance and support.

While anxiety can come about for many reasons, trauma is definitely one of the factors that makes anxiety a possibility both immediately following a traumatic event and later in life. When we have experienced such scary violations of our bodies - we may experience residual effects of fear for many years to come. This is normal, natural and in many ways helpful - at least initially. This fear is in some way a sign that your body/mind is taking good care of you - trying to keep you on your toes in order to protect you from anything terrible happening to you again. However, as it sounds like you know, anxiety feels awful and there are certainly ways of learning to reduce anxiety. In order to get the tools you need to manage anxiety and also understand where it comes from and how it works in your life, I would encourage you to seek professional help and check out anxiety resources online.

However, it's important to recognize that your own well-being is crucial in this situation. The signs of exhaustion, headaches, insomnia, and irritability that you've been experiencing are indicators of caregiver burnout. Caregiver burnout is a common issue among individuals who provide long-term care for their loved ones, and it can have serious consequences for both the caregiver and the care recipient.

To address your current situation, I would recommend a few strategies. First, it's essential to prioritize self-care. This can include activities such as regular exercise, a healthy diet, adequate sleep, and engaging in hobbies or activities that bring you joy. How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

In my therapy practice the decision to end therapy is mutually made together with the patient.Otherwise, the person can end up with a sense of tremendous rejection and abandonment.The way you'll both know therapy is coming to a close is that the discussion will feel lighter and move easily.The person's mood will be better, they will smile more, sit in their seat in a more relaxed way, look more at ease, take better care of their appearance.One of the ways to end therapy is to gradually decrease the frequency of the sessions.Sometimes people who are in my practice start to come each three weeks, then monthly, then every three months.This gives a sense of security, friendliness, and casualness to the therapy, and de-medicalizes it as though the person was treated for a medical symptom and the symptom stops completely one day.Talk therapy is about life and life problems usually end gradually.I end my therapy in a way which mirrors the life process in which many interaction and situation problems show their effects gradually and show different effects over time.

First of all, I want to say, I am so sorry you are not feeling accepted by your family. I know how  isolating and lonely this can be. The most important step you can take right now is building a community of supportive people who do accept you. Creating your own sense of community is very powerful for helping you love yourself. If you can find a trans support or LGBTQ support group in your area, I recommend seeking that out right away through your local LGBTQ center or PFLAG. If you don’t have access to that, I recommend calling Trans Lifeline US: 877-565-8860 Canada: 877-330-6366 https://www.translifeline.org/. You can talk to other trans-identified people anonymously for support, calling them from wherever you feel safe. This is a great way to begin to connect with other people who have similar experiences to you. Next, think of this time in your life as your time to explore your gender identity, just for yourself. Make room to explore you gender identity in ways that are private and comfortable for you. Consider reading a book like: https://www.newharbinger.com/queer-and-transgender-resilience-workbook to explore who you are and build resilience. Also, consider learning about other religions that are accepting of LGBTQ folks for another perspective - there are many out there! Once you feel you have a strong support system outside of your family and a positive sense of self-love (which can take time, be patient, don’t rush it), then you can consider what action steps you want to take with your family. If you are still living with your family or financially depend on them, having other supports in place first is very important. It’s a very personal choice how you want to navigate your family relationships, talk it through in-depth with a trusted friend, other trans folks, or therapist to help you decide what’s right for you.And remember, there are tons of people out there who will love and accept you. We are rooting for you!In solidarity,-Lindsey

It's completely normal to feel the way you're feeling after a long-term relationship ends. Breakups can be incredibly challenging, especially when they come as a surprise. Adjusting to the idea of being alone can take time and it's important to give yourself permission to grieve the loss.

One suggestion I have is to allow yourself to fully process your emotions. It's okay to think about the past memories and even feel sadness or anger about the breakup. Journaling can be a helpful tool in this process, allowing you to explore and release your feelings on paper. Additionally, talking to trusted friends or family members who are good listeners can provide some relief and support during this difficult time.

Finding new activities or hobbies can also help in the healing process by providing an opportunity to focus your energy and attention elsewhere. Whether it's trying out a new workout class, joining a club or group that aligns with your interests, or anything else that brings you joy and fulfillment, engaging in positive and enriching experiences can aid in creating a sense of happiness and purpose.

Furthermore, practicing self-care is vital for healing. This means taking care of both your physical and emotional well-being. Make sure you prioritize getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and exercising regularly. Additionally, finding ways to nurture your mental health, such as through meditation, deep breathing exercises, or mindfulness practices, can help create a sense of inner peace and calmness.

Lastly, remember that healing takes time. There is no specific timeline for moving on from a breakup, but by focusing on self-growth and taking small steps towards building a fulfilling life for yourself, you will gradually find happiness again. Be patient and compassionate with yourself throughout this journey.

I hope these suggestions can offer you some guidance and support as you navigate through this difficult period. Remember, healing is possible, and you deserve to find peace within yourself.

1. Communication is key: Start by creating opportunities for open and honest conversations with your partner. Set aside dedicated time to talk about your feelings, desires, and concerns. Listen actively to each other without judgment or criticism, and strive to understand each other's perspectives.

2. Initiate small gestures of affection: Show your partner love and care through small acts of kindness and appreciation. This can include giving compliments, holding hands, hugging, or doing little things that make them feel valued and loved. These gestures can go a long way in rekindling intimacy.

3. Prioritize quality time together: Make a conscious effort to spend quality time with your partner regularly. Engage in activities that both of you enjoy, whether it's having a romantic dinner, going for a walk together, or watching a movie. Creating shared experiences can help reignite the spark in your relationship.

4. Explore new activities together: Trying out new experiences as a couple can freshen up your connection and bring excitement back into your lives. Consider participating in a hobby together, joining a dance class, or taking a cooking course. Discovering new interests as a team can provide opportunities for growth and bonding.

5. Practice empathy and understanding: Being empathetic towards your partner's struggles and emotions cultivates an environment of emotional safety and trust. Seek to understand their point of view and validate their feelings, even if you don't agree. Avoid blaming or criticizing each other, and work towards finding constructive solutions as a team.

6. Seek professional support if needed: If despite your efforts, the issues persist or become more complex, consider seeking couples counseling or therapy. A trained professional can assist you in navigating the challenges you're facing and provide guidance tailored to your unique circumstances.

Remember, rebuilding intimacy takes time and effort from both partners. Be patient with each other and celebrate the progress you make along the way. With dedication and a willingness to work on your relationship, you can strengthen your bond and reclaim the intimacy you desire.

For some of the couples I work with in my practice, I find that helping to organize a time apart, which I call a "Therapeutic Separation" can do wonders for the relationship. I offer homework to be done during this time. Reading, worksheets and individual counseling helps people learn more about themselves and what they desire out of their relationship.
