Marriage

"I'm seeking counseling because I am currently facing challenges within my marriage, and I hope to address them through therapy. The goal is to improve our relationship dynamics and strengthen our bond. My spouse and I are having difficulty communicating effectively, leading to feelings of frustration and disconnection."

"For example, we struggle to express our needs and desires openly. Instead, it feels like we're constantly tiptoeing around each other, afraid of starting an argument. As a result, our conversations lack depth and meaningful connection."

"These symptoms have been present for over a year now. The frequency and intensity of these communication struggles depend on various factors, such as stress levels and external circumstances. However, they tend to arise multiple times a week and can last for hours."

"When considering our backgrounds, my spouse grew up in a family where open communication was discouraged, while I had parents who were overly critical and quick to anger. It's possible that these experiences have influenced our current communication difficulties."

"I would greatly appreciate any advice on how we can improve our communication as a couple. Are there specific techniques or exercises we could try together?"

Improving communication within a marriage is a common goal, and seeking therapy is a great step towards addressing these challenges. It's understandable that you want to strengthen your bond and have more effective conversations with your spouse.

To begin improving your communication dynamics, it may be helpful to focus on creating a safe and supportive environment for both you and your spouse to express yourselves openly. Start by setting aside dedicated time for regular conversations where you can discuss your needs, desires, and concerns without fear of argument or judgment. This could be a weekly check-in or a designated date night where you prioritize open and honest dialogue.

One technique that might be useful is active listening. Instead of just waiting for your turn to speak, make an effort to fully understand what your partner is saying by giving them your undivided attention. Show genuine interest in their perspective, ask clarifying questions, and restate their thoughts to ensure you've understood correctly. This can help foster deeper understanding and connection between the two of you.

Another practical exercise you could try is practicing empathy and validation. Take turns expressing your feelings and experiences, allowing each other to truly feel heard. Remember to acknowledge and validate your spouse's emotions, even if you don't necessarily agree with their perspective. By doing so, you create a sense of safety and understanding within the relationship.

It might also be beneficial to explore any underlying emotional patterns from your respective backgrounds. Consider how your spouse's upbringing and your own childhood experiences may affect your current communication struggles. Understanding these influences can provide insight into potential areas for growth and help you approach conversations with more compassion and patience.

Lastly, keep in mind that improving communication takes time and effort from both partners. Be patient with yourselves as you navigate this process together, and celebrate small victories along the way. If needed, consider reaching out to more resources such as books, articles, or workshops on effective communication in relationships.

Remember, building better communication skills requires active participation and willingness from both you and your spouse. With dedication, practice, and a commitment to growth, it's possible to improve your relationship dynamics and foster deeper connection.

We weren't long distance until he joined the military.  I love him and I know he loves, me but it's complicated. He said he's not going to find someone else, but I'm afraid. How do I keep our relationship going?

Hello. You are asking a very good question about how to sustain a long-distance relationship. Although maintaining a long-distance relationship has its challenges, with the proper communication, commitment, and understanding, many long-distance couples are able to thrive and maintain a close connection. Without knowing more about the "complicated" nature of your relationship, I wonder whether your boyfriend has given you reason not to trust him that makes afraid that he will find someone else. Has he cheated on you in the past and has shown romantic interest to another person that made you fear losing him?  Or, is your thought just a fear but not based on evidence? Knowing that distinction is important because if it is the latter, you may benefit from refocusing on the wonderful qualities about your partner that makes you feel good about him and the relationship rather than focusing on the unknown or uncertainty of the future. The more you focus on "what if" situations, the more you may feel anxious about a reality that is not accurate and make you act in ways that are insecure. However, if there is reason for you to question his fidelity, you may have to speak to your boyfriend about how to build trust in the context of a long-distance relationship. To help the conversation, you may need to consider what you may need to experience or receive as support to feel safe in the relationship to build trust. Is that you wish him to contact you regularly, or to include you more in his life, or to make a clear commitment? For many of my clients in my private practice, that may include talking to their partner often and using a variety of modalities including text, phone, and Skype. It's hard to believe in a relationship when you never talk to your partner, and it's hard to build a relationship when you don't know what's going on in your partner's life. Other times, it is Making sure they talk often to their long-distance partner so that they can participate in each others lives and to feel their presence.. Regular communication, understanding and caring is the key to sustaining any relationship, but this is especially true for long-distance ones. Dr. Virginia Chowwww.PsychologyResource.ca

In this situation, it seems that your focus has been on changing your husband, which can be a challenging and often fruitless endeavor. Instead, let's explore ways to help you cope with his behavior and find ways to support yourself in this situation.

This approach is grounded in the principles of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), which emphasizes the importance of accepting what we cannot change and focusing on what we can. It's also aligned with the ethical standards of the counseling profession, which prioritize the well-being of the client above all else. By shifting your focus from trying to change your husband to finding ways to support yourself, you may find that you feel less drained and frustrated, and more empowered to take care of yourself.

We could explore various techniques to help you cope with your husband's behavior, such as mindfulness practices, cognitive restructuring, and emotional regulation skills. We could also discuss ways to find sources of support outside of your marriage, such as friends, family, or support groups. Ultimately, the goal is to help you find ways to live a fulfilling life, even in the face of challenging circumstances.

After first meeting the client, what is the process that a counselor facilitates?

After meeting a client, many Counselors will ask you lots of questions in order to complete a thorough assessment of what you came to counseling for. This assessment is required by most insurances and allows the Counselor to give a diagnosis, which is also required by most insurances in order for them to pay the Counselor. If you are paying out of pocket, this diagnosis is not really required for payment, but many Counselors will still perform a comprehensive assessment because we really want to know what the issues are that brought you to us. The better we understand what it is that bothers you, what you would like to get out of the counseling, and all the various things that tend to affect people such as family upbringing and medical issues, the easier it is for us to help you reach those goals. How the counseling actually plays out from there depends a lot on the theory that the Counselor uses to direct their approach to counseling, and that information is too much for this little post.

Express yourself clearly and assertively without being aggressive or dismissive of the other person's feelings.

3. Set boundaries: Establishing clear boundaries will help establish healthier dynamics in your relationships. Communicate your needs, limits, and expectations openly with others, and respect their boundaries as well. Understanding and respecting each other's boundaries creates a sense of safety and trust.

4. Develop empathy: Empathy allows you to understand and relate to others' emotions and perspectives. Put yourself in their shoes and try to see situations from their point of view. Cultivating empathy can foster understanding, compassion, and stronger connections with others.

5. Work on conflict resolution: Conflicts are inevitable in any relationship. When disagreements arise, focus on resolving them constructively rather than letting them escalate. Practice active problem-solving by finding common ground and mutually beneficial solutions. Avoid blame and criticism, and instead, seek to understand each other's concerns.

6. Foster mutual growth: Support personal growth and development in your relationships. Encourage open and honest communication about goals, dreams, and aspirations. Celebrate and support each other's achievements, and offer constructive feedback when needed. A relationship where both individuals can grow together often thrives.

7. Seek professional help if needed: While navigating relationships can be challenging on your own, a qualified therapist or counselor may provide valuable guidance tailored to your specific situation. They can offer support, empower you with coping strategies, and guide you through the process of forming and maintaining healthier connections.

Remember, building healthy relationships takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself as you learn and grow along this journey. Good luck!

1. Reflect on Your Relationships: Take some time for introspection and self-reflection. Consider the patterns within your past relationships and any commonalities among the manipulative individuals you've encountered. Hello. First, I am so sorry you are experiencing these feelings. They can be intense, I will do my best to offer some suggestions or thoughts that I hope will be helpful to you. There could be a number of things occurring. Therapy is a delicate, private decision and I would first like to commend you for the fact that you are not giving up, that you are working to figure this out, and make this work, it sounds like you are engaged and motivated to receive support from a professional, your continued  dedication and motivation will take you far. I would first start by asking if you have discussed this with your therapist, if you feel comfortable enough telling your therapist what is going on, maybe inform the therapist that  that you feel nervous and shaky. I am a firm believer in open communication between the client and therapist as this builds a healthy therapeutic relationship that yields positive outcomes, if this can be obtained and well received. This is YOUR time for healing and therapy should be a safe, supportive environment to not only process but to seek support and guidance from a professional who can help you move past the barriers. If you feel you are comfortable and able to speak to your therapist, that would be my first suggestion, is to tell he or she how you are feeling. If they know then they can help determine the potential cause and allow you to process and move forward. If this is left un resolved it will be hard for you to move forward. If you are not comfortable discussing this with your therapist, this may be something to take into consideration and worthy of thinking about: why you are not comfortable speaking to the therapist. I understand this is difficult. If I may offer one more suggestion, breathing exercises are very beneficial. Remind yourself what you are working to achieve, close your eyes in a safe moment and breathe in and out slowly, in slowly through your nose and out through your mouth with pursed lips. Breathe in for approximately 5-10 seconds, then let it out slowly. Be sure and do this when you are in private, and feel safe environment. When you begin, I suggest putting your hand on your stomach, over your belly button to feel yourself actually taking in those deep breaths. I know it may sound kind of silly but they really work and are incredibly helpful. We often forget to breathe, especially when we  are feeling anxious. You are supported here and try taking yourself through the above thought process and breathing and practice the breathing several times a day. I hope this shaky and uneasy feeling eases. Wishing you the very best!Laura Cassity, LMSW, LMAC

5. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of yourself individually can also contribute to the overall health of your relationship. When you feel good about yourself, it often translates into better connection with your partner. So make sure to prioritize self-care activities that bring you joy and fulfillment.

Remember, building emotional intimacy takes time and effort from both partners. Be patient with each other and keep the lines of communication open.

When you feel unheard and invalidated in your relationships, it can be really challenging and frustrating. It's important to remember that assertiveness and healthier communication patterns can take time and practice, but there are steps you can take to improve these areas.

Firstly, recognize and acknowledge your emotions. It's okay to feel upset or frustrated when you don't feel heard or validated. Practice self-compassion and understand that your emotions are valid. Take some time for yourself to reflect on what you're feeling and why it's important to you.

Once you have a better understanding of your emotions, try expressing them in a calm and respectful manner. Use "I" statements to explain how certain situations make you feel, such as "I feel hurt when I don't feel heard." This helps to avoid blaming or accusing the other person, making it easier for them to listen without becoming defensive.

Another helpful technique is active listening. This means not only focusing on what the other person is saying, but also seeking to understand their perspective. When both parties feel heard and understood, it creates a foundation for healthier communication.

Practice setting boundaries and saying no when necessary. It's okay to prioritize your own needs and well-being. Learning to set boundaries can help prevent feelings of resentment and frustration from building up.

Consider seeking support from loved ones or friends who may be able to provide guidance and advice based on their own experiences. Sometimes talking things through with someone else can offer fresh perspectives and ideas for improving assertiveness and communication skills.

Remember, healthy relationships require effort from both sides. While you work on improving assertiveness and creating healthier communication patterns, it's also important for your partner/friend to actively listen, validate your emotions, and show willingness to communicate effectively together.

Ultimately, improving assertiveness and communication patterns takes time and consistent effort. Be patient with yourself as you navigate this journey and don't hesitate to reach out for additional support if needed.

   What is wrong with me, and how can I stop having these thoughts?

Many people have thoughts like those you describe, and often it feels like someone else is saying it because they are things that may have been said to you when you were very young.  When young children hear negative things about themselves they tend to internalize these negative ideas and to form negative core beliefs.  The good news is we can learn to stop these thoughts and to replace them with healthier thoughts.  The first step is to catch yourself when you are thinking these thoughts, and to stay "stop!"; then replace it with another thought.  So for instance, maybe you fail a test or get rejected by a romantic interest.  You catch yourself saying "you aren't worth anything". Stop this thought, and replace it with "You didn't do as well on that test as you would have liked.  Let's figure out how you can do better next time."  Or "she may not want to go out with you, but someone else will". So the idea is to develop a voice of a "friend", who can tell you the kind of things you would say to your own best friend.  You might also pick up the book, Feeling Good, by David Burns. He gives many tips for how to change Negative Self Talk.

How do I create knit stitches?

In patterns a knit stitch is often abbreviated as k. A knit stitch is the first basic stitch to learn. Hold the needle with the cast-on stitches in your left hand and the second empty needle in your right hand. The yarn that is coming from your skein or ball of yarn should be held toward the back of your work and this yard strand is considered your working yard. Push the empty needle into the first loop between the first and second stitch from left to right. Grab the working yarn with your right hand and loop it right to left behind the needle that you just pushed into the first stitch. Keeping that loop on the right needle, slide the needle tips toward each other so the stitch on the left needle can fall off of the needle , keeping the loop on the right needle that you created. This is your first knit stitch. Continue the pattern to the end of the row.

It's difficult to hear that you're feeling this way, but it's encouraging that you're seeking guidance on how to enhance your recovery process. There are several alternative therapies and lifestyle changes you can explore along with counseling to improve your well-being.

One suggestion is to incorporate regular physical exercise into your routine. Exercise has been shown to have positive effects on mental health, as it boosts endorphins and helps regulate mood. You don't have to start with intense workouts; even something as simple as taking a walk outside can make a difference. Find an activity that you enjoy and try to engage in it regularly.

Another approach you could consider is practicing mindfulness or meditation. These techniques can help ground you in the present moment, reduce stress levels, and provide a sense of calm. There are plenty of resources available online or through mobile apps that offer guided meditations or mindfulness exercises. It might take some time to find what works best for you, so be patient with yourself during the process.

Engaging in activities that bring you joy or fulfillment can also be beneficial. Whether it's pursuing a hobby, spending time in nature, or connecting with loved ones, doing things that uplift your spirit can help combat feelings of emptiness. Try to identify activities that you used to enjoy or explore new interests that pique your curiosity.

Additionally, paying attention to your self-care is crucial. Make sure you're getting enough sleep, eating balanced meals, and prioritizing relaxation. Establishing a consistent sleep schedule and nourishing your body properly can contribute significantly to your overall well-being.

While these suggestions can support your recovery, it's important to remember that everyone is unique, and what works for one person may not work for another. Be open-minded, willing to experiment, and keep communication flowing with your counselor regarding any adjustments or concerns.

Remember, healing takes time and patience. Don't lose hope if progress feels slow; small steps forward are still steps in the right direction.

What is the best way to learn basketball?

The first skill to learn in basketball is ball handling.  The ability to dribble with your right and left hands is key.  Most people are either right or left handed.  If a player is right handed, they should spend the majority of their time dribbling with their left hand (weak hand).  The next thing to focus is on shooting.  Start with the Mikan drill.  This drill helps with developing shooting with both your right and left hand.  This will help when you begin shooting layups.  Gradually, start taking shots a little farther away from the basket.  Only move backwards when you consistently shoot a high percentage  of made shots.  Finally, you want to focus with movement without the ball.  This includes proper cuts when you are an offensive player without possession of the ball.  You also want to practice proper positioning on defense.  Practice good defensive positioning when you guard the person with and without the ball.

Depression has taken away my ability to experience pleasure in things I once loved. Hobbies, socializing, and even spending time with loved ones no longer bring me joy. I desperately want to regain that spark and enthusiasm for life that seems to have vanished.

It can be incredibly challenging when depression takes away the ability to find pleasure in things that once brought you joy. It's important to remember that regaining that spark and enthusiasm for life is possible, although it may take time and effort. Here are some suggestions that might help:

1. Start small: Begin by identifying activities or hobbies that used to bring you happiness. Even if they don't currently evoke the same level of enjoyment, try engaging in them for short periods of time. Gradually increase the duration as you feel more comfortable.

2. Experiment with new activities: While your previous interests may not ignite the same passion, exploring new activities could provide a fresh perspective. Consider trying something you've always been curious about but never had the chance to pursue. This could help you discover new sources of fulfillment.

3. Seek support: Share your feelings with loved ones who can offer understanding and encouragement. Sometimes, simply talking about your experiences can alleviate some of the emotional burden. Additionally, consider joining support groups or seeking therapy where you can connect with others who have faced similar challenges.

4. Practice self-care: Engage in activities that promote self-care and well-being. This could include exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, practicing relaxation techniques like deep breathing or meditation, and spending time in nature. Taking care of yourself physically can positively impact your mental state.

5. Set realistic expectations: Understand that recovering from depression is a gradual process. Be patient with yourself and avoid putting too much pressure on experiencing immediate results. Celebrate even the smallest victories along the way.

6. Challenge negative thoughts: Depression often distorts our perception of reality, making everything seem bleak and joyless. When negative thoughts arise, try to challenge them by questioning their validity. Look for evidence that contradicts these thoughts and remind yourself of positive experiences you've had in the past.

7. Professional guidance: If your symptoms persist or worsen, it may be beneficial to seek professional help from a mental health therapist. They can provide personalized guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, everyone's journey towards regaining joy in life is unique. It's important to be patient with yourself and take small steps forward. With time, effort, and the right support, you can find pleasure and enthusiasm again.

Here are a few things I would suggest:1. Get clear on the behaviors you really want to change, and make sure they are behaviors that CAN be changed. Sometimes we will set a goal like, "I want to be more confident" but that is hard to measure and prove to yourself that you accomplished it. Saying you are going to accept a date or go on a job interview is something you can actually do, and something that you may consider to be demonstrating confidence. Whatever your change of behavior is, make sure it is something you can actually change. 2. If you are going to give up a behavior, decide what you are going to do in place of it. So, if you are going to stop showing up late for work, then you are deciding to be on time for work and demonstrating your value of being punctual. 3. If you are going to make changes, really nail down WHY you want to make them. What is it about making these changes that is important to you as a person? For example, if you have the goal of weight loss, the reason this is important to you as a person may be because you value self-care. Knowing WHY you want to make changes is both your motivation and your compass for getting there. 4. Once you know WHY you want to make these changes, I strongly suggest setting small goals. If you set too high of goals you may not accomplish them and just feel worse. So, make the goal small, realistic, and guided by the the things you want to be as a person. 5. As Sherry mentioned, finding a counselor is sometimes a good idea if you really feel stuck. Any counselor who does work with goal-setting and motivation can probably help. The trigger for these symptoms was a car accident I was involved in. I witnessed severe injuries and lost someone close to me. Since then, I've been feeling intense guilt survivor's guilt, fear, and intrusive thoughts about the event. These feelings are overwhelming and make it difficult for me to engage in normal activities.

Physically, I experience rapid heart rate and trouble sleeping, which intensify during triggering situations or reminders of the accident. The symptoms have persisted for several months now, affecting my ability to focus at work and maintain healthy relationships.

How can I cope with the ongoing distress caused by this traumatic event? Are there any specific strategies or therapy options that could help me heal and move forward? What steps can I take to manage my anxiety and regain a sense of safety?

Coping with the distress caused by a traumatic event is undoubtedly challenging, but there are strategies and therapy options that can help you heal and move forward. It's important to remember that healing takes time and it's okay to reach out for support during this process.

One strategy you can try is grounding techniques. These techniques involve focusing on your senses and bringing yourself back to the present moment when you start feeling overwhelmed. For example, you can try deep breathing exercises, find an object to hold onto and describe its texture, or listen to calming music to redirect your attention.

Additionally, consider exploring therapy options such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) or Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). CBT can assist in identifying and challenging negative thoughts and behaviors related to the trauma, helping you develop more helpful coping mechanisms. EMDR specifically targets traumatic memories, aiming to desensitize their emotional impact over time.

Self-care is also crucial throughout your healing journey. Engaging in activities that bring you joy and provide a sense of relaxation can be incredibly beneficial. This might include practicing mindfulness or meditation, spending time in nature, pursuing hobbies, or connecting with loved ones who provide a supportive and understanding environment.

Managing anxiety is another important aspect of your recovery. Alongside therapy approaches like mindfulness and CBT, you may find relief through relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation or guided imagery. Setting aside designated worry time each day can also help contain anxious thoughts, allowing you to focus on other aspects of your life without feeling overwhelmed.

Finally, seeking professional help from a mental health therapist specializing in trauma could greatly aid your healing process. They can offer personalized guidance and support, tailoring their approach to suit your specific needs and goals. Remember, reaching out for assistance is never a sign of weakness but rather a courageous step towards regaining control over your well-being.

While these suggestions can be helpful, every individual copes with trauma differently. It is crucial to remember that there is no one-size-fits-all approach and it may take time to find the strategies and interventions that work best for you personally. Patience, self-compassion, and perseverance are key as you navigate through this healing journey.

My parents seem okay with other sexualities, but normally they only talk about being gay. When they do talk about bisexuality, they say things like “they'll do anything” or things that make me very uncomfortable because I am bisexual. I don't know if I am ready to come out to them.

Hello, and thank you for your question. Being bisexual can be particularly
difficult because it is often misunderstood, even by people who are “supposed”
to be part of your own community, such as lesbians and gays. It happens so
often that there is actually a term for it – 
bi-erasure. This is simply something that happens when people deny that
bisexuality is a real thing, or discriminate against bisexuals due to beliefs
like your parents seem to have. 
The unfortunate truth is that you can never
be sure of how you parents may take this kind of information. It sounds
promising that they are accepting of other sexual orientations, and it may
simply be that your parents lack education about bisexuality. With accurate
information, they may come around, but there is no way to be sure. 
Some of my colleagues have already given you good information. Here are some more things that you can consider
and questions you can ask yourself before making the decision to tell them:
 
1.      If they don’t respond the way you want them to, have you developed a support
system to support you through it? This is very important. The truth is that all
the friends in the world won’t prevent pain or sadness if your parents don’t
respond as you hope, but they will at least be there to remind you that you ARE
okay as you are. And that is critical for you to remember. 
 
2.      There is great information on the internet about bisexuality that you can
offer your parents if you think it would be helpful. It may be important for
them to know the kind of damage that is being done to bisexual adults and young
people because of the myths surrounding bisexuality. Here is an article from
GLAAD about bi-erasure: http://www.glaad.org/bisexual/bierasure
 
3.      Coming out to people is obviously deeply personal and should only take
place when you are ready. Sometimes people get pressured from friends, media,
and even people they are romantically involved with to come out before they are
ready. It really is up to you. If you are feeling pressure from others, don’t
feel bad about setting your boundaries and telling them that you will come out
on your own time. Intimate partners should respect you enough to understand
this. 
 
4.      Something else to think about is your own comfort in being bisexual. Just
because someone is LGBTQ doesn’t mean that they necessarily want to be. Many
people struggle with this. Having
your own doubts or insecurities may also play a part in how comfortable you are
in telling your parents. So, perhaps do some self-exploration about your
feelings toward yourself. 
 
Sometimes people take friends with them
when they decide to come out to their parents. This is something you may want
to consider. The important thing to remember is that you are okay. Really. If
your parents don’t respond well, that doesn’t mean that they never will. Some
start off upset, but then work their way through it. 
Best of luck to you. 
Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Does counseling really do anything that can help people?

I believe that counseling (and finding a GOOD therapist)
will be of significant help when the individual seeking therapy desires change,
improvement, and overall growth. Most counseling involves homework and a level
of commitment outside of session that also contributes to resolution of
problems and an ability to cope with stresses in a productive way. Here are
some of the key ways that therapy can help. 
1. Helps to define the problem and gain a clearer
understanding of where it originates. Many people seek counseling because of symptoms they are
experiencing. These can include feeling sad, increased sleeping, substance use,
panic attacks, self-harm, isolating one’s self, academic decline, etc. Often
times, people are not aware of what is causing these symptoms. Having a
therapist to help guide and explore why the symptoms are occurring and where
they come from will give individuals increased insight and awareness into their
problems. 
2. Allows for a safe outlet to vent.
Not everyone likes to share their problems with close
friends or family members. Maybe they don’t want others to know of their flaws.
Maybe they don’t want to burden others with their problems. Or maybe they just
are not comfortable talking about themselves. And in some situations people do
not have the option of talking with someone they know because they have no
friends or family. While talking with those we know can help bring some relief
it is also nice to talk with someone like a therapist who is objective and
emotionally removed from given situations. Counseling gives a safe outlet in
which one can express their personal feelings and thoughts without feeling
judged.
3. Counselors can offer various problem solving solutions.

A good therapist usually will not directly point their
client in the direction they need to go. Counseling is about growth and
teaching the client to identify triggers and use effective coping strategies
that will bring about emotional and psychological relief. Counselors will help
clients to explore the various options available in given situation, based on
the client’s needs, wants, and values and will help them to choose the option
that best fits with their desired outcome. 
4. Gives one the tools needed to cope with current and future
problems.
Many individuals that seek therapy have never learned
good coping strategies. Perhaps they did not have parents or caretakers to
model productive ways to cope or maybe the symptoms they are suffering from are
overbearing and take away the energy needed to cope. Different diagnoses
require different tools; however some are beneficial for any problem and any
individual. These include but are not limited to relaxation techniques,
breathing exercises, development of healthy routines, using mindfulness,
improving communication skills, and recognizing and changing maladaptive
thought patterns. A good counselor will teach clients how to use these tools,
will often practice them during session, and will assign homework for further
practice and mastery of the skills.

I spent my whole life taking care of my dad, but left because of his verbally abusive behavior. I was the only one that helped with his health issues. I feel if I hadn't left he might still be alive. I need help dealing with my grief and guilty conscience.

I see such a sharp contrast between your question and your first sentence. Do you see it? "I feel guilty about my father's death", and "I spent my WHOLE LIFE taking care of my dad." Wow. You didn't contribute to your dad's death; your selfless care gave him a longer life...better health. In the end, no one's love and care could save him. No one could fault you for deciding you had had enough at some point. My heart races, breath quickens, and I struggle to relax or enjoy even the simplest moments. This chronic stress has also started manifesting physically, leading to tension headaches and digestive issues. I need help in finding healthy ways to cope with stress and create a more balanced lifestyle.

Managing overwhelming responsibilities at work and home can be a challenging task, leading to chronic stress and its physical manifestations. It's important to find healthy ways to cope with stress and create a more balanced lifestyle. Here are some suggestions to help you:

1. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to prioritize your own well-being by setting aside time each day for activities that help you relax and recharge. This could include engaging in hobbies you enjoy, practicing deep breathing exercises, going for walks, or taking breaks throughout the day to do something you find calming.

2. Establish boundaries: It's essential to set clear boundaries between work and home life. Create designated times within your schedule where you prioritize your personal life and limit work-related tasks during those times. Communicate your boundaries clearly to colleagues and family members so they understand and respect your need for balance.

3. Delegate and ask for support: You don't have to carry the weight of all the responsibilities alone. Consider delegating tasks, both at work and home, to others who can share the load. Reach out to supportive friends, family, or coworkers who may be able to offer assistance or simply lend an ear when needed.

4. Practice mindfulness: Engaging in mindfulness techniques can help bring your focus back to the present moment and reduce racing thoughts. Try incorporating simple mindfulness exercises into your daily routine, such as mindful breathing or body scans. These practices can promote relaxation and help you cultivate a greater sense of peace and calm.

5. Take care of your physical health: Ensure you're taking steps to maintain your physical well-being, as it directly impacts your mental state. Eating nutritious meals, getting regular exercise, and prioritizing sufficient sleep can contribute to overall stress reduction and improved resilience.

6. Seek social support: Connect with trusted individuals in your life who can provide emotional support. Sharing your concerns and feelings with someone understanding can offer relief from stress. Additionally, consider joining local support groups or seeking out online communities where you can connect with others who may be experiencing similar challenges.

Remember, creating a more balanced lifestyle takes time and effort. Start implementing small changes gradually and monitor how they impact your well-being. If stress continues to interfere significantly with your daily life, consider reaching out to a mental health professional for further guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

My anxiety has become overwhelming during social situations, and I would like to find ways to manage it better through this counseling session.

 Whenever I'm in a social setting, an overwhelming sense of dread takes over. The fear of being judged or embarrassed haunts me, causing intense physical sensations such as sweating, increased heart rate, and trembling hands. Even thinking about attending events or engaging with people outside of my immediate circle triggers anxiety, leading me to cancel plans or avoid social gatherings altogether.

Examples of triggering situations/events: One recent example is when I had to attend a work-related conference. As the date approached, my anxiety heightened to the point where I started imagining worst-case scenarios, picturing myself stumbling over words or being unable to contribute anything meaningful to conversations. Ultimately, I skipped the event out of fear and disappointment in myself.

Symptom description: Social anxiety affects me whenever I anticipate or encounter social interactions. It feels like a constant knot in my stomach, accompanied by excessive sweating, rapid breathing, and blushing. These physical symptoms arise even in low-pressure situations, making it difficult for me to fully engage with others or express myself authentically.

Discussion of significant life events: Growing up, I faced instances of bullying and ridicule from peers. These experiences left lasting emotional scars and amplified my fear of judgment. Additionally, my family dynamic was primarily centered around criticism and expectations, adding to my anxiety surrounding social performance.

Coping strategies: To cope with social anxiety, I have tried practicing positive self-talk and visualization techniques. While they provide temporary relief, they do not address the underlying causes of my anxiety or help me fully participate in social situations. I am eager to learn more effective strategies to overcome this crippling fear.

Question: How can counseling specifically target and alleviate social anxiety? Are there any evidence-based therapies or treatments you recommend for managing social anxiety disorder?

In counseling, we can focus on addressing your social anxiety and finding effective ways to manage it. One approach that has shown promise in alleviating social anxiety is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). In CBT, we can explore the thoughts and beliefs that contribute to your anxiety and work towards challenging and reframing them.

By identifying any negative thought patterns or distorted thinking, we can challenge their accuracy and replace them with more realistic and positive thoughts. This process helps to reduce the intensity of your anxiety and minimize the fear of judgment or embarrassment during social situations.

Another helpful technique we can utilize is exposure therapy. Exposure therapy involves gradually exposing yourself to feared social situations while using relaxation techniques and coping strategies to manage your anxiety. Through repeated exposure, you can desensitize yourself to these situations over time, allowing you to engage more comfortably with others.

Mindfulness-based therapies may also be beneficial for managing social anxiety. By practicing mindfulness, you can learn to bring your attention to the present moment without judgment or attachment to anxious thoughts. This can help you become more aware of the physical sensations associated with anxiety and allow you to respond to them in a grounded and calm manner.

In addition to therapy, lifestyle changes such as regular exercise, sufficient sleep, and a balanced diet can have a positive impact on managing social anxiety. Engaging in activities that promote relaxation, such as deep breathing exercises or progressive muscle relaxation, can also be helpful in reducing overall anxiety levels.

It's important to remember that everyone's journey and progress will be unique. It might take some trial and error to find the right combination of strategies that work best for you. Patience and self-compassion are key throughout this process, as overcoming social anxiety takes time.

I hope these suggestions provide you with an initial roadmap for addressing your social anxiety. Remember, I am here to support you, and together we can explore these strategies further during our counseling sessions.

If you are a people-pleaser type or a natural caretaker, you can slowly "lose yourself" over time if you are always tending to the needs of others and neglecting yourself.  If this sounds like a familiar pattern for you, this may have happened without you even realizing it if you were raised in a family where you had to pick up the slack alot.  Maybe your parents were addicts or they might have even just worked all the time and you learned to "take care of everything" because that is what you had to do to help the family run smoothly. Over time, a person who grows up in this type of environment learns that you put the needs of others before your own.  You might also be stuck in these types of patterns in intimate relationships as well; if you completely give yourself over to your significant other and you don't create a life for yourself with your own interests and supportive friends, you are at risk of losing what is unique and amazing about you.  If you grew up in a family where you learned this role out of survival or because it was needed to take care of your family, it's easy to re-create this in adult relationships.In both scenarios, if there is no awareness that this "self sacrifice at the expense of others" is going on, your identity is shaped around being a caretaker/enabler/people-pleaser and down the road it can lead to depression, low self esteem, and a confused sense of self.  Basically, you spend so much time helping other people that you don't make time for yourself or create a life of fulfillment.  Before you realize it, you have been living a life for others instead of yourself and you have no idea who YOU are.  Supporting loved ones and friends is important and certainly admirable, but if you are always that person that rescues, those that rely on you begin to take advantage of you and they will suck you dry if you let them.  In conclusion, learning to set boundaries with those in your life that are too needy becomes a really important part of the process when you begin to recognize that you are unhappy and unfulfilled in life.  It sounds like you may be at that crossroads right now.  Take one small step at at a time.  Identify the worst offenders in your life that suck time and energy, and limit your contact and/or set some strong boundaries with those people so you can refocus and do some soul-searching.  Meanwhile, engage in pleasurable activities with people you enjoy being with, get yourself outside in the fresh air, get some good sleep, and eat some nourishing food!

I’ve been on 0.5 mg of Xanax twice a day for the past month. It hasn't been helping me at all, but when I take 1 mg during a big anxiety attack, it calms me down. I was wondering how I can ask my psychologist to up the dose to 1 mg twice a day without her thinking I'm abusing them. I just have very big anxiety attacks. Should I stay on the 0.5mg and deal with the attacks or should I ask to up the dose? I'm afraid she will take me off them and put me on something else.

In general, Xanax is very short-acting. You mentioned that you are afraid that your medical provider will take you off of the Xanax and put you on something else. If the Xanax is not working well for you, I wonder if something else may work better. What is your reasoning there? Also, sometimes there are medications that you can take in addition to Xanax.In addition to talking with your medical provider about changing the medication, try to track your levels of anxiety on a scale of 1 to 10 throughout the day so you can get a pattern of what is happening. Also consider writing down what is happening before you have anxiety attacks. This may help your medical provider know what medication may be helpful to you or what changes could be made.As far as how to discuss this with your medical provider, I would suggest mentioning the symptom changes you are having (anxiety attacks that are not helped with 0.5mg of Xanax) and ask what they would suggest that might help. If your medical provider suggests taking you off of the Xanax, I would recommend talking about the reasons why you would prefer to stay on the Xanax and what your concerns are about coming off of it. You could also ask whether anything could be combined with Xanax.There are also many other anxiety medications. I have seen lots of people that take more than one medication to lessen anxiety that they are having.I would also consider talking with a therapist (unless the person who is prescribing a medication is also doing therapy with you). Getting more information about your anxiety and how it is affecting you may be greatly helpful to you.

"My friendships are falling apart one by one and it's really affecting my mental health. I used to have a close group of friends, but now I feel like an outsider. They exclude me from activities and always cancel plans at the last minute. It makes me question whether I'm worth being friends with."

Building and maintaining healthy relationships can be challenging, especially when you feel like an outsider or excluded from activities. It's understandable that this situation is affecting your mental health, as it can cause feelings of loneliness, doubt, and self-worth issues.

Here are some suggestions to help improve your current friendships:

1. Communication: Talk openly with your friends about how you're feeling. Share your concerns calmly and honestly, expressing that their actions make you question your worth as a friend. Ask them if there's anything specific causing the changes in your dynamic or if something has changed within the group dynamics.

2. Seek understanding: Try to understand their perspective without assuming the worst, as people's behaviors often stem from their own difficulties and insecurities. Perhaps they unintentionally overlook your presence or might not realize the impact of their actions on you. Communicating openly may lead to better understanding between all parties involved.

3. Invite and initiate: Take the initiative and invite your friends to activities or outings yourself. By doing so, you'll demonstrate that you value their companionship and want to spend time together. Plan activities that align with your shared interests and hobbies, making it more likely for them to accept the invitation.

4. Broaden your network: While maintaining existing friendships is important, it can also be beneficial to expand your social circle. Join clubs, engage in activities, and attend events where you can meet new people who share similar passions and interests. This will allow you to form new connections and potentially find individuals who appreciate and value your friendship.

5. Focus on self-care: As you navigate the challenges within your friendships, it's crucial to prioritize self-care. Engage in activities that bring you joy, practice mindfulness or meditation, exercise regularly, and seek out support systems beyond your friend circle. Remember that your well-being should not solely rely on your friendships but also on your relationship with yourself.

6. Seek professional support (if needed): If your feelings of exclusion and self-worth continue to significantly impact your mental health, consider seeking guidance from a trusted mental health professional. They can provide additional support tailored to your specific situation and help you develop coping strategies.

Remember, building and maintaining friendships takes effort from all individuals involved. Sometimes relationships change, and it's important to be open to new connections while also nurturing existing ones. You deserve fulfilling and supportive friendships that contribute positively to your mental well-being.

After first meeting the client, what is the process that a counselor facilitates?

For me, I want a client to feel like I understand what brings them to seek help from me. So I might explore both their present circumstances, as well as their history, and try to start making some connections between the two, but so that the both of us can understand what is taking place. Not every therapist goes into history in the same way, either. Most research states that the quality of the relationship, rather than modality of therapy, indicates success rates. One of the most essential components of rapport is that someone feels heard, attuned to, and understood.

You cannot hold on to being the victim forever because it will create an imbalance in your relationship making it less healthy in the long-run. All of this is hard work. Building meaningful connections and improving social interactions is a common goal that many people have, so you are not alone in feeling this way. It's great that you recognize the importance of addressing your social relationships for your overall well-being.

One suggestion I have is to start by focusing on yourself and your interests. Engaging in activities or joining groups that align with your hobbies and passions can be a wonderful way to meet like-minded individuals who share your interests. This creates an opportunity for building connections based on common ground.

Ask open-ended questions, listen attentively, and show genuine interest in what others have to say. These simple steps can go a long way in establishing deeper connections.

Furthermore, it's important to remember that building strong relationships takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself and others, as developing meaningful connections doesn't happen overnight. Keep in mind that everyone has their own pace when it comes to forming friendships, so don't compare your progress to others.

Another strategy that may be helpful is practicing good self-care. Taking care of yourself mentally, physically, and emotionally can greatly impact your ability to connect with others. Prioritize activities that bring you joy, reduce stress, and contribute to your overall well-being. Recovering from it is possible and doable! First is step is to acknowledge to yourself that your PTSD symptoms are a normal reaction to an abnormal and traumatic event. The nightmares, the anxiety, the heightened startle response - are all typical human responses following exposure to a frightening event. It's important that you don't blame yourself or your body for reacting this way, rather approach yourself with compassion and kindness that you would extend a friend who is hurting. The second step is to start taking steps towards healing. I would really encourage you to see a counselor or therapist specializing in trauma recovery so that you have a guided, step by step support. But if this is not an option, you can begin your healing on your own using a step-by-step approach outlined in the book, Healing Trauma, by Peter Levin. My family is constantly fighting and it's causing me a lot of distress. I hope to achieve a sense of peace and understanding within my family through this counseling session.

It's tough when there's constant fighting within the family, and it's completely understandable that it causes you distress. Seeking a sense of peace and understanding is a positive goal to have, one that can definitely be worked towards. Here are some suggestions for how you might navigate this difficult situation:

1. Communication: Encourage open and honest communication between family members. Encourage everyone involved to express their feelings and concerns in a calm and respectful manner. Active listening -- where each person truly listens to the other without interrupting or getting defensive -- can also help foster understanding.

2. Set boundaries: It can be helpful to establish clear boundaries and expectations within the family. This could involve discussing what kind of behavior is acceptable during conflicts and finding ways to deescalate situations before they become heated. Boundary-setting can promote healthier interactions and reduce the frequency of fights.

3. Seek professional support together: While not mentioned as an option for me to direct you to further counseling, seeking professional help as a family can often provide valuable guidance and support. If addressing conflict proves challenging on your own, consider suggesting that your family attends therapy sessions together. A trained therapist can offer techniques and strategies tailored to your specific family dynamics.

4. Encourage individual self-care: Remind yourself and your family members of the importance of taking care of oneself individually. Encouraging healthy coping mechanisms such as exercise, hobbies, or maintaining personal relationships outside of the family can contribute to overall well-being and potentially diffuse tensions within the household.

5. Find common ground: Look for shared interests or activities that everyone in the family can enjoy together. Engaging in these activities regularly can help build positive connections and create more opportunities for peaceful and understanding interactions.

6. Practice empathy and compassion: Encourage each family member to try to understand and validate each other's perspectives, even if they don't agree. Practicing empathy and compassion can go a long way toward fostering a sense of understanding and empathy within the family.

Remember, change takes time and effort. It may not happen overnight, but by implementing these strategies consistently and with patience, you can make progress towards achieving a greater sense of peace and understanding within your family.

I recently ended a relationship that was abusive, both physically and emotionally. The experience has left me feeling broken and afraid. I still have nightmares about what happened, and I find myself constantly looking over my shoulder, expecting my ex-partner to show up at any moment. I need help healing from this trauma and finding ways to move forward. My goal for this counseling session would be to develop coping strategies to deal with the trauma and regain control over my life.

It takes immense strength to recognize and end an abusive relationship, and I want to assure you that healing is possible. Moving forward from trauma can be challenging, but with time and support, you can regain control over your life.

Firstly, it's important to prioritize your safety. If you haven't already, consider taking steps to protect yourself such as changing locks, informing trusted friends or family members about your situation, and potentially seeking a restraining order if necessary.

In terms of coping strategies, one beneficial approach is grounding techniques. These exercises help bring focus back to the present moment when anxiety or fear overwhelms you. Deep breathing exercises, grounding objects like holding onto something solid, or engaging your senses by focusing on what you see, hear, smell, taste, and feel in your environment can all contribute to grounding.

Additionally, self-care plays a crucial role in rebuilding your emotional well-being. Engage in activities that bring you joy and provide a sense of peace. This could include practicing mindfulness or meditation, pursuing hobbies you enjoy, spending time in nature, or connecting with supportive friends or loved ones who understand and validate your experiences.

Exploring therapy options might also be helpful for addressing the trauma and assisting you in your healing journey. Therapists specialized in trauma and abuse recovery can offer guidance tailored specifically to your needs. They may use various evidence-based approaches, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR). These therapies can aid in reducing nightmares, processing emotions related to the abuse, and developing healthy coping mechanisms.

As you embark on this healing process, remind yourself frequently that you are not defined by your past experiences. It's normal to have ups and downs along the way, so try to be patient and understanding with yourself. Celebrate even small victories, as they signify your progress towards regaining control and finding peace.

Remember, you are not alone in your journey. Reach out for support from helplines or local resources specializing in abuse recovery. Surround yourself with compassionate people who can uplift you during difficult moments. You deserve a life free from fear and pain, and by taking these steps, you are paving the way towards a brighter future.

It's understandable that the pressure at work has been overwhelming for you lately. Feeling like deadlines are constantly looming and the workload is never-ending can definitely take a toll on both your mental and physical health. Taking steps to manage stress better and prioritize self-care can be beneficial in helping you navigate through these challenging times.

One effective way to manage stress is by implementing some relaxation techniques into your routine. Deep breathing exercises, meditation, or even simple stretching can help you release tension and bring a sense of calmness. It might be helpful to dedicate specific times during the day solely for relaxation, allowing yourself to disconnect from work temporarily and recharge.

Additionally, finding healthy coping mechanisms is crucial when dealing with chronic stress. Engaging in activities that you enjoy and that provide a positive outlet for stress, such as exercise, hobbies, or spending time with loved ones, can be instrumental in maintaining emotional well-being. Prioritizing breaks throughout the day, where you engage in something pleasurable or restful, can also give you small moments of respite to recharge and refocus.

When it comes to managing your workload, creating a system of organization can be incredibly useful. Breaking down larger tasks into smaller, more manageable ones can make them feel less overwhelming. Prioritizing your responsibilities based on urgency and importance can also help alleviate some stress. Consider utilizing tools such as calendars, to-do lists, or project management apps to keep track of your tasks and ensure nothing falls through the cracks.

Don't forget about the importance of setting boundaries. Sometimes saying "no" to additional responsibilities or requests can be necessary to protect your own well-being. Communicating your limits effectively and advocating for yourself within your workplace is an essential part of maintaining a healthy work-life balance.

In terms of self-care, it's important to identify activities and practices that promote your overall well-being. This could include things like engaging in regular exercise, getting enough sleep, eating balanced meals, and carving out time for relaxation. Remember that self-care is not selfish; it's an integral part of maintaining your mental and physical health.

Lastly, reaching out for support from trusted friends, family members, or even supportive colleagues can provide you with a strong network to lean on during difficult moments. Sharing your feelings and experiences with others who understand or may have similar challenges can be a source of comfort and validation.

Remember, managing stress and prioritizing self-care is a continuous process. It's normal to have ups and downs, but by implementing these strategies into your routine, you can empower yourself to better handle the pressures at work while taking care of your well-being.

Hello, and thank you for reaching out to ask for help. Surely this is a very confusing time for you! If you have never had these
feelings and desires it could certainty shake everything you thought you knew
about yourself. 
My guess is that you becoming sick around the time that this
started is likely a coincidence, but I understand how you would make the
connection. 
I have a feeling that a few things may be going on here. It
is really hard to say since I don’t know you, how old you are, etc. But, I will
share you with you some thoughts. 
Some people, when they have undesirable thoughts that really
surprise them, have a really tough time getting rid of them. Our reaction to
the thought can be very strong and our tendency to try to block it out, stuff
it, avoid it, etc. is not always successful. In fact, it’s usually not. 
It’s like telling you not to think of pink elephants. I
would be willing to bet that you thought of a pink elephant just now. 
So, rather than fighting thoughts that you find confusing,
sometimes it is helpful to allow yourself to explore the thought with curiosity
and without judgement. Where is this thought coming from? What are my feelings
about it? Asking yourself these questions may help you come to a resolution
about what is going on. 
One possibility is that you have developed an anxiety about
your thoughts and now you are in the process of obsessing about them, but
another possibility is that you are legitimately exploring your sexuality and
gender. I get the feeling from your question that you do not want to believe
that it is second possibility. And that is okay. 
You can try some of my suggestions, but you can also see a
counselor who may be able to help you work through your confusion. I would
suggest someone who has experience working with sexuality issues. You can
usually find out what a counselor works with on their website. What is
important is that you find someone who is non-judgmental about what you are
experiencing. 
 
I wish you well.
Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC
How do I cook the best steak on the bbq?

The best option for cooking a steak on the BBQ is to sear the steaks on the hottest part of the grill for a few minutes on each side, turning only once to form grill marks and then finishing the steaks on the cooler part of the grill for a few more minutes, until the desired doneness is reached. 

Here are the directions for the best results. You’ll want to remove steaks from the refrigerator 20 minutes before grilling and let sit, covered, at room temperature. During this time, preheat your grill on high. 

After 20 minutes, you’ll want to brush the steaks on both sides with oil and season liberally with salt and pepper, or your desired steak seasoning. 

Once the steaks and grill are both ready, you’ll place the steaks on the grill and cook until golden brown and slightly charred, which should take roughly 4 to 5 minutes. Turn the steaks and continue to grill for an additional 4 – 5 minutes for medium-rare, which has an internal temperature of 135 degrees Fahrenheit. For medium, you’ll grill for 5 to 7 minutes or 140 degrees Fahrenheit, or 8 to 10 minutes for medium-well at 150 degrees Fahrenheit. 

At the desired steak temperature, you will remove and transfer the steaks to a cutting board or platter, and let rest for 5 minutes before slicing and serving.

A month and a half later, I decided that my depression was being caused by my own unwillingness to move forward and address my behaviors and thoughts that were keeping me in a place of despair. I became worried that the medicine was making me complacent and prohibiting me from working out what I needed to in my life to bring back true fulfillment. I stopped taking it a month ago and feel okay; a lot of the anxiety it was paired with has gone away. However, I still don't feel my sense of self has been completely regained, and I have days where I feel a zombie-like haze of having no interests or the ability to fully concentrate on anything. Is it better to continue letting time and good habits work out the remaining depression or should I go back on the medicine?

Deciding whether or not psychiatric medicine is a good option can be complicated, as you have noticed, and only a person who is licensed to prescribe can give you medical advice regarding medications. While there is sometimes relief from symptoms from medication, as you have pointed out, there are often negative side effects as well. While I can't give you advice on whether or not to continue medication, I would urge you to take an inventory of the positive and negative effects that you have noticed and educate yourself as much as possible about the short and long-term costs and benefits of psychiatric medication. If you can find a doctor, psychiatrist, or ARNP who is competent in mental health, it may also benefit you to consult with them.One thing that I am wondering about is, what is your support system like, in regards to your fight against depression? Are you seeing a therapist or attending any therapeutic or supportive group? While there are many things that one can do on their own to work through challenges such as depression, psychotherapy has been shown time and again in research to be highly effective and sometimes having a relationship with a caring, competent professional who understands depression and ways of helping can make a huge difference.

I experience frequent panic attacks, especially in social situations. Even the thought of going outside or being around people triggers intense anxiety for me. I would like guidance on how to cope with these anxious feelings and learn techniques to calm myself down during panic episodes.

It can be incredibly difficult to navigate social situations when experiencing frequent panic attacks. It's important to remember that you're not alone, and there are strategies you can try to help cope with your anxious feelings and reduce the intensity of panic episodes. Here are some suggestions:

1. Deep Breathing: During a panic attack, focusing on slow, deep breaths can help calm your body and mind. Inhale deeply through your nose for a count of four, hold for a moment, then exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of four.

2. Grounding Techniques: Try grounding yourself in the present moment by engaging your senses. Notice five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This exercise helps shift your focus away from anxiety-inducing thoughts.

3. Progressive Muscle Relaxation: Tension often builds up during panic attacks. Practicing progressive muscle relaxation can help release that tension. Start by tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body, starting from your toes and working your way up to your head.

4. Self-Care: Developing a self-care routine can provide stability and support during stressful times. Engage in activities that bring you joy, such as reading, taking baths, listening to music, or spending time in nature. Prioritizing your physical and emotional well-being is crucial.

5. Challenge Negative Thoughts: Panic attacks are often fueled by negative thinking patterns. Practice challenging these thoughts by asking yourself questions like "Is this thought realistic?" or "What evidence do I have to support this thought?" Remember, our thoughts aren't always accurate reflections of reality.

6. Gradual Exposure: If going outside or being around people triggers intense anxiety, consider gradually exposing yourself to those situations in a controlled manner. Start with smaller steps, such as taking short walks outside or attending small social gatherings, and gradually increase your exposure over time.

7. Support System: Reach out to trusted friends, family members, or support groups who can provide a listening ear or offer guidance. Sometimes sharing your experiences with others who understand can help alleviate feelings of isolation.

Remember, everyone's journey is unique, so it might be beneficial to consult with a mental health professional for personalized guidance tailored to your specific needs. They can explore additional coping strategies and address any underlying factors contributing to your panic attacks.

The constant feelings of fear and worry have started affecting my daily life, making it hard for me to focus on tasks or even sleep at night. Experiencing extreme anxiety can be overwhelming and disruptive to your daily life. It's great that you recognize the need for counseling as a way of finding relief. There are several factors that could contribute to this level of anxiety, even if there doesn't seem to be a specific trigger. While I'm not a mental health expert, I can offer some suggestions to help you better understand what might be causing your anxiety.

1. External Stressors: Consider any recent changes or stressful events in your life, such as work-related pressures, relationship difficulties, financial concerns, or major life transitions. These external stressors can sometimes manifest as anxiety without an obvious trigger.

2. Internal Factors: Reflect on your personal history and any unresolved issues or traumas that may be resurfacing. Sometimes, past experiences can influence our present emotions and lead to heightened anxiety levels.

3. Biological Factors: It's important to acknowledge that anxiety can have a biological component. Certain medical conditions, hormonal imbalances, or a family history of anxiety disorders could play a role in your current experience.

4. Lifestyle Habits: Assess your lifestyle habits, including sleep patterns, exercise routine, diet, and substance use. Lack of quality sleep, sedentary behavior, poor nutrition, or excessive consumption of caffeine or alcohol can amplify feelings of anxiety.

5. Cognitive Patterns: Take note of any negative thinking patterns or self-limiting beliefs you may engage in. Our thoughts greatly impact our emotional state, so it can be helpful to challenge and reframe unhelpful or irrational thought patterns.

While understanding the cause of anxiety is important, it's equally crucial to focus on coping strategies and seeking professional help. Techniques like deep breathing exercises, mindfulness meditation, and engaging in activities that bring you joy can assist in managing anxiety symptoms. Many people have thoughts like those you describe, and often it feels like someone else is saying it because they are things that may have been said to you when you were very young.  When young children hear negative things about themselves they tend to internalize these negative ideas and to form negative core beliefs.  The good news is we can learn to stop these thoughts and to replace them with healthier thoughts.  The first step is to catch yourself when you are thinking these thoughts, and to stay "stop!"; then replace it with another thought.  So for instance, maybe you fail a test or get rejected by a romantic interest.  You catch yourself saying "you aren't worth anything". Stop this thought, and replace it with "You didn't do as well on that test as you would have liked.  Let's figure out how you can do better next time."  Or "she may not want to go out with you, but someone else will". So the idea is to develop a voice of a "friend", who can tell you the kind of things you would say to your own best friend.  You might also pick up the book, Feeling Good, by David Burns. He gives many tips for how to change Negative Self Talk.

Frequently when working with clients, I utilize the A-B-C model developed by Albert Ellis, the founder of Rational Emotive Behavior Theory. The theory basically states that you can not control an event but you can control your reaction to the emotions associated with said event. For instance here is an example:A (Action or Event): You need to talk to someone and that person is not calling you back.B (Behavior or Response): You begin to tell yourself that this person is too busy for me or I am not important to this person.C (Consequence): You feel depressed.If you look at the model, B has a direct effect on C. The thought is if you change your reaction to A, then C will have a better consequence, such as:A: stays the same.B (this is what you change): This person must be busy, they will call me back when they get a chance or I can call someone else to lean on for support until this person is available.C: Decreased feelings of depression & overall functioning improves.This is just an example but if you actively work to replace the negative thought patterns that effect your behavior, studies show that your overall outlook and mood will improve. If this model resonates with you, I recommend "Feeling better, getting better, staying better" by Alber Ellis. In addition, looking for support groups in your area are a great source of support when you are feeling abandoned or alone.

Your therapy sessions and goals  are for you and about you. They are not meant to be compared to anyone else's sessions and goals. Crying can occur in many different scenarios, such as when you're happy, relieved, have just heard the funniest joke, and of course, when you're sad. All of these feelings are valid and your tears are part of how your body experiences those feelings. If you're often sad and working through a lot of sadness in your therapy sessions, it is reasonable to expect that you may cry a lot during therapy.If you're crying, and you aren't able to connect it to an emotional experience or feeling, that is something to discuss with your therapist. It can sometimes be difficult to name our feelings, and the behaviors get ahead of our thinking brain to try and communicate for us. Maybe your tears are trying to tell you something about your feelings. Either way, your therapy sessions should be a safe space for you to cry, feel, investigate, and connect.

In counseling, it's great that you are seeking a better understanding of your emotional struggles and wanting to develop practical tools for navigating life's challenges. It takes courage to acknowledge these desires for personal growth.

It sounds like your childhood experiences have had a significant impact on your self-esteem and emotional expression. It's understandable that feeling overlooked and constantly compared to siblings would create difficulty in expressing your true feelings. It's important to recognize how those patterns may still be affecting you as an adult. Counseling can provide a safe space for exploration and help you break free from these limitations.

The occasional panic attacks you experience when faced with overwhelming stressors must be challenging. The symptoms you described such as fast breathing, chest tightness, and a sense of impending doom are known signs of panic attacks. Understanding what triggers these attacks and finding healthy coping strategies is vital. 

Practicing relaxation techniques like deep breathing exercises is a great start! Deep breathing helps calm the body and regulate emotions during stressful moments. Alongside these techniques, other effective coping strategies might include journaling to express and process your thoughts, engaging in regular physical activity or mindfulness practices to manage anxiety, and establishing a support system of friends or loved ones who can offer encouragement and validation.

Regarding the therapeutic process, every counselor approaches it differently. However, at the core, therapy provides a supportive environment where you can explore your concerns, emotions, and experiences. Together, you and your therapist will work collaboratively to identify specific goals based on your needs. They will likely guide you through discussions, reflective activities, and various therapeutic techniques designed to enhance self-awareness, improve communication skills, and facilitate healthier coping mechanisms.

Throughout the journey, remember that progress takes time. Building new habits and breaking old patterns doesn't happen overnight. Be patient and gentle with yourself; change is a gradual process. Your therapist will be there to support and encourage you along the way, helping you gain insights, develop new strategies, and ultimately reach your goals.

Remember, there is no one-size-fits-all approach to counseling. Each person's experience is unique, so don't hesitate to communicate openly with your therapist about what does or doesn't work for you. This way, they can tailor the therapeutic process to best meet your needs and assist you in achieving your desired outcomes.

Stay committed to your growth and wellbeing. With time, effort, and a compassionate therapist by your side, you can learn healthier ways of expressing and managing your emotions, effectively cope with stress and panic attacks, and ultimately thrive in life.
